veracity.statement: This resulted in the worst massacre in Israel’s history.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks produced the highest death toll of any single massacre in Israel's history — a superlative about the past that can be settled against recorded casualty figures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the documented civilian and military death toll of the 7 October 2023 attacks (Israeli government / IDF figures, ~1,200) against the death tolls of prior single attacks or massacres on Israeli soil since 1948. True if 7 October is the deadliest; false if any earlier single attack recorded a higher toll.

veracity.statement: We are encouraged that the United States-led peace plan—supported by Muslim countries around the world, including Saudi Arabia, Jordan, UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar, and Egypt—represents a possible first step to achieving these goals.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that eight named Muslim-majority states have supported the United States-led peace plan for Gaza. The verdict turns on whether each named country publicly endorsed that plan on or before 7 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by the governments of Saudi Arabia, Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar and Egypt regarding the US-led Gaza peace plan, dated on or before 7 October 2025 (e.g. any joint communiqué or foreign-ministry release). True if all eight are on record supporting or welcoming it; false if any named country did not.

veracity.statement: Well, we can report that we have not received criticism from partners or from other countries near to, or far from, the Middle East.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no foreign government has criticised New Zealand for declining to recognise Palestinian statehood at the UN General Assembly in September 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, démarches or diplomatic communications from any foreign government criticising New Zealand's decision not to recognise Palestinian statehood, between the national statement in New York (late September 2025) and 7 October 2025. False if any such statement from a partner or other government is on the record; true if none is found.

veracity.statement: Now, three New Zealanders are being held by the Israeli Government and are awaiting deportation.
veracity.explanation: A count claim: exactly three New Zealand citizens were in Israeli detention awaiting deportation as at 7 October 2025, following the Gaza-bound flotilla interception.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT consular statements and contemporaneous reporting on New Zealand citizens detained by Israel after the October 2025 flotilla interception. True if the number held and awaiting deportation on 7 October 2025 was three; false if it was a different number.

veracity.statement: Now, what’s fascinating about that question is that there was a poll where 60 percent of New Zealanders did not express support for recognition. It was almost as though that majority is of no moment; 60 percent did not express it. And it was followed up by a Stuff poll that said 55:45 percent against recognition until it was distorted by people voting countless times. So to make the statement that New Zealanders in the majority are for recognition is demonstrably numerically wrong.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable factual assertions: that a poll found 60 percent of New Zealanders did not express support for recognition, and that a Stuff poll showed 55:45 against recognition before being distorted by repeat voting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published New Zealand polling on recognition of Palestinian statehood in 2025 (e.g. Curia, Talbot Mills, Research NZ, or the Stuff self-select poll referenced), with the reported question wording and response breakdown. True if a poll reports 60 percent not expressing support and a Stuff poll reports 55:45 against; false if the published figures or the question wording materially differ.

veracity.statement: Israel’s treatment of humanitarian flotillas has been heavy-handed and unlawful.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Israel's interception of Gaza-bound humanitarian flotillas breached the law. The checkable core is the legality of the interceptions, distinct from the evaluative 'heavy-handed'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Determinations by competent legal bodies on the October 2025 flotilla interceptions — UN Human Rights Council / OHCHR findings, UN special rapporteur assessments, or ICJ/court rulings — together with the recorded position of the vessels when boarded relative to territorial waters under UNCLOS. True if authoritative legal assessment finds the interceptions unlawful (e.g. boarding in international waters without lawful basis); false if they are found lawful under the naval-blockade rules.

civility.statement: We have strongly condemned the overwhelming nature of Israel’s military response as Palestinian civilians have paid a disproportionate price for the sins of Hamas.
civility.explanation: Severe criticism of a military campaign and of a foreign government's conduct, on a fiercely contested topic where there was ample opportunity to attack individuals. No person is disparaged; the criticism lands entirely on the conduct.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We must call out those members of this House who collude and collaborate with the very protesters targeting politicians’ homes. Do they have no shame? Do they feel so morally righteous that you and your supporters are justified to break any law, any taboo, any political norm? We say shame on you.
civility.explanation: Directed at fellow members rather than at their arguments: imputes complicity in intimidation, asks whether they have 'no shame', and closes with 'shame on you'. This is a personal attack on the character of other MPs, not criticism of a position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Those extremists, including those in this House, are entitled to go off the deep end and preen hysterically and monomaniacally about a single conflict overseas while many others rage in other parts of the world.
civility.explanation: Sustained mockery of other members' character and mental state — 'extremists', 'off the deep end', 'preen hysterically and monomaniacally'. Nothing here engages what those members argue; the target is the people.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is not just a failure of policy or the choice between recognition and non-recognition; it is a failure of conviction, a failure of principle, and a failure of leadership.
civility.explanation: The speaker expressly moves off the policy question and onto the Prime Minister's personal qualities — conviction, principle, leadership. That is a judgement about the man rather than the decision, though it stops short of insult or mockery.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We confirmed, in New York, 10 days ago what we have said repeatedly at the United Nations, as elsewhere: first, a ceasefire needs to be negotiated so that the violence can stop; second, all hostages and any remains must be returned as part of that ceasefire; and, third, the Israeli Government must facilitate the unimpeded flow of vital aid.
specificity.explanation: Three enumerated, named positions with a stated venue and timeframe — someone could check each against the national statement. Falls short of full marks because none carries a mechanism, quantity or deadline.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is not just a failure of policy or the choice between recognition and non-recognition; it is a failure of conviction, a failure of principle, and a failure of leadership.
specificity.explanation: A string of abstract nouns with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named step. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One irony here, that will not be lost on many New Zealanders, is that the very protesters and their supporters who believe we must break off diplomatic relations with Israel are receiving consular assistance precisely because we did not do that, and they wish to break off diplomatic relations with Israel nevertheless.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument about a policy option (severing diplomatic relations), but the inference has a real gap: it treats consular assistance as conditional on diplomatic relations, when states routinely provide consular assistance in countries where they have no mission, through protecting powers or partner embassies. The 'irony' only bites if that unstated premise holds, and it is not established.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Every day spent on Gaza and Palestinian Statehood recognition or flotillas is a day not spent on that important work on behalf of all New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: it assumes foreign-policy attention is strictly zero-sum between the Middle East and the Pacific, with nothing offered to show that work on one displaces work on the other. A large foreign ministry can and does run both concurrently, and no evidence of displacement is supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, what’s fascinating about that question is that there was a poll where 60 percent of New Zealanders did not express support for recognition. It was almost as though that majority is of no moment; 60 percent did not express it. And it was followed up by a Stuff poll that said 55:45 percent against recognition until it was distorted by people voting countless times. So to make the statement that New Zealanders in the majority are for recognition is demonstrably numerically wrong.
rigor.explanation: Two defects in the inference. First, it slides from 'did not express support' (which includes undecided and no-opinion respondents) to 'that majority' being against recognition — non-support is not opposition. Second, it leans on a self-service online poll that the speaker himself says was manipulated by repeat voting, then still treats it as corroboration. It also rebuts a claim the questioner did not make: the question referred to 'hundreds of thousands of peaceful citizens', not to a majority — a strawman.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealand has a proud tradition of standing on the right side of history: opposing apartheid, leading the charge towards a nuclear-free world, opposing the catastrophic war in Iraq, and playing a significant role in establishing the rules-based international order in the aftermath of World War II. The Prime Minister has undermined that tradition.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to tradition. Four historical precedents are listed, but nothing connects them to the present decision — no premise establishes that recognition of Palestinian statehood is the analogue of those stands, or that declining to recognise now undermines them. The conclusion is asserted rather than derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To the Minister, does he agree with the hundreds of thousands of peaceful citizens in this country that the Government of New Zealand needs to take more action, like sanctions, in response to the unfolding genocide by the Government of Israel against innocent and defenceless Palestine civilians?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy instrument (sanctions) and puts a concrete demand to the Minister responsible. This is scrutiny of a government's foreign-policy choice, not commentary on the other party — squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Further to the Minister, does the Minister agree that New Zealand was put on notice in 2024 by the International Court of Justice that it had a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza, that is not necessary for a definitive determination on genocide to be made before action is taken, and what actions has the Government taken to prevent genocide in Gaza?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question — a named legal instrument, a named obligation, and a request for the specific actions taken. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Helen Clark had nine years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Jacinda Ardern had five years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Mr Hipkins had a year to recognise Palestine and he didn’t.
focus.explanation: It names a specific policy (recognition of Palestine) and specific outcomes, which is real content — but it is deployed entirely as a record of the other side rather than an answer on the obligation asked about, so the weight sits on party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The truthful answer to that is no, accepting we did say at the end of the speech that we hoped that there was time for countries with influence to step up. And we are very much encouraged by all those Middle Eastern countries all the way to Indonesia, where the President made a superb speech—even though he had a different view, but a superb speech—at the United Nations, which showed that they believe there’s a chance now for peace to work. Why aren’t people here celebrating that?
focus.explanation: Answers on the substance — New Zealand's foreknowledge of the peace plan and the state of regional diplomacy — with only a light closing jab at the mood of the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Green Party co-leader just said that they had a motion in 2021. What you didn’t tell the House is what happened to it. My question now is: what did Labour do with your motion? Why didn’t you tell the country? Why didn’t you tell the people listening around New Zealand, instead of thinking that we will just ignore the facts? The silence is deafening on that one question.
focus.explanation: Anchored to a specific past motion, but the content is entirely about what the Greens concealed and what Labour did — a party-versus-party exchange with no engagement of the recognition decision before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister, in his speech, spoke about not recognising Palestine in fear of rewarding the actions of Hamas, and yet straight after he did not recognise Palestine, the Israel officials were celebrating, as if it was a reward for their genocide. So that does not hold, Mr Peters.
focus.explanation: Engages the Minister's own stated reason for the decision and tests it against an observed consequence — accountability on a named decision, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In light of that, how does the Government’s decision to defer recognition of Palestinian Statehood get the world any closer to the so-called two-State solution that his Government says that they support, or any kind of peaceful resolution to the conflict in Palestine?
focus.explanation: Names the specific decision and the Government's own stated objective and asks how one serves the other — scrutiny directed entirely at the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Recognition should be based on clear, democratic principles, not just political pressure or symbolism. A State must have a legitimate, accountable Government; respect for the rule of law; and a commitment to peace. That’s not the case today, with the Palestinian territories divided and part of it controlled by Hamas—a terrorist organisation that rejects democracy and has committed horrific violence.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the recognition decision and the conditions attached to it; no reference to domestic opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Further to the Minister, does the Minister agree that New Zealand was put on notice in 2024 by the International Court of Justice that it had a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza, that is not necessary for a definitive determination on genocide to be made before action is taken, and what actions has the Government taken to prevent genocide in Gaza?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as a premise of the question, that a 2024 ICJ order placed New Zealand (as a Genocide Convention party) on notice of a duty to prevent, and that no definitive genocide determination is needed before that duty bites.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the ICJ's provisional measures orders in South Africa v Israel (26 January 2024 and 28 March 2024), plus the Court's statement of third-State obligations under the Genocide Convention; true if the Court in 2024 found a plausible risk of genocide and stated that States parties' duty to prevent is engaged without a definitive merits determination, false if no such finding or statement exists.

veracity.statement: Helen Clark had nine years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Jacinda Ardern had five years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Mr Hipkins had a year to recognise Palestine and he didn’t.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific tenures and that no Labour prime minister recognised Palestine during them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Prime ministerial tenure dates (Clark 1999–2008, Ardern 2017–2023, Hipkins 2023) and the MFAT/New Zealand Government record of formal recognition of the State of Palestine; true if none of the three governments extended recognition and the stated durations are approximately right, false if any did or the durations are materially wrong.

veracity.statement: The reality is, there has been no International Court of Justice ruling to that effect. Or does he think that we should just ignore the International Court of Justice and just come to our own interpretation, legally qualified or otherwise?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the absence of any ICJ ruling establishing the obligation Henare described. Turns on how narrowly 'to that effect' is read — a merits determination naming third States versus the 2024 provisional measures findings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ICJ docket in South Africa v Israel and any advisory opinions to 7 October 2025; true if no ICJ ruling has determined that New Zealand holds a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza, false if such a ruling or order exists.

veracity.statement: Let us be clear that recognising Palestinian Statehood, the likes of which the Green Party put forward a motion to propose to do exactly that in 2021, was opposed by National and ACT MPs, is an important part of being very clear that Israel must not be rewarded for its genocide.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Greens advanced a 2021 motion to recognise Palestinian statehood and that National and ACT MPs blocked or opposed it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2021 Hansard record for a Green Party motion or request for leave on recognising Palestinian statehood; true if such a motion was put and National and/or ACT members objected or voted against, false if no such motion exists or if the objection came from elsewhere.

veracity.statement: Because any world that normalises over 20,000 - plus children’s lives being taken by the violence of Israel, any State—any country—that normalises the intentional killing of doctors and nurses and journalists and the winding back of the health system, surely, that needs to be part of our responsibility.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a figure of more than 20,000 children killed by Israeli military action in Gaza as at the date of the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Gaza Ministry of Health and UN OCHA casualty data as at October 2025 for deaths of children; true if the recorded figure exceeds 20,000, false if it is materially below that.

veracity.statement: It has democracies in 19 years of consistent free fall, where now autocratic regimes are more plentiful than democracies that we support; more plentiful than countries that foster and use the democratic process.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions attributed to the Freedom House index: a nineteen-year unbroken decline, and that autocracies now outnumber democracies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Freedom House Freedom in the World 2025 report; true if it records a 19th consecutive year of decline in global freedom and shows authoritarian states outnumbering democracies on its own classification, false if the run of decline is a different length or the balance of regime types is the other way.

civility.statement: We are sick of people who are lions in Opposition and lambs in Government.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith and cowardice to the named former prime ministers rather than engaging the substance — a sneer at character, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The reality is, there has been no International Court of Justice ruling to that effect. Or does he think that we should just ignore the International Court of Justice and just come to our own interpretation, legally qualified or otherwise?
civility.explanation: 'legally qualified or otherwise' is a dig at the questioner's competence to read the Court, edging off the substance and onto the member — pointed rather than a clear personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Green Party co-leader just said that they had a motion in 2021. What you didn’t tell the House is what happened to it. My question now is: what did Labour do with your motion? Why didn’t you tell the country? Why didn’t you tell the people listening around New Zealand, instead of thinking that we will just ignore the facts? The silence is deafening on that one question.
civility.explanation: Repeatedly imputes deliberate concealment to the co-leader — 'what you didn't tell the House', 'why didn't you tell the country' — which is an accusation of bad faith rather than a contest of her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister, in his speech, spoke about not recognising Palestine in fear of rewarding the actions of Hamas, and yet straight after he did not recognise Palestine, the Israel officials were celebrating, as if it was a reward for their genocide. So that does not hold, Mr Peters.
civility.explanation: A direct, hard challenge addressed to the Minister by name that stays entirely on his reasoning; nothing is said about him as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reality is, there has been no International Court of Justice ruling to that effect. Or does he think that we should just ignore the International Court of Justice and just come to our own interpretation, legally qualified or otherwise?
rigor.explanation: False dilemma: presents the only alternative to his reading as ignoring the Court entirely and substituting a home-made interpretation, when acting on a treaty duty in the absence of a merits ruling is a third option he does not address.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, again, the primary answer to the question began with the criteria from the Montevideo convention about recognition. That has not been satisfied.
rigor.explanation: A real inference — recognition requires the Montevideo criteria; they are unmet; therefore no recognition — but the conclusion is asserted rather than shown, with no indication of which criteria fail or why.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister, in his speech, spoke about not recognising Palestine in fear of rewarding the actions of Hamas, and yet straight after he did not recognise Palestine, the Israel officials were celebrating, as if it was a reward for their genocide. So that does not hold, Mr Peters.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference against the Minister's stated rationale, but there is a gap: Israeli officials welcoming non-recognition does not by itself establish that recognition would not also have rewarded Hamas, so the conclusion outruns the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Recognition should be based on clear, democratic principles, not just political pressure or symbolism. A State must have a legitimate, accountable Government; respect for the rule of law; and a commitment to peace. That’s not the case today, with the Palestinian territories divided and part of it controlled by Hamas—a terrorist organisation that rejects democracy and has committed horrific violence.
rigor.explanation: Sets out a criterion, applies it, and gives grounds — territorial division and Hamas control — for the conclusion that the criterion is unmet. The inference tracks the premises, though the stated criteria are asserted rather than derived from any recognised legal test.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Peace, of course, will come only through direct negotiation between two democratic partners willing to co-exist, not through declarations that ignore reality.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy asserted without support — recognition and negotiation are presented as mutually exclusive routes, and no reason is offered for why one forecloses the other.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, again, the primary answer to the question began with the criteria from the Montevideo convention about recognition. That has not been satisfied.
specificity.explanation: Names the governing convention, which is checkable, but supplies none of the four criteria, no evidence against them, and no threshold for when they would be satisfied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we are truly interested in enduring peace, it means that we must properly afford their sovereignty and mana motuhake for them to come up with what they, as a people, believe is the best way forward for their State.
specificity.explanation: States a principle for how recognition should work but names no mechanism, instrument, condition or timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It has democracies in 19 years of consistent free fall, where now autocratic regimes are more plentiful than democracies that we support; more plentiful than countries that foster and use the democratic process.
specificity.explanation: Names the source index and gives a precise figure for the run of decline, so a reader can go and check it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Violence is not the answer to the objective nature of debate. Emotions must be removed from the difficult situations so we all hear the debate in its entirety, and debated objectively, thus ensuring the best outcomes for all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A general sentiment about how debate should be conducted; no measure, mechanism, figure or commitment that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But this didn’t start on 7 October 2023, and I think that we have to remind ourselves of what happened 75 years ago, when Palestinian land was taken, when houses were destroyed, and when people were displaced and, in fact, their self-determination—their mana motuhake—was denied.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 75 years before the statement Palestinian land was expropriated, houses were destroyed and the population was displaced, with self-determination denied — a historical claim about the 1948 events, not an opinion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The historical record of the 1948 Palestine war/Nakba (UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine and UNRWA displacement figures, standard scholarly surveys). True if land was expropriated, villages destroyed and a large Palestinian population displaced in that period; false if the record does not show this. Note the stated interval: 75 years before October 2025 is 1950, while the events referred to are 1948.

veracity.statement: We acknowledge the three New Zealanders who were detained by Israel after being illegally intercepted in international waters, because they had the courage to actually do what this Government doesn’t.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that three New Zealand citizens were detained by Israel following the interception of the aid flotilla, and that the interception occurred unlawfully in international waters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and MFAT/NZ government statements on the Global Sumud Flotilla interception of early October 2025. True if exactly three New Zealand citizens were detained by Israeli authorities after the interception; false if the number differs or none were detained. The 'illegally … in international waters' element resolves against the recorded interception coordinates and the legal characterisation given by the UN human rights bodies or relevant courts.

veracity.statement: There was a statement made there about genocide that is not authorised, supported, or precedented by any international court whatsoever, but they make the statement anyway, and, sadly, that’s been far too often the case on this very, very sad issue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no international court has authorised, supported or set a precedent for characterising events in Gaza as genocide.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The orders and rulings of the ICJ and ICC concerning Gaza up to October 2025. True if no international court has issued any finding or order lending support to a genocide characterisation; false if such an order exists — e.g. the ICJ's provisional measures orders in South Africa v Israel (January, March and May 2024) finding a plausible risk to rights under the Genocide Convention.

veracity.statement: Well, here’s the reality: there are clear guidelines out in the 1990s Montevideo Convention on recognition, which is not met.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the Montevideo Convention dates from the 1990s and that its criteria for statehood are not met in the case of Palestine.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States — its date of signature (public treaty record) and its four stated criteria for statehood, applied to Palestine. True if the Convention dates from the 1990s and Palestine plainly fails those criteria; false if the Convention dates from another decade, or if the application of the criteria is genuinely contested among states that have recognised Palestine.

veracity.statement: You’ve got these Muslim countries: Saudi Arabia, Jordan, United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar, and Egypt all seeking to work with the American-led peace plan to get a solution.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that eight named states were all engaging with and supporting the US-led Gaza peace plan at the time of the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by the governments named — Saudi Arabia, Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Türkiye, Qatar and Egypt — from September–October 2025 on the US-led Gaza plan, including any joint statement. True if all eight publicly endorsed or engaged with the plan; false if any of the eight had not.

veracity.statement: And might I say, on the so-called aid programme, the flotilla was offered—by the Italian Government—a military ship to take all of their so-called aid on those boats and to make sure they got to the destination. Guess what? They refused it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific offer by the Italian government of a naval vessel to carry the flotilla's aid to its destination, and that the flotilla declined it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Italian government statements and contemporaneous reporting on the Global Sumud Flotilla, late September 2025. True if Italy offered a navy vessel to carry the flotilla's aid to its destination and the flotilla declined; false if no such offer was made, if the offer was on materially different terms (e.g. transfer of aid to a third party rather than delivery to Gaza), or if it was accepted.

civility.statement: To imply that there hasn’t been anything before 7 October denies, as we heard earlier, the decades of occupation, apartheid, and human suffering.
civility.explanation: Forceful disagreement directed entirely at a position and at the historical record, not at any member. No one is insulted or accused of bad character — this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it because they’re black that you don’t care, or what?
civility.explanation: Directly accuses the questioner of racial indifference. This is an attack on the member's character and motives rather than on any argument they advanced.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And here you’ve got sympathisers trying to make a defence today in this House.
civility.explanation: Labels the members questioning him 'sympathisers' in a context where the implication is sympathy for Hamas. It imputes bad faith to individual members rather than engaging what they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They refused it because they’re virtue signallers—they are performative; they aren’t real.
civility.explanation: Sneering attribution of motive: the participants are characterised as insincere and performative rather than their decision being argued against.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To imply that there hasn’t been anything before 7 October denies, as we heard earlier, the decades of occupation, apartheid, and human suffering.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: no one in the exchange asserted that nothing happened before 7 October. The conclusion (that the opposing view 'denies' decades of occupation) is drawn against a position nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we have to say is that condemning the flotilla is then condemning any efforts that we’re trying to humanely do to get aid into a nation of people who are enduring the most inhumane suffering disproportionately—disproportionately.
rigor.explanation: False equivalence: criticism of one particular convoy is treated as entailing criticism of all humanitarian aid efforts. Nothing is offered to bridge the specific case to the general one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve had decades and decades of political parties supporting this criteria when all of a sudden, despite Clark having the 90s to do that, despite Jacinda Ardern having five years to do that, and despite Mr Hipkins having one year to do that, they all of a sudden want to change the criteria. Now that doesn’t bespeak, surely, to the ethics and morality of their argument.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the conclusion that the opposing argument lacks ethical and moral standing rests only on the claim that previous leaders of that party did not act earlier. Past inaction bears on consistency, not on whether the recognition criteria are correctly applied now.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They go to oil and mining, they go to gas, and they do a bunch of things over there that he’s refused to create opportunities for here at home. That’s why we’re very happy to support quarrying, mining, and oil and gas.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, with a large gap: the premise that departing New Zealanders predominantly take extractive-sector jobs is asserted rather than evidenced, and even if true it would not establish that extraction policy is what drives emigration.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My next question is: in what way would recognising Palestinian Statehood complicate achieving a ceasefire?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy decision (recognition of Palestinian statehood) and presses the Minister on the stated reason for it. Entirely about the measure, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When he said, “If you want a job, you go where the jobs are. I encourage anyone to do what it takes to get a job.”, did he mean: “go to Australia”?
focus.explanation: There is a real policy question underneath (job availability and emigration to Australia), but the question is built around catching the Prime Minister out with his own words rather than engaging a named measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Holidays Act will be repealed and replaced with a simpler, more workable alternative: what will be known as the employment leave bill. The new legislation will be based on hours-based accrual, something I know businesses have been asking for for a long time now.

rigor.statement: We have had conversations in recent times with leaders and foreign Ministers, with senior officials from dozens and dozens of countries both in the Middle East and closer to home. rigor.explanation: The conclusion (reputation 'very much intact') rests on unverifiable private conversations — an appeal to the speaker's own anecdotal, privileged evidence. It also slides from 'our position is understood' to 'our reputation is intact', which does not follow: a position can be perfectly well understood and badly received.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The first was from the leader of the Labour Party, the second was from the justice spokesman of the Labour Party, but both of them voted against the bill. It appears that at least Duncan Webb is more consistent than his leader.

specificity.statement: We have had conversations in recent times with leaders and foreign Ministers, with senior officials from dozens and dozens of countries both in the Middle East and closer to home. veracity.statement: That’s why our energy package tackles the root causes: limited fuel supply, a shortage of back-up generation in dry years, and years of policy uncertainty. The issues add a risk premium of between $240 and $400 annually on Kiwis’ household power bills.

veracity.statement: The report specifically cited the ban on offshore exploration, the 100 percent renewable target, and Lake Onslow as to why we are short on investment in fuel and firming, and that has left us dangerously short of reliable back-up generation.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Frontier Economics electricity market report: true if it names all three of those policies as causes of reduced investment in fuel and firming; false if it names none, or attributes the shortfall to other causes without citing them.
