focus.statement: It'd be good if the members on this side of the House made up their mind about the fee. Some of them think it's not sufficient of a barrier; others think it's too much of a barrier.
focus.explanation: The named measure (the prescribed fee) is genuinely at issue, but the weight of the remark is on the opposing benches' internal inconsistency rather than on whether a fee should be charged. A real policy point wrapped in party framing. No individual is attacked, so this is Focus's territory, not Civility's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How will new section 360D(6)’s inclusion of proposed company, prospective director, and prospective shareholder work in practice when the company does not yet exist? The definitions in new section 360D(6) seem to create some complex scenarios. Who will maintain alternative address records during company formation, for example?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the committee: the drafting of a named subsection and how it would operate. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How will new section 360D(6)’s inclusion of proposed company, prospective director, and prospective shareholder work in practice when the company does not yet exist? The definitions in new section 360D(6) seem to create some complex scenarios. Who will maintain alternative address records during company formation, for example?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision, the three extended definitions it inserts, and the concrete operational gap being probed — who holds the alternative address record before the company exists. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer. Short of 1.0 because no figure, timeframe or proposed mechanism is supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, already we have a differentiation in the test between section 360G(2)(b), which is “as soon as practicable”, and section 360D(2)(b), which is “ensure the alternative address is publicly available from the New Zealand register.”, which would then lead any interpretation to conclude that it must be an absolute test, because, if the Parliament had wanted to put a qualifier in, such as “take reasonable steps” or “as soon as practicable”, it would have put it in there.
rigor.explanation: A genuine interpretive inference (expressio unius / deliberate-omission reasoning): the qualifier appears in one provision and not the parallel one, therefore the silent provision imposes an absolute duty. The conclusion tracks the premise; the gap is that drafting inconsistency is not always deliberate, which is why it is not a 1.0.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So our officials and, particularly, the drafters from the Parliamentary Counsel Office said, actually, if we really want to capture the intent of this bill, if we want to capture the nuances, then this is the way to draft it. So we very gratefully accepted their drafting recommendations to try to capture the various different situations that might occur, and it’s all designed to put that in place.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority. The objection was that two parallel provisions carry different tests and may be internally inconsistent; the answer is that the Parliamentary Counsel Office drafted it that way. Who wrote the wording is not a reason why the differing wording is correct, so the conclusion does not follow from what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are already a number of methods for delivering documents for service. All this clause does is enable an alternative address to be used as one of the many methods, and lawyers are quite accomplished at delivering those documents already, despite the plethora of methods that are already available to them.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: service already has multiple concurrent methods with no hierarchy, so adding one more creates no new problem. Reasonable, but there is a gap — the question asked which of two now-listed addresses a practitioner should choose, and 'lawyers manage already' answers by analogy rather than addressing the choice.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you look at a lot of commercial addresses around New Zealand that have multiple businesses, they are not overly well signposted. You just need to be a delivery driver and have a bit of experience in this, but, actually, it’s very hard, even if it’s labelled as a business address, to actually find some of these businesses because of poor signage and it’s not clear where it is.
rigor.explanation: A real argument about a real provision — shared commercial premises are hard to locate, so service at an alternative address may fail — but the premise rests on generalised personal experience rather than any evidence about failed service rates.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Therefore, already we have a differentiation in the test between section 360G(2)(b), which is “as soon as practicable”, and section 360D(2)(b), which is “ensure the alternative address is publicly available from the New Zealand register.”, which would then lead any interpretation to conclude that it must be an absolute test, because, if the Parliament had wanted to put a qualifier in, such as “take reasonable steps” or “as soon as practicable”, it would have put it in there.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provisions (360G(2)(b), 360D(2)(b)) and quotes the competing statutory wording. Anyone could open the bill and check the point.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So there’s nothing really in new section 360E that actually talks about the serviceability of the alternative address.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause and the missing element (serviceability), but does not say what the fall-back mechanism should be or how it would work.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will there be any hierarchy of service methods or will alternative addresses under these provisions have equal status with residential addresses?
specificity.explanation: A checkable question with a determinate answer: it identifies the two competing address types and asks specifically about ranking between them. A precise question counts as specific even though it announces nothing.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There are multiple different tests here, and I am actually reasonably concerned, for want of a better word, that the drafting here is confused and may be incorrect and may need rectification before we potentially vote on this clause or any other clauses before the end of the evening.
civility.explanation: A blunt charge that the drafting is confused and possibly wrong, aimed entirely at the text of the bill. No person is impugned — hard criticism of a measure is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How would I as, say, a legal practitioner, maybe a chartered accountant that was slandered recently by the Hon Dr Duncan Webb—how will legal practitioners know which address to use for service?
civility.explanation: A live policy question carrying a gratuitous accusation that a named member slandered someone. The imputation of wrongdoing is aimed at the person, not at any argument, and nothing in the service question required it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The job of members of Parliament is not to stir up hate in the community, not to incite things to take place.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — stirring up hate and inciting — to the interjecting member and their party. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes malice to a person rather than engaging what was said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He’s the one that actually does the heavy lifting. I’m surprised he hasn’t resigned yet.
civility.explanation: A sneer at another member — mock praise followed by the suggestion he should have quit. It targets the person's position and standing, not any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are multiple different tests here, and I am actually reasonably concerned, for want of a better word, that the drafting here is confused and may be incorrect and may need rectification before we potentially vote on this clause or any other clauses before the end of the evening.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the internal consistency of the clause and whether it is fit to be voted on. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So there’s nothing really in new section 360E that actually talks about the serviceability of the alternative address.
focus.explanation: Names the specific provision and identifies a specific gap in it — whether an address that fails in practice is still legally effective for service. Entirely on the substance of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will there be any hierarchy of service methods or will alternative addresses under these provisions have equal status with residential addresses?
focus.explanation: A precise question about the operation of the clause under debate — the relative status of two service addresses. Names the mechanism at issue, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How would I as, say, a legal practitioner, maybe a chartered accountant that was slandered recently by the Hon Dr Duncan Webb—how will legal practitioners know which address to use for service?
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy question inside this — which address a practitioner serves on — but half the sentence is an aside about a named opponent's conduct rather than the clause.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The job of members of Parliament is not to stir up hate in the community, not to incite things to take place.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure is named. It is a characterisation of what the other side does with its time, prompted by an interjection, with no content about the bill before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He’s the one that actually does the heavy lifting. I’m surprised he hasn’t resigned yet.
focus.explanation: Entirely about an individual opposite and their party's internal state. No policy, clause, figure or outcome is mentioned.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, when we’re looking at this clause, clause 6, which says that says that service of documents on directors in legal proceedings must be done by leaving them at the director’s alternative address as that address is shown in the register, that alternative address cannot be the company that they work for, which is the legal address of service. So there’s a contradiction in terms there.
rigor.explanation: A genuine textual argument, but it equivocates: clause 5 restricts what may be *recorded* as a director's alternative address, while clause 6 lists the alternative address as one of several places where documents *may* be served. The conclusion that the two provisions contradict each other does not follow from the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m just going back to clause 6, amending section 387A. It gives a number of different places where documents may be served. If we go back to new section 360E, inserted by clause 5: the alternative address must not be the company’s registered office, but the company’s registered office can still be used for service.
rigor.explanation: Draws the distinction the opposing argument elides — a restriction on what may be recorded as an alternative address is not a restriction on where service may occur — and the conclusion that there is no contradiction follows directly from that distinction plus the list of service addresses in s 387A.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is confusion in the law because section 387A(1) of the Companies Act is in regard to a director in their capacity as a director. Now, you can serve legal proceedings on someone in their capacity as a director or you can serve legal proceedings on someone because they've defamed you and called you an untrustworthy accountant, having nothing to do with their directorship.
rigor.explanation: The capacity distinction is real and is offered with a concrete illustration, but the conclusion overreaches: service depending on the capacity in which proceedings are brought is a pre-existing feature of the law, not something these clauses create, so "there is confusion in the law" does not follow from the premise given.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Therefore, when we’re looking at this clause, clause 6, which says that says that service of documents on directors in legal proceedings must be done by leaving them at the director’s alternative address as that address is shown in the register, that alternative address cannot be the company that they work for, which is the legal address of service. So there’s a contradiction in terms there.
specificity.explanation: Names clause 5, clause 6, new section 360E and the exact operative wording, so anyone can go to the bill and check the reading. Precision is high whether or not the reading is right.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There is confusion in the law because section 387A(1) of the Companies Act is in regard to a director in their capacity as a director. Now, you can serve legal proceedings on someone in their capacity as a director or you can serve legal proceedings on someone because they've defamed you and called you an untrustworthy accountant, having nothing to do with their directorship.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (s 387A(1)) and works a concrete scenario — proceedings against a director qua director versus a defamation claim against the same individual — that a reader could test against the section.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think we’ve had a pretty good crack tonight at being quite serious and quite upfront about actually addressing the content before us, and to be heckled about that is quite unacceptable. So if the member is able to address that point, I’m sure we’d really appreciate it.
civility.explanation: Objects to the conduct of the debate and asks for an answer without attacking any individual; the complaint about heckling is pointed but lands on behaviour in the chamber rather than on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think the member is making a mountain out of—it’s not even a molehill, it’s just a blip in his mind somewhere. I think filibustering is all very well but at least it should have some point.
civility.explanation: Moves off the drafting question and on to the member: mockery ("a blip in his mind somewhere") plus an imputation of bad faith (filibustering). A clear personal jab rather than a rebuttal, and she had already made the substantive rebuttal without it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I do take umbrage from across the House at being asked whether we are taking this seriously. We are taking it extremely seriously, Mr Abel.
civility.explanation: Responds directly to a heckler, naming him, but the objection is to the accusation rather than to the man; no attack on his character, competence or motives.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is great. You’re embarrassing yourself wonderfully.
civility.explanation: A direct personal jibe at the member speaking — sarcastic mockery of her as a person, engaging none of the drafting point under debate.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just to challenge one of the points that Mr Abel made in his interjections, which we are entitled to respond to, where he said, “Take another five-minute call.”, well, if he'd been here for long enough, he’d realise that actually most of us are taking succinct calls to ask direct questions of the member and to seek answers, and we still haven't had answers to questions asked a long time ago.
civility.explanation: Mostly a defence of how the debate has been conducted, but "if he'd been here for long enough" is a dig at the member himself rather than at his interjection — edging past robust into condescension without becoming an outright insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It doesn’t say you cannot use the company’s office for serving documents, it just simply says that the alternative address cannot be the company’s registered office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the bill's text actually provides: that new s 360E only limits what may be recorded as a director's alternative address, and does not remove the company's office as a place where documents may be served.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill at this committee stage — new s 360E(3) inserted by clause 5, and s 387A of the Companies Act 1993 as amended by clause 6. True if s 360E(3) restricts only what may be recorded as a director's alternative address while the amended s 387A still lists the company's registered office/address for service among the permitted places of service; false if the amended s 387A removes or forbids service at the company's office.

veracity.statement: That's the contradiction we've created, because most company directors around the country would have the address for service as being their company.
veracity.explanation: An empirical premise about the prevailing practice of NZ company directors: that for a majority of them, the address at which documents would be served on them is their own company's address.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Companies Office / Companies Register data on the addresses recorded against New Zealand company directors and their companies. True if, for a majority of directors, the address recorded for serving documents on them is their company's registered office or address for service; false if most are recorded against a residential or third-party (e.g. solicitor's or accountant's) address.

focus.statement: And to be heckled by members of the Green Party for saying that we're sitting here filibustering, when they sit there day after day after day abusing members of Parliament in title changes of bills, is really disappointing and it only reflects more on them than it does on us.
focus.explanation: Once the complaint about the Green Party's general chamber conduct is removed there is nothing left — no clause, no figure, no policy consequence. Pure inter-party point-scoring in the middle of a clause-by-clause debate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question remains: how will the clause 7 amendments to section 388A affect legal practitioners serving documents on directors? Will there be any hierarchy of service methods, or will alternative addresses, under these provisions, have equal status with residential addresses? How will legal practitioners know which address under section 388A to use for service?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: names clause 7 and the specific section it amends, and asks about the operative effect on service. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What if they are driving a Toyota Corolla and it’s supposed to be for four-wheel drives, hypothetically? What if people want to fly business class but there is only economy available? What would you do if you were a member of the Green Party, with that option? What would you do? What would your option be?
focus.explanation: A digression about the Green Party's travel choices with no connection to service of documents, section 388A, or any named policy. Nothing about the clause survives if the party reference is removed. No individual is insulted, so this is a Focus failure rather than a Civility one; no argument is advanced, so nothing is emitted for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There’s a whole variety of methods someone may use—whichever one is most convenient. They are not in any hierarchy.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the mechanism that was in dispute — whether the listed service methods are ordered — with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Surely, the second clause here actually supersedes the first clause, really, because, otherwise, we’re not really adding anything more under (ba). I think it’s maybe a bit of a drafting error here, and we have ended up adding a bit of complexity.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the drafting of the clause before the committee — which subclause does the work and whether the insertion is redundant. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I felt very uncomfortable walking those first few steps, and I looked down, and my left shoe was on my right foot, and my right shoe was on my left foot. I thought, “That’s what’s making me feel uncomfortable. The shoe is on the other foot.” That can make some of us feel very uncomfortable, but, for me, it was an enlightening experience this morning.
focus.explanation: A measure (clause 8, service on shareholders and creditors) was before the committee, so there was a policy question available to engage. This anecdote engages none of it; the payload is the "shoe is on the other foot" dig at the roles being reversed, with no mechanism, cost, figure or named provision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just wonder whether the member thought for a second about taking the opportunity to once and for all eradicate facsimiles from the record and make our lives just a little bit easier.
focus.explanation: A real point about the provision under discussion — the retention of facsimile as a method of service in section 391(1)(c) — put to the member in charge of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question remains: how will the clause 7 amendments to section 388A affect legal practitioners serving documents on directors? Will there be any hierarchy of service methods, or will alternative addresses, under these provisions, have equal status with residential addresses? How will legal practitioners know which address under section 388A to use for service?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the section, and the precise mechanism at issue (hierarchy versus equal status of the two addresses). Checkable and answerable; short of 1.0 only because it poses the question rather than supplying figures or a rule.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just wonder whether the member thought for a second about taking the opportunity to once and for all eradicate facsimiles from the record and make our lives just a little bit easier.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete change to a named method of service, but supplies no drafting, no transitional handling, and no timeframe for how the removal would work.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I note that the same arguments apply for the next clause as well, and I note that they are possibly just as irrelevant.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the opposing contributions as irrelevant. It lands on the arguments rather than on the member, so it stays civil, but the tone edges toward the person and is more than robust engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There’s a whole variety of methods someone may use—whichever one is most convenient. They are not in any hierarchy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the methods of service listed in section 388A are alternatives of equal standing, with no required order of attempt.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Companies Act 1993 s 388A as amended by this bill: true if the paragraphs are joined disjunctively ("may be served on a director as follows: (a) … or (b) … or (c) …") with no provision requiring one method be attempted before another; false if the section, or any related rule of service, prescribes an order of preference among the listed methods.

veracity.statement: But I invite the member to mention to his colleague, the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, that now would be a good time to remove facsimile machines—although I understand some medical doctors and pharmacists still use them quite a lot.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a present fact that fax machines remain in substantial use among New Zealand doctors and pharmacists.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Evidence on fax use in NZ primary care and community pharmacy as at 2025 — Health NZ / Ministry of Health digital-health or e-referral reporting, RNZCGP or Pharmacy Guild statements, or contemporaneous reporting on faxed referrals and prescriptions. True if fax remains in routine use by a non-trivial share of GPs or pharmacies; false if fax has been effectively phased out of those settings.

rigor.statement: Surely, the second clause here actually supersedes the first clause, really, because, otherwise, we’re not really adding anything more under (ba). I think it’s maybe a bit of a drafting error here, and we have ended up adding a bit of complexity.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure, but with a real gap: the conclusion that subclause (2) supersedes subclause (1) assumes the two insertions do the same work, without checking what paragraph (ba) actually provides for. It covers leaving a document at the alternative address, while (b) covers posting — so the premise of redundancy is not established. Reasoning about the policy, and reasoning loosely.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The briefing materials associated with the legislation note that there are currently almost 3,200 registered John Smiths on the company's register—almost 3,200.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of directors named John Smith on the Companies Register, sourced to the bill's briefing materials.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE/Companies Office register data and the departmental briefing supplied to the select committee on this bill; true if the register shows approximately 3,200 director records under the name John Smith, false if the figure is materially different or absent from the briefing.

veracity.statement: I understand that the Minister has indicated that he intends to introduce comprehensive reforms which include director identification numbers (DINs).

veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial statements and the Government's announced legislative programme for Companies Act reform; true if the Minister has publicly signalled a bill introducing director identification numbers, false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: We know that some of the other contributors to that horrendous abuse that took place in State care and in faith-based institutions was also a consequence of having untrained staff members, a lack of institutional safeguards, a lack of safe regulations, and also the location that some of these institutions were at—for example, Great Barrier Island or Aotea in the 1970s during the Whakapakari boot camp.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific contributing causes of abuse in State and faith-based care, and places the Whakapakari programme on Great Barrier Island/Aotea in the 1970s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia) and its case studies; true if the report identifies untrained staff, absent safeguards and institutional remoteness as contributors and records Whakapakari operating on Great Barrier Island in the period stated, false if it identifies different causes or dates the programme outside the 1970s.

specificity.statement: The briefing materials associated with the legislation note that there are currently almost 3,200 registered John Smiths on the company's register—almost 3,200.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a named register and a precise figure — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have given the Minister the commitment that if his bill is through the first reading before the end of the year, I will withdraw my member’s bill—I will hold off on the third reading.
specificity.explanation: A precise conditional with a named trigger (first reading), a deadline (end of the year) and a named consequence (holding off the third reading).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Labour is supporting these changes, because they’re a first step, but we are absolutely committed to a much more comprehensive response to what has been an appalling practice in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: States a position but the promised "much more comprehensive response" carries no mechanism, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that some of the other contributors to that horrendous abuse that took place in State care and in faith-based institutions was also a consequence of having untrained staff members, a lack of institutional safeguards, a lack of safe regulations, and also the location that some of these institutions were at—for example, Great Barrier Island or Aotea in the 1970s during the Whakapakari boot camp.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete causal factors, a named institution and a location, though the date range is loose and no figures are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The removal of residential addresses under these provisions, in my view, will make it even harder to distinguish between directors with 3,200 John Smiths currently registered.
rigor.explanation: Premise (residential address is the current disambiguator) supports the conclusion (removing it degrades identification) fairly directly; the gap is that he does not address whether the alternative address system also disambiguates, which he asks about separately.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have a small country and it’s quite possible for us to close that gap, and really that overseas convictions gap was really that one. We don’t have the same complexity as people who can move from state to state.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a real structural premise (New Zealand has no federal states, so no inter-state information transfer problem) to the conclusion that closing the overseas-convictions gap is feasible here. The inference holds, though the analogy does more work than the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That scrutiny is deserving because we know that one of the reasons why the scale of abuse of children, the scale of torture, the scale of violence that took place between the years of 1975 and 1999 is because of a lack of institutional safeguards, because of a lack of children’s safety and indeed, children’s rights being put at the forefront of legislation and of all of the rules and conditions around that State care.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal premise (absent institutional safeguards produced the historical abuse) to support the conclusion that close scrutiny of this bill's safeguards is warranted. The inference follows, but the causal premise is asserted rather than evidenced here.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a concern that the Labour Party has had too, that there hasn’t been the consultation that had been expected.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a specific process failure on the bill before the House — survivor consultation — rather than general criticism of the other party.

civility.statement: Does the Minister concede that perhaps we can do better in the future iterations and changes to respond to this abuse inquiry?

veracity.statement: First thing: we had a royal commission for six years, and they were very clear in their recommendations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care ran for six years.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions' establishment date (Order in Council) and the date its final report was delivered; true if the elapsed period is approximately six years, false if materially shorter or longer.

veracity.statement: There are hundreds of recommendations that need to be looked at, considered, and enacted, potentially, and we’re going through that work.

veracity.statement: Budget 2025 funded a safe and capable workforce, for example.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 Estimates/Vote documents and the Budget 2025 initiatives summary; true if an identifiable appropriation for care-workforce safety/capability appears, false if no such initiative was funded.

veracity.statement: Just to be clear, this part already exists in the legislation for core workers who have a conviction in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an appeal right of this kind already exists in current law for core workers with New Zealand convictions, so the bill only extends it.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The existing safety-checking provisions of the Children's Act 2014 and its regulations; true if they already confer on a core worker with a New Zealand conviction a right of appeal to the High Court against a confirmed determination, false if no such existing right is found.

rigor.statement: This part of the bill was relatively uncontroversial. We didn’t have many—hardly anyone, in fact, I believe—saying anything about this part of the bill that meant they were opposed to it. It’s a widely supported, relatively straightforward change that fills a known gap and responds to the royal commission report.
rigor.explanation: Infers that the change is 'widely supported' from the absence of opposing submissions — an argument from absence of evidence, further weakened by the hedge 'I believe'. The inference about the policy is real but the conclusion outruns what silence can show.

rigor.statement: I think to do due diligence is to actually spend a bit more time, because people are listening and wanting to make sure that we are held accountable.

rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Many people were involved in that, but, more broadly, I have set up a ministerial advisory group of representative survivors to help guide the Government in its work over the next few years.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (a ministerial advisory group of survivors) but supplies no membership, terms of reference, timeframe or numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I know that we're moving hopefully to a law where we change the rules around trafficking and they're quite a significant change, and I really welcome the work done in that area where we move away from consent.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a specific area of law and the particular element being changed, but gives no clause, timeframe or figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We think it’s already clear, in this bill, that we are adding specified offences, as I mentioned in my opening speech. It’s very clear that, as things come up, we will consider adding them to the specified offences list, as we’ve done in this bill today.
specificity.explanation: Answers a question about whether new offences can be added with a general assurance that they 'will consider' additions; no mechanism (regulation-making power vs primary legislation), no criteria and no timing are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the main ones that we hear about is the request for an independent survivor-led redress system, but I understand that there were other recommendations that haven’t been followed through.
specificity.explanation: Names one concrete recommendation (an independent survivor-led redress system) but leaves the 'other recommendations' unenumerated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of a survivor going through the process, they will be able to apply, they will be able to go to the chief executive, but then, in terms of, again, the support for a survivor who has been through trauma, who has been harmed and hurt by the State, and the State then requiring them to potentially pay to have their appeal heard by the High Court—I’d appreciate for that to be illuminated to understand a bit more about, again, for a survivor, who is paying the cost when they’ve already paid the highest cost.
specificity.explanation: Traces a concrete procedural pathway (application, chief executive, High Court appeal) and identifies the cost question, though no figures or fee schedules are supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re just aligning the law so that people who have an overseas conviction and now fall under this piece of legislation also have an appeal right.
specificity.explanation: States precisely who the provision covers (core workers with overseas convictions), what it gives them (an appeal right) and how it relates to existing law — checkable against the clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know that we're moving hopefully to a law where we change the rules around trafficking and they're quite a significant change, and I really welcome the work done in that area where we move away from consent.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance — a named legal change (trafficking law, removal of the consent element) and how it interacts with the specified-offences list in Part 1. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the main ones that we hear about is the request for an independent survivor-led redress system, but I understand that there were other recommendations that haven’t been followed through.
focus.explanation: Names a specific recommendation from the inquiry report and asks why it was not implemented. This is scrutiny of a named policy commitment, not party-directed attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In terms of a survivor going through the process, they will be able to apply, they will be able to go to the chief executive, but then, in terms of, again, the support for a survivor who has been through trauma, who has been harmed and hurt by the State, and the State then requiring them to potentially pay to have their appeal heard by the High Court—I’d appreciate for that to be illuminated to understand a bit more about, again, for a survivor, who is paying the cost when they’ve already paid the highest cost.
focus.explanation: Engages a named provision and its practical consequence — who bears the cost of a High Court appeal under the new section — rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think to do due diligence is to actually spend a bit more time, because people are listening and wanting to make sure that we are held accountable.
civility.explanation: Opposes a closure motion — a genuinely contested moment where he could have accused the Government of shutting down scrutiny — and argues the point without touching any member personally.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In new section 28B(2), there is a reference to a chief executive receiving an application and the ability to hand that application for review on to another chief executive. I just have a question about the rationale for that and when it would be used.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (new section 28B(2)) and the precise mechanism at issue — the transfer of a review application between chief executives. A minister could act on this directly; it carries no figures or timeframes, so short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, yeah, I’m seeking to understand why we’ve specified that only core workers must not be engaged or employed in this business, and what safeguards are in place to make sure that every person that interacts—guides, teaches—in any way, small or big, with vulnerable children are not going to pose any danger or risk to their wellbeing and safety.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named term in a named clause and the class of workers she thinks is excluded, but the alternative she wants is left as 'every person that interacts... in any way, small or big' — no proposed definition, threshold or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The key is that when people are working with children and have unsupervised access to children, they are teachers, learning support people, teacher-aides and those types of people who generally have unrestricted access to children that we need to protect children from.
specificity.explanation: Gives the operative test (unsupervised access to children) and names the occupational categories it captures. Falls short of the top because it enumerates examples rather than the statutory boundary, so it does not settle which third-party or volunteer roles fall inside.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we are talking about here is Part 2, and we’re talking about the significance of the use of the words “vulnerable adult” and the potential replacement of those words with “adult at risk”.
specificity.explanation: Names the Part, the exact wording in the bill and the exact wording proposed to replace it — a change that could be drafted straight into an amendment. No detail on which provisions the substitution would touch.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: A comment on repeat was around the Limitations Act and whether consideration had been given in terms of that very key limitation on people being able to access their rights of complaint—which was six years, I understand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, with a hedge, that the limitation period constraining abuse-in-care complainants' access to legal remedy is six years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Limitation Act 2010, s 11 (primary limitation period for money claims, including claims arising from abuse): true if the primary period is six years from the act or omission; false if the statute sets a materially different primary period.

veracity.statement: In response to that member’s question, “core worker’ is an existing term defined in the Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 'core worker' is not new drafting in this bill but a definition already carried in the principal Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Children's Act 2014 as it stood before this amending bill: true if 'core worker' is a defined term in the principal Act; false if the term is introduced or first defined by this bill.

veracity.statement: The select committee rejected the suggestion out of concern for what was seen as unintended consequences.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fact about the committee's stated reasoning for not adopting the submitters' preferred terminology.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee's report on this bill: true if the majority report records declining the 'adult at risk' substitution and gives unintended consequences as the reason; false if the report gives a different reason, or does not record the suggestion being rejected.

focus.statement: So, yeah, I’m seeking to understand why we’ve specified that only core workers must not be engaged or employed in this business, and what safeguards are in place to make sure that every person that interacts—guides, teaches—in any way, small or big, with vulnerable children are not going to pose any danger or risk to their wellbeing and safety.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the scope of the employment restriction in the amended section 28 and the coverage gap it leaves. Names the policy category at issue rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Listening, in this case, and responding here today to this suggestion by altering the language or accommodating the worries of the people involved in this process would actually be its own step in terms of trust, rather than overriding it with something that can be seen as an institutional override.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the committee — the specific words in Part 2 and the case for amending them. No party framing at all, despite an available line of attack about consultation.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My assumption would be, after the scale of abuse and torture that was experienced for decades and, in some ways, still endures today, how much of that abuse took place by people who are just simply around and had the ability to be around?
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy — that historical abuse was committed by peripheral adults, so a restriction confined to core workers is under-scoped. But the load-bearing premise is offered explicitly as an assumption and put as a rhetorical question, with nothing from the Royal Commission's findings supplied to establish who the perpetrators actually were. A real gap between what is shown and what is concluded, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Listening, in this case, and responding here today to this suggestion by altering the language or accommodating the worries of the people involved in this process would actually be its own step in terms of trust, rather than overriding it with something that can be seen as an institutional override.
rigor.explanation: A real argument about the measure: because the harm was institutional, adopting the survivors' preferred wording would itself rebuild trust. The inference is coherent but the connecting step — that a terminology change produces trust rather than merely symbolising it — is asserted rather than supported, and the counter-consideration (the unintended consequences she is asking about) is left unaddressed in the reasoning.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The one thing that I think has been done well is the select committee process, and this is what the people said, so it’s a really heavy thing not to listen to it.
civility.explanation: Pressing the Government for departing from submitters' wishes on a highly charged bill, where an accusation of bad faith or indifference toward survivors was readily available. She criticises the decision, credits the process, and turns on nobody.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, I guess, the question we’re trying to understand is: what was the decision making behind connecting the existence of a disability and the term “vulnerable adult”?
focus.explanation: Directly interrogates a specific drafting choice in the bill — the linkage between disability and the statutory definition of "vulnerable adult". No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d like a plain explanation of what this change is intended to do and what kinds of grey areas there have been in the past, and the concern over the previous way that this was written in the law and why we are now, in particular, moving to articulating that the commencement of the period is actually at the time when the person is first placed in secure care.
focus.explanation: A precise scrutiny question about one clause: what the drafting change does, what problem in the old wording prompted it, and why commencement is being fixed at first placement. Entirely on the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Ongoing Resource Scheme (ORS) funding, which gives that extra funding to kids in the education system with disabilities—if you’ve got FASD, you can’t even access that, and that’s not the only disability that is not recognised or funded or supported in this country.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific funding scheme (ORS), a specific condition (FASD), and a specific consequence (no access). Checkable and actionable, though no figures are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve also tabled Amendment Paper 354, which is looking at clause 17 of the bill, which defines terms related to the new search on entry provisions in secure youth residences.
specificity.explanation: Names the Amendment Paper by number, the clause it amends, and what that clause does. Anyone could look it up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s a lot of work going on in the background that doesn’t require legislation, but with the help of this legislation, our youth justice and care and protection will have better tools to be able to make sure that our young people are safe.
specificity.explanation: "A lot of work going on in the background" and "better tools" name no programme, mechanism, quantity or timeframe. Nothing here is checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What has happened in the amendment of the law, or will happen, is that we’ll move from a continuous period of 72 hours of detention, and we’ll be moving to a situation where there is clarity over the period that there hasn’t been before, including the actual period “commencing on the day on which the child or young person is first placed in secure care”.
specificity.explanation: Names the existing 72-hour period and quotes the new commencement wording from the clause, so the change described is precise; the "clarity that there hasn't been before" half is left general.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Ongoing Resource Scheme (ORS) funding, which gives that extra funding to kids in the education system with disabilities—if you’ve got FASD, you can’t even access that, and that’s not the only disability that is not recognised or funded or supported in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that children with foetal alcohol spectrum disorder cannot access Ongoing Resourcing Scheme funding in the New Zealand education system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education Ongoing Resourcing Scheme eligibility criteria: true if a foetal alcohol spectrum disorder diagnosis is not itself an ORS eligibility category and children with FASD alone are declined ORS verification; false if FASD is a listed qualifying impairment for ORS.

veracity.statement: The royal commission’s conclusion and their recommendation to us was to acknowledge the concerns from the broader disability community about describing people as “vulnerable”, but they recommended changing the Crimes Act to strengthen the protections for disabled people in the current legislative framework.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Royal Commission actually recommended: retain the existing Crimes Act "vulnerable adult" framework while adding disability to it, rather than adopt a different term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report recommendations concerning the Crimes Act and the definition of "vulnerable adult": true if the report both records disability-community concern about the term "vulnerable" and recommends amending the Crimes Act to extend/strengthen those protections to disabled people; false if it recommended replacing the term or made no such Crimes Act recommendation.

veracity.statement: It clarifies the duration in secure care, which will be three days before court authority is required, and it also makes two changes to youth justice residences.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual description of the bill's effect on the secure-care time limit — three days before court authority is needed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill's clause amending section 370 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989: true if the amended provision sets a three-day period in secure care before court authorisation is required, false if the period is a different length or no court-authority trigger is set at that point.

rigor.statement: FASD is very prevalent in our prison population, and I would assume, based on my one visit to a youth justice residence last year, Te Puna Wai in Christchurch, that foetal alcohol spectrum disorder is probably prevalent in a lot of the young people in there.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single site visit to the youth justice population — an inference from anecdote. Mitigated because the speaker explicitly labels it an assumption and flags the sample as one visit, and because the prison-prevalence premise gives some independent support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you were to change “vulnerable adult” to another definition such as “at risk”, well, that obviously has consequences much more broadly than this particular instance because it would change that for everything that applies in that situation in the Crimes Act, with ramifications that may be unintended and not necessarily helpful to other elements of that regime.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference: a term defined once in the Crimes Act carries into every provision that uses it, so redefining it necessarily has effects beyond this bill. The conclusion follows from the premise offered; the unspecified "ramifications" leave a small gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We understand that there will be a variety of views on this, but we do take some confidence in the process of the royal commission and the very extended process and significant amount of consultation that went into that in order to recognise that that was a sensible thing to recommend, and that’s why we’re carrying it through.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority and process: the recommendation is treated as sensible because the body making it consulted extensively and took a long time, not because of anything about the merits of the definition itself. Length of consultation is evidence of thoroughness, not of correctness.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It doesn’t always mean that you’d necessarily agree with the suggestions made, but that does not equate with ignoring.
civility.explanation: Rebuts an implied charge that the Government ignored submitters by drawing a distinction about the process. Contested exchange, but nothing is directed at any person.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It’s very serious in its implications and the actual tension and the time period is part of that, but so is, obviously, the invasiveness of searching and the humiliation that is involved in the control over people in that situation—but probably the most contentious part will be the issue over force used in that situation.
divination.explanation: Forecasts which part of the bill will prove most contested in the rest of its passage — the use-of-force provisions rather than the detention duration or the search provisions.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the remaining committee-stage and third-reading debate on this omnibus bill, plus Amendment Papers tabled: true if the provisions on use of force attract more debate time and more contested amendments than the secure-care duration and search-on-entry provisions; false if either of those other parts draws more.

focus.statement: So on the time limits on detention in secure care, we’ve got an Amendment Paper which reduces the 72 hours to three hours—mostly because we’re cognisant of the psychological and physical impacts that it can have on any human being who is detained in secure care for prolonged periods of time.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the Committee — a named clause, a named Amendment Paper, and the specific change it makes. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So on the time limits on detention in secure care, we’ve got an Amendment Paper which reduces the 72 hours to three hours—mostly because we’re cognisant of the psychological and physical impacts that it can have on any human being who is detained in secure care for prolonged periods of time.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (an Amendment Paper to the time-limit clause) and the exact figures involved (72 hours reduced to three hours). Checkable and actionable; falls short of 1.0 only because the stated rationale is a general harm claim rather than a quantified one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The problem is that when you have two separate definitions, if a child or young person was placed in secure care at 6 p.m. on the Tuesday, that is day one, so, when counting three days, they need to be out by midnight on the Thursday; in contrast to when counting 72 hours after 6 p.m. on a Tuesday, it is 6 p.m. on a Friday, 18 hours later than when counting three days.
specificity.explanation: Fully concrete: specific placement time, both counting methods, both resulting release times, and the 18-hour difference between them. Anyone could check the calculation.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Obviously, at the extreme end, we see that quite a lot in the adult prison system, where you have reports like the report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit (PERU) at Auckland Prison, where there were people in there who spent 900 consecutive days in, essentially, solitary confinement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit at Auckland Prison documented at least one prisoner held for 900 consecutive days in conditions amounting to solitary confinement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Chief Ombudsman's published report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit (PERU) at Auckland Prison: true if the report records a prisoner held in PERU for 900 or more consecutive days in conditions it characterises as effectively solitary confinement (or equivalent prolonged isolation); false if the longest continuous period recorded is materially shorter, or if the report does not describe the regime as effectively solitary.

veracity.statement: I just want to clarify, because it’s been repeated a couple of times that we landed on a 72-hour time frame: actually, this legislation will be deleting the 72-hour time frame to make sure that we are very clear that it clarifies that three days in secure care before court authority is needed is what was landed upon; not 72 hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill before the Committee removes the existing 72-hour reference and substitutes a three-day period as the limit on secure care before court authority is required.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the clause under debate (clause 16) in the bill as reported back, and the Oranga Tamariki Act provisions it amends: true if the clause deletes the 72-hour formulation and the operative limit before court authorisation is expressed as three days; false if the 72-hour wording is retained anywhere in the operative provision, or if the three-day period is not the trigger for court authority.

veracity.statement: They don’t sit for three days with no contact with a person.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of fact that young people placed in secure care in youth justice residences are not held without human contact for the three-day period — that they have staff contact and access to a day room within the secure unit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki secure care policy and residence records, together with OPCAT inspection reports of youth justice residences by the Ombudsman and the Independent Children's Monitor covering the period to October 2025: true if those records show young people in secure care have routine staff contact and day-room access throughout, false if inspections document instances of young people confined alone to a room without contact for extended periods during a secure care placement.

rigor.statement: Because when people exit that secure care eventually, if they haven’t had any human or social interactions or contact for too long, it can cause even more adverse problems.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: prolonged isolation causes reintegration harm, therefore the permitted period should be shorter. A mechanism is offered (readjustment to social contact) rather than a bare assertion, but the supporting evidence is an analogy from 900-day adult solitary confinement to a 72-hour youth limit — a large scale gap that is not bridged, so the conclusion outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem is that when you have two separate definitions, if a child or young person was placed in secure care at 6 p.m. on the Tuesday, that is day one, so, when counting three days, they need to be out by midnight on the Thursday; in contrast to when counting 72 hours after 6 p.m. on a Tuesday, it is 6 p.m. on a Friday, 18 hours later than when counting three days.
rigor.explanation: A worked deduction whose conclusion follows from its stated premise. Given day-of-placement counting, 6 p.m. Tuesday to midnight Thursday is three days, and 72 hours from 6 p.m. Tuesday is 6 p.m. Friday — 18 hours later, exactly as claimed. The arithmetic is correct and it supports the conclusion that the three-day formulation is the shorter of the two. No fallacy; short of 1.0 only because the day-one counting convention is assumed rather than sourced.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So this picture of sitting in a cell, with the door locked, dark and dank, and not being able to leave their room, and have no contact with people for three days, is absolutely untrue and overexaggerated.
civility.explanation: A forceful rebuttal aimed entirely at the characterisation of secure care, not at the member who made it. She disputes the picture as inaccurate rather than imputing bad faith or attacking the member's motives or competence — robust disagreement of the kind the re-anchored scale treats as the standard. Slightly below 1.0 because 'overexaggerated' edges toward suggesting the member overstated deliberately.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And I’ve tried to visit Korowai Manaaki as well but have been denied three times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific factual record: three refused requests by the member to visit the Korowai Manaaki youth justice residence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki records / OIA response or ministerial answer on requests by Tamatha Paul to visit Korowai Manaaki before 8 October 2025; true if three or more such requests were declined, false if fewer or none were declined.

veracity.statement: Because one of the core recommendations from the abuse in State care report Whanaketia was the institutionalisation of those residences or programmes and how that could lead to a lifetime of staying in institutions, whether those be in mental hospitals or in prison.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Royal Commission's Whanaketia report identified as a core concern: institutionalisation of residences and its link to lifelong institutional pathways into mental health facilities and prison.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care report 'Whanaketia — Through pain and trauma, from darkness to light' (2024); true if institutionalisation of residential settings and the pathway from care into psychiatric or penal institutions appears among its central findings/recommendations, false if the report does not treat this as a core issue.

specificity.statement: So my questions are around the use of force, and I’m going to be talking specifically to our Amendment Paper No. 366, and this is an amendment that looks to remove all provisions for the use of force against youth justice residents.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact instrument (Amendment Paper No. 366) and states precisely what it would do — remove all use-of-force provisions for youth justice residents. Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In prisons, when there is a use of force, the best practice is that there’ll be a bit of a multidisciplinary team that come together. They look at the body camera footage, they look at the CCTV footage and they ask themselves, did we have to use force?
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete comparator process — a multidisciplinary post-incident review using body camera and CCTV footage — though without naming the Corrections policy or any figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my questions are around the use of force, and I’m going to be talking specifically to our Amendment Paper No. 366, and this is an amendment that looks to remove all provisions for the use of force against youth justice residents.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the measure before the committee; names a specific amendment and its mechanism, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And that means that there is better practice because people are more aware of the different tools that they can utilise before resorting to force.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: post-incident review raises staff awareness of alternatives, therefore practice improves. The mechanism is plausible but the causal step is asserted rather than evidenced — no outcome data or evaluation is offered to connect review processes to reduced force.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But how do you make sure that that’s not just institutionalising an entire generation of young people where it becomes normalised to them to have force used against them by people in authoritative positions in their lives?
civility.explanation: A hard challenge on a genuinely contested question — she could readily have imputed bad faith to the Minister — but it goes entirely to the effect of the policy and attacks no one personally.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The other issue is that secure care is also tied to very broad discretion in terms of when that can occur, and just looking at the scope of searches that can be done under these provisions as well, it is quite considerable.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure before the House — the breadth of discretion and the scope of the search powers in the bill. No party framing at all. Specificity is deliberately not scored high here; the point is directional rather than detailed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it should be appreciated that not everybody can go into youth justice residences and into these State care institutions.
focus.explanation: About the subject matter — access to youth justice residences, which bears on how the House can scrutinise secure care — rather than about the other party. It stops short of naming a specific policy, provision or figure, so it does not reach the top of the scale.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So under new section 384A(2) in clause 17(2), search can be any article.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact new section and clause of the bill and the operative scope ('any article'). Anyone could open the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When I was working at YouthLaw Aotearoa, I visited Whakatakapokai, and we used to go in to deliver sessions with educators, and there were times, on multiple occasions, when simple objects would go missing and that would restrict the provision of those legal services to those young people.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real provision: firsthand experience is offered to support the conclusion that a broad 'any article' search power restricts young people's access to services. But it rests on personal anecdote from one residence generalised to the operation of the clause — an appeal to anecdote, and no data or mechanism is offered to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I've just spoken to one of the roles I used to play entering a youth justice residence, and so I have just an observation that I think it would have been useful to consult with some of those entities that are regularly entering youth justice facilities to hear their views on the pat-down searches.
civility.explanation: A direct criticism of the Minister's consultation process on a contested amendment, put entirely on the substance. No imputation of bad faith, no jibe at the person. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the explanatory note, it amends the current definition of a “pat down search” in section 384A to ensure that it covers not only the youth justice resident but those who enter a youth justice residence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Minister's Amendment Paper 354 does: extends the existing statutory definition of 'pat down search' in section 384A so that it applies to persons entering a youth justice residence, not only to residents themselves.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text and explanatory note of Amendment Paper 354 to the youth justice bill amending clause 17, read against section 384A of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. True if the amendment extends the pat-down search definition to persons entering a youth justice residence; false if it does not, or if it alters section 384A in some other way.

veracity.statement: A first question here would be what advice did the Minister seek regarding how the use of force is consistent with the royal commission's findings and recommendations that found that laws and regulations surrounding the use of force were often ignored when they were in place, and, in reality, legitimised the use of force, leading to severe harm, abuse, and trauma in far too many cases.
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual assertion about what the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found: that rules governing use of force in State care were frequently ignored, and that where in place they served to legitimise force, resulting in severe harm, abuse and trauma in many cases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care (Whanaketia, 2024) and its findings/recommendations on use of force, restraint and seclusion in State care institutions. True if the report makes findings that use-of-force rules were routinely disregarded and/or operated to legitimise force causing severe harm; false if the report contains no such findings or characterises use-of-force regulation differently.

rigor.statement: The existing time limit applies to the period before approval must be sought from the court for an extension. Reducing the period to three hours is not a practical time frame in which a court decision can be sought.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the amendment: the premise (the limit is a window before court approval must be sought) supports the conclusion (three hours is impractical for obtaining a court decision). The gap is that no evidence is offered on how long court approval actually takes, so the practicality claim rests on assertion rather than data.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would say, without this provision to use force in the context of a search on entry, Oranga Tamariki would have no authority to touch the child or young person who is not cooperating—for example, even to just guide them to a scanner.
rigor.explanation: An argument from consequence against removing the force provision, with a concrete illustration (guiding a young person to a scanner). It reasons validly from the premise that the provision is the only source of the authority, but that premise is asserted rather than shown — other statutory or common-law bases for minimal physical guidance are not addressed, leaving a gap between what is offered and the absolute 'no authority' conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We allow adults to make those choices, but, in this situation, we’re kind of clamping down really hard—so you’ve got a child who’s coming in and they’re just stripped of all these things that have been used probably for comfort, etc., and they’re in an extremely challenging situation.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument about the harmful-item schedule, reasoning by analogy from adult autonomy over tobacco and vaping to the treatment of young people entering a residence. The analogy has a real gap she does not close: the comparison class differs materially (detained minors in a custodial setting versus adults at liberty), so the conclusion about proportionality is weaker than the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The existing time limit applies to the period before approval must be sought from the court for an extension. Reducing the period to three hours is not a practical time frame in which a court decision can be sought.
focus.explanation: Engages the named Amendment Paper, the clause it amends and the specific mechanism (the secure-care time limit and the court-extension process). No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m just asking, in this situation, why has this been prohibited in this way rather than some sort of proportional assessment at the time, or is that built in?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the drafting of the harmful-item prohibition in clause 17 and whether a proportionality test is available. No party framing or characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would say that this bill is clear that the scanner search images must be disposed of within 24 hours, meaning that they can be disposed of sooner if necessary.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism and a hard timeframe (disposal of scanner images within 24 hours) that anyone could check against the bill text or act on. Falls short of 1.0 only because no figure is attached to the 'sooner if necessary' discretion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I wanted to ask the Minister to explain the process around how that decision would be made given what I have suggested, which is that we’ve got a fairly spare, a minimal principle of harm in the first clause.
specificity.explanation: Points at an identified mechanism — the regulation-making power to declare further harmful items, and the thinness of the harm test it would be applied against. Concrete enough to be answered, but carries no figures, no proposed threshold and no alternative wording, so it stops at a direction rather than a checkable proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Privacy Commissioner in his submission on this bill found the restriction on the retention of images was generally appropriate, so we won’t be supporting that amendment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Privacy Commissioner's written submission on this bill contained a finding that the image-retention restriction was generally appropriate. The check is on what the submission actually says, not on whether the restriction is in fact appropriate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privacy Commissioner's written submission to the select committee on this Oranga Tamariki amendment bill (published on the Parliament bill page / OPC website). True if the submission states that the restriction on retention of scanner images is generally appropriate or equivalent; false if it raises objections to that restriction, is silent on it, or recommends tightening it.

civility.statement: I can certainly understand the thought behind this amendment.
civility.explanation: Responding to an opposition amendment on a contested youth justice bill — a real opportunity to impute bad faith or sneer. Instead she credits the intent behind it before explaining her disagreement on practical grounds. Attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just in regard to the questions that have just been asked around harmful items: the harmful items are the same as the list in the Corrections Act, for starters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the harmful-items list under this bill is the same as the list in the Corrections Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The harmful/unauthorised items list in the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Abuse in Care and Other Matters) Amendment Bill and its draft regulations, compared with the unauthorised-items provisions of the Corrections Act 2004; true if the items are drawn from the same list, false if the bill's list covers materially different items.

veracity.statement: Standard operating procedure is that physical intervention can only be used when verbal de-escalation techniques have failed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current content of Oranga Tamariki's standard operating procedure on physical intervention in youth justice residences.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki's published standard operating procedure / practice guidance on physical restraint in youth justice residences; true if it states physical intervention may be used only after verbal de-escalation has been attempted and failed, false if it permits it on other grounds.

veracity.statement: This bill’s not changing the existing time limits for secure care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill leaves the existing statutory maximum periods for secure care unamended.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill as reported back from select committee, compared with the secure-care provisions of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989; true if no clause amends the maximum permitted periods in secure care, false if any clause alters them.

veracity.statement: The Whanaketia report shows very clearly that they were not exaggerations; they were the horror that people lived through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whanaketia report documents that descriptions such as 'dark and dank' were accurate accounts of conditions in State care rather than exaggerations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whanaketia – Through pain and trauma, from darkness to light, the final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care (July 2024); true if it records first-hand survivor accounts of residence conditions matching such descriptions, false if it does not or if it characterises them as overstated.

specificity.statement: The bill was also amended at select committee stage to include guiding criteria for this legislation-making power. This will require the Minister for Children to consult with the Minister of Justice and be satisfied on reasonable grounds that the harm that could be caused by the items justifies it being added to the list or even removed from the list if requested.
specificity.explanation: Names the stage of amendment, the two Ministers involved and the statutory test ('satisfied on reasonable grounds') that must be met; a reader could go to the bill and check the mechanism. Falls short of 1.0 only because no timeframe or threshold of harm is quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, now, staff are trained in verbal de-escalation with restorative practice in addition to proactive prevention of events like fights. After the use of force, it will be reviewed by a team leader. It will also have a process to escalate internally to the Oranga Tamariki escalation team where any concerns about the appropriateness of the use of force can be investigated.
specificity.explanation: Names the training content (verbal de-escalation, restorative practice), the reviewer (team leader) and the named escalation body. Missing the how-many, the by-when and any completion figures for the training programme.
specificity.subject: speaker
