focus.explanation: Names three parties and nothing else — no clause, figure, mechanism or outcome. Interjected into a clause-by-clause debate on evidential thresholds, it engages none of it. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Much money has been spent and the predictions are that we have another 20 or 30 years of litigation, and so there are many elements of this legislation that need further work.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that applications and litigation under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act will still be running two to three decades from 2025.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: High Court and Ministry of Justice records of undetermined Takutai Moana applications. True if customary marine title applications or appeals under the Act remain before the courts in 2045; false if all applications have been finally determined or the pathway has been closed by then.

focus.statement: I want to ask the Minister this: why will he not exclude the case of Ruapuke Island from the further customary marine title amendments?
focus.explanation: Names a specific case (Ruapuke Island) and a specific legislative mechanism (the customary marine title amendments) and asks the Minister to engage with it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are a number of questions there, but in terms of where the date of taking effect came from—and this is in relation to the date that we had in June last year—I mean, in essence, the goal was to ensure that we had as much consistency with the rest of the vast majority of cases that haven't yet come forward, to have a consistent test, but to recognise that those that had been concluded and granted before the date, we didn't want to unscramble.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the transitional provision — where the commencement date came from and what it is meant to achieve. No reference to the other party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Ngāi Tahu have suffered at the hands of colonisation and have been dispossessed of their lands in Te Waipounamu for many generations, and Ruapuke Island is no exception.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as historical fact that Ngāi Tahu were dispossessed of land in the South Island over many generations, and that Ruapuke Island falls within that pattern.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's Ngāi Tahu Report (1991) and the Crown apology in the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998; true if those records find extensive Crown-caused dispossession of Ngāi Tahu land in Te Waipounamu, false if they find no such dispossession. The Ruapuke Island element is checkable against the Tribunal's and settlement record for that island specifically.

veracity.statement: I want to underscore this point to you: that decision found from the expert evidence that the applicant group had held this specified area in accordance with tikanga and that they had whakapapa connections to that area, but they also had exercise control in that area through mahinga kai, through kaitiakitanga, through rāhui that they exercised, and through protection of biodiversity—regular use, physical use, use in a customary sense, use of land rights, and the use of British land rights, and that is something which meets all of the tests which the Minister has talked about today.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: (a) that the High Court decision on Ruapuke Island made specified findings on expert evidence — holding in accordance with tikanga, whakapapa connection, and exercise of control through mahinga kai, kaitiakitanga, rāhui and protection of biodiversity; and (b) that those findings satisfy the tests the Minister has described in the amendments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The High Court judgment on the Ruapuke Island customary marine title application: true if the judgment records findings of holding in accordance with tikanga, whakapapa connection, and exercise of control by those named means; false if it made no such findings. Element (b) is checkable against the text of the amended test in the Bill as reported — true if each element of the new test maps onto a finding in the judgment, false if the new test adds a requirement the judgment did not address.

rigor.statement: I want to underscore this point to you: that decision found from the expert evidence that the applicant group had held this specified area in accordance with tikanga and that they had whakapapa connections to that area, but they also had exercise control in that area through mahinga kai, through kaitiakitanga, through rāhui that they exercised, and through protection of biodiversity—regular use, physical use, use in a customary sense, use of land rights, and the use of British land rights, and that is something which meets all of the tests which the Minister has talked about today.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: the decision's specific findings are listed, then mapped onto the amended test to conclude the title would be granted again anyway. The listed findings do support the tikanga and connection limbs, but the conclusion that it 'meets all of the tests' is asserted rather than walked through limb by limb — a gap between the evidence offered and the sweeping conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Given that there are a limited number of cases that fall in here, what is the massive policy objection to saying “Well, you got in under the law as it was”, which is how it works, we generally like to think that this is the concept of the rule of law; the Minister may not be familiar with it, but the idea is that you apply the law as it stands and you don’t pull the legal rug from under people and change legal history, but that seems to be exactly what’s going on here.
rigor.explanation: The inference stands on its own and does not rest on the jibe: few cases fall in the affected band, and the rule of law implies applying the law as it stood when the claim was made, so the retrospective voiding needs a justification proportionate to the small benefit. The gap is that 'limited number of cases' is asserted, not quantified, so the cost-benefit step is unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are a number of questions there, but in terms of where the date of taking effect came from—and this is in relation to the date that we had in June last year—I mean, in essence, the goal was to ensure that we had as much consistency with the rest of the vast majority of cases that haven't yet come forward, to have a consistent test, but to recognise that those that had been concluded and granted before the date, we didn't want to unscramble.
rigor.explanation: Offers a genuine rationale — consistency of test across the bulk of undetermined cases, balanced against not unscrambling concluded grants. But the conclusion does not reach the objection actually put: it explains why a cut-off exists without explaining why decisions made after the announcement and before enactment should be treated as never having had legal effect. The premise supports having a date, not this date.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why must they go back—using taxpayers’ money, the $15 million, or a portion of that—to be reheard?
specificity.explanation: Carries one checkable figure ($15 million) and a concrete consequence (a rehearing of an already-decided application), but hedges the amount ('or a portion of that') and gives no timeframe or breakdown of the cost.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of having to go back to the start, no, it's not our expectation that the cases that have been heard have to go right back to day one and start the whole process again, merely that they would presumably need to reconsider or hear any extra evidence that's required in relation to the amended test or the clarified test.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete outcome — cases already heard would not restart, only additional evidence for the amended test would be required — which is checkable against how the courts then proceed. But 'presumably' and 'any extra evidence that's required' leave the actual scope of rehearing undefined, with no timeframe or cost.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: My friend and colleague Arena Williams just went through a particular claim that has been decided but will have to be relitigated, which raises the transitional provisions.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the already-decided Ruapuke Island customary marine title claim will have to be litigated again once the transitional provisions in new Schedule 1AA take effect.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Court records for the Ruapuke Island customary marine title application after enactment: true if the application must be reheard or redetermined under the amended test, false if the existing High Court order stands undisturbed (including if the Bill is amended to carve it out or does not pass).

civility.statement: Given that there are a limited number of cases that fall in here, what is the massive policy objection to saying “Well, you got in under the law as it was”, which is how it works, we generally like to think that this is the concept of the rule of law; the Minister may not be familiar with it, but the idea is that you apply the law as it stands and you don’t pull the legal rug from under people and change legal history, but that seems to be exactly what’s going on here.
civility.explanation: 'the Minister may not be familiar with it' is a sneering aside about the Minister's grasp of the rule of law — condescension aimed at the person rather than the provision. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the man, not the clause.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In terms of having to go back to the start, no, it's not our expectation that the cases that have been heard have to go right back to day one and start the whole process again, merely that they would presumably need to reconsider or hear any extra evidence that's required in relation to the amended test or the clarified test.
civility.explanation: Answers a hostile line of questioning, including a jibe about his familiarity with the rule of law, entirely on the substance of the transitional provision. No retaliation, no imputation of motive.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Part 1 of the bill holds the real meatiness around what the meaning of “exclusive use and occupation” is, as well as the meaning of “substantial interruption”, and that’s included in new sections 57A and 57B, inserted by clause 7.
specificity.explanation: Names the part of the bill, the two defined terms at issue, the two new sections and the inserting clause — anyone could open the bill and check the reference. Falls short of 1.0 only because it locates the issue rather than quantifying anything.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And I want to speak to this particular one, the Amendment Paper under the name of my colleague Arena Williams, which looks towards the deletion of the words “and occupation”, and it is in there, clause 10(2)(b), “had exclusive use and occupation of the specified area from the start to the end of the applicable period”.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the Amendment Paper, its sponsor, the exact words proposed for deletion and the subclause, and quotes the provision. Fully actionable — the Minister can answer it without asking what is meant.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So if you have, I don’t know, dragon boats going up and down for a dragon boat festival; entirely unrelated to tikanga but it is wholly or partly in the area, by a person or persons who don’t belong to the group, and it is a lawful activity.
specificity.explanation: A concrete worked example mapped element-by-element onto the limbs of the statutory test, so the Minister can answer it directly. Short of the top because it is a hypothetical rather than a figure, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The supplementary analysis came after Cabinet had actually taken the decision to proceed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a sequencing fact about the bill's regulatory impact analysis: that the supplementary analysis was produced only after Cabinet had already resolved to proceed, rather than informing that decision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Regulatory Impact Statement / supplementary analysis report for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill and the dates on the associated Cabinet papers and minutes. True if the supplementary analysis is dated after the Cabinet decision to proceed; false if it was before Cabinet ahead of that decision.

veracity.statement: I'm not too sure if the Minister knows this—how toheroa spat works—but you might find the toheroa on the beach or closer to the waterline, but actually, the spat finds itself in the sand dunes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about toheroa biology: that while adult toheroa are found on the beach near the waterline, the spat (juvenile settling stage) is found in the sand dunes rather than in the intertidal zone.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published toheroa (Paphies ventricosa) biology from NIWA, MPI, DOC or peer-reviewed marine ecology literature on where spat settle. True if spat are documented occurring in dune sand landward of the waterline; false if settlement is documented only in the intertidal or surf zone.

focus.statement: The concern that I have is that for substantial definitions such as the meaning of “exclusive use and occupation”, it appears, from looking through the regulatory impact statement, that the ability for substantive analysis was completely restrained.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: a named definition in the bill and a named document assessing it. This is exactly the scrutiny an opposition member is there to do — no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s quite conceivable that there are customary rights which occur only once every few months or only once a year or conceivably once a generation, or even longer than that, but that doesn’t make them any less customary rights.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of new section 57B(c) and how the 'substantial interruption' test would operate. No party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because it’s looking like all arrows are pointing towards this being simply a provision within the coalition agreement that was enacted without proper due analysis.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: from the enumerated gaps she has just listed (no regulatory impact analysis before the Cabinet decision, no financial forecasting, consultation as short as a couple of weeks) she concludes the analysis was inadequate. That part tracks the evidence. The added conclusion about motive — that it is 'simply a provision within the coalition agreement' — is a further step the listed evidence does not establish, so short of the top.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s quite conceivable that there are customary rights which occur only once every few months or only once a year or conceivably once a generation, or even longer than that, but that doesn’t make them any less customary rights.
rigor.explanation: The inference — that infrequency of exercise does not extinguish a right's customary character, so a test keyed to interruption by other lawful activity may misfire — follows from the statutory language he has just quoted. Marked down because the key premise, that frequency is irrelevant to the legal character of the right, is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because it’s looking like all arrows are pointing towards this being simply a provision within the coalition agreement that was enacted without proper due analysis.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism, but aimed at the process and the decision rather than at the Minister as a person. It edges toward imputing that the legislation was driven by a coalition deal instead of analysis, which is what keeps it below the standard 1.0.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just in relation to the question, I'm not of a mind to support the Amendment Paper that the member refers to.
civility.explanation: Declines an opposition amendment on a bitterly contested bill without any dig at the member who moved it or the one who raised it. The expected standard, met.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But it does not mean interruptions caused by confiscation of adjacent land by the Crown; it does not mean legislation, including the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004; it does not mean the Crown's policies that prevented or restricted Māori access; it does not mean interruptions caused by the establishment of ports, harbours, or other infrastructure without the group's consent; and it does not mean commercial activities licensed by the Crown.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates five named, checkable carve-outs and cites a specific statute (Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004). Someone drafting or applying the clause could act on this directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Amendment Paper—and I mentioned the use of occupation amendment, there's another Amendment Paper in my colleague Arena Williams’ name which refers directly to Part 1, clause 7, and it looks towards the removal of, under Part 1, clause 7 new 57B: replace every instance of “and occupation” with “stewardship”.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact provision (Part 1, clause 7, new section 57B) and the exact textual change proposed — replacing 'and occupation' with 'stewardship'. Precisely checkable against the Amendment Paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to ask him first in respect of his change to the interim period, which at new clause 4 in new Schedule 1AA says, “Certain CMT [customary marine title] decisions made in interim period,”—so say, Ruapuke—“and related agreements and orders made, have no legal effect and never have had legal effect”; what does that mean for the cases where other decisions have been made in reliance upon them, and has the Minister had advice about what decisions may have been made in reliance upon them?
specificity.explanation: Names the Amendment Paper, the page, the new clause and schedule, quotes the operative words, and identifies a specific affected case (Ruapuke Island). A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer — the Minister could not mistake what is being asked.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But it does not mean interruptions caused by confiscation of adjacent land by the Crown; it does not mean legislation, including the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004; it does not mean the Crown's policies that prevented or restricted Māori access; it does not mean interruptions caused by the establishment of ports, harbours, or other infrastructure without the group's consent; and it does not mean commercial activities licensed by the Crown.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the measure before the House — what does and does not constitute substantial interruption under his tabled amendment No. 8. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A marine farm should not be a thing that interrupts customary title. It is a commercial activity that may be permitted and may be consistent with it so long as it is by the consent of the iwi, but it is not an interruption.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the Minister's stated mischief and a specific factual scenario under the clause. On-policy throughout, notwithstanding the weak inference.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d just invite people to imagine that if you have customary marine title in a spot where a port is and the ability to pass resource consents or not, then I think most New Zealanders could understand the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country, and so I won’t be supporting that.
focus.explanation: Squarely addresses Abel's tabled amendment and the operational mechanism it would affect. No party framing; the weakness is in the inference, not the subject matter.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So any arrangements that have been entered into would have been done in the knowledge that there was a risk that this legislation would pass and that the legislation would require those examples to be heard again under the new test, so I think everybody would have gone into it with eyes wide open.
focus.explanation: Engages the transitional-provisions question about the interim period rather than the questioner's party. On-policy, even though the reasoning does not carry the conclusion.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Amendment Paper—and I mentioned the use of occupation amendment, there's another Amendment Paper in my colleague Arena Williams’ name which refers directly to Part 1, clause 7, and it looks towards the removal of, under Part 1, clause 7 new 57B: replace every instance of “and occupation” with “stewardship”.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the drafting of the measure before the committee. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to ask him first in respect of his change to the interim period, which at new clause 4 in new Schedule 1AA says, “Certain CMT [customary marine title] decisions made in interim period,”—so say, Ruapuke—“and related agreements and orders made, have no legal effect and never have had legal effect”; what does that mean for the cases where other decisions have been made in reliance upon them, and has the Minister had advice about what decisions may have been made in reliance upon them?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named transitional provision and its consequences for identified cases. Names the policy, the clause and the outcome at issue; contains no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A marine farm should not be a thing that interrupts customary title. It is a commercial activity that may be permitted and may be consistent with it so long as it is by the consent of the iwi, but it is not an interruption.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion largely restates the premise — near-circular. The reason offered ('may be permitted... so long as it is by the consent of the iwi') only covers the consented case, which is precisely the case not in dispute; it does nothing to show that a marine farm established without consent is not an interruption, which is the Minister's actual example.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’d just invite people to imagine that if you have customary marine title in a spot where a port is and the ability to pass resource consents or not, then I think most New Zealanders could understand the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country, and so I won’t be supporting that.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an appeal to popularity and self-evidence — 'most New Zealanders could understand' — in place of an argument. The mechanism (CMT holders' role in resource consents) is gestured at but never connected to a stated consequence; the difficulty is asserted as obvious rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So any arrangements that have been entered into would have been done in the knowledge that there was a risk that this legislation would pass and that the legislation would require those examples to be heard again under the new test, so I think everybody would have gone into it with eyes wide open.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur between the premise and the conclusion. That a risk was signalled does not establish that every affected party — councils, landowners, whānau who entered relationship agreements — had that knowledge, and 'eyes wide open' converts a general public signal into imputed universal awareness. It also concludes nothing about the legal-effect question actually put, which was what happens to decisions made in reliance.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just in relation to that question, when this policy to overturn the Court of Appeal decision was announced originally in July 2024, the Government signalled, of course, right at that point that we would seek to have the legislation take effect from that point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about the past: that the policy to overturn the Court of Appeal's Re Edwards decision was announced in July 2024, and that the announcement at that time signalled the legislation would take effect from the announcement date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet paper and Minister's/Government press release announcing the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill in 2024, plus the bill as introduced. True if a public announcement was made in July 2024 and that announcement (or accompanying Cabinet material) stated the new test would apply from the date of announcement to undetermined applications; false if the announcement fell outside July 2024 or if the retrospective application date was first signalled later.

rigor.statement: It stipulates that applicants must prove that they have had exclusive use and occupation over the land since the application period without substantial interruption, right, since “substantial interruption” can include an extinguishment of title. So the new section 106(2), in effect, mandates that the applicants prove that their customary interests have never been extinguished, as to amount to a substantial interruption; therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
rigor.explanation: A real inference chain: from the wording of new s 106(2), to what 'substantial interruption' encompasses, to the conclusion that the presumption is practically reversed. The conclusion follows if the premise about what counts as a substantial interruption holds; the small gap is that this premise is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So is this, you know, his own idea or is this his officials? Because I’m pretty sure that a good parliamentary counsel—and we have excellent parliamentary counsel in this Parliament—would not have advised this messy, duplicate, verbose, and largely redundant drafting.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to authority: the conclusion that the drafting is defective rests on what a hypothetical 'good parliamentary counsel' would have advised, rather than on the textual reasons he gave elsewhere. The point is reasonable but the inference here leans on the appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It stipulates that applicants must prove that they have had exclusive use and occupation over the land since the application period without substantial interruption, right, since “substantial interruption” can include an extinguishment of title. So the new section 106(2), in effect, mandates that the applicants prove that their customary interests have never been extinguished, as to amount to a substantial interruption; therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the committee — a named clause and its operative effect. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It asks a very specific question about the announcement that the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations made with respect to the moves that he’s making to amend this particular legislation through this bill, which is that at the end of the Schedule, inserting New Schedule 1AA, it does say in there at new clause 6, “No entitlement to compensation”, “A person is not entitled to compensation of any kind on account of the operation of the CMT amendments.”, which begs the question, once again: does that only apply to the ones that are listed here?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named provision — asks who the compensation bar actually covers given the listed cases. Names the schedule, the clause and the issue; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It stipulates that applicants must prove that they have had exclusive use and occupation over the land since the application period without substantial interruption, right, since “substantial interruption” can include an extinguishment of title. So the new section 106(2), in effect, mandates that the applicants prove that their customary interests have never been extinguished, as to amount to a substantial interruption; therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the subsection, the statutory test and the precise mechanism by which the burden shifts. Anyone could go to the amendment paper and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It asks a very specific question about the announcement that the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations made with respect to the moves that he’s making to amend this particular legislation through this bill, which is that at the end of the Schedule, inserting New Schedule 1AA, it does say in there at new clause 6, “No entitlement to compensation”, “A person is not entitled to compensation of any kind on account of the operation of the CMT amendments.”, which begs the question, once again: does that only apply to the ones that are listed here?
specificity.explanation: Cites the new schedule, the clause number and the operative words, and puts a precise question about their scope. Checkable against the amendment paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Also, to the announcement that the Minister said they are setting aside $15 million—to do exactly what?
specificity.explanation: Attaches a concrete figure and a named announcement, but the question itself asks for the detail rather than supplying it — no mechanism, recipients or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But my question here is, where you see examples in legislation, it’s a kind of interpretive convention that examples are not the rules themselves.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a general fact about New Zealand statutory interpretation: that material presented as an 'example' in an Act does not itself carry operative force, and is read as illustrating the provision rather than constituting it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislation Act 2019 s 13 (examples in legislation) and Parliamentary Counsel Office drafting guidance: true if examples are stated not to limit the provision they illustrate and the provision prevails where the two are inconsistent; false if examples are given the same operative force as the provision itself.

civility.statement: So is this, you know, his own idea or is this his officials? Because I’m pretty sure that a good parliamentary counsel—and we have excellent parliamentary counsel in this Parliament—would not have advised this messy, duplicate, verbose, and largely redundant drafting.
civility.explanation: Robust and pointed. The harsh words ('messy, duplicate, verbose, redundant') are aimed at the drafting, which is fair game, but the rhetorical question about whose idea it was edges toward implying the Minister personally overrode expert advice. It stops short of landing on him as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we are to have a seriously plural legal system, one that takes account of the fact that we have, over the course of time and jurisprudence, got a blending of tikanga and common law as the foundation of our legal system in this country, then we need to enshrine and recognise that tikanga has, at least, the same standing as common law, and that it must not meet the test of common law.
rigor.explanation: A conditional argument: given the stated goal of a plural legal system and the premise that tikanga and common law are already blended in NZ jurisprudence, the conclusion that tikanga should not be tested against common law standards does follow. The gap is that the premise of an existing 'blending' is asserted rather than shown, and 'plural legal system' does the work of a premise as well as a goal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It seeks not to take away rights—nobody will wake up tomorrow with less ability to enjoy the coastal area or have a connection with it.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation on 'rights'. The objection was about customary marine title held by successful applicants — a property interest — and the rebuttal offers evidence about a different thing, the general public's ability to enjoy and connect with the coast. The conclusion that no rights are taken away does not follow from the premise supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The name is reflective of what it’s going to do, because the thresholds being set and the hoops that our people will need to jump through, effectively, sees the raupatu of our customary Māori rights to the takutai moana.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered — the thresholds and procedural burden — but the step from 'harder to meet' to raupatu (confiscation) is not made out; procedural difficulty and extinguishment are different things, and nothing connects them here. A real inference about the measure, and a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It requires the court to recognise tikanga as evidence and sets out the nature and forms of the evidence that may take.
specificity.explanation: Names the actor (the court) and the mechanism (a statutory evidential requirement) but conveys no threshold, test or operative wording in this sentence — a direction with detail missing, sitting mid-scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It does not break any deals; it is set out in its goal to find that balance between enabling Māori to establish customary marine rights and title, while also recognising the wide interests that all New Zealanders have in the marine and coastal space.
specificity.explanation: States a goal in the language of 'balance' and 'wide interests' with no threshold, figure, clause or mechanism — a direction rather than checkable content, though it is not a bare slogan.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Wairarapa have customary marine title (CMT) granted in interim judgment in December 2024.
specificity.explanation: Names the applicant group, the exact legal instrument (interim judgment), the relief granted (CMT) and the month and year. Someone could go and check it against the judgment record.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The law has been changed not just to make it harder for future litigants, but to strip people who have had their day in court and won their case.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the amendment operates retrospectively on applicants who have already obtained a favourable customary marine title determination, not merely prospectively on future applications.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill as at 14 October 2025 — specifically its application, transitional and commencement provisions. True if the Bill applies the new test to applications in which the High Court has already issued a judgment granting CMT (including interim judgments); false if it applies only to applications not yet heard or determined.

veracity.statement: Wairarapa have customary marine title (CMT) granted in interim judgment in December 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the High Court issued an interim judgment granting customary marine title to the Wairarapa applicant group in December 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court judgment records under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 for the Wairarapa CMT applications. True if an interim judgment granting CMT to Wairarapa applicants was issued in December 2024; false if no such judgment exists, if it was issued in a materially different month/year, or if it declined CMT.

civility.statement: That is the kind of behaviour you’d expect from somewhere with a weak democracy that doesn’t respect the rule of law.
civility.explanation: A severe comparison, but aimed at the Government's legislative conduct rather than at any individual member. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a decision is civil; this edges toward imputing disregard for the rule of law, so it sits just below the standard rather than at it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It does not break any deals; it is set out in its goal to find that balance between enabling Māori to establish customary marine rights and title, while also recognising the wide interests that all New Zealanders have in the marine and coastal space.
civility.explanation: Replies to a sustained and pointed attack ('a shameful day for the rule of law') entirely on the substance of the Bill's purpose, without turning on any member. This is the expected standard, met.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We could, of course, call it the “Hobson’s Pledge Memorial Bill” because that’s really where these politics come from: the politics of attacking Māori simply for looking for the recognition of the rights that they have historically exercised.
focus.explanation: Locates the Bill's origin in a lobby group's politics and characterises the other side's motives rather than engaging the measure. There is a thread of policy content (the recognition of historically exercised rights), but the weight of the sentence is on where 'these politics come from', not on any named provision or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: All of these groups, as well as other whānau, who have very important rights will have their judgments null and void, so they will not be entitled to any compensation for the loss of time, for the loss of opportunity, and for the sweat and tears that they have put into their hearings.
divination.explanation: Forecasts two outcomes once the Bill takes effect: that existing CMT judgments held by the named northern groups cease to have effect, and that no compensation is payable to those applicants for costs, time or opportunity already expended.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act as enacted, plus any accompanying appropriation or ex gratia scheme. True if the enacted Act sets aside or requires redetermination of existing CMT judgments AND provides no compensation or costs recovery to affected applicant groups; false if existing judgments are preserved, or if any compensation, costs or ex gratia payment mechanism for those applicants is established.

specificity.statement: The member did refer to a lot of numbers, and I can assure the member that the Government has received advice and allocated up to $15 million to the rehearing of cases.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure ($15 million) and what it is allocated to (the rehearing of cases), so it is checkable; but no timeframe, appropriation line or breakdown is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what I have done is I have drafted an Amendment Paper, Amendment Paper 388, explicitly modelled after new section 339—the same section around federation polytechnics—that will enable anchor polytechnics to be designated and removed from the designation of anchor polytechnics, using the exact same language and the exact same processes that the Minister has outlined for federations.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (Amendment Paper 388), the model provision (new section 339), and the exact mechanism it would create. Someone could pick it up and check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To ensure that a polytechnic is successful, it must be very engaged with their community, must be very integrated with their community, and must understand their community.
specificity.explanation: Answering a direct question about how Māori will be represented on ITP councils, this offers a string of generic virtues — engaged, integrated, understanding — with no mechanism, threshold, appointment process or figure attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The member did refer to a lot of numbers, and I can assure the member that the Government has received advice and allocated up to $15 million to the rehearing of cases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has received advice and has allocated up to $15 million for the rehearing of cases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Justice / Vote Courts appropriations and Ministry of Justice or Crown Law budget documents for 2025/26; true if an allocation of up to $15 million for the rehearing of cases is recorded, false if no such allocation exists or the amount is materially different.

veracity.statement: However, there is currently no clause that enables anchor polytechnics to be removed from the designation as an anchor polytechnic in this amendment legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill as drafted contains no clause providing for removal of anchor polytechnic designation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill as reported back (clause 22, new sections 315, 337, 338, 339); true if no provision expressly enables removal of anchor polytechnic designation, false if such a provision exists.

veracity.statement: The Minister has publicly stated and pledged to my local polytechnic, the Otago Polytechnic, and also to the Otago Daily Times, that if they meet the road to viability, which they’re on track to do, they will be able to exit the federation and exit their anchor polytechnic status.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister for Vocational Education publicly committed, including to the Otago Daily Times, that Otago Polytechnic will be able to exit both the federation and its anchor polytechnic status if it meets viability requirements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Daily Times reporting and the Minister's public statements/press releases in 2025 on Otago Polytechnic; true if a statement to that effect (exit of both federation and anchor status on meeting viability) is on record, false if no such commitment was made or it was limited to federation membership only.

focus.statement: While we do not support this bill, we do support legislation functioning as intended, and, at the moment, I do believe that there is a glaring omission at the heart of the Minister’s bill—the omission is, as drafted, that there is currently no way for an institution that has been established as an anchor polytechnic to be removed out of its designation; nor is there, arguably, a way for anchor polytechnics to be designated as an anchor polytechnic outside of being established as one from its inception.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanics of the bill before the House — a specific drafting gap in the anchor polytechnic designation provisions. No party framing at all, despite the speaker openly opposing the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m interested, Minister, in understanding how Māori will be represented on the ITP councils.
focus.explanation: A government backbencher putting a substantive question about a named feature of the bill — the appointment and composition of ITP councils. No party content whatever, where a patsy or tribal question was equally available.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would argue that the section is clearly for newly established polytechnics—so if you’re starting a polytech at the start, not intending to designate polytechs that already exist and are currently in existence and have been established.
rigor.explanation: A real textual inference: the section sits under the heading “Establishment of polytechnics”, therefore it applies only to newly established institutions. The inference is legitimate but leans on a heading rather than the operative words, and headings are not conclusive of scope — a genuine gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s no need for us to have that explicit in the legislation; it would be via an Order in Council.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion offered with a reason, but the reason does not reach it: the Order in Council power the member identified sits under “Establishment of polytechnics”, which was precisely the objection. Asserting the mechanism exists without addressing the scope argument leaves a real gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, if a polytechnic was operating in a community which was predominantly Māori, you would expect that polytechnic’s council to be predominantly Māori.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise actually supplied — that councils must reflect the make-up of their community — applied to a specific case. Valid given its assumption; whether the reflection principle is the right one is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I know that this cannot be the Minister’s intention.
civility.explanation: On a bill the speaker has vigorously opposed, he expressly credits the Minister with good intent rather than imputing bad faith. Attacks no one; the disagreement stays on the drafting.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So the anticipation is that there would be a lot more movement of federation polytechnics than there would be of anchor polytechnics.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, once the new system is operating, federation polytechnics will change status considerably more often than anchor polytechnics do.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Gazette notices and Orders in Council recording polytechnic designation changes under the new Part 4 regime between commencement and 31 December 2030; true if more federation polytechnics enter or leave federation status than institutions gain or lose anchor polytechnic status, false if anchor designation changes equal or exceed federation movements.

veracity.statement: Just another reminder to the members in this committee that today marks the 50-year anniversary since our tupuna Dame Whina Cooper led the march from the Far North here to Wellington.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the sitting day (14 October 2025) is exactly 50 years to the day since the Whina Cooper–led land march reached Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary records of the 1975 Māori land march (Te Rōpū o te Matakite) and of its arrival at Parliament: true if the hīkoi led by Dame Whina Cooper reached Parliament on 14 October 1975, i.e. exactly 50 years before the day of this statement; false if the arrival date differs materially from the anniversary claimed.

veracity.statement: Well, I’d like to thank the member for his history lesson, and I’ll give him another date, which is it is now coming up to 21 years since the Labour Government, in 2004, passed the Foreshore and Seabed legislation that took the coastal area for the Crown.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Labour Government enacted the Foreshore and Seabed legislation in 2004 and that it vested the coastal area in the Crown, roughly 21 years before this statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enactment record of the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004: true if it was passed in 2004 under the Fifth Labour Government and vested the public foreshore and seabed in the Crown; false if the year, the responsible government, or the vesting effect is materially different.

veracity.statement: This Act that we’re amending at the moment—the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act—was an agreement between the National Party and the Māori Party in 2011, to come up with a process by which Māori could establish their customary rights to the foreshore and seabed area—a significant advance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the 2011 Act was the product of an agreement between National and the Māori Party and created a process for Māori to establish customary rights.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The passage record of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 and the National–Māori Party relationship/confidence-and-supply agreement of that Parliament: true if the Act was enacted in 2011 with Māori Party support under such an agreement and established a customary rights recognition process; false if the record shows it was not the product of that agreement.

veracity.statement: It certainly moves away from it in so far as it puts the burden of proof on iwi Māori and the onus on iwi Māori, rather than the onus being on the Crown to prove extinguishment, which was clearly articulated by the Minister at the time, Chris Finlayson, in that the onus had to be borne by the Crown to prove extinguishment; not that iwi Māori had to prove customary title.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Chris Finlayson, as the Minister responsible in 2011, stated that the Crown bore the onus of proving extinguishment rather than iwi Māori bearing the onus of proving customary title.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Chris Finlayson's statements during the passage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill in 2011 (Hansard, select committee material, and the Bill's explanatory note): true if he stated the onus of proving extinguishment lay with the Crown; false if the record shows him placing the onus of proof on applicant groups.

veracity.statement: Nobody’s bloody been successful in direct negotiations.
veracity.explanation: An absolute claim that no applicant group has ever succeeded via the Crown's direct-negotiation pathway for recognition of customary marine title. Stated as sarcasm, but it is a checkable factual assertion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti records of the Crown engagement (direct negotiation) pathway under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011: false if any applicant group had obtained a customary marine title recognition agreement or recognition order through direct engagement with the Crown as at October 2025; true if none had.

veracity.statement: I want to call back to what the officials told us in the supplementary analysis report, where Te Arawhiti said in their overall analysis—Te Arawhiti considered this reform was unlikely to address the primary concerns Māori have with the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, as identified through the Waitangi Tribunal 266O inquiry, and any amendments proposed to address the coalition commitments only make it harder under the current law to prove customary marine title.
veracity.explanation: She is relaying, not asserting: the claim is that Te Arawhiti's overall analysis in the supplementary analysis report reached these two conclusions about the reform.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report published with the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill: true if Te Arawhiti's overall analysis states the reform was unlikely to address the primary Māori concerns identified in the Waitangi Tribunal inquiry referred to and that the proposed amendments make customary marine title harder to prove; false if the report's analysis says otherwise or contains no such conclusion.

civility.statement: When I look towards the commencement of this particular bill, let it be another stain on the record of this committee and the treatment of the Māori people.
civility.explanation: A severe moral condemnation of the committee's decision and of the legislation, in a plainly contested debate where he had every opportunity to turn on the Minister or other members. He does not: no individual's character, competence or motives are impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I’d like to thank the member for his history lesson, and I’ll give him another date, which is it is now coming up to 21 years since the Labour Government, in 2004, passed the Foreshore and Seabed legislation that took the coastal area for the Crown.
civility.explanation: "Thank the member for his history lesson" is condescension aimed at the member rather than at his argument — it dismisses the contribution as a lecture instead of engaging it. Mild and conventional, but it lands on the person, so short of the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The “Zombie Foreshore and Seabed Act” could be an appropriate name for it because it has the effect of being a confiscation.
civility.explanation: Derisive in the extreme — but every bit of the derision is aimed at the legislation, not at the Minister or any other member. Fierce criticism of a policy is the civil standard, not a breach of it.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Act that we’re amending at the moment—the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act—was an agreement between the National Party and the Māori Party in 2011, to come up with a process by which Māori could establish their customary rights to the foreshore and seabed area—a significant advance.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the year, the two parties to the agreement and the mechanism it created. Someone could go and check every element of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I propose, as I did in my earlier kauwhau, October 2026 as a commencement date, to allow the system to catch up—allow the system to catch up—unless I’m missing something.
specificity.explanation: A named commencement date and a stated purpose, i.e. an actionable amendment. What "caught up" would consist of, and how it would be measured, is left open.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to call back to what the officials told us in the supplementary analysis report, where Te Arawhiti said in their overall analysis—Te Arawhiti considered this reform was unlikely to address the primary concerns Māori have with the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, as identified through the Waitangi Tribunal 266O inquiry, and any amendments proposed to address the coalition commitments only make it harder under the current law to prove customary marine title.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document, the agency, the inquiry it draws on and the specific finding relied on. A reader could locate and check the passage.

rigor.statement: The Parliament set a high threshold, and that is what this amendment bill is seeking to re-establish, following a couple of court cases that went through.
