veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Budget/health policy record for the prescription co-payment: the date free prescriptions took effect under the Labour Government, and the date the $5 co-payment was reinstated. True if both the Labour attribution and a July 2025 reinstatement date are correct; false if the co-payment was reinstated in a different month or year.

veracity.statement: They have a new code of practice that was introduced in 2016, with updates in 2024, with a real understanding that for the public to trust these institutions, they need to know that they're independent, and they need to trust not only the individuals who are in those roles but the way in which they were appointed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the United Kingdom introduced a new code of practice governing public appointments in 2016 and updated it in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The UK Governance Code on Public Appointments as published by the Cabinet Office / Commissioner for Public Appointments. True if a code was introduced in 2016 and a revised version issued in 2024; false if the introduction or revision dates differ materially, or no such code exists.

rigor.statement: However, there is also the secondary issue which came up in multiple submissions about medicines not being funded by Pharmac, and external providers not seeing that as a viable opportunity. So while this certainly does address one of the issues, it doesn't address the second leg of the issues, and so there's, actually, a big question mark about whether this will go the whole way in resolving the issue of ensuring that there is access to medicines.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: two distinct barriers to access are identified (approval speed, Pharmac funding), the bill is said to address only the first, and the conclusion drawn — that access will not be fully resolved — follows from those premises. No fallacy; the small gap is that the relative weight of the two barriers is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The third reading of this bill continues a long legacy of this House, over many, many years, of treating Māori as second-class citizens.
civility.explanation: Severe criticism of the bill and of the House's collective record over decades. No individual is targeted, no bad faith imputed to a named person — under the re-anchored scale this is the expected standard, and the harshness of the judgement about the measure does not cost anything.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The third reading of this bill continues a long legacy of this House, over many, many years, of treating Māori as second-class citizens.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House — the bill's third reading and the effect he says it has on Māori rights. It names no figure or mechanism, but it is directed at the legislation rather than at the other party's character, so it is on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yet, for whatever reason, this Government continues to say co-governance, co-management, or working alongside Māori, is not the thing to do, and would rather score political points instead of underscoring the good frameworks that are already in place that allow management of places like the marine and takutai moana—in this instance, the Ninety Mile Beach.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — an existing co-management framework for a named stretch of coast, and the Government's stance on co-governance — but a substantial part of the weight is carried by an assertion about the Government's motives rather than by the policy itself.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have an arrangement there to look after the Ninety Mile Beach on behalf of all New Zealanders, which was agreed on by this House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a statutory co-management arrangement for Ninety Mile Beach (Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē), covering the beach on behalf of all New Zealanders, was enacted by Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand statute book for Te Hiku o Te Ika settlement legislation: true if an Act passed by Parliament establishes a board or equivalent body with statutory functions for the management of Ninety Mile Beach / Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē covering public access and use; false if no such statutory arrangement exists or if it was created by something other than an Act of the House (e.g. a council bylaw or a private deed alone).

veracity.statement: They work hard to make sure that they can fix those injustices of the past, and when we became Government in 2017, it was one of the first things the Rt Hon Jacinda Ardern did, in recognising that what Labour had done in 2004 was wrong and unjust.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on taking office in 2017 Jacinda Ardern, among her first acts, publicly acknowledged that Labour's 2004 foreshore and seabed legislation was wrong and unjust.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record (Hansard, Beehive releases, contemporaneous news reports) of statements by Jacinda Ardern in the opening months of the 2017 Labour-led Government: true if she made a public apology or repudiation of the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 early in that term; false if no such statement by her is on record, or if Labour's apology for the 2004 Act was made by a different leader at a materially different time.

specificity.statement: We have an arrangement there to look after the Ninety Mile Beach on behalf of all New Zealanders, which was agreed on by this House.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific place and a specific legislated arrangement, and says who it is for, but gives no mechanism, body, statute name or date — a direction with some detail rather than a checkable account of how the arrangement works.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yet, for whatever reason, this Government continues to say co-governance, co-management, or working alongside Māori, is not the thing to do, and would rather score political points instead of underscoring the good frameworks that are already in place that allow management of places like the marine and takutai moana—in this instance, the Ninety Mile Beach.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, and a weak one. The premise offered is that workable co-management frameworks already exist; the conclusion drawn is that the Government's opposition is motivated by point-scoring. That is an unsupported leap to motive — nothing is offered to rule out a principled disagreement about co-governance, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act was enacted by the National-led Government in 2011 following significant consultation and widespread dissatisfaction with Labour’s earlier Foreshore and Seabed Act.
focus.explanation: Names two specific pieces of legislation and the policy history that motivates the bill. There is party framing ('Labour's earlier'), but it identifies a named Act rather than characterising the other party in general, so it stays on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The current wording of section 58 of the Act plainly states that in addition to holding the specified area in accordance with tikanga, the applicant groups need to have had exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the statutory test in s 58 currently requires — two limbs, a start date of 1840, continuity to the present, and a 'without substantial interruption' qualifier. The word 'plainly' is a gloss; the checkable content is whether those elements appear in the section as enacted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacted text of section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 on the New Zealand Legislation website. True if s 58 requires both (a) holding the area in accordance with tikanga and (b) exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption; false if either limb, the 1840 start date, or the 'without substantial interruption' qualifier is absent from the section.

veracity.statement: Last year’s Supreme Court judgment in Re Edwards confirmed that the earlier judgments, particularly in the Court of Appeal, did not apply the test in line with Parliament’s intent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court's judgment endorsed the proposition that the lower courts, especially the Court of Appeal, had misapplied the statutory test against Parliament's intent. What must be settled is whether the judgment actually found error in the Court of Appeal's application of the test, as opposed to differing on some elements while accepting the overall approach.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court's judgment in Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) on the s 58 customary marine title test. True if the Court held that the Court of Appeal had erred in its application or interpretation of the s 58 test relative to Parliament's intent; false if the Supreme Court upheld the Court of Appeal's approach to the test, or if it corrected only ancillary points and not the application of the test itself.

veracity.statement: However, the Supreme Court’s own interpretation of the test has since been applied in the lower courts, with no apparent change to the outcomes, resulting in extensive awards of customary marine title, including the entire coast from Kāpiti to Manawatū and in southern Wairarapa.
veracity.explanation: Two linked factual assertions: that post-Re Edwards High Court decisions produced outcomes no different from the earlier line of cases, and specifically that CMT was awarded over the entire Kāpiti-to-Manawatū coast and in southern Wairarapa.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court customary marine title judgments issued after the Supreme Court's Re Edwards decision and before 21 October 2025. True if those judgments awarded CMT covering the whole of the coastline between Kāpiti and Manawatū and areas of southern Wairarapa; false if the awards over those coasts were partial, refused, or not yet decided at the date of the statement.

veracity.statement: During readings of this Act in the House back in 2011, the Hon Chris Finlayson and the Hon Tariana Turia both emphasised the Act was intended to recognise customary marine title in specific parts of the coastline. No mention was made of the entire coastlines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both what two named members said in 2011 (that recognition was aimed at specific parts of the coastline) and an absence — that neither contemplated whole coastlines. The absence claim is the harder half to settle and is what makes the pair checkable against the 2011 debates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the 2011 readings of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill. True if the speeches of Chris Finlayson and Tariana Turia describe CMT as applying to particular or specific parts of the coast and contain no statement contemplating recognition over entire coastlines; false if either member described the Act as capable of applying to whole coastlines, or if neither characterised the coverage as specific areas.

veracity.statement: As I’ve said previously, the Government recognised the impact this has had on affected applicants and has provided $15 million to support costs for re-hearings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a $15 million fund for applicants' re-hearing costs has been provided, not merely proposed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government funding announcements, Budget or Cabinet papers relating to the takutai moana re-hearing support fund. True if $15 million was appropriated or committed to support applicants' costs for re-hearings; false if the figure is materially different, or if the money was announced but not provided.

rigor.statement: So our starting proposition is that all New Zealanders—all New Zealanders—have an interest in what happens in the coastal area and usually expect to have a say in things like resource consents. That is why a high hurdle was put in the legislation before moving away from that basic proposition.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: a general public interest in the coastal area is offered as the reason for setting a high statutory threshold before that interest is displaced. The conclusion tracks the premise, but the step from 'everyone has an interest' to 'therefore the threshold must be high' is asserted rather than argued — no account is given of how competing customary interests were weighed against it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: During readings of this Act in the House back in 2011, the Hon Chris Finlayson and the Hon Tariana Turia both emphasised the Act was intended to recognise customary marine title in specific parts of the coastline. No mention was made of the entire coastlines.
rigor.explanation: An argument from silence: because the sponsoring members did not mention entire coastlines in 2011, the current awards are taken to contravene Parliament's intent. Ministerial speeches are not the enacted text, and the absence of a stated scenario in debate is weak evidence that the statutory words exclude it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Retrospective provisions in legislation are reserved for exceptional circumstances and these are exceptional. The current approach to the test by the courts is damaging to the takutai moana process as a whole.
rigor.explanation: The load-bearing premise — that these circumstances are exceptional — is simply asserted after stating the standard it must meet, which is close to circular. The support offered, that the courts' approach is 'damaging to the takutai moana process as a whole', is itself a bare assertion with no evidence of the damage.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Government’s view is that the courts have interpreted the requirements for the test for customary marine title in a way that has materially reduced their intended effect, to the point where it was necessary to take action to ensure the Act operates as originally intended.
civility.explanation: Contested ground — criticising the judiciary in a third reading is a real opportunity to be uncivil — and the criticism lands entirely on the interpretation adopted, not on any judge or member. No imputation of bad faith or incompetence.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Key elements include more tightly defining what “exclusive use and occupation” means, requiring decision makers to base any influences on a firm basis of physical evidence, not just cultural associations in that second part of the test, and thirdly, placing the burden of proof more squarely on applicants to demonstrate that they meet both legs of the test.
specificity.explanation: Three named mechanisms the bill uses — a tightened statutory definition, an evidential requirement of physical evidence over cultural association, and a shifted burden of proof. Concrete enough to check against the bill's clauses, though it gives no clause numbers or thresholds.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The test, as amended by the bill, will apply to all undecided applications from 25 July 2024.
specificity.explanation: A precise scope and a precise date for the bill's retrospective reach; anyone could check it against the bill and act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve said previously, the Government recognised the impact this has had on affected applicants and has provided $15 million to support costs for re-hearings.
specificity.explanation: A named figure attached to a named purpose — funding for re-hearing costs — although no allocation mechanism, per-applicant limit or timeframe is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The sole purpose of these amendments is to ensure that that balance continues to be struck and is an enduring one.
specificity.explanation: A purposive statement carrying no mechanism, figure, threshold or timeframe. 'Balance' and 'enduring' commit to nothing that could be checked or acted on, even though the surrounding speech does supply detail elsewhere.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister is more concerned with giving away seabed rights to Aussie miners and bottom trawlers than with recognising the customary rights of indigenous New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad-faith priorities to the Minister personally — that he cares more about foreign miners than about Māori rights — rather than criticising the bill's effect. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes motive to the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There's no decent future for us as a country if we keep doing shitty legislation like this.
civility.explanation: Coarse and brutal about the legislation, but it attacks no person: no motive imputed, no individual disparaged. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a policy sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Get thee hence, Satan—this is the worst pettiness and nastiness.
civility.explanation: Directed across the Chamber at the bill's promoters, this is mockery imputing bad character, even though he immediately clarifies that the epithet is aimed at the idea rather than the person. A real failure of civility, short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As such, this legislation has—and I said this in the first speech—a treasonous character, because its first service is not to New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: The stated premise (the bill's 'first service is not to New Zealanders') does not support the conclusion that it is 'treasonous', a term with a specific legal meaning involving levying war or aiding an enemy. Non sequitur via a loaded label; no bridging argument offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premises he laid out immediately before: old s 106(3) presumed non-extinguishment; new s 106(2) requires applicants to prove use without substantial interruption; substantial interruption encompasses extinguishment; therefore the presumption is reversed. Valid inference, whatever the accuracy of the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we will be supporting this because it does restore what Parliament intended, it does restore an exacting test, and I commend this bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: The structure is sound — courts departed from the 2011 test, this bill restores it, therefore support it — but the central premise that the bill restores Parliament's original intent is asserted rather than shown. A real gap between what was offered and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Section 106(3) of the MACA Act states that, unless there is evidence to the contrary, non-extinguishment of customary interest will be assumed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of s 106(3) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 — that non-extinguishment of a customary interest is presumed absent proof to the contrary.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of s 106(3) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 as in force on 21 October 2025 (legislation.govt.nz). True if the subsection presumes, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that a customary interest has not been extinguished; false if it says something materially different or does not exist.

veracity.statement: The Minister acknowledged in the Committee of the whole House that he was concerned about the impact on the fishing industry of recognising customary rights.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of record that during the committee of the whole House on this bill, the Minister expressed concern about the effect of recognising customary rights on the fishing industry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of the committee of the whole House stage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill. True if the Minister states a concern about the fishing industry's exposure to recognised customary rights; false if no such statement appears in that stage.

veracity.statement: It is a thing that is recognised in other colonised lands that don't have treaties, such as Australia, and it was recognised from even the earliest days of Government in this country.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that native/customary title is legally recognised in Australia despite the absence of a treaty, and that customary title was recognised in New Zealand law from the earliest colonial governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: For Australia: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) 175 CLR 1 and the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) — true if native title is recognised at common law/statute without any treaty. For New Zealand: early colonial authority such as R v Symonds (1847) and the Native Lands Act 1865 — true if customary title was legally recognised then. False if either limb is unsupported.

veracity.statement: This bill fulfils a specific coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement contains a commitment that this amendment bill implements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–New Zealand First coalition agreement of November 2023 (published text). True if it contains a commitment to amend the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 to restore or clarify the customary marine title test; false if no such clause appears.

veracity.statement: I think we go back to when the first claims were lodged under this Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, that every single centimetre of our coastline was subject to a claim.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the applications lodged under the MACA Act covered the entirety of New Zealand's coastline, with no stretch unclaimed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The register of applications lodged under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 by the 3 April 2017 deadline (Te Arawhiti / Ministry of Justice records of High Court applications and Crown engagement applications), mapped against the New Zealand coastline. True if the applications collectively cover effectively the whole coastline; false if material stretches were never subject to any application.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister of the time, John Key, made it very clear that there would be very limited numbers of successful claims because of the need to prove uninterrupted title for the duration since 1840.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of record that John Key, as Prime Minister during the 2011 passage of the MACA Act, publicly said successful customary marine title claims would be very limited because of the continuous-title-since-1840 requirement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and contemporaneous press statements/interviews by John Key during the 2010–2011 passage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill. True if he stated that successful claims would be very few owing to the test of exclusive use and occupation since 1840 without substantial interruption; false if no such statement is on record.

specificity.statement: The new section 106(2) now stipulates that applicants must prove that they have exclusive use and occupation over the land since the applicable period, without substantial interruption.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision and states the precise legal test it imposes — exclusive use and occupation, since the applicable period, without substantial interruption. Directly checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That has, unfortunately, been undermined by a number of court decisions, including, obviously, the Edwards decision.
specificity.explanation: Names one decision (Edwards) but leaves the rest as 'a number of court decisions', with no account of what those decisions held or how the test was changed. A direction with some detail, missing the how.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a party, we are committed to one law for all and that every New Zealander is treated equally regardless of race, religion, or background.
specificity.explanation: A statement of creed offered in place of content: no figure, mechanism, provision or timeframe, and nothing here that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The practical effect of this bill shifts the burden of proof onto Māori.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the mechanism of the measure before the House — who bears the burden of proof — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So we will be supporting this because it does restore what Parliament intended, it does restore an exacting test, and I commend this bill to the House.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House and its effect on the statutory test; no party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It's the worst kind of rubbish that has come before this House, and it will be undone by a future Government, and we will have to stand up and apologise, Minister, for this nasty piece of legislation to somehow try and restore the honour of the Crown that you are disdaining.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a future New Zealand government will repeal or reverse this amendment and that the Crown will apologise for it. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — the Greens are not in government and the forecast is about what some later administration will do.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand statute record: whether the burden-of-proof amendment to s 106 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 made by this bill is repealed or reversed by a subsequent Parliament, and whether a Crown apology is issued in respect of it. True if the provision is repealed or reversed; false if it remains in force in substantially its enacted form.

rigor.statement: This means that what this Government is doing now guarantees that the fight for Te Tiriti justice only deepens from this point on, and continues on into the next generations.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the measure before the House: the bill causes, and 'guarantees', generational conflict. The step from the legislation to a guaranteed multi-generational outcome is asserted, not connected — an overreach from a single cause to a certain long-run effect with no mechanism offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Governments continue to lie, deny, obscure, obfuscate, and deliberately confuse to keep the public from seeing, knowing, and truly understanding the truth of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and that is that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is good for everyone.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of what governments in general are 'really like' — dishonest and deliberately deceptive. No measure, clause, figure or outcome is named; the weight is entirely on the other side's character rather than on the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because that’s the thing: you change the goal posts because the courts start endorsing us.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — that the amendment responds to, and reverses, favourable court determinations — but it is carried as a motive attribution to 'you' rather than as an engagement with the test or clause being changed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is Parliament, not the courts, that makes the laws of this land, and this bill makes clearer what “exclusive use and occupation” means, and it strengthens the requirement for physical evidence of exclusive use.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure: what the bill changes and to which statutory test. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is not, as the Government insists, a tidy clarification of an old law; it is an incredibly blunt instrument that tears at the very foundation of justice, up-ends our court processes, and undermines a hard-fought relationship between te iwi Māori and the Crown.
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at what the bill does — its retrospective reach into court processes — rather than at the other party's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reality is that Casey Costello was a spokesperson for Hobson’s Pledge, a group that is on the record, clear for being fundamentally opposed to indigenous rights.
focus.explanation: The provenance of the coalition commitment is a legitimate line, but as put here the content is about who a member used to speak for rather than about any clause, test or effect of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s rising in our youth, it’s rising in our children, and as it rises—and it will continue to rise, generation after generation—the old, pale, stale, deeply held racist views of Te Tiriti o Waitangi will set like the sun.
civility.explanation: 'Old, pale, stale' attaches the criticism to who people are — age and ethnicity — rather than to the position held, and 'racist' imputes bad faith. Aimed at a class of people rather than a named member, so short of a direct personal insult, but past the point of engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The reality is that Casey Costello was a spokesperson for Hobson’s Pledge, a group that is on the record, clear for being fundamentally opposed to indigenous rights.
civility.explanation: Goes to the Minister's affiliations rather than to the bill, and the framing ('a group ... fundamentally opposed to indigenous rights') imputes a motive to her personally. Not a direct insult, but past engaging the substance — Costello immediately raised a point of order that her reputation had been impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: When we get rid of this one-term Government, we’ll repeal this legislation back to 2003—2003.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the current National/ACT/NZ First coalition will serve only one term, i.e. will not be returned to government at the next general election. (The repeal half of the sentence is a promise about the speaker's own action and is not scored here.)
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official Electoral Commission result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it: true if the National-led coalition (National, ACT, NZ First) does not form the next government; false if that coalition is returned to office.

veracity.statement: Yet Māori did not ask for the marine and coastal area, takutai moana legislation, nor the foreshore and seabed legislation that was before it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neither the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 nor the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 originated from a Māori request — both were Crown initiatives.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of both Acts (Cabinet papers, the Crown's response to the Court of Appeal's Ngāti Apa decision, select committee records, the 2004 hīkoi and Waitangi Tribunal Wai 1071 report): true if both Acts were Crown-initiated rather than sought by Māori claimants or Māori organisations; false if the record shows Māori bodies requested either statute.

veracity.statement: But what we have is a counterfeit kāwanatanga, changing the rules again; an illegitimate use of kāwanatanga as per what the Waitangi Tribunal has already declared, and this massive hara that ripples through to te ao Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal has already found the Crown's exercise of kāwanatanga in relation to this takutai moana amendment to be illegitimate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's reports on the takutai moana amendment (the urgent inquiry into the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment proposal, Wai 3400): true if the Tribunal found the Crown's proposed amendment to be an unjustified or illegitimate exercise of kāwanatanga in breach of Treaty principles; false if the Tribunal made no such finding.

veracity.statement: Right now, people are burning the bill on the coastline, affirming that they are there now and they will be there tomorrow because we are not going anywhere.
veracity.explanation: A claim about a present event: that protesters were burning copies of the bill at coastal locations at the time of the debate (21 October 2025).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous news reports and organiser/social media records from October 2025 for the Northland and Bay of Plenty locations named later in the speech: true if bill-burning protests on the coastline are documented around 21 October 2025; false if no such protests occurred.

veracity.statement: It delivers on a coalition agreement commitment with New Zealand First, and I commend it to the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that this bill implements a commitment contained in the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (November 2023): true if it contains a commitment to amend the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 to restore Parliament's original intent on the customary marine title test; false if no such commitment appears there.

veracity.statement: The reality is that Casey Costello was a spokesperson for Hobson’s Pledge, a group that is on the record, clear for being fundamentally opposed to indigenous rights.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that Casey Costello held a spokesperson role for Hobson's Pledge, and that Hobson's Pledge is on the record as fundamentally opposed to indigenous rights.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hobson's Pledge media releases, campaign material and news interviews naming its spokespeople, plus its published position statements: true if Costello is documented as a Hobson's Pledge spokesperson and the group's own published material opposes Māori-specific rights and Treaty-based provisions; false if she never held that role or the group's stated positions do not bear that characterisation.

veracity.statement: No, I did not, and I would just like to highlight that the regulatory impact statement to this bill refers to the coalition agreement, which includes this legislation to take away customary rights, so that was mentioned as one of the key reasons that this decision was taken by the Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's regulatory impact statement cites the coalition agreement as one of the reasons for the policy decision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Regulatory Impact Statement for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill: true if it references the coalition agreement commitment among the drivers of the proposal; false if the RIS makes no such reference.

specificity.statement: It is Parliament, not the courts, that makes the laws of this land, and this bill makes clearer what “exclusive use and occupation” means, and it strengthens the requirement for physical evidence of exclusive use.
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory phrase being redefined and the specific change to the evidential requirement, so the effect is checkable against the bill text — but gives no thresholds, clause references or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is not, as the Government insists, a tidy clarification of an old law; it is an incredibly blunt instrument that tears at the very foundation of justice, up-ends our court processes, and undermines a hard-fought relationship between te iwi Māori and the Crown.
specificity.explanation: Almost entirely metaphor ('blunt instrument', 'tears at the very foundation of justice'). No clause, test, figure or mechanism is named, so nothing here could be checked or acted on. High focus, low specificity — she is on the policy but not yet in it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It was a deal done as a dirty deal that legislated away Māori customary rights to gain power, and I want that on the record.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith and a corrupt motive ("dirty deal"... "to gain power") to the governing parties rather than engaging the bill's substance. No individual is named or insulted, so this sits at the imputing-bad-faith level, not a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Oh, don't you tell me about Ngāti Porou. We all know you wanted to be Ngāti Porou, but anyway, we're talking about Takutai Moana, which this Government have no evidence that public have been denied access to.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at the Minister about his own identity and motives, which has nothing to do with the measure. The second half returns to the substance, but the opening lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The substantial interruption I referred to, under the current law, occasional authorised public activity did not automatically break customary occupation, but under this bill, any other use, authorised or not, can destroy a claim. This, effectively, means that even when we maintained ongoing connection, any intrusion by others, no matter how brief, no matter what, it counts as an interruption.
rigor.explanation: A stated premise about the change in the substantial-interruption test, and a conclusion that tracks it: if any other use authorised or not can destroy a claim, then brief intrusions count. The inference follows from the premise offered; whether the premise describes the bill accurately is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When their own senior architect says the Government is dismantling the very framework he built, that should give you cause to pause.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to authority. It is a relevant authority — the author of the 2011 Act speaking to its original intent — but the conclusion rests on who is objecting rather than on any offered reason why the amendments fail, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The bill is also part of the agreement of the coalition Government and agreed to and supported by all Government parties. Therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: An explicit "therefore" resting on an appeal to authority: that the coalition parties agreed to it is offered as the reason to commend it, which bears on its political provenance rather than on its merits. The inference does not support the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Cabinet was explicitly warned by officials not to proceed in this way. That advice was ignored and, as a result, up to seven cases may now need to be reheard, affecting more than 280 kilometres of coastline and consuming millions of dollars in costs.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named source of advice, a case count, and a coastline figure — checkable content, not a slogan. Missing only the identity of the cases.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The amendments align the recognition of the customary marine titles more closely with tikanga and address concerns addressed by the courts.
specificity.explanation: States a direction of travel but names no clause, no test, no court decision and no figure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill seeks to restore the clarity to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, it seeks to protect property rights that foster legal clarity, and it seeks to reduce legal disputes and ambiguity.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act but otherwise a string of generic aims — clarity, property rights, fewer disputes — with no clause, test, figure or timeframe. Nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Cabinet was explicitly warned by officials not to proceed in this way. That advice was ignored and, as a result, up to seven cases may now need to be reheard, affecting more than 280 kilometres of coastline and consuming millions of dollars in costs.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named consequence of the measure before the House — official advice, case numbers, cost. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The self-proclaimed party of property rights, trampling all over the rights guaranteed to us, even though they were our rights before the courts were even established in this land.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — that the bill overrides existing property rights — but the weight of the sentence is a hypocrisy charge against the other party's self-description rather than the mechanism at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Your reign as Government is for one more year, so don't get too comfortable.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's hold on office. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Cabinet was explicitly warned by officials not to proceed in this way. That advice was ignored and, as a result, up to seven cases may now need to be reheard, affecting more than 280 kilometres of coastline and consuming millions of dollars in costs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that officials advised Cabinet against the retrospective approach, (b) that up to seven decided cases may require rehearing, and (c) that more than 280 km of coastline is affected.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice advice to Cabinet and the Regulatory Impact Statement for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill: true if officials recommended against retrospective application and the advice estimates roughly seven affected cases and >280 km of coastline; false if the advice contains no such recommendation or materially smaller figures.

veracity.statement: It applies the new test back to 24 July 2024, meaning that any case heard before the New Zealand courts can be reopened.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific retrospective commencement date of 24 July 2024, and that the consequence is that any case heard by the courts can be reopened.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Bill's application/transitional provisions as reported back from the Justice Committee: true if the new test applies to applications determined on or after 24 July 2024 and the reopening extends to all previously heard cases; false if the date differs, or if reopening is confined to a narrower class (e.g. only determinations made on or after that date), which would make "any case heard" an overstatement.

veracity.statement: In 2004, the Foreshore and Seabed Act caused huge upheaval within New Zealand. Tens of thousands of people protested, political parties fractured, and trust between Māori and the Crown was broken.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2004 Foreshore and Seabed Act drew protests numbering in the tens of thousands and caused a party split.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and police/organiser estimates for the May 2004 foreshore and seabed hīkoi to Parliament, plus the record of Tariana Turia's resignation from Labour and the founding of the Māori Party: true if the hīkoi is credibly estimated at 10,000+ and a party split is documented; false if attendance estimates are an order of magnitude lower or no party fractured.

veracity.statement: Former Attorney-General Chris Finlayson—again, hardly a left-wing radical—warned that this legislation would be extremely harmful to race relations and it will rip away the good work that was done.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Chris Finlayson about the effect of the amendments on race relations. What is checkable is whether he said it, in those terms.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Chris Finlayson's public statements, media interviews or select committee submission on this Bill: true if he described the amendments as extremely harmful to race relations; false if no such statement exists or his stated position is materially different.

veracity.statement: Hoi anō rā, I think the best way for me to address this bill is as a wīwī Nāti, as Ngāti Porou being the first and only iwi to have our own takutai moana bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ngāti Porou is the only iwi with its own dedicated takutai moana statute.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand statute book: true if Nga Rohe Moana o Nga Hapu o Ngati Porou Act 2019 is the sole iwi-specific foreshore/takutai moana Act; false if any other iwi has an equivalent standalone Act.

divination.statement: This bill will not bring certainty; it will bring more litigation.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that enactment will increase, rather than reduce, litigation over customary marine title.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Count of Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act proceedings filed or reheard in the High Court and Court of Appeal in the two years after enactment, compared with the two years before: true if the volume rises; false if it falls or is flat.

divination.statement: Your reign as Government is for one more year, so don't get too comfortable.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the current National-led coalition will be out of government after the next general election, roughly a year hence.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The result of the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed after it: true if the National-led coalition does not form the next government; false if it is returned to office.

civility.statement: In fact, he should be ashamed of the bill, and he should be ashamed of himself.
civility.explanation: Moves from criticism of the bill to a direct personal reproach of the Minister himself ('ashamed of himself'). A clear personal attack rather than an attack on the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You are scared of Māori asserting themselves in this world, and you have learned nothing, Mr Goldsmith, nothing, because Mr Potaka has been able to teach you nothing.
civility.explanation: Attacks two named members' character and capacity — accusing one of fear and of having 'learned nothing', and the other of being unable to teach him anything. Contemptuous of the persons, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And the kaupapa will be to fight this Government on every issue where they attack Māori, which is coming weekly, which is coming fortnightly.
focus.explanation: A bill is before the House, but this engages no measure, mechanism, figure or named commitment — it is a declaration about fighting the other side in general. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is the tribal framing Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As the previous speaker, Tracey McLellan, pointed out, working towards bringing councils closer to the decision making; giving a strengthening to the provisions on the way that revenue that is above operating costs will be used to improve traffic locally, because New Zealanders want to see the costs of this system—that they will pay in to make sure that traffic can move more efficiently—going towards ways to improve traffic in their area.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: the select committee changes to council decision-making and the hypothecation of above-cost revenue to local traffic improvements. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You know, and I look at what Cushla Tangaere-Manuel was saying: our people, they trust the law; they go through the process—our kaumātua work through the process; they chuck everything at this; they come and win at court level—then Government changes the rules.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: claimants used the statutory process and succeeded in court, and the legislature is now amending the rules, which supports the implied conclusion that the amendment defeats a legitimate expectation. The gap is that it never establishes the amendment actually reverses the court outcomes rather than altering procedure prospectively, so the conclusion runs slightly ahead of the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I rise to speak on the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill, in support because New Zealanders already face a high cost, sitting in traffic.
rigor.explanation: A genuine premise-to-conclusion move about the measure — congestion imposes real costs, therefore support the charging bill — but the middle step is missing: nothing is offered to connect time-of-use charging to a reduction in that cost, so the conclusion leans on an assumed mechanism rather than a shown one.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You see, their former mentor, Chris Finlayson, has said: “These amendments do not restore the original intention of Parliament. They undermine them.”—they undermine them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Chris Finlayson, the former Attorney-General who piloted the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, publicly stated that the current amendments undermine rather than restore Parliament's original intention. The claim under test is the accuracy of the attributed quote.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of Chris Finlayson's statements on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill — his select committee submission, published opinion pieces, or media interviews up to 21 October 2025. True if he made a statement in these or materially equivalent terms; false if no such statement exists or if his stated position is that the amendments do restore Parliament's original intention.

veracity.statement: We've never stopped access to the foreshore.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the period since the 2011 Act, Māori applicants or holders of customary marine title have not excluded the public from access to the foreshore.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 public-access provisions (which preserve free public access to the common marine and coastal area) together with the register of customary marine title orders and recognition agreements to October 2025. True if no CMT order or agreement has operated to exclude general public access to a foreshore area; false if any documented instance of public access being stopped under the Act can be identified.

veracity.statement: As the last speaker on this third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, I don’t want to drag it out, but I do want to just put on record that Ngāti Porou has got a carve-out from this Act and their takutai moana is not going to be affected by this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ngāti Porou's takutai moana is dealt with under separate legislation that is excluded from the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, and so is unaffected by the amendment bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nga Rohe Moana o Nga Hapu o Ngati Porou Act 2019 and the text of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill as passed. True if the Ngāti Porou arrangement sits outside the amended Act and the bill contains no provision applying to it; false if the amendment bill's customary marine title provisions extend to the Ngāti Porou rohe moana.

specificity.statement: This bill is about freeing up traffic so we can have a more free-flowing system.
specificity.explanation: States an aim in the most general terms available — no charge levels, no corridors, no timeframe, no mechanism. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As the previous speaker, Tracey McLellan, pointed out, working towards bringing councils closer to the decision making; giving a strengthening to the provisions on the way that revenue that is above operating costs will be used to improve traffic locally, because New Zealanders want to see the costs of this system—that they will pay in to make sure that traffic can move more efficiently—going towards ways to improve traffic in their area.
specificity.explanation: Names two actual amendments — council involvement in decision-making and surplus revenue directed to local improvements — but carries no figures, no thresholds and no timing for either.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is also very much in alignment with the Infrastructure Commission, which has encouraged us to price things so that it spreads peak demand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the NZ Infrastructure Commission (Te Waihanga) has advocated demand-based pricing to spread peak demand across infrastructure generally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Waihanga / NZ Infrastructure Commission published advice, its 30-year National Infrastructure Plan and its congestion-pricing work; true if the Commission has recommended demand pricing (including congestion charging) as a means of spreading peak demand, false if no such recommendation exists in its published output.

veracity.statement: I can recall, in introducing the second reading, the Hon Chris Bishop’s comments on the New York scheme, which he’d just been to see, which has just started, and saying, “This is working really, really well and people are actually going, ‘We didn’t like the idea, but now we like it—we see what it’s doing’ ”.
veracity.explanation: Relays Bishop's assessment that New York's congestion pricing scheme is working well and that public opinion has shifted from opposition to approval since it began.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NYC MTA congestion relief zone reporting on traffic volumes and travel times since January 2025, plus published polling on New Yorkers' support; true if traffic entering the zone fell materially and polling shows support rising from a minority to a majority, false if traffic/travel-time measures are unchanged or polling shows sustained opposition.

rigor.statement: The one we did argue about was public transport, because the whole rationale for time of use charging is to change the time or the mode, and public transport is about the mode.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (public transport should be exempt) follows from the stated premise: the charge exists to shift travellers to another mode, so charging the alternative mode would work against the scheme's own purpose. Coherent means-ends reasoning, no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If 10 percent of the people change the way they travel, it means that, instead of being stuck in traffic, you’ve got relatively free-flowing traffic.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but a leap: the step from a 10 percent behavioural shift to 'relatively free-flowing traffic' is asserted with nothing offered to connect them — no modelling, evidence or account of the non-linearity claimed. A genuine gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The one we did argue about was public transport, because the whole rationale for time of use charging is to change the time or the mode, and public transport is about the mode.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the measure before the House — which vehicle classes are exempt and why — rather than the other party. Names the specific exemption at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we proposed, and I think that’s had broad acceptance—it’s one of the ones we pushed with the Minister—an independent chair appointed jointly and unanimously by NZTA and by the councils, and that’s set out in section 65V(1)(d), in clause 4.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact governance mechanism (independent chair, jointly and unanimously appointed) and cites the clause and new section that implement it. Fully checkable against the bill as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It puts in place something in the tool kit that local government has been asking for, for a long time, which hopefully should save the country a significant amount of money in congestion and, potentially, in capital programmes.
specificity.explanation: Identifies two real channels of benefit (congestion cost, deferred capital spend) but quantifies neither — 'a significant amount of money', no figure, no timeframe, no scheme. A direction with some detail and no how much.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think, at the time, you said, Mr Twyford, that you didn’t want another tax before the 2020 election, but it might be worth revisiting after the 2020 election.
civility.explanation: Recounts an opposing member's electoral caution on the record. Pointed — it touches on political timing rather than the merits — but it imputes no bad faith, mocks no one, and stays on the funding question; he immediately includes himself in the same charge.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific funding/policy changes by the current Government: that the walking and cycling budget was halved, and that the public transport farebox recovery requirement was increased.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 (and Budget 2024 NLTF allocations) walking and cycling activity class funding compared with GPS 2021: true if the allocated range is roughly half the previous one; plus the GPS/NZTA farebox recovery ratio target: true if the required ratio was raised above the previous setting. False if either the cycling allocation was not materially reduced or the farebox recovery requirement was unchanged or lowered.

veracity.statement: Because congestion is only one negative impact of our car dependency, the health costs from air pollution actually exceeds the cost of congestion itself, and yet this bill ignores that evidence entirely, presumably because it’s an inconvenient truth that air pollution from motor vehicles—and this is the 53rd Parliament, so no doubt the costs have increased, like everything else—causes approximately $10 billion in social costs every year, including 13,000 cases of childhood asthma prevalence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that vehicle air pollution causes approximately $10 billion in social costs a year in New Zealand and about 13,000 cases of childhood asthma, and that air pollution health costs exceed congestion costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health and Air Pollution in New Zealand (HAPINZ 3.0) study, checking the social cost and childhood asthma figures attributed specifically to motor vehicles rather than to all air pollution sources; and NZTA/Ministry of Transport congestion cost estimates for comparison. True if the motor-vehicle share of social costs is ~$10bn with ~13,000 childhood asthma cases and exceeds published congestion cost estimates; false if those figures are the all-sources totals rather than the vehicle share, or if congestion costs are higher.

veracity.statement: The city raises $50,000—or $50 million I should say—each month from the scheme that it can then plough back into public transport, and buses travel faster in Manhattan as a result.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New York's congestion pricing scheme raises about $50 million a month, that the revenue is directed to public transport, and that Manhattan bus speeds have improved. The "$50,000" is an immediately self-corrected mis-speak, not a claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MTA published monthly Congestion Relief Zone revenue reports for 2025: true if gross monthly revenue is approximately $50 million, false if materially different (e.g. under $35m or over $70m). Plus MTA bus speed data for Manhattan crosstown/CBD routes before and after 5 January 2025: true if average speeds rose.

veracity.statement: The noise complaints in the city of Manhattan have fallen by 70 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 70 percent fall in noise complaints in Manhattan, offered in the context of New York's congestion charging scheme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NYC 311 complaint data for the Congestion Relief Zone comparing 2025 with the equivalent 2024 period, for the noise/honking complaint categories: true if the fall is approximately 70 percent, false if materially smaller, or if the reduction is not attributable to the charging zone (e.g. a citywide trend of the same size).

focus.statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
focus.explanation: Names specific policy levers — the walking and cycling budget and the farebox recovery ratio — and a specific consequence (fares). Legitimate scrutiny of named commitments, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s been a real win all around for the city of Manhattan, and now we’re going to be able to trial it here in New Zealand, and that’s a great thing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and the evidence for it — the mechanism, its results elsewhere, and the trial proposed here. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
civility.explanation: A contested debate where she could have turned on the Minister; instead the criticism lands entirely on the Government's policy decisions. Hard criticism of a policy is the standard, not a deduction.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because congestion is only one negative impact of our car dependency, the health costs from air pollution actually exceeds the cost of congestion itself, and yet this bill ignores that evidence entirely, presumably because it’s an inconvenient truth that air pollution from motor vehicles—and this is the 53rd Parliament, so no doubt the costs have increased, like everything else—causes approximately $10 billion in social costs every year, including 13,000 cases of childhood asthma prevalence.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, a health-outcome count and a named comparison against congestion costs. Someone could go and check it against the underlying study.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are not against all road improvements, by any means; we just think that the bulk of the billions ahead over the next 60 years are not the best investment.
specificity.explanation: States a position on spending priorities but with no named projects, no amounts and only a gestural timeframe — "the bulk of the billions" over "the next 60 years" commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The city raises $50,000—or $50 million I should say—each month from the scheme that it can then plough back into public transport, and buses travel faster in Manhattan as a result.
specificity.explanation: A named jurisdiction, a monthly dollar figure and a named destination for the revenue. Precise enough to act on or check.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s been a real win all around for the city of Manhattan, and now we’re going to be able to trial it here in New Zealand, and that’s a great thing.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is supported by the figures he actually offered (travel times, traffic volumes, noise, revenue, bus speeds), so it is not a bare assertion. The gap is the generalisation: a single overseas case is carried across to New Zealand cities without anything offered to connect the two contexts — a weak argument from example rather than a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We have some major problems to unlock, particularly in our largest cities, that have the legacy of really poor 20th century policies that, essentially, locked in the 1950s, very dispersed, urban form cities that are utterly dependent on motorway systems, that cannot efficiently move people and goods around.
civility.explanation: Harsh criticism aimed squarely at historic planning and transport policy — "really poor 20th century policies" — with no person, and no member, targeted. This is the expected standard: brutal about the policy, civil about people.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is simply not possible, because when you have a growth in population, a growth in demand to move goods and people around, every time you expand the roads, in that context, you simply induce more demand.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: premise (population and freight demand growth) plus mechanism (induced demand) supporting the conclusion that road-building cannot clear congestion. The conclusion tracks the premises; the only weakness is the absolute framing ("simply not possible") where the mechanism supports a weaker claim about diminishing returns.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We can say with certainty that it has the potential to reduce 10 percent or more of drivers at a particular time of day when the charging is in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the international evidence base from implemented congestion-charging schemes shows a reduction of 10 percent or more of drivers during charged periods.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published evaluations of the schemes he names (Transport for London congestion charge impact monitoring reports; Stockholm congestion tax evaluations; Singapore ERP studies; Milan Area C; NYC congestion pricing data). True if peak-period vehicle volumes in charged zones fell by 10% or more in multiple schemes; false if the documented reductions are materially below 10%.

veracity.statement: Good things often take time, and I'm very pleased to see that policy work that I started as transport Minister, probably seven or eight years ago, has finally found its way, through a succession of other Ministers, to this House in the form of this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the policy work underpinning this time-of-use charging bill was begun by Twyford himself while Minister of Transport, roughly seven or eight years before October 2025 (i.e. 2017-18).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport and Auckland Council records for "The Congestion Question" work programme and any related ministerial announcements. True if that congestion-pricing work programme was initiated under Twyford as Minister of Transport in 2017-18 and is the lineage of the current bill; false if the work began under a different Minister or materially later.

specificity.statement: By adding a small charge to the use of that particular roading network at particular times of the day, it will incentivise people to change their transport behaviour, to take another mode, to get on the train or the bus or the ferry or to time their journey for a less expensive hour when they don't have to pay that extra fee.
specificity.explanation: Sets out a real mechanism — a time-varying charge on a defined cordon or motorway stretch, and the specific behavioural responses it targets (mode shift, retiming) — but carries no charge levels, no zones, no dates and no expected magnitudes. A direction with detail, short of checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, I made it clear in the select committee that I only support this bill with one clear condition: if any revenue is collected in the Mt Roskill electorate, I want it to return to Mt Roskill—for future transport infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete condition (hypothecation of locally-collected revenue back to the electorate for transport infrastructure), but supplies no amounts, no mechanism for enforcing it, and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We have to find other ways to fund our transport system and the technology that's in use here, and what will very likely be a shift to electronic GPS-based road-user charges for all vehicles—a technology that's already in place for a significant section of our trucking fleet—will mean that petrol excise can be phased out and replaced with a much more comprehensive way of raising revenue based on people's real-time use of the transport network.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand will move to electronic GPS-based road user charges across the whole vehicle fleet, and that fuel excise duty will consequently be phased out. Not a promise about his own action — he is in opposition and forecasting a system-wide transition.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand legislation and NZTA implementation records. True if fuel excise duty has been phased out for light petrol vehicles and replaced by electronic road user charges applying to the general vehicle fleet; false if petrol excise remains the primary charging mechanism for light vehicles at the resolve-by date.

focus.statement: However, I made it clear in the select committee that I only support this bill with one clear condition: if any revenue is collected in the Mt Roskill electorate, I want it to return to Mt Roskill—for future transport infrastructure.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — where scheme revenue goes and on what condition his support rests. No party framing, no reference to opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I am going to reject one of Dr Cheung’s claims that the money collected in Mount Roskill should be spent in Mount Roskill.
civility.explanation: A named colleague's claim is rejected head-on, but the disagreement lands entirely on the substance of the hypothecation argument — nothing is said about Cheung himself. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Of course, the Auckland motorway and roading network is a network, and the spending needs to go across the network to ensure that the network functions effectively, which of course will, in turn, help people in Mount Roskill.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: because the roading system is interconnected, revenue should be spent network-wide rather than hypothecated to the collection area. The premise-to-conclusion step is reasonable, but it leans on a near-tautology ('the network is a network') and simply asserts the flow-on benefit to Mount Roskill without offering anything to support it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We do spend a lot of time sitting in traffic, and so that’s a behaviour that clearly needs to change.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on the speaker's own commuting anecdote and a supposition about a colleague's commute — an argument from anecdote. The leap from 'people sit in traffic' to 'this behaviour needs to change' also skips over whether the behaviour is chosen or forced, which is the contested question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And there’s an interesting little supposition underlying that: that somehow school kids don’t deserve to be on the roads—they don’t deserve to use the roads because the roads are better when they’re not there.
rigor.explanation: A strawman. Using school-holiday traffic as a benchmark for uncongested flow implies nothing about whether school children 'deserve' road access; the speaker attributes a value judgement that the comparison does not carry, then argues against it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That’s a viable solution along State Highway 16 now that a busway is at last being retrofitted into State Highway 16.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that busway infrastructure is currently being retrofitted onto State Highway 16 (the Northwestern corridor) in Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project records and funding decisions for the Northwestern Busway / SH16 bus improvements. True if dedicated busway infrastructure on SH16 was under construction as at October 2025; false if only bus shoulder lanes or interim improvements existed and the busway itself remained unfunded or unstarted.

veracity.statement: London and Stokholm are both great examples of congestion charging working where traffic reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent in London; 20 to 25 percent in Stokholm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific measured traffic reductions attributable to congestion charging schemes: 15–30 percent in London and 20–25 percent in Stockholm.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transport for London's Congestion Charging Impacts Monitoring reports and the published evaluations of the Stockholm congestion tax. True if measured traffic-volume reductions in the charged zones fall within the stated bands; false if the documented reductions are materially outside 15–30% for London or 20–25% for Stockholm.

specificity.statement: There are a number of reasons why congestion charging is a great idea: the environmental benefits, the revenue generation beyond what we already have, the sustainable infrastructure, improved cities, and, of course, economic efficiency, which is what we’re all about on this side of the House: economic growth and efficiency.
specificity.explanation: A list of generic benefit categories — 'environmental benefits', 'sustainable infrastructure', 'improved cities' — with no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named provisions of the bill. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: London and Stokholm are both great examples of congestion charging working where traffic reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent in London; 20 to 25 percent in Stokholm.
specificity.explanation: Named jurisdictions with numeric ranges attached to each — precise enough that anyone could go to the published evaluations and check it. Missing only the time period and the measure being counted.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are a number of reasons why congestion charging is a great idea: the environmental benefits, the revenue generation beyond what we already have, the sustainable infrastructure, improved cities, and, of course, economic efficiency, which is what we’re all about on this side of the House: economic growth and efficiency.
focus.explanation: The statement is genuinely about the measure before the House, but a third of it is party self-identification ('what we're all about on this side of the House') rather than anything about how the charging scheme works.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need buses, we need trains, we need bus fares and train fares that take into account people’s circumstances and that also enable people like children, for example, to be able to attend sports games, to be able to attend training.
specificity.explanation: Names modes and a beneficiary group, but carries no figures, no fare level, no funding source and no timeframe — a direction rather than a checkable proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We also think that new section 65C(2), inserted by clause 4, allows too much ministerial control, and that’s about protecting local autonomy.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (new section 65C(2), inserted by clause 4) and the concrete objection to it; anyone could go to the bill and check the claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need buses, we need trains, we need bus fares and train fares that take into account people’s circumstances and that also enable people like children, for example, to be able to attend sports games, to be able to attend training.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the transport policy question the bill raises (what accompanies a congestion charge); no party content at all. Vague but on-policy — the contrast with its low specificity is the intended split.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a little bit like hearing Simeon Brown say that doctors have crossed an ethical line when they assert their right to stand up for their patients and talk about safer staffing and better pay and conditions to make sure that people receive adequate healthcare.
focus.explanation: A hypocrisy point about an opponent's conduct in an unrelated portfolio; it does name a specific remark rather than being pure party-bashing, but it carries no content about the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, in the interest of brevity, I was really pleased to see in the introduction, mechanisms for a scheme board to adjust to charges, manage scheme operations, etc., because I remember going to the Mount and paying the gold coin at the little toll booth with the people in the booth.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific mechanism in the bill (the scheme board's power to adjust charges and manage operations) and an actual tolling experience; no party content, though the substance is thin.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We did have these half-price fares; the Government has removed them, so I’m keen to know what this Government is going to do to make sure the other side of the ledger of the congestion charge is about enabling people to get other forms of transport.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a half-price public transport fare scheme existed and that the current Government ended it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA records and Budget documents on the half-price public transport fares scheme introduced under the previous Government: true if half-price fares existed and were discontinued under the current Government; false if they were never in place, or if they remain in force.

veracity.statement: The other thing, I suppose, is just really noting that former Minister of Transport Simeon Brown has said we want to make sure we’re not adding further cost to people using roads during a cost of living crisis.
