rigor.statement: This creates a significant administrative burden. More summonses must be sent out, more follow-ups are required, and more time is spent managing excusal requests. By raising the excusal age, we reduce that burden, making the system more efficient and more representative.
rigor.explanation: A real mechanism is offered — high excusal rates force extra summonses and processing, so shrinking the automatic-excusal pool reduces that work — and the conclusion tracks it. The gap is that it assumes 65–72-year-olds will not simply seek discretionary excusal instead, which would leave the processing load largely unchanged.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The age of 72 strikes the right balance. It reflects capability, it respects contribution, and it aligns with other civic roles.
rigor.explanation: Only the third limb ('aligns with other civic roles') connects to anything previously offered, namely the Ombudsman's retirement age of 72. The first two limbs are bare assertions, and the conclusion that 72 specifically is the right point does not follow from a benchmark range spanning 70 to 80.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is a bill where, when there is difficulty in fulfilling the numbers required for a jury duty trial, reducing the reasons that a person may be excused makes it easier for the Ministry of Justice to be able to fulfil those numbers in a jury and to be able to allow people to be heard in the way that they hope to be heard.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: premise (juries are hard to fill), mechanism (fewer grounds for excusal), conclusion (the pool is easier to fill). The conclusion follows from the premises; the only gap is that no magnitude is offered for how much the change would help. No fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a bill where, when there is difficulty in fulfilling the numbers required for a jury duty trial, reducing the reasons that a person may be excused makes it easier for the Ministry of Justice to be able to fulfil those numbers in a jury and to be able to allow people to be heard in the way that they hope to be heard.
focus.explanation: Engages the bill's mechanism and who it affects, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We think there are other ways and, again, other things that could be introduced and could be considered, in terms of the remuneration aspect when it comes to jury service, that, again, allow more people to be able to partake in jury service, particularly people who are younger.
focus.explanation: Squarely on policy: names a specific lever (juror remuneration) and the group it would affect, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It doesn’t even reflect the minimum wage.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fee paid to jurors is lower than what an equivalent period of work would pay at the statutory adult minimum wage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice jury service fee schedule in force on 2025-10-22 (daily/half-daily juror fee), compared against the statutory adult minimum wage for an equivalent day's attendance; true if the juror fee is below that figure, false if it is equal to or above it.

veracity.statement: When I think of the Manukau court in my electorate, it’s one of the busiest courts in the country and there is certainly a need there for more people who want to fulfil this duty, also a real need for more justices of the peace who can sit as magistrates in that court to be able to participate in that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Manukau court is among the busiest courts in New Zealand. (The reference to justices of the peace 'sitting as magistrates' is loose terminology in live speech, not a separate factual claim, so it is not extracted.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice District Court caseload statistics by court location for 2024–2025; true if Manukau ranks among the highest-volume courts nationally by cases filed or disposed, false if it sits mid-range or lower.

veracity.statement: Now, just to kind of cast our minds back to when this bill was introduced and the first reading: in the first reading, we did oppose the bill, but then we were interested to hear, in the select committee process, exactly some of the potential fishhooks that this does create.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of record that the Green Party voted against the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill at its first reading. Reported about his own party, so the subject is the speaker.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division/vote record for the first reading of the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill; true if the Green Party is recorded voting against, false if it is recorded voting in favour or the bill passed first reading without opposition.

specificity.statement: When I think of the Manukau court in my electorate, it’s one of the busiest courts in the country and there is certainly a need there for more people who want to fulfil this duty, also a real need for more justices of the peace who can sit as magistrates in that court to be able to participate in that.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific court and two specific unmet needs (jurors, justices of the peace), but supplies no caseload figures, shortfall numbers or timeframe — a direction with detail, missing the how much.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We think there are other ways and, again, other things that could be introduced and could be considered, in terms of the remuneration aspect when it comes to jury service, that, again, allow more people to be able to partake in jury service, particularly people who are younger.
specificity.explanation: Points at remuneration but commits to nothing checkable — no rate, no mechanism, no cost, no timeframe, only 'other ways' and 'other things'. High focus, low specificity.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Personally, I'm a big fan of juries. I think there's a long history that's proven that it is a core part of the demos having a say in the way justice and law is created and dished out in our society, our country, and through our history.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to tradition. The conclusion — that juries are a core part of democratic participation — rests entirely on the assertion that a 'long history' has 'proven' it; no mechanism, evidence or comparison with non-jury systems is offered, and longevity of a practice does not establish its value.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If the House has been so open to raising this age, I wonder about how the House might look at raising the superannuation age gradually, carefully, over time. It would be an important thing to make sure that our country is financially stable into the future.
rigor.explanation: Weak inference on two counts: the bridge from the House's willingness to raise the jury excusal age to its willingness to raise the superannuation age is a non sequitur (unrelated policies with different rationales), and the fiscal payoff is asserted rather than shown — no costing or projection connects a higher super age to 'financially stable'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There's a good reason for that; people work pretty hard, especially those in manual labour.
rigor.explanation: A genuine reason is offered for keeping the superannuation age where it is — the physical toll of manual work — and it bears on the conclusion. But there is a real gap: the premise that manual work is hard does not by itself establish 65 as the right threshold, and no evidence on health, life expectancy or workforce participation is supplied to close it.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If the House has been so open to raising this age, I wonder about how the House might look at raising the superannuation age gradually, carefully, over time. It would be an important thing to make sure that our country is financially stable into the future.
specificity.explanation: Names a real policy (the superannuation eligibility age) and a direction (raise it), but supplies no target age, no start date, no rate of increase and no fiscal figures. 'Gradually, carefully, over time' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The challenge for us is to continue to grow our economy strongly so we can afford to have those that get to 65 retire with some dignity and some security in their earnings, particularly those that have gone through a life of manual labour, for which 65 is quite a threshold to get to.
specificity.explanation: The goal is named (affording superannuation at 65), but the entire mechanism is 'grow our economy strongly' — no policy, no growth target, no fiscal figure and no timeframe. Nobody could check or act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I would take a little bit of issue with Cameron Luxton's take on lifting the super age; I don't think that's going anywhere fast, but we're here.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the proposal to lift the superannuation eligibility age will not progress. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — it is a prediction about what Parliament and the Government will do. Resolve-by date has not passed, so the prior is left at 0.5.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary bills register and Government policy announcements: false if a bill or Government policy raising the New Zealand Superannuation eligibility age above 65 is introduced to the House or adopted as Government policy before 31 December 2027; true if no such bill or policy is introduced or adopted by that date.

veracity.statement: The volunteer sector in New Zealand would collapse without the contribution of our seniors.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that seniors' contribution is load-bearing for the whole volunteer sector, to the point that removing it would cause collapse. Extracted as hyperbole with a checkable core — the underlying share-of-volunteering claim can be measured even though 'collapse' is an overstatement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ General Social Survey / time-use data and Volunteering New Zealand sector reports on volunteering rates and hours by age band: true if people aged 65+ supply a dominant share of formal volunteer hours (say, a plurality well above their population share) such that their withdrawal would leave the sector non-viable; false if their share of volunteer hours is broadly comparable to other adult age groups.

focus.statement: And obviously, I mean, our leader the Rt Hon Winston Peters is certainly well past this threshold and still running rings around most, if not all, politicians in this Parliament.
focus.explanation: Party framing in place of policy content. It gestures at the bill's 72-year threshold, but the substance is a testimonial to his own party leader rather than anything about the measure — who it affects, how it works, or what it costs.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Old people bring a lot of really valuable experience, so I think it’s good that this will enable a wider range of participation.
rigor.explanation: A genuine but thin inference about the measure: the premise (older people carry valuable experience) supports the conclusion that broader participation is good, but nothing connects experience to jury performance, and the premise is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In listening to the kōrero to my left and to my right, from experience having parents who are in the category—the demographic group that is being spoken of, mid-60s—in Māori communities, it's very, very rare nowadays to see many 70-year-olds turning up to the marae, coming to hui, actually out and about in the community. Many of them are very frail.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: the observation of her own parents and her local community is generalised to the whole 65–72 Māori population, and no data is offered to bridge the gap between that experience and a population-level claim about capacity to serve.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If she'd actually read the legislation, she would know that, for example, if they had healthcare issues or issues of a similar nature, they still have the ability to apply to withdraw from being part of the jury process.
rigor.explanation: A sound rebuttal on the merits: if the excusal-on-health-grounds provision survives the amendment, the objection that the bill ignores individual circumstances does not hold. The conclusion follows from the premise offered (the snideness of the framing is a Civility matter, not a defect in the inference).
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Look, congratulations to the member Carl Bates on getting your bill drawn, and it looks like it will have unanimous support from the House.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill will pass its remaining stages with no party voting against.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division/voice-vote record for the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill's subsequent readings in the NZ House; true if it passes with no party recorded against, false if any party votes against.

civility.statement: I find it quite interesting to hear this bill being proposed by someone not in that demographic group, but speaking for them.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the person rather than the bill — it questions the member's standing to propose the measure rather than the measure itself, with a mildly sardonic 'quite interesting', but stops well short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because you’re not in the Māori community.
civility.explanation: Disqualifies the member personally rather than answering him — his standing to comment is attacked on the basis of who he is, not what he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But had she read the legislation? Not a chance, not a chance at all, and it showed, in that shameful two-minute contribution.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the member's diligence and competence — asserting she did not read the bill and branding her speech 'shameful' targets the person rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a generalisation of everybody within the 65- to 72-year-old age group. It is putting a blanket response on everyone within the demographic without giving weight to the individual circumstances of these people.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: it engages the specific age band the bill changes and the mechanism's treatment of individual circumstances, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By changing it from 65 to 72, it reduces bureaucracy and it improves jury diversity.
focus.explanation: Names the exact change the bill makes and the outcomes claimed for it — entirely about the measure, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We received 31 submissions on the bill and unanimously—unanimously; Oriini Kaipara’s own colleague from Te Pāti Māori—recommended that this bill pass.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts about the Justice Committee's consideration of the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill: that it received 31 submissions, and that its recommendation to pass was unanimous, including the Te Pāti Māori member on the committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill (parliament.nz select committee papers); true if the report records 31 submissions and a unanimous recommendation that the bill be passed with no Te Pāti Māori minority/differing view, false if the submission count differs materially or a differing view was recorded.

veracity.statement: We are living longer in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that life expectancy in New Zealand has been rising, offered as the factual basis for lifting the jury excusal age.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life-expectancy-at-birth series for New Zealand; true if life expectancy in the most recent releases is higher than in earlier decades, false if the series is flat or declining over that span.

specificity.statement: This can either be for a particular occasion, under section 15(2)(aa) of the Juries Act 1981, or permanently, under section 15A(2).
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and two specific provisions and distinguishes the occasion-by-occasion excusal from the permanent one — anyone could go and check exactly what is claimed.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have people that I’ve met in that context in that village who would ace a jury. They’d be absolutely wonderful on it because they’d be thinking about the situation with all that rich experience, and coming to it with a proportionality.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that older people would make excellent jurors — rests entirely on an appeal to anecdote: a self-selected group of residents she happens to have met at public meetings in one retirement village. No evidence is offered that rich experience produces better deliberation, and the sample is exactly the kind (people who turn up to meet their MP) least likely to generalise to the wider over-70 population. The inference is about the policy and it is weak, so it belongs here rather than to Focus.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have people that I’ve met in that context in that village who would ace a jury. They’d be absolutely wonderful on it because they’d be thinking about the situation with all that rich experience, and coming to it with a proportionality.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it engages who the bill affects and why extending the jury age would change the pool of jurors. No party framing at all. Scored high despite the weak inference, which is Rigor's business, not Focus's.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I took the case because that was a breach of the law—you can’t discriminate on the basis of age.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of New Zealand law that an employer could not lawfully force an employee to retire on reaching a set age at the time of the case she describes (around 15 years before the speech, so roughly 2010). The claim is about the legal position, not about the merits of her client.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Human Rights Act 1993 s21(1)(i) and s22, and the Employment Relations Act 2000: true if age (for employees aged 16 and over) was a prohibited ground of discrimination in employment in New Zealand at the time, such that a contractual compulsory-retirement clause was unenforceable; false if compulsory retirement on age grounds remained lawful then.

specificity.statement: I think that this bill has got a really strong, firm affirmation of a group of people who often feel that they are not being valued and whom we should value, and so I commend the bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: A summing-up of what the bill does that carries no checkable content: no age threshold, no numbers of additional eligible jurors, no mechanism, no timeframe. 'A strong, firm affirmation of a group of people' is a sentiment rather than a description of the measure. The nearby text supplies no figures to credit either — the only number in the speech, 72, appears as an aside about her own prospects of jury service.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The member came to the conclusion that it was a balanced midpoint where judges retire at the age of 70 but can serve until the age of 75, and the Ombudsman’s retirement age, at this stage, is 72.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete statutory retirement ages (70, 75, 72) and ties them to a specific design choice in the bill; anyone could check the figures and follow the reasoning for why 72 was chosen.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to invest time to reinforce how important it is to have the contribution of our older and wiser folk in the exercise of law.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey a substantive point but carries no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named step — 'invest time to reinforce how important it is' commits to nothing checkable, even though the surrounding speech does contain the 65-to-72 detail elsewhere.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The member came to the conclusion that it was a balanced midpoint where judges retire at the age of 70 but can serve until the age of 75, and the Ombudsman’s retirement age, at this stage, is 72.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that judges' retirement age is 70 with service possible to 75, and that the Ombudsman's retirement age is 72.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Senior Courts Act 2016 (judicial retirement age and the age limit for acting judges) and the Ombudsmen Act 1975 provision on when an Ombudsman vacates office; true if the statute sets judicial retirement at 70 with acting service available to 75 and the Ombudsman vacating at 72, false if any of the three ages differ.

veracity.statement: As this is a second reading speech, I just wanted to comment that I have read through the submissions that were presented at select committee, and you can see from that that most of the select committee submissions did agree that there was an issue here, that the courts are being pressured at the moment, and that this would go some way to alleviate them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority of the submissions to the Justice Committee on the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill agreed there was a problem, that courts are currently under pressure, and that the bill would partially relieve it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published submissions to the Justice Committee on the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill; true if more than half of them identify a juror-availability problem and support the change as relief, false if most were neutral or opposed. Court pressure separately checkable against Ministry of Justice jury trial backlog/waiting-time statistics for 2025.

veracity.statement: The practical reasons include reducing the need for having to issue more summons, as people aged 65—who are, at this stage, still given jury summons—will ask for excusal at age 65.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current position: people aged 65 are still summoned for jury service and seek excusal on reaching 65, generating additional summonsing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Juries Act 1981 provisions on excusal as of right for people aged 65 and over, plus Ministry of Justice data on summonses issued and excusal applications by age; true if 65-year-olds are still summoned and excusal at 65 is routinely sought, false if the over-65s are excluded from the summons pool or if excusal at 65 is uncommon. The universal 'will ask' is the part most likely to be overstated.

rigor.statement: Some of the positives of this are that we know that it will help in making sure that we can have more people to contribute to jury duty so that we can get through our cases in a quicker and faster way as well, because we’d have that that extra seven years of people that fall into that pool for jury duty being able to contribute as well.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: a seven-year wider eligibility band enlarges the juror pool, therefore cases move faster. The first step follows; the second leaps, assuming pool size is what limits case throughput rather than court time or scheduling, and 'we know' asserts more certainty than the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I'm sure my peers in this House and my more senior colleagues would agree, lived experience allows for a far greater and more balanced judgment of the facts of any case that may be before a juror.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that lived experience produces better fact-finding — rests entirely on an appeal to popularity ('I'm sure my peers would agree') and, earlier in the speech, on the speaker's own observation. No evidence about juror age and verdict quality is offered to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It's no secret to New Zealanders that in my community of Nelson, we do have a higher proportion of older people, many of whom, upon their retirement, continue to contribute in a number of voluntary ways—volunteering for organisations, sitting on committees, and actually being able to undertake jury service is the type of contribution that I know a lot of older people in Nelson really appreciate being able to do.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Nelson electorate/region has a higher-than-typical share of older residents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census/subnational population estimates for the Nelson region or electorate: true if the proportion aged 65+ exceeds the national proportion, false if it is at or below the national figure.

veracity.statement: Just to be really clear, the current law doesn't preclude anyone over the age of 65 from participating in a jury already, but what it does do is it allows somebody over the age of 65 to be able to excuse themselves, whereas that age is now going to be lifted to the age of 72.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that existing law lets people over 65 excuse themselves from jury service rather than barring them, and that the bill raises that threshold to 72.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Juries Act 1981 s 15 (excusal as of right) and the text of the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill as reported back: true if the current threshold is an excusal right at 65 (not a disqualification) and the bill substitutes 72, false if either the mechanism or either age differs.

veracity.statement: I also just note that the Justice Committee did make a couple of small amendments to the bill with some savings provisions, particularly, to ensure that when the bill has its commencement and receives its Royal assent that it doesn't become retroactive to people who have already been issued their first notice for being on a jury, their first summons, so that was a sensible position from the select committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Justice Committee recommended savings/transitional provisions so the new excusal age does not apply to people already summonsed before commencement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill and the bill as reported back: true if the reported-back bill contains a savings/transitional provision preserving the position of people already issued a summons, false if no such provision was recommended.

specificity.statement: Just to be really clear, the current law doesn't preclude anyone over the age of 65 from participating in a jury already, but what it does do is it allows somebody over the age of 65 to be able to excuse themselves, whereas that age is now going to be lifted to the age of 72.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact legal mechanism (excusal as of right, not disqualification) and both the current and proposed ages; directly checkable against the Act and the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And again, some of the changes they're looking to make so that people aren't inconvenienced by having to turn up and present themselves from jury duty and hang around and wait there, they're actually looking at some more modern techniques which actually will support what Mr Bates has done here, in this bill.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at operational reform of jury summoning but names no technique, no agency commitment, no cost and no timeframe — 'some more modern techniques' is not checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So what this will mean is that there is a bigger pool of people who will be required to participate in a jury. That is a good thing, because we know that there's a real pressure on our court system, and often part of that pressure is actually having the availability of jurors to sit on a jury.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: juror availability is a contributor to court delay, therefore enlarging the juror pool helps. The conclusion tracks the premise, but the premise is asserted on 'we know' with no evidence offered and no attempt to size the effect — a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Again, I think it's just an art that we—or something we just need to remember, that just because your bill's being drawn, it doesn't actually mean the select committee's going to do all the work, because it doesn't have the same vested interest as the member in charge does.
rigor.explanation: An argument from incentives: the committee lacks the member in charge's stake in the bill, therefore the member cannot rely on the committee to carry it. The conclusion follows from the stated premise, though the premise about committee incentives is simply asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The life expectancy for people will get longer and longer and they will need to continue to think about the ways that they can contribute to society.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a continued rise in New Zealand life expectancy. The speaker gave no timeframe, so the earliest fair test is the next full NZ life tables release cycle.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ New Zealand period life tables (life expectancy at birth): true if the figure published in a release after this statement exceeds the most recent figure available at the time of speaking, false if it is flat or lower.

veracity.statement: Drowning has been cited as the third-highest cause of unintentional death in New Zealand for children up to the age of 14.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific ranking for drowning among causes of unintentional death for New Zealand children aged 0-14.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Water Safety New Zealand / Ministry of Health injury mortality data for the 0-14 age group; true if drowning ranks third among causes of unintentional (accidental) death for that age band, false if it ranks otherwise or if the cited ranking is for a different population (e.g. all ages).

veracity.statement: Our overall fatal drowning rate is among the worst in the developed world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's per-capita fatal drowning rate sits near the top of comparable developed countries.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD / WHO Global Health Estimates drowning mortality rates per 100,000; true if New Zealand sits in the worst quartile of OECD countries, false if it sits near or below the OECD median.

veracity.statement: Maritime Rule 91 requires that all recreational vessels carry life jackets for every person on board but it doesn’t mandate that children wear them at all times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of Maritime Rule Part 91: a carriage requirement for every person on board, but no blanket wearing requirement for children.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Maritime Rule Part 91 (Navigation Safety) as in force in October 2025; true if it requires personal flotation devices to be carried for each person on board and imposes no at-all-times wearing obligation on under-15s, false if it contains such a wearing mandate or lacks the carriage requirement.

veracity.statement: Last year alone, Maritime New Zealand was notified of 17 deaths, of all ages, involving recreational craft.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of recreational-craft fatalities notified to Maritime New Zealand in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Maritime New Zealand's recreational craft fatality notifications for the 2024 calendar year; true if the notified total is 17, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The scope of this bill is limited to those under 15, which is tied to the minimum age which someone can legally skipper a boat.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 15 is the minimum age at which a person may lawfully skipper a boat in New Zealand, and that the bill's threshold matches it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Maritime Transport Act, Maritime Rule Part 91 and regional navigation safety bylaws; true if a legal minimum age of 15 for operating a recreational vessel exists nationally, false if there is no national minimum age (i.e. it is set only by some regional bylaws, or only for particular vessel types or speeds).

specificity.statement: It makes the wearing of life jackets compulsory for anyone under 15 years of age while on board recreational vessels 6 metres or less in length.
specificity.explanation: States the operative rule with an exact age threshold, an exact vessel-length threshold and the class of vessel covered — someone could check or apply it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My only query about this is the affordability for life jackets. A good quality life jacket is not cheap, and so we need to think about how we make those things accessible to whānau, because everybody's life is valuable and no price should be put on that.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a real issue but commits to nothing checkable: no price figures, no subsidy or distribution mechanism, no timeframe — 'we need to think about how we make those things accessible'.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They are inconsistent, can be confusing, and hence ineffective.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the existing bylaw regime: inconsistency implies confusion, which is offered as entailing ineffectiveness. The final step is asserted rather than supported — no compliance or outcome evidence links confusion to ineffectiveness, so there is a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The 2024 numbers not wearing a life jacket have yet to be confirmed, given ongoing investigations, but what we do know is that life jackets would have saved several last year.
rigor.explanation: The sentence concedes the underlying data is unconfirmed and pending investigation, then concludes in the same breath that 'what we do know' is a counterfactual about lives saved. The conclusion is stronger than the premise it is drawn from — an assertion of certainty from evidence just described as unavailable.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We teach our kids to wear seatbelts in a car. We make them wear helmets on bikes. Wearing a life jacket on a small boat should just be as obvious.
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy to seatbelt and helmet mandates. The analogy is apt in kind but the relevant similarity is asserted rather than established — no comparison of risk exposure, enforceability or compliance is offered to carry the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill simply codifies what many regional councils already have in place; it codifies what most families already put in practice; and it codifies what almost every Kiwi, rightly, expects is already happening.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to popularity and common practice — that most families already do it and most people assume it is law — as the reason to legislate. There is a legitimate consistency argument underneath (aligning national rules with existing bylaws), but the weight is carried by what people already believe and do rather than by an effect on the outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My only query about this is the affordability for life jackets. A good quality life jacket is not cheap, and so we need to think about how we make those things accessible to whānau, because everybody's life is valuable and no price should be put on that.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure before the House — raises cost as a barrier to compliance with the proposed mandate. On-policy, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, just in the spirit of jest, while we do support this bill, I just want to say, oh, whānau, I hope you don't need to get your life jacket repaired, because that bill didn't get passed because the Nats didn't let it get heard tonight.
focus.explanation: There is a real legislative point here — another member's bill on repair not proceeding — but it is not named or specified, and the weight of the remark is a jab at 'the Nats' rather than engagement with either measure.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I agree with life jackets on small boats. It’s like seatbelts, and it’s regulation that will save lives.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (this regulation will save lives) offered with a single supporting reason: an analogy to seatbelts. The analogy is asserted rather than established — no evidence is offered that life jackets on small craft behave like seatbelts in cars, and the two differ in the risk profile and the population affected. A real inference about the policy, but a thin one leaning on argument from analogy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill doesn't target bad parenting. It doesn't respond to a pattern of preventable deaths. It imposes a one-size-size-fits-all rule on every boating family in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that a blanket mandate is not warranted — tracks the premises the member laid out immediately before it (one covered death in a decade, and that death already unlawful under existing law). The inference from 'no pattern' to 'no blanket rule' is a reasonable cost-benefit step, though it leaves a gap: a low observed death count under current voluntary behaviour does not by itself show the rule would add nothing, and the member does not close that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I'd put a counter example to that, which is: how do you know it's not a safe condition? I mean, in the calmest of waters, bad things can happen.
rigor.explanation: A real inference engaging the opposing argument: if risk cannot be assessed in advance, a conditions-based exemption is unworkable. The point is valid as far as it goes, but the support offered is an assertion plus (immediately after) a remembered family anecdote about seatbelts — an appeal to anecdote and analogy rather than any evidence on how often calm-water incidents actually occur. A genuine gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: None of the five people on the 4.8-metre boat was wearing a life jacket when it was struck by two waves in short succession and capsized in Auckland’s Manukau Harbour a short time later.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the moment of the 6 November 2022 Clarks Beach capsize in the Manukau Harbour, none of the five occupants of the 4.8m vessel was wearing a life jacket.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Coronial findings, the Maritime NZ investigation, and court records for the Clarks Beach / Manukau Harbour capsize of 6 November 2022; true if the record states no occupant was wearing a life jacket at the time of the capsize (and that there were five occupants on a ~4.8m vessel), false if any occupant is recorded as wearing one at that moment or the vessel/occupant figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: There are already some regions where it is compulsory for any age to wear a life jacket.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at least one NZ region already has a bylaw requiring life jackets to be worn by persons of any age (not just children) on relevant vessels.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Regional council navigation safety bylaws (e.g. Auckland Council, Environment Canterbury, Otago Regional Council) as at October 2025; true if any bylaw mandates the wearing of life jackets by all persons regardless of age on specified recreational craft, false if every regional bylaw only requires carriage rather than wearing, or applies only to children.

veracity.statement: Even as our population grows, the overall trend in child drownings is falling.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number (or rate) of child drownings in New Zealand is on a declining trend despite population growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Water Safety New Zealand's DrownBase annual drowning statistics for the 0-14 age band over the last one to two decades; true if the series shows a declining trend in child drowning deaths (absolute or per capita) across that period, false if flat or rising.

veracity.statement: I ask the House, last year, how many children drowned who would have been covered by this bill? None. In 2023, none.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in each of 2024 and 2023, no child under 15 drowned while on a recreational craft under six metres — i.e. no drowning in either year fell within the bill's coverage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Maritime New Zealand OIA response and Water Safety New Zealand data the member tabled, cross-checked against DrownBase records for recreational-craft drownings of under-15s in 2023 and 2024; true if both years record zero such deaths, false if either year records one or more.

veracity.statement: Over the past decade, from 2014 to 2024, there has been only one such case.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that across 2014-2024 there was exactly one drowning of a child that would have fallen within the bill's coverage (under-15, recreational craft under six metres).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Maritime New Zealand and Water Safety New Zealand drowning data for 2014-2024 filtered to under-15s on recreational craft under six metres; true if exactly one such death is recorded, false if the count is zero or two or more.

veracity.statement: The skipper was charged and pleaded guilty to manslaughter.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the skipper in the 2022 case referred to was charged with manslaughter and entered a guilty plea to that charge.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand court records and reported judgments for the prosecution arising from the November 2022 Clarks Beach / Manukau Harbour capsize; true if the skipper is recorded as pleading guilty to manslaughter, false if the charge or plea differed (e.g. a lesser Maritime Transport Act charge, a not-guilty plea, or conviction after trial).

veracity.statement: Right now, we have very fragmented rules across New Zealand, based on the territorial authorities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that life jacket requirements for recreational craft currently differ from one local authority area to another rather than being nationally uniform.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Regional council navigation safety bylaws made under the Maritime Transport Act as at October 2025; true if the wearing requirements (ages, vessel lengths, conditions) differ materially between regions, false if a single national rule applies uniformly.

specificity.statement: None of the five people on the 4.8-metre boat was wearing a life jacket when it was struck by two waves in short succession and capsized in Auckland’s Manukau Harbour a short time later.
specificity.explanation: Carries a date, a location, a vessel length, an occupant count and a described mechanism — every element is checkable against the public record. Precise and concrete.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I ask the House, last year, how many children drowned who would have been covered by this bill? None. In 2023, none.
specificity.explanation: A precise, year-by-year count tied to an explicitly defined coverage class (children who would have been covered by this bill), and the member offers to table the underlying data. Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yet the parties on the other side of the House, at the moment at least, think a 15-year-old can decide life or death, a 16-year-old can get married and can pay tax, but they can’t vote.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point buried here — consistency of statutory age thresholds, and the voting age in particular — but the weight of the sentence is directed at what 'the parties on the other side of the House' think, and it leaves the measure before the House entirely. The speaker herself signals the drift immediately afterwards ('before I’m reminded, I’ll get back to this bill'). A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of course, local government does a lot of work in water safety and pools and swimming, but please don’t make this another unfunded mandate that regional councils are required to enforce without any support from central government.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: names the enforcement body, the funding mechanism and the cost-shifting consequence of the bill. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: ACT believes that approach is wrong. We believe children should wear life jackets in risky conditions, but on a still day, anchored on a shallow bay, with parents nearby, should you really be criminalised for lying on the deck without a life jacket or for jumping off the boat to cool off?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the operation of the measure: what conduct it would criminalise, under what conditions, and where the member would draw the line instead. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is what this bill is trying to do, to standardise and make it clear what is expected from skippers, whether you're up North or down South in Dunedin.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the bill directly — what it standardises and who it binds. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I really am concerned that if this bill goes through with the title Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill, we will be advised that changing the age will not be within the scope of the bill.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that once the bill is with the select committee, the committee will be advised that amending the age threshold falls outside the bill's scope, because of how the bill is titled. This is a forecast about advice the committee will receive, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill, plus the departmental/Clerk's scope advice published with it; true if the committee is advised that raising or removing the age limit is outside the bill's scope, false if the committee is advised the age threshold may be amended within scope (or amends it).

civility.statement: I commend the member for his concern and congratulate him on having his bill drawn, however, ACT cannot in good conscience support this bill.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested position — announcing opposition to a coalition colleague's bill on a subject involving dead children — where there was ample opportunity to impugn motives. The member confines himself to the bill and credits the sponsor's motive. This is the expected standard, met.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I've listened intently to your speech, Cameron Luxton, and while I disagree, I really respect that within a coalition we can have these types of debate on principle and on policy.
civility.explanation: Direct disagreement with a named member, expressed entirely as a disagreement on principle and policy with no imputation of motive or capacity. Contested ground, no attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I just wanted to say, first off, in junior and youth sailing in this country, it is mandatory to wear life jackets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that life jacket wearing is already compulsory in organised junior and youth sailing in New Zealand, as distinct from recreational sailing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Yachting New Zealand racing rules and class/event rules for junior and youth classes; true if a personal flotation device is required to be worn at junior/youth racing events, false if wearing is optional or left to the sailor.

veracity.statement: In 2020, the rate is about 1.62 per 100,000 people. It’s higher than a comparable country like Australia, which is 1.1, and Canada, which is 1.3.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand's 2020 drowning death rate was about 1.62 per 100,000, above Australia's 1.1 and Canada's 1.3.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Water Safety New Zealand / WHO Global Health Estimates drowning mortality rates per 100,000 for New Zealand, Australia and Canada for 2020; true if the three figures match to within rounding and the ordering holds, false if any figure is materially different or the ordering reverses.

veracity.statement: In 2024 alone, 18 New Zealanders lost their lives in boat-related incidents. Of those, 17 were not wearing a life jacket.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2024 count of 18 boating-related deaths in New Zealand and that 17 of the 18 victims were not wearing a life jacket.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Maritime New Zealand and Water Safety New Zealand 2024 drowning/boating fatality reports; true if the recreational boating fatality count for 2024 is 18 and the reported no-lifejacket cases number 17, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: I think you were probably there with Mark Mitchell and the Prime Minister that Surf Life Saving New Zealand and Coastguard received a funding boost of $63.6 million over four years last year—over four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Government announced a $63.6 million, four-year funding increase for Surf Life Saving New Zealand and Coastguard New Zealand in the previous year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget documents and the Government's water-safety funding announcement; true if a package of $63.6 million over four years for Surf Life Saving NZ and Coastguard NZ was announced in the year before October 2025, false if the amount, recipients or period differ materially.

rigor.statement: Why would we not support a bill that would make that rule consistent for all young people in this country? It just seems ludicrous when you think that even the best people can get caught out if they are not wearing those life jackets.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single family anecdote to a national rule, and leans on an appeal to incredulity ('ludicrous', 'why would we not'). The anecdote does genuinely establish the premise it is used for — that skill does not remove the risk — so the inference is weak rather than broken.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They believe that personal responsibility or the burden is on the skippers, or they’re scared the Government is going to overreach, but I want to remind them that the cost of a life jacket is far less than the cost of a funeral.
rigor.explanation: States the opposing objection (personal responsibility, regulatory overreach) and answers it with an appeal to emotion. The funeral comparison is about cost and grief; it does not engage the liberty argument it is offered against, so the conclusion does not follow from what was put.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We still go through some quite strict security regimes at the airport. The chances, thankfully, in our country of someone wanting to harm us on a plane is very, very small, but we’re prepared to do that for the greater good. This piece of legislation is one of those: for the greater good.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy that largely holds: both cases impose a small universal burden against a low-probability, high-harm outcome. It is not airtight — nothing is offered on the disanalogies of cost or setting — but the conclusion tracks the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think we should, along with this piece of legislation, look forward to another National Party MP bringing forward a piece of legislation that says it is compulsory for all schools to teach kids to swim because, in fact, that has been squeezed out of the curriculum, out of school responsibilities. That’s part of the reason that we’re seeing too many people drown in this country.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal attribution: the decline of school swimming is asserted to be part of the cause of the drowning toll, with no data, trend or study offered linking the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill introduces national consistency and a clear legal requirement that anyone under 15 years old on a boat 6 meters or smaller must wear a properly fitted life jacket—no excuse and no grey areas.
specificity.explanation: States the exact mechanism of the bill: an age threshold (under 15), a vessel size threshold (6 metres or smaller) and the obligation (a properly fitted life jacket, worn). Fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this is about a consistent, nationwide rule that everyone understands, that kids under the age of 15 on vessels 6 metres or less will wear a life jacket—will wear a life jacket.
specificity.explanation: Names the age threshold, the vessel size and the obligation. Slightly less complete than the bill's full text (no mention of fit or enforcement), but concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They know a law like this could save many lives, and it’s very sad and very disappointing to hear that the ACT Party are not supporting this bill.
civility.explanation: Criticises a party's position on the bill in mild terms. No individual is attacked and no bad faith is imputed — expressing disappointment at an opposing vote is squarely civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The idea that parents could look after their kids is complete idiocy when they’re in the water—and most of the time stepping on to a boat with the expectation that they will be safe, and for the most part, they are—but we have many, many pieces of legislation and regulation around this country for the small minority of people who might find themselves unfortunately in this situation, or harm themselves or harm us or whatever; it’s for the minority.
civility.explanation: 'Complete idiocy' is aimed at the opposing position rather than at a named member, but it is dismissive mockery of the view and, by implication, of those holding it — short of a personal insult, but past civil engagement with the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was disappointing to hear from the ACT Party that they can’t see the logic to this, that the ideology of libertarianism that you can make up your mind is going to protect everyone when you go in the water.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — whether individual choice is sufficient protection on the water — but it is carried mainly as a characterisation of another party's ideology rather than of the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I relish the opportunity to reply and thank the members for their contributions and the overwhelming majority of parliamentarians that will be supporting this to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill will pass its first reading with the support of an overwhelming majority of MPs and be referred to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the first reading of the Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill; true if the bill passed and was referred to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee with well over a simple majority (ACT's votes the main opposition), false if it failed or the vote was close.

specificity.statement: I went to a life jacket hub at Sport Waitākere, in West Auckland, where they, at nominal or no charge, give out life jackets to those groups and families that need them for occasions.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific organisation, location and the mechanism (free or nominal-cost distribution to families in need). No figures on volume or funding, so short of fully concrete.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, we need to create a whole bunch of jobs in order to have the transition to renewable electricity; in order to have affordable, warm, dry housing; in order to have sustainable transportation; to have high quality processed wood products that can be used in structural timber buildings.
specificity.explanation: Names four sectors but supplies no job numbers, no timeframe, no funding mechanism and no policy instrument — 'a whole bunch of jobs' commits to nothing checkable, though the sectors named lift it above a pure slogan.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But we do—and I encourage the Transport and Infrastructure Committee to look at that genuine access, look at the affordability, look at communities, Grant McCallum, in the Far North, and their realistic access to life jackets, and on the East Coast, Dana Kirkpatrick.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what the select committee should examine (access, affordability, particular communities). Engages an opposition-raised point on its merits rather than the party that raised it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve known that for 10, 20, 30 years, and it saddens me that members in this House—who no doubt have children or grandchildren or other family members, and surely they care about the future world that those children and their children will inherit—are continuing to live in denial of the basic reality of what we need to do to have a livable future.
focus.explanation: The weight is on characterising the state of mind of members opposite ('living in denial') rather than on the bill's mechanism. There is a thin policy referent, but no named measure, figure or outcome carries the sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What this bill does is it draws that line in the sand: no new coal mines, no expansion of existing coal mines.
focus.explanation: States exactly what the measure before the House would do. Entirely on the policy, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know that a certain Minister in this Government would laugh and brag about causing these species to become extinct—that’s how out of touch some of the Government members are.
focus.explanation: There is a policy referent (species loss from mining), but the sentence is built around what Government members are like rather than around the bill's mechanism or any named decision.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You go through—and I’m not going to read them all out, because they’re all discoverable, but there are so many stories that have happened on so many occasions in recent years where life jackets would have saved lives.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy, but it rests on an accumulation of media anecdotes and an unstated counterfactual ('would have saved lives') rather than drowning statistics. Argument from anecdote; the conclusion is plausible but under-supported by what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You crunch the numbers, you do the maths; we cannot have a livable climate if we continue to explore and produce fossil fuels, particularly coal.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but it leans on an appeal to an unstated calculation — 'do the maths' is asserted rather than shown, and no carbon budget figures are supplied to connect continued coal production to the stated outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As if, somehow, money were something other than a symbol. It’s just a symbol.
rigor.explanation: Answers the economic objection by redefining money rather than engaging it — an equivocation. That money is a symbolic medium of exchange does not bear on whether the jobs and revenue at stake are real, so the conclusion (the economic case can be set aside) does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So there’s a lot to think about for the Transport and Infrastructure Committee to get their head around, but this is a bill that has the support of over 90 percent of New Zealanders—90 percent of New Zealanders want children in small boats to wear life jackets, and this will achieve that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over 90 percent of New Zealanders support requiring children in small boats to wear life jackets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published NZ polling or survey work on mandatory life jacket wearing for children in small vessels (e.g. Water Safety New Zealand or Maritime New Zealand public attitude surveys, or polling cited in the bill's explanatory material). True if a survey of the general public shows support at or above 90 percent; false if the best available polling is materially below 90 percent, or if no such survey exists and the figure is unsourced.

veracity.statement: It would strip mine an area the size of 1,700 rugby fields.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the proposed open-cast coal mine on the Denniston Plateau would strip mine an area equivalent to about 1,700 rugby fields (roughly 1,700 hectares).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The mine footprint stated in the fast-track approval application for the Denniston Plateau open-cast coal mine (applicant's application documents / EPA fast-track register). A rugby field is approximately one hectare. True if the proposed disturbed area is approximately 1,700 ha (within about 20 percent); false if the application's footprint is materially smaller or larger.

veracity.statement: The Department of Conservation ranks this plateau as one of the most valuable ecological sites on mainland New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that DOC itself classifies the Denniston Plateau among the most ecologically valuable mainland sites in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC ecological assessments of the Denniston Plateau (Protected Natural Areas Programme surveys, DOC submissions on mining applications, or DOC's published conservation values assessments). True if a DOC document ranks or describes the plateau as among the most ecologically valuable sites on the mainland; false if no such DOC assessment exists or DOC's own documents rank it lower.

veracity.statement: It is the only home on Earth for the avatar moth and New Zealand’s very own endangered giant carnivorous snail.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both the 'avatar moth' and an endangered giant carnivorous snail are found nowhere on Earth except the Denniston Plateau.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Distribution records for the Denniston 'avatar moth' and for the Powelliphanta snail taxon concerned (DOC threatened species listings, NZ Threat Classification System, published taxonomy). True only if both taxa are endemic to the Denniston Plateau; false if either occurs elsewhere — noting that giant carnivorous Powelliphanta snails as a group are distributed widely across the West Coast and Nelson, so the claim stands or falls on the specific species meant.

veracity.statement: They brag and laugh about the destruction of entire species.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Government members have publicly boasted and joked about causing entire species to be destroyed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The public record (Hansard, press releases, reported interviews) of statements by Government ministers about species affected by mining and fast-track consenting. True if a minister has publicly boasted about or joked approvingly about a species being wiped out; false if the record shows advocacy for mining or dismissal of environmental objections without any such remark about extinction.

veracity.statement: Indeed, the cost of the runoff from the acidified water, as a result of the open-cast coal mine, costs more for the Government to repair than the royalties they earn on the mining.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Crown's cost of remediating acid mine drainage from open-cast coal mining exceeds the coal royalties the Crown receives from it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown accounts and agency figures for acid mine drainage remediation liabilities on West Coast coal mines (DOC / Crown Minerals / Treasury unappropriated liability disclosures, and the Stockton remediation programme costings) set against NZ Petroleum & Minerals published coal royalty revenue for the same mines and period. True if remediation cost exceeds royalty revenue; false if royalties exceed remediation cost.

civility.statement: I know that a certain Minister in this Government would laugh and brag about causing these species to become extinct—that’s how out of touch some of the Government members are.
civility.explanation: Imputes to an identifiable Minister the motive of taking pleasure in driving species extinct — an attack on the person's character rather than on the mining policy. The added 'out of touch' judgement lands on people, not arguments.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The wholesale power price doubled overnight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the wholesale electricity price doubled immediately following the previous government's oil and gas exploration ban.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electricity Authority EMI wholesale spot price series around the 12 April 2018 exploration-ban announcement: true if the wholesale price roughly doubled within days of the announcement; false if the rise was materially smaller, or occurred gradually over months/years, or is attributable to a separate event such as the Pohokura outage.

veracity.statement: So consequently, suddenly, we became the only country in the world that instead of transitioning to renewables, we’re going away from gas to coal—to coal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand is the sole country in the world whose generation mix shifted from gas back to coal rather than toward renewables.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IEA / Ember electricity generation data 2018-2025: true if New Zealand is the only country whose coal share of generation rose while gas share fell over the period; false if any other country shows the same shift.

veracity.statement: We have a huge pile of coal there that we’re importing from Indonesia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand is currently importing coal from Indonesia in significant quantity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ merchandise import statistics for coal by country of origin, plus Genesis Energy disclosures on Huntly coal stockpiles, 2023-2025: true if material Indonesian coal imports and stockpiles are recorded; false if imports are negligible or sourced elsewhere.

rigor.statement: It won’t reduce our impact on emissions in this country; it’ll make it worse because the coal’s got to be imported.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: restricting domestic mining means coal is shipped in, so transport emissions rise. The gap is an unstated assumption that total coal consumption is fixed — the conclusion only follows if the bill changes the source of coal but not the quantity burned, which is precisely what is in dispute.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It won’t reduce our impact on emissions in this country; it’ll make it worse because the coal’s got to be imported.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the bill's predicted effect on emissions — the substance of the measure before the House, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And wouldn’t it be better if we were to use coal that we had in our own country rather than importing it?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question the bill raises — domestic extraction versus imported coal — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Gee, they’re really excited on the other side of the house, aren’t they?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the reaction of the other side. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the content is purely the opposing party's behaviour.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because it’s just the idealistic nonsense you get from people on the other side who don’t understand the implications of making these sorts of decisions.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other side's general outlook rather than any specific policy; strip out the part about opponents and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have a plan, and we’re pragmatic.
specificity.explanation: Claims a plan while conveying nothing about it: no mechanism, no figures, no timeframe, no named policy. A bare assertion of competence where the content was the whole point.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The truth is clearly hurting some on the other side of the House—clearly hurting people.
civility.explanation: Sneering aside at members opposite, imputing that their objections are discomfort with the truth rather than disagreement. Short of a direct insult, but it engages the members rather than the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The sad part about this, as I just heard the previous Government member talk about people laughing—and they are laughing: they are laughing at the lack of vision that this Government has and the absolute embarrassment that it has for the future generations who want to hear what is the solution.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government in general terms — its 'lack of vision' and 'embarrassment' — without naming a measure, figure or outcome. Party-directed rather than policy-directed, though it gestures at wanting a solution.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Where is the transition this Government keeps talking about, because it’s not evident in any of the discussions?
focus.explanation: Names a specific government commitment (the energy transition) and asks for evidence of it. Legitimate scrutiny of a stated policy, not party-bashing, though it carries no detail of its own.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But under our colleagues, of course, this has gathered dust. There hasn’t been much action, like many things under this Government in the past two years.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — the comprehensive energy strategy has not been progressed — but it is immediately widened into a general swipe at the Government's record over two years, which names nothing. A policy claim in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill does not immediately shut down active mines, despite what Government members will say.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what the measure before the House actually does — correcting the claimed effect on operating mines. Engaging the content of the bill, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I think, you know, again, the only people that really benefit from this are the shareholders.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: the universal conclusion that only shareholders benefit is drawn from the speaker's own observation of what the industry does in Taranaki. Nothing is offered on employment, royalties or regional spend to bridge the gap between one region's experience and 'the only people'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s a scare tactic, really, where they constantly use the line that we need more mines in order to keep the lights on when it comes to energy, and anyone who knows anything about the subject matter knows that that would only get us part of the way.
rigor.explanation: The rebuttal of the security-of-supply argument rests entirely on 'anyone who knows anything about the subject matter knows' — an appeal to self-evidence and unnamed expertise. No generation figures, no share of the grid, nothing offered to establish that new mines would only get us 'part of the way'.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because you’re comfortable sitting in the mud and the filth of what the sector does and brings to our whole nation.
civility.explanation: A direct personal charge against the members opposite — not that their policy is wrong but that they are personally complacent and morally soiled. Imputes bad character rather than engaging the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I really like the MP for North Shore, he’s a great man, but this is hard yakka, when it comes to important stuff before us.
civility.explanation: In a contested first-reading debate the speaker goes out of his way to compliment an opponent personally while pressing the difficulty of the issue. The mild jab lands on the difficulty of the work, not on the member.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And when are we going to stop sitting there and being in denial that coal is the dirtiest fuel on the earth—the dirtiest?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that coal is the most polluting fuel in use, superlatively — dirtier than any other fuel, and that this is not seriously contestable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative emissions-intensity data for fuels from the IEA/IPCC and NZ's Ministry for the Environment emission factors: CO2 per unit of energy delivered, plus SO2, NOx, mercury and particulate output. True if coal (including lignite and sub-bituminous grades) ranks highest among fuels in general use on carbon intensity and on the major pollutants; false if another fuel in common use ranks higher on those measures.

veracity.statement: This bill prohibits new coal mines and any expansion of existing coal mines after the 1 January in 2025.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill as introduced actually does: bars new coal mines and expansions of existing ones, with effect from 1 January 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill as introduced, on legislation.govt.nz/bills. True if its operative clauses prohibit the grant of permits for new coal mining and for expansion of existing coal mining operations, with the stated 1 January 2025 date; false if the scope or the date differ materially (e.g. it also revokes existing permits, or uses a different commencement date).

specificity.statement: This bill prohibits new coal mines and any expansion of existing coal mines after the 1 January in 2025.
specificity.explanation: States the mechanism (prohibition on new mines and on expansion of existing ones) and the commencement date. Anyone can check it against the bill or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think, after that standup comedy routine, I’d like to bring some serious analysis to this debate—some very serious analysis to this debate.
civility.explanation: Opens by characterising the previous member's speech as a "standup comedy routine" and implying only she brings seriousness — mockery and condescension aimed at the speaker rather than the substance, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She says it’s a climate plan; I say it’s a plan to manufacture energy scarcity, and that it’s frankly immoral.
civility.explanation: Calling a policy immoral is harsh criticism of the policy and passes cleanly, but "a plan to manufacture energy scarcity" imputes deliberate intent to create harm to the member who wrote it. That is an attribution of bad faith rather than an engagement with the mechanism.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now let’s talk about what she refuses to: real people.
civility.explanation: Imputes to the member a refusal to consider ordinary people — an assertion about her indifference rather than about her policy. Bad-faith imputation, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Willie Jackson: it’s an elite fantasy where other people pay your power bill.
civility.explanation: A clear personal attack on a named member: casts him as an elite who expects others to carry his costs. Directed at the person's character and circumstances, not at any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason that power prices have been so high is because there are so many unbuilt but consented renewables available to us—wind farms that could have been built.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause explanation of high power prices asserted without connecting evidence; the existence of unbuilt consents is offered as though it establishes causation, leaving a real gap between premise and conclusion (no account of dry-year hydro, gas supply, or market structure). Not a fallacy so much as an under-supported inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why would we carry on mining coal in New Zealand when there is no need for coal for process energy in New Zealand—when we do not need to mine it?
rigor.explanation: The premise contradicts what the speaker conceded moments earlier — "There is a need still, in some cases, for coal for process power, and that's a recognised need." The conclusion is drawn from an assumption she has already abandoned, so the inference is internally inconsistent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Energy poverty isn’t an academic talking point. It’s a child doing homework in a cold house because Parliament decided to grandstand and that’s what we had from Labour and the Greens for six years.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to emotion carrying an unsupported causal claim: the image of a cold house is offered in place of any link between the previous government's decisions and household energy poverty. Nothing is supplied to connect "Parliament decided to grandstand" to the outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Prohibiting modern, monitored higher standard mining, here, shifts demand to jurisdictions with lower environmental standards, longer shipping routes, and higher emissions.
rigor.explanation: A genuine carbon-leakage argument with a stated mechanism — demand persists, supply relocates, transport emissions rise. The inference holds only if demand is inelastic and the substitute jurisdictions really are dirtier, neither of which is established, so there is a real but not fatal gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And when it comes to keeping the lights on, physics beats politics every day, because hydro needs rain, wind needs wind, solar needs sun, and when they don’t show up, New Zealand still needs reliable and affordable energy, and that is in the form of thermal coal.
