focus.statement: I look opposite me and I see tobacco lobbyists, I see gun lobbyists, I see Hobson’s Pledge lobbyists, I see absolute profiteers, landlords, conspirators, and climate change deniers.
focus.explanation: Entirely about who the other side supposedly are. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Unlike the elite, flightless birds who want to focus on protecting the rich, we care for all whānau in Aotearoa.
focus.explanation: A contrast drawn entirely in terms of what sort of people the other parties are versus what sort her own party is. No policy, mechanism or outcome is named on either side of the comparison.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is unfair to our new Prime Minister is that you have started your legacy as a Prime Minister by attacking Māori and attacking our environment, but, worse, attacking our mokopuna.
focus.explanation: There is a real grievance about the Government's direction, but it is carried entirely by the word "attacking"; no specific measure, figure or outcome is identified.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because, as you can see, Winston has gone off track somewhat and Jonesy just can’t shut his mouth.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the behaviour and standing of two individuals in the other parties. No policy content survives if you remove them.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These attacks are around Māori health, where they’re shutting down our Māori Health Authority.
focus.explanation: Names a specific institution and a specific Government decision about it — scrutiny of a concrete policy, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That is what these small parties who make up this Government, ACT and New Zealand First’s combined vote is less than the 20 percent who you have offended the hell out of—the hell out of.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ACT and New Zealand First's combined party vote at the 2023 general election was below 20 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the 2023 New Zealand general election; true if ACT's party vote share plus New Zealand First's party vote share sums to less than 20 percent, false if it reaches 20 percent or more.

veracity.statement: So I want to say today that, when I woke up this morning and I read about Nicola Willis talking about te reo and cutting back in terms of some of our bureaucrats getting paid extra for speaking te reo Māori, I was shocked.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Nicola Willis had publicly signalled cutting the additional payments public servants receive for te reo Māori proficiency, in reporting on or shortly before 6 December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous news reports and Nicola Willis's own public statements around 5–6 December 2023; true if she stated an intention to end or curtail te reo proficiency allowances/bonuses for public servants, false if no such statement was made.

veracity.statement: I was shocked, because I was the Minister who was in charge of overseeing the language, and part of that strategy is getting 1 million speakers by 2040.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Crown's Māori language strategy he oversaw as Minister carries a target of one million te reo Māori speakers by 2040.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Maihi Karauna Crown strategy for Māori language revitalisation; true if it sets a target of one million New Zealanders able to speak te reo Māori by 2040, false if the target figure or date differs.

veracity.statement: These attacks are around Māori health, where they’re shutting down our Māori Health Authority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming Government is disestablishing the Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–ACT and National–New Zealand First coalition agreements of November 2023 and the subsequent Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) legislation; true if the Government committed to and legislated the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, false if no such commitment exists.

specificity.statement: I am proud as heck that we showed those who paid $440,000 to get a single MP in that our little $17,000 per candidate goes a long way.
specificity.explanation: Carries two concrete dollar figures and a per-candidate unit, so a reader could go and check the campaign spending comparison being drawn — though who the $440,000 belongs to is left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want to have a tax policy where we would have 2.2 million people living better.
specificity.explanation: A figure is attached to the claimed effect, but the tax policy itself — rates, thresholds, mechanism, timing — is not described, so there is a number without anything to act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I was shocked, because I was the Minister who was in charge of overseeing the language, and part of that strategy is getting 1 million speakers by 2040.
specificity.explanation: Names the office held, a numeric target and a date — a claim someone could look up and hold him to.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: You think about that: when we have the North come on, and the East Coast come on, and all around the nation, you’ll get a hīkoi 10, 20 times bigger than yesterday.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a future nationwide Māori mobilisation will produce a hīkoi ten to twenty times the size of the 5 December 2023 action at Parliament.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Police and media crowd estimates for subsequent nationwide Māori protest marches compared with estimates for the 5 December 2023 action; true if a later hīkoi is credibly reported at ten times or more that turnout, false if no such march reaches that scale by the resolve-by date.

civility.statement: Seymour knows nothing about the Treaty.
civility.explanation: A flat assertion that a named member is ignorant — the target is David Seymour's personal knowledge and competence, not any argument he has made. No policy claim is engaged, so this is a clear personal attack rather than robust criticism of a position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Tell that stupid Seymour this.
civility.explanation: A direct insult naming another member — an attack on the person's intelligence with nothing of the substance attached. Contempt, at the bottom of the scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve seen a shambolic start to Government from this three-headed being that is our Government. We’ve seen the two junior partners in the coalition running rings around the Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: Pointed and mocking about the coalition's functioning and edging toward the Prime Minister's authority, but it stops short of attacking him personally and imputes no bad faith to any individual.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He’s been expelled by his own iwi. He got kicked out of the tribe the other day.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that David Seymour has been formally expelled from his iwi, attributed later in the speech to Mana Epiha.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A formal statement or resolution from Seymour's iwi (Ngāpuhi) or its runanga, or contemporaneous reporting of one, expelling or disowning him; true if such a decision by the iwi authority is documented, false if no iwi body took such a decision and the claim rests only on an individual's remarks (whakapapa membership is not revocable by an iwi authority).

veracity.statement: I asked him, “What was your legal training, David Seymour?” He has none.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Seymour has no legal training or legal qualification.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: David Seymour's tertiary qualifications as recorded by the University of Auckland and his parliamentary biography; true if he holds no law degree or legal professional qualification, false if he holds a law degree or has been admitted to the bar.

veracity.statement: They were brought in to stop the Government in terms of privatisation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a historical purpose for the Treaty principles: that they were legislated in order to constrain the Government's privatisation of assets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of the Treaty principles clauses — the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 and section 9 of the State-Owned Enterprises Act 1986 — plus the 1987 Court of Appeal judgment in New Zealand Māori Council v Attorney-General; true if the principles clause was introduced in the context of restraining Crown asset transfer/corporatisation, false if the principles entered law independently of asset sales.

veracity.statement: What we have seen from the Government that is sitting on the Treasury benches today is a decision that they are going to roll back world-leading smoke-free legislation—that would have seen smoke-free generations in New Zealand—with a Minister of Finance who thinks it is OK to baldly say that the revenue is needed to fund the tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Finance openly said the revenue from reversing the smokefree legislation was needed to fund the Government's tax cuts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by Nicola Willis in November–December 2023 and the coalition's fiscal plan documents; true if Willis publicly stated that revenue from retaining tobacco excise/the smokefree repeal was counted towards funding the tax package, false if she made no such statement and the repeal revenue was not booked in the tax plan.

veracity.statement: There are 21,000 new public housing places funded by the previous Governments between 2017 and 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific number of public housing places funded by the 2017–2023 Governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Housing and Urban Development public housing supply figures and Budget appropriations for 2017–2023; true if funded public housing places over that period total approximately 21,000, false if the funded total is materially different (e.g. below 18,000 or above 24,000).

veracity.statement: Already, we have seen, at the current climate talks, that New Zealand received the “Fossil of the Day” award.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand received the Fossil of the Day award at the climate conference then under way.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Climate Action Network International's Fossil of the Day announcements from COP28 (Dubai, December 2023); true if New Zealand was named a Fossil of the Day recipient at that conference, false if it was not.

focus.statement: All that the principles talk about is partnership. They talk about good faith. They talk about participation. That’s what the principles are about.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure at issue — what the Treaty principles actually contain — rather than on the character or record of the other parties. This is the substantive part of the speech.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now we have the most separatist Government we’ve seen in history, the most dangerous Government we’ve seen in history, and we’re committed as a Māori caucus and as a Labour Party to fight it and advance the aspirations and rights of our people.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government in general terms and declares a party commitment to fight it. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named in the statement, so there is nothing here to hold anyone accountable against — party framing rather than scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we have seen from the Government that is sitting on the Treasury benches today is a decision that they are going to roll back world-leading smoke-free legislation—that would have seen smoke-free generations in New Zealand—with a Minister of Finance who thinks it is OK to baldly say that the revenue is needed to fund the tax cuts.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (repeal of the smokefree legislation), the mechanism (tobacco excise revenue) and the purpose it is put to (funding the tax package). Legitimate scrutiny of a named government decision, which is the job of an Opposition MP.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve seen a shambolic start to Government from this three-headed being that is our Government. We’ve seen the two junior partners in the coalition running rings around the Prime Minister.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the coalition's internal dynamics — who is dominating whom — with no policy, measure or outcome named. This is the tribal-framing case rather than accountability against a commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All that the principles talk about is partnership. They talk about good faith. They talk about participation. That’s what the principles are about.
specificity.explanation: Names three particular principles (partnership, good faith, participation), which is more than a platitude, but supplies no source, statutory reference or wording that would let someone check the enumeration.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are 21,000 new public housing places funded by the previous Governments between 2017 and 2023.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure attached to a named programme and a defined period — someone could go to the housing supply data and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the funny thing here is that Seymour and this Government will be playing into Māori hands, who never supported the Treaty principles anyway.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: because Māori never supported the principles, reopening them helps rather than harms Māori. The premise is offered (Matike Mai, article 2) but is stated absolutely — 'never supported' — while the same speech says Māori health professionals and others defend Treaty-based institutions, so the conclusion overreaches a premise with real exceptions. A gap between what was shown and what was concluded, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don’t think there are many New Zealanders who voted—thinking they might like a tax cut—that thought they were voting for a tax cut that was premised on increased revenue from cigarettes and rolling back world-leading legislation.
rigor.explanation: An inference about what voters understood themselves to be voting for, offered with nothing to support it — no polling, no survey, no campaign material. It engages the actual policy rather than the other party's character, so it is a real argument, but the conclusion rests on an assumed public opinion (an appeal to the speaker's own sense of what voters thought).
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I said there would be civil disobedience—not my choice. I said you’ll get protests worse than the Springbok Tour. That’s all going to come to fruition, all because of this Government—this Government who said they’re going to get rid of division; they’re going to make things equal for everyone.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that opposition to the Government's Treaty principles policy will produce civil disobedience and protest exceeding the 1981 Springbok Tour.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Comparison of Treaty-related protest activity in this parliamentary term against the 1981 Springbok Tour protests on the measures that define that benchmark — number of participants, duration, and arrests (1981: sustained nationwide protest over ~two months, roughly 150,000 participants and around 2,000 arrests). True if Treaty protest in this term exceeds the Springbok Tour on participation and involves comparable sustained civil disobedience and arrests; false if protest, however large, remains lawful, brief, and without comparable arrest numbers.

focus.statement: Labour were a party at the election who stood for nothing.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party in general terms — no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. This is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The most egregious thing that happened under the last Government—in fact, under Chris Hipkins’ watch as Minister of Education—was the fact that our achievement went backwards.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific portfolio and a specific outcome (student achievement declining) rather than the other party's character. Holding a former minister to account for a measurable result is on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Labour were a party at the election who stood for nothing.
civility.explanation: Attacks a party, not a person; no individual is insulted, so it passes Civility cleanly even though it is content-free.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: David Parker, the most senior Minister in Government, threw his toys, gave up his revenue portfolio, because his vision for tax reform: gone by lunchtime under Chris Hipkins.
civility.explanation: "Threw his toys" is a personal jibe at a named member, imputing a childish temper rather than engaging the tax-policy disagreement. The substantive point could have been made without it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When Jan Tinetti said on the news, after Labour’s defeat, that she felt a great weight had been lifted off her shoulders when she lost her job as education Minister, I say it is my great privilege and great honour to take on this huge responsibility: of ensuring that our children experience academic success and we bring it back to the heart of our education system.
civility.explanation: Uses a named member's personal remark about relief to imply she did not value the responsibility, contrasting it with the speaker's own dedication. It is an insinuation about a person's commitment rather than a criticism of anything she did in office.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The worst defeat of any Government in this country ever was this previous Government because they stood for nothing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2023 result was the largest defeat suffered by any incumbent New Zealand government in history.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission / historical NZ general election results: change in the governing party's vote share and seat count at each election since 1890. True if Labour's 2023 loss (50.0% to 26.9%, 65 to 34 seats) is the largest such fall on record; false if any earlier government lost more, e.g. the 1935 Coalition.

veracity.statement: David Parker, the most senior Minister in Government, threw his toys, gave up his revenue portfolio, because his vision for tax reform: gone by lunchtime under Chris Hipkins.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that David Parker was the most senior minister in the Hipkins Government, and that he relinquished the Revenue portfolio because his tax reform plan was dropped.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet ranking list of the Hipkins ministry (published by DPMC in 2023) and the ministerial list record for Parker's Revenue portfolio. True if Parker was ranked most senior below the PM and gave up Revenue following the tax-policy decision; false if he was ranked lower or retained/left the portfolio for another reason.

veracity.statement: The Programme for International Student Assessment results last night just confirmed that decline.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the PISA results released the previous evening showed a continuing decline in New Zealand student performance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD PISA 2022 country results for New Zealand (released 5 December 2023), mean scores in mathematics, reading and science compared with the 2018 and earlier cycles. True if the 2022 means are significantly lower and continue a downward trend; false if they are stable or improved.

veracity.statement: We will remove the distraction of cellphones in our schools, because we know that the evidence shows that our kids improve their achievement and also their wellbeing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that research evidence shows school cellphone restrictions improve student achievement and wellbeing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed studies and meta-analyses of school cellphone bans and student outcomes (e.g. Beland & Murphy 2016; subsequent replication and review studies). True if they consistently show significant gains in achievement and wellbeing; false if effects are null, mixed, or confined to narrow subgroups.

veracity.statement: Let me just remind this House how Labour proposed to teach mathematics through a critical awareness of wider political and ideological and economic issues, addressing issues of power, social justice, and equality.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government's draft mathematics curriculum framed maths teaching in terms of political, ideological and economic critique, power, social justice and equality.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 draft Mathematics and Statistics learning area of the refreshed New Zealand Curriculum (Te Mātaiaho), as published for consultation by the Ministry of Education. True if it contains framing in those terms; false if that language is absent or is being read in from a different document.

rigor.statement: Nothing about improving achievement outcomes for our kids. Nothing about how many kids we got to curriculum. Nothing about how we improved our NCEA results. Nothing about getting our kids to school. And there’s a reason for that. It’s because they failed abysmally.
rigor.explanation: Argument from silence: the premise is what an opponent omitted from one speech, and the conclusion drawn is abysmal policy failure. What a speech leaves out does not establish the underlying result; the achievement data she cites elsewhere would, but it is not what is offered here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We will remove the distraction of cellphones in our schools, because we know that the evidence shows that our kids improve their achievement and also their wellbeing.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, but it rests on an unnamed appeal to authority — "the evidence shows" — with no study, effect size or source given, and it jumps from a ban to gains in both achievement and wellbeing without connecting them.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: National is a party that stands for delivery; we stand for outcomes; we stand for evidence, front-line results, and improving people’s lives.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — delivery, outcomes, evidence, results — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have set a very ambitious target of getting 80 percent of our kids to curriculum by the time they leave intermediate.
specificity.explanation: A named figure (80 percent), a defined population and a defined milestone (end of intermediate). Checkable against curriculum-level achievement data; loses a little for carrying no date by which the target must be met.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We already know that most schools do this, but we are ensuring that it’s formalised and that there is consistency across the country so that every child—no matter where they go to school—has access to an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths.
specificity.explanation: A concrete quantum (an hour a day), the subjects named, and the mechanism stated (formalising an existing practice as a national requirement). Someone could check whether it happened.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Under our Government, the trends of decline, the decline in performance, the trends of teacher retention: they stop.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the measured decline in New Zealand student performance halts during this parliamentary term. Not a promise of a specific action but a claim about an outcome in the world.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: OECD PISA 2025 results for New Zealand (due for publication in December 2026), mean scores in mathematics, reading and science compared with 2022. True if none shows a statistically significant further decline; false if any continues to fall.

civility.statement: But that’s not John Key that you’ve got over there; that’s a corporate middle manager who himself said today, from that chair, that the Government’s “Under new management”.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the Prime Minister personally as "a corporate middle manager" — a jibe at the person's stature and calibre rather than at any policy. Contested setting with a real opportunity to stay on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If you want to have boot camps, be honest and say you want to have boot camps because you don’t like these people. The people, the families, the communities that they come from are not your communities, so you don’t care about them and you want to shut them off and you want to cart them off and shut them away.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith and indifference as the real motive for the policy — members opposite are said not to care about the communities affected and to be dissembling about why. That is an attack on motive rather than on the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, a lot of what the Key Government did was more progressive than what that Government’s proposing, so you should be utterly and totally ashamed of yourself.
civility.explanation: The comparison itself is a fair policy point, but it is delivered as a demand that members opposite be "utterly and totally ashamed" of themselves — shaming the people rather than criticising the programme.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member for Banks Peninsula, Vanessa Weenink, GP, would have had people come into her practice with emphysema caused by smoking addiction. Will she vote for it or will she uphold her Hippocratic Oath that says “Do no harm.”?
civility.explanation: Singles out a named member and frames her forthcoming vote as a choice between her party and her medical ethics. Pointed and personal — it questions her integrity as a doctor — though it stops short of insult and is tethered to an actual vote.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And here’s one of the things that this Speech from the Throne says: “for the past several years the number of people employed in the public service has grown at a rate that has not been matched by a commensurate increase in the level of services provided to the public.” Does that sound like Christopher Luxon to you? No, that’s the 2008 Speech from the Throne.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the quoted passage about public service headcount outgrowing service levels comes from the 2008 Speech from the Throne, not the 2023 one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Speech from the Throne delivered at the opening of the 49th Parliament (December 2008), published in Hansard; true if it contains that sentence substantially as quoted, false if the wording does not appear there.

veracity.statement: And here’s a new idea, a regulatory standards bill will be passed—like this one from 2011 that wasn’t passed, or this one from 2021 that wasn’t passed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Regulatory Standards Bill was before the House in 2011 and again in 2021, and that neither was enacted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills register / Hansard first-reading division records for the Regulatory Standards Bill 2011 and the Regulatory Standards Bill 2021; true if both were introduced and neither passed into law, false if either was enacted or if no such bill existed in either year.

veracity.statement: The evidence on boot camps is that it disenfranchises and alienates the young people that go there. It makes them network with other disenfranchised young people and it makes reoffending greater and it puts those people into a cycle of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the research evidence shows boot camps increase reoffending via alienation and criminal peer networks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ evaluations of military-style activity camps (MSD/Oranga Tamariki, and the Department of Corrections' own reviews) plus international meta-analyses of correctional boot camps (e.g. Campbell Collaboration / Washington State Institute for Public Policy); true if the weight of that evidence shows recidivism unchanged-to-worse for boot-camp participants, false if it shows a reliable reduction in reoffending.

veracity.statement: On that note, I’d like for him and his colleagues to, potentially, actually think about how, under the previous Labour Government, they had a 65-seat majority—it was a complete majority ever in the history of, you know, MMP, and they haven’t actually achieved anything, really. They haven’t delivered for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour Government held 65 seats and that this was the only single-party majority in the history of MMP in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the 2020 general election and the seat allocations for every MMP Parliament since 1996; true if Labour was allocated 65 seats in 2020 and no other party has held an outright majority under MMP, false if the seat count differs or another single-party majority exists.

rigor.statement: As Richard Ekins said in the New Zealand Universities Law Review, it’s “reckless lawmaking”—it’s unconstitutional, it politicises the Public Service, and it threatens the rule of law.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the three substantive conclusions (unconstitutional, politicises the Public Service, threatens the rule of law) rest entirely on a cited academic's say-so, with no reasoning offered as to why the bill has those effects. A named scholarly source in a law review is a legitimate thing to lean on, so this is a real gap rather than a bare fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is laughable. You know, so you’re going to have an entire machinery to cut costs. That is absolutely ridiculous.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to ridicule. There is an implicit argument about a real policy — that a new department to cut regulatory cost is self-defeating — but nothing is offered to support it beyond declaring it laughable and ridiculous.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The evidence on boot camps is that it disenfranchises and alienates the young people that go there. It makes them network with other disenfranchised young people and it makes reoffending greater and it puts those people into a cycle of crime.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal chain is set out — alienation, peer association, higher reoffending — which supports the conclusion that the policy fails on its own terms. Marked down because the "evidence" is asserted rather than cited to any study or evaluation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member for Banks Peninsula, Vanessa Weenink, GP, would have had people come into her practice with emphysema caused by smoking addiction. Will she vote for it or will she uphold her Hippocratic Oath that says “Do no harm.”?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the question is posed as voting for the bill OR honouring the Hippocratic Oath, with no room for any reading in which a member could support the measure and still consider herself doing no harm. The emphysema anecdote is offered as emotional support rather than evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Rolling back the protections that John Key started, that Kris Faafoi finished, that means that you don’t have truck shops cruising around South Auckland selling essential goods on 100 percent interest rates.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy lineage (the consumer credit protections begun under Key and completed by Faafoi), the concrete practice being prevented (truck shops in South Auckland), and an interest-rate figure. Short of full marks: no bill, section or date is named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As for Māori, this Government is intending to do nothing other than roll back: roll back the Treaty, roll back the equity progress that’s been made, roll back the functions of the Waitangi Tribunal—which has a fundamental role in pointing out the missteps of Government—and roll back the Māori Health Authority.
specificity.explanation: Two of the four items are concrete institutions (the Waitangi Tribunal's functions, the Māori Health Authority); the other two — "the Treaty" and "the equity progress" — are directional with no mechanism, figure or timeframe attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So why don’t you have an original idea of your own to face the real problems that are facing New Zealand today: the problems of climate change, the problems of housing, the problems of the health system.
focus.explanation: Three real policy domains are named, but the weight of the sentence is the party charge that the other side has no original ideas rather than engagement with any of the three.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On that note, I’d like for him and his colleagues to, potentially, actually think about how, under the previous Labour Government, they had a 65-seat majority—it was a complete majority ever in the history of, you know, MMP, and they haven’t actually achieved anything, really. They haven’t delivered for New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: A sweeping verdict on the other party's whole term with no measure, figure or programme named — the policy example (light rail) only arrives in the following, unfinished sentence. This is the party-record framing Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They had 65 members, a complete majority in this House; they could not deliver a centimetre of that light rail—it’s a light fail.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (Auckland light rail), the specific commitment (all the way to Auckland Airport, by 2021) and the specific outcome (nothing built). This is scrutiny of a named commitment, which is the job of a government MP holding the previous government to account — high focus, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They had 65 members, a complete majority in this House; they could not deliver a centimetre of that light rail—it’s a light fail.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) Labour held 65 seats and an outright majority in the 2020–23 Parliament and (b) no light rail was constructed at all.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Parliament composition after the 2020 general election (Labour's seat count) and Auckland Light Rail project construction records to December 2023; true if Labour held 65 seats with a single-party majority and no light rail track was laid, false if the seat count is materially different or any track was constructed.

veracity.statement: Instead, what did they deliver? 14,000 public servants and 1,400 KiwiBuild homes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2017–2023 Labour government added about 14,000 public servants and completed about 1,400 KiwiBuild homes against a 100,000-home pledge.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public Service Commission workforce data for headcount/FTE growth 2017–2023, and Ministry of Housing and Urban Development KiwiBuild completion figures as at late 2023; true if the public service grew by roughly 14,000 and KiwiBuild completions were roughly 1,400, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: So the profile for emissions in New Zealand was worse under that Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's emissions were higher during the 2017–2023 Labour government than previously.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment New Zealand Greenhouse Gas Inventory, gross and net emissions for 2017–2022 compared with the preceding period; true if emissions rose over that term, false if they were flat or falling.

veracity.statement: They didn’t deliver on anything when they had a majority.
veracity.explanation: An absolute claim that the 2020–2023 Labour government delivered none of its commitments. Extracted as hyperbole, which is now a veracity matter: an overstated claim is an inaccurate claim, and this one is checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative and policy record of the 2020–2023 Parliament — bills passed and manifesto commitments implemented (e.g. Fair Pay Agreements, minimum wage increases, the smokefree legislation); false if any significant commitment was delivered, true only if none was.

specificity.statement: Instead, what did they deliver? 14,000 public servants and 1,400 KiwiBuild homes.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable figures against a named programme. Someone could go and verify both numbers. Whether they are accurate is Veracity's question, not this one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can just guarantee that I won’t be wasting $20 million trying to actually dream up something called ANZPM—Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media bill—and literally pay nearly $20 million to consultants who had absolutely no clue about broadcasting.
specificity.explanation: A named programme, a named bill, a dollar figure and the specific object of the spending. Concrete enough that the spend could be looked up and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As the Prime Minister the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon stated, our 100-day plan is focused on rebuilding the economy, easing the cost of living, restoring law and order, and delivering better public services.
specificity.explanation: Names a real, identifiable instrument (the coalition's 100-day plan), which lifts it above a pure slogan, but the four goals listed are generic directions with no mechanism, cost, target or date attached. A listener could not check or act on anything here beyond the existence of the plan.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I guess it’s actually—I think we need to look at the emission profile of the previous Government’s performance when they have to import so much coal from Indonesia because they couldn’t actually power the generators, so they had to actually import coal from overseas. So the profile for emissions in New Zealand was worse under that Labour Government.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy area, but a weak one: it moves from a single input (imported Indonesian coal for electricity generation) to a conclusion about New Zealand's entire emissions profile. That is a hasty generalisation from one sector to the national inventory; nothing is offered to show the coal imports outweighed movements in the other emitting sectors. Scored here rather than under Focus because there is a genuine argument about a policy outcome left once the party framing is stripped out.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You know, there was no reason to bring Radio New Zealand and TVNZ together, and they weren’t going to deliver for New Zealanders something that they didn’t already deliver separately as Radio New Zealand and TVNZ.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: the preceding sentence's premise is that the Minister 'couldn't give us a realistic answer', from which the speaker concludes there was 'no reason' at all. Not having heard a satisfactory rationale does not establish that none exists, and the second clause simply restates the conclusion rather than supporting it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I can just guarantee that I won’t be wasting $20 million trying to actually dream up something called ANZPM—Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media bill—and literally pay nearly $20 million to consultants who had absolutely no clue about broadcasting.
civility.explanation: The criticism of the ANZPM programme itself would be fine at any volume, but 'consultants who had absolutely no clue about broadcasting' is a swipe at the competence of the people involved rather than at the policy, and it is set up as a contrast with the named predecessor Minister. That is imputed incompetence, short of a direct insult — a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale rather than the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I witnessed earlier in the House isn’t the House that I think represents our people.
civility.explanation: Criticises the conduct of the earlier debate — a genuine opportunity to be uncivil, since he could have named and attacked the members involved — but keeps it entirely on the behaviour and the standard expected, naming nobody and imputing no bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t want to hear any celebration of the new migrant members of the Government’s caucus, who are complicit—who are completely complicit—in driving a divide between our migrant communities and Māori.
civility.explanation: Turns on identifiable people — the new migrant MPs in the Government caucus — and imputes bad faith to them personally ("completely complicit" in dividing communities) rather than criticising a policy. Repetition sharpens it into a character charge.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It makes me sad to think that Te Aka Whai Ora has not been given a chance; that Te Aka Whai Ora is not just about the delivery of equitable services in our community, but more importantly—and we’ll approach this when we come to the debate—it is about holding the Pākehā system or the actual health system in this country to account, making sure that that system can continue to deliver better services for our people.
focus.explanation: Engages a named measure before the House (the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora) and what it was designed to do — accountability of the mainstream health system. No party framing; entirely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t smoke and I’m proud of that, and my tamariki don’t smoke, my nephews and nieces, they don’t smoke—simply because of the changes that a brave Government in their day made many years ago.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the smokefree measures the Government proposes to reverse, not about the other party. On-policy even though the argument for it is weak — the classic high-focus/low-rigor pair.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a dog whistle that hides the fact that this Government will be criminalising people, because when you strip people of their only legal source of surviving, you put people in a position where their only way to survive is to commit a crime, and so this Government is actually working against the goal of reducing crime by creating a generation of people who will have no means of surviving.
focus.explanation: Directed at a named policy — benefit sanctions and the "tough on crime" agenda — and argues about its mechanism and effects, rather than about what the other party is like. Weak reasoning does not make it off-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t want to hear any celebration of the new migrant members of the Government’s caucus, who are complicit—who are completely complicit—in driving a divide between our migrant communities and Māori.
focus.explanation: Entirely about who the other side's MPs are and what they are like. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don’t smoke and I’m proud of that, and my tamariki don’t smoke, my nephews and nieces, they don’t smoke—simply because of the changes that a brave Government in their day made many years ago.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy — smokefree legislation caused his family not to smoke — but it rests entirely on personal anecdote and asserts sole causation ("simply because of") from a single household. Appeal to anecdote plus post hoc reasoning.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s a dog whistle that hides the fact that this Government will be criminalising people, because when you strip people of their only legal source of surviving, you put people in a position where their only way to survive is to commit a crime, and so this Government is actually working against the goal of reducing crime by creating a generation of people who will have no means of surviving.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal argument about the sanctions policy, but each step overreaches what was offered: benefit sanctions are treated as removing the *only* legal income, that in turn as leaving crime the *only* means of survival, and the outcome is scaled to "a generation". Sequence of unsupported jumps rather than a supported inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, the person who I’d like to call the godfather of Māori health, Sir Mason Durie, was the leader of that particular kaupapa and initiative—not me, not the Minister of Health in the day, but actually Sir Mason Durie.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Sir Mason Durie, not ministers, led the design and establishment of the Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of the establishment of Te Aka Whai Ora — Ministry of Health and Cabinet papers, and the membership/chairmanship of the interim Māori Health Authority board announced in 2021. True if Sir Mason Durie held the leading design or chair role; false if the initiative was led by ministers or officials with Durie in an advisory or nominal capacity.

veracity.statement: Now I wish those eloquent words were mine, but they were indeed the words of my grandfather, the late Sir James Hēnare, who in September of 1988—in Parliament House, here—addressed the members of Parliament and used those words 35 years ago.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the quoted passage about a referendum on the Treaty and being "numerically inferior to our other treaty partner" to Sir James Hēnare, delivered to MPs at Parliament House in September 1988.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Archival/parliamentary record of an address by Sir James Hēnare at Parliament House in September 1988 (e.g. AJHR, select committee records, Ngā Taonga or newspaper reports of the day). True if such an address occurred in that month and contains the quoted wording; false if no such address exists, the date is materially wrong, or the words belong to someone else.

veracity.statement: In fact, the words “poverty” and “inequality” did not get a single mention in today’s speech.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neither the word "poverty" nor the word "inequality" appears anywhere in the Speech from the Throne delivered on 6 December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published text of the Speech from the Throne, 6 December 2023 (Hansard / Governor-General's website). True if a word search for "poverty" and "inequality" returns zero hits; false if either word appears even once.

veracity.statement: We were talking about 17,000 mothers who were being sanctioned at that time for not naming the father of their children.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a figure of roughly 17,000 sole mothers subject to the section 70A benefit deduction for not naming the other parent, as at around 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development benefit-sanction statistics for the section 70A deduction (or the equivalent OIA releases) for 2017. True if the number of sole parents under that sanction was approximately 17,000; false if it was materially different (e.g. under 12,000 or over 22,000).

veracity.statement: The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) in Wellington has been unable to even keep track, for example, of the number of people that attend those seminars.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MSD does not hold or record data on how many beneficiaries attend the mandatory work seminars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD responses to Official Information Act requests or written parliamentary questions about attendance at work seminars. True if MSD has stated it does not hold or cannot produce attendance numbers; false if MSD publishes or has supplied those figures.

specificity.statement: We were talking about 17,000 mothers who were being sanctioned at that time for not naming the father of their children.
specificity.explanation: Carries a figure, a population, a time reference and the precise ground of the sanction — someone could go and check it against MSD data.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Do you know, I actually had a time before, when I was listening to some of the speeches, that I thought, “Do the Government realise they’re in Government now, or are they still thinking they’re in Opposition?”—because their speeches were more about us, and more about Labour than what they’re going to do, and that is what I have heard all day: I have heard only about us, repealing, and going backwards.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's conduct — that they talk about Labour rather than govern. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing on-policy to hold onto. This is party-directed commentary, not scrutiny of a named commitment. Nothing is emitted for Rigor: strip out the part about the other team and no argument remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’ve even heard that the Minister has been saying, “Well, most schools do teach an hour a day of reading, writing, and mathematics; it’s just the odd few that don’t.” So what’s the problem that we’re trying to solve here?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure itself — the one hour a day of reading, writing and mathematics — and on what problem it is meant to solve. A named policy, engaged on its merits.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New Zealand is going backwards under this Government and will go backwards and not forwards.
specificity.explanation: A bare directional assertion. No figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy — nothing a listener could check or act on. Not emitted for Divination either: 'going backwards' has no stateable falsification criterion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Child poverty: 77,000 fewer children in poverty than when we took office.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable figure tied to a named domain and a stated baseline ('when we took office'). Missing only the measure used, which is what stops it being a 1.0.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Child poverty: 77,000 fewer children in poverty than when we took office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of children in poverty fell by 77,000 between Labour taking office (2017) and the time of speaking, on the measure the speaker implies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics release: compare the number of children below the 50% of median equivalised household income after-housing-costs threshold for the 2017/18 baseline year against the most recent year published before December 2023. True if the reduction is approximately 77,000 children on that or the primary headline measure; false if the reduction is materially smaller, or if it only reaches 77,000 on a measure not in the official set.

veracity.statement: All of the wonderful things happening in health: things like three million free prescriptions; the increase in Pharmac’s funding by 51 percent.
veracity.explanation: Two factual claims about the previous government's health record: that roughly three million prescriptions have been dispensed free since the $5 co-payment was removed, and that Pharmac's funding rose by 51 percent under that government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) Te Whatu Ora / Ministry of Health reporting on prescriptions dispensed without the $5 co-payment since 1 July 2023 — true if the count is around three million by December 2023. (b) Pharmac annual reports and Vote Health budget documents comparing the combined pharmaceutical budget for 2023/24 against 2017/18 — true if the increase is approximately 51%, false if materially different or if the 51% figure only holds for a differently-defined baseline.

veracity.statement: The 2020 guidelines brought a bigger focus on to consent, not gender diversity—gender diversity was already there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2020 Ministry of Education relationships and sexuality education guidelines expanded the treatment of consent, and that gender diversity content was already present in the earlier (2015) guidelines rather than newly introduced in 2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the Ministry of Education 'Sexuality Education: A Guide for Principals, Boards of Trustees and Teachers' (2015) with 'Relationships and Sexuality Education' (2020). True if gender diversity content appears in the 2015 guide and the 2020 revision materially expands consent content; false if gender diversity content is absent from the 2015 guide, or if consent coverage was not expanded in 2020.

rigor.statement: Well, first of all, what are charter schools if they are not ideology? That’s exactly what charter schools are—exactly; they are exactly ideology.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the conclusion ('charter schools are ideology') simply restates the rhetorical question that was offered as its support, with emphasis substituting for evidence. No criterion for what makes a policy ideological is given, and none is applied to charter schools. This does engage a policy before the House, so it is properly assessed here rather than dismissed as a jibe — the argument is real, and weak.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve even heard that the Minister has been saying, “Well, most schools do teach an hour a day of reading, writing, and mathematics; it’s just the odd few that don’t.” So what’s the problem that we’re trying to solve here?
rigor.explanation: A sound inference: if the practice the policy mandates is already near-universal by the Minister's own account, the mandate addresses little. The step from premise to conclusion holds. Marked down from the top only because it rests on a second-hand report of what the Minister said and treats 'most' as though it were 'all' — the 'odd few' are precisely the case a mandate would target.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, guess what! That sounds like national standards mark two, and how well did that work out for the Government last time? What a failure for our kids, and they are still feeling the outfall from that, even today.
rigor.explanation: The equivalence between the new assessment policy and national standards is asserted by resemblance ('sounds like') and never demonstrated — no feature of the two schemes is compared. The conclusion then rests on a rhetorical question and an appeal to emotion ('what a failure for our kids') rather than on evidence of the earlier policy's effects. Guilt by association plus appeal to consequences.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, the Government need to go through and make certain that they read those before they make such rash statements, because they are only harming communities who are already under threat and in a minority in this country.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism aimed at the Government's process and the effect of its policy, not at any individual. The suggestion that they have not read the guidelines is pointed and edges toward imputing carelessness, which keeps it just below a clean 1.0, but no person's character, competence or worth is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have heard three contributions from the Government, and each and every single one of them slagged us off.
focus.explanation: A debate on the Speech from the Throne is squarely a policy occasion, but this sentence is entirely about the other side's rhetorical conduct — no measure, figure or outcome is named. It is a complaint about the other team, which is what Focus exists to catch. (No Rigor item: strip out the part about the Government and there is no inference left to assess.)
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why have they not mentioned that they are going to bring in a rule that allows employers to sack people within 90 days without giving any single reason?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy of the Government and its concrete mechanism. Demanding the Government account for a measure it has not mentioned is scrutiny, which is the job of an opposition MP, so this scores at the top regardless of the rhetorical framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I wonder if the reason why they haven’t mentioned those is because, within the first week, their Cabinet had leaked the document to the media that contained advice that said very clearly that repealing fair pay agreements would disproportionately disadvantage women, Māori, Pasifika, youth, and low-wage workers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that Cabinet material was leaked to media within the new Government's first week and (b) that the leaked advice identified those five groups as disproportionately disadvantaged by repealing fair pay agreements. The rhetorical 'I wonder if' frames the motive, but the factual content about the document is asserted, not speculated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The official advice on repeal of the Fair Pay Agreements Act that reached media in the first week of the coalition Government (MBIE advice / regulatory impact material, as reported late November–December 2023). True if that advice states that repeal would disproportionately disadvantage women, Māori, Pasifika, youth and low-wage workers; false if no such advice reached the media, or if it does not identify those groups as disproportionately affected.

veracity.statement: Why have they not mentioned that they are going to bring in a rule that allows employers to sack people within 90 days without giving any single reason?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a stated intention of the incoming Government that trial periods of 90 days, during which an employee can be dismissed without any reason being given, will be available to employers generally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements and the resulting employment law amendment. True if 90-day trial periods are extended to employers of all sizes with dismissal in that period requiring no stated reason and attracting no personal grievance for unjustified dismissal; false if the policy is narrower (e.g. small employers only) or requires reasons to be given.

veracity.statement: They didn’t add up before the election; they certainly don’t add up after they’ve given Shane Jones $1.2 billion and given the ACT Party interest deductibility backdated to April.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable commitments are asserted: a $1.2 billion allocation attached to Shane Jones, and restoration of interest deductibility backdated to April, both said to post-date the campaign costings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–NZ First and National–ACT coalition agreements published 24 November 2023. True if the NZ First agreement commits $1.2 billion to a regional infrastructure fund associated with Shane Jones and the ACT agreement restores interest deductibility for residential property with effect backdated to an April start date; false if either figure or the backdating is materially different.

rigor.statement: The reason this Government wants to get rid of the Māori Health Authority is because of the first word in those three words. That’s it: “Māori”.
rigor.explanation: This engages a named policy, so it is a real inference rather than a jibe — but the inference is weak. The support offered is an argument from asymmetry (the rural health strategy is not being repealed, and rural people vote for them) plus an appeal to absence of any other explanation. Neither establishes the motive claimed; other reasons for abolishing the Authority are simply not addressed, so the conclusion outruns the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So when you’ve got a $10 billion hole in your transport budget and at least a $2 billion hole in your tax budget, and then you add on $1.2 billion for Shane Jones and God knows how many millions for the ACT Party, that’s a massive hole—a massive hole that Nicola Willis is desperately trying to put on us, even though the thing she’s pointing to was already out there in the public domain, and two of them are already factored into their fiscal plan.
specificity.explanation: Carries named figures against named budget lines ($10b transport, $2b tax, $1.2b) and identifies who is said to be shifting the blame, so the arithmetic could be checked against the fiscal plan. It falls short of the top because the amounts are not sourced and 'God knows how many millions' is left open.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So when you’ve got a $10 billion hole in your transport budget and at least a $2 billion hole in your tax budget, and then you add on $1.2 billion for Shane Jones and God knows how many millions for the ACT Party, that’s a massive hole—a massive hole that Nicola Willis is desperately trying to put on us, even though the thing she’s pointing to was already out there in the public domain, and two of them are already factored into their fiscal plan.
civility.explanation: Pointed, and it does land on a named individual — 'desperately trying to put on us' imputes a motive to Nicola Willis rather than only disputing her numbers. But it stops well short of attacking her character, competence or worth, and the substance of the exchange is about the fiscal plan.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It made the massive hole in their fiscal plan just a little bit smaller, and what it will mean by reversing the smokefree rules that have been coming in is that, for those young people who wouldn’t have taken up smoking, some of them will, and some of them will die from it.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the smokefree measures will cause young people who would otherwise not have started smoking to take it up. This is a prediction about the effect of another party's policy, not a promise about the speaker's own action; the second limb (some will die of it) is the long-run consequence and is not separately observable within the window.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / NZ Health Survey daily-smoking and smoking-initiation rates for 15–24-year-olds, measured against the pre-repeal trend. True if youth smoking uptake stops falling or rises after the December 2023 repeal of the Smokefree Environments amendments (denicotinisation, retailer reduction, smokefree generation), relative to the trajectory in the years before repeal; false if youth uptake continues to fall at or above the pre-repeal rate.

rigor.statement: Indeed, we campaigned on those; we gained a mandate on the basis of doing so. It would be strange, and indeed anti-democratic, were we not to follow through with those policies—so we will.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about policy: campaigned on X, won, therefore reversing X is democratically required. The step is coherent but leans on an appeal to mandate — an election win does not establish majority support for each individual policy in the platform, and the leap to 'anti-democratic' overstates what the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I’m pleased to say that along with other aspects of the Government’s programme in removing the wasteful industry transformation plans, or ITPs, likewise in the building construction sector, while we commit very firmly and strongly to talking with the sector, we won’t do it through a mechanism that has not been productive at all in the way that the Government had intended. We will save the taxpayer money by doing so, and therefore we will make a contribution to reducing those cost of living pressures that we rightly talked about during the campaign and on which basis New Zealanders have given us a mandate to go forward and govern.
rigor.explanation: A real chain of reasoning about a real measure, but with a large unbridged gap: scrapping the industry transformation plans saves money, therefore cost-of-living pressures fall. No magnitude is offered to connect a departmental programme saving to household costs, so the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: With all due respect to Ms Tinetti, when she talks about issues and decries our focus on ensuring that at least one hour of math, reading, and writing takes place every day, well, it’s not very much help if we don’t have school classrooms in which to be able to actually conduct those.
rigor.explanation: The inference does not answer the objection it is aimed at. A shortage of classrooms is a separate problem from whether the one-hour requirement is sound policy; offering it as a rebuttal to Tinetti's criticism of that requirement is a change of subject rather than a refutation.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In building and construction, we’ve seen far too little progress lately on the question of how we can allow the building sector to be more productive, less bound by regulation; while acknowledging, of course, where safety is an issue of workers, but of course in terms of the abilities of buildings to be safe and secure environments too.
specificity.explanation: The incoming Minister for Building and Construction sets out his portfolio direction with no named regulation, no mechanism, no timeframe and no figure — 'more productive, less bound by regulation' with a balancing nod to safety. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I’m pleased to say that along with other aspects of the Government’s programme in removing the wasteful industry transformation plans, or ITPs, likewise in the building construction sector, while we commit very firmly and strongly to talking with the sector, we won’t do it through a mechanism that has not been productive at all in the way that the Government had intended. We will save the taxpayer money by doing so, and therefore we will make a contribution to reducing those cost of living pressures that we rightly talked about during the campaign and on which basis New Zealanders have given us a mandate to go forward and govern.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific mechanism — removing the industry transformation plans in the building and construction sector — which is checkable and actionable, but supplies no saving figure, no timeframe and no account of what replaces the consultation mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will improve the situation with law and order in our New Zealand cities, towns, and indeed rural areas. We will improve health and education services.
specificity.explanation: A list of directions with nothing attached: no target, no measure, no timeframe, no mechanism. 'Improve health and education services' commits to nothing that anyone could later check against.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Some valuable work was undertaken two terms ago, led by the Hon Ron Mark, who was very passionate about this work, and consultation was undertaken in relation to the idea of a covenant—or a kawenata—to reflect that special bond of service between New Zealand and these fine women and men who put themselves forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during the 2017–2020 term, under Minister for Veterans Ron Mark, work was undertaken and public consultation held on a proposed veterans' covenant (kawenata).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Veterans' Affairs New Zealand / Ministry of Defence records and ministerial releases from the 2017–2020 parliamentary term: true if a consultation on a veterans' covenant or kawenata was run under Ron Mark as Minister for Veterans, false if no such consultation or work programme existed in that term or if it was led by another Minister.

veracity.statement: They need the space; this is an important project, but it turns out that through considerable mismanagement, over-promising, under-delivering, announcements being favoured over the hard reality of delivery, and a mismatch of rhetoric and reality, this project now appears not to be able to be funded given the state of the books that have been left with us.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the planned major innovation centre at Kaipara College cannot now be funded, and that this follows from the state of the accounts inherited from the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property and capital works records for Kaipara College as at late 2023: true if the innovation centre project was unfunded, deferred or removed from the capital programme at that date, false if funding for it was allocated and available.

focus.statement: They need the space; this is an important project, but it turns out that through considerable mismanagement, over-promising, under-delivering, announcements being favoured over the hard reality of delivery, and a mismatch of rhetoric and reality, this project now appears not to be able to be funded given the state of the books that have been left with us.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project at a specific school in his electorate and a specific outcome — that it now appears unfundable. That is scrutiny of a named commitment, which is on-policy. Marked down only because a third of the sentence is generic 'rhetoric and reality' party framing rather than the project itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: With all due respect to Ms Tinetti, when she talks about issues and decries our focus on ensuring that at least one hour of math, reading, and writing takes place every day, well, it’s not very much help if we don’t have school classrooms in which to be able to actually conduct those.
focus.explanation: Squarely on education policy: it names the incoming one-hour-a-day literacy and numeracy requirement and sets it against school property capacity. A specific measure is engaged, not the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, actually, some of those Government Ministers should be looking in a mirror and reflecting, quite literally, upon the cause of some of the malaise across this country and including, particularly, as I say, in the education system.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the people opposite and their blameworthiness. 'Malaise across this country' names no measure, no figure and no outcome; the only policy content is the passing gesture at the education system.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I say to her: it would be helpful for her to reflect on her legacy and her Government’s legacy.
civility.explanation: Pointed and condescending toward the individual — an invitation to reflect on her 'legacy' is a sneer directed at the person rather than an argument about the policy — but it stops short of a direct insult or an attack on her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: His desire is to do away with the funding for staff of the Crown that are proficient in the Māori language.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an incoming Minister announced, on or about 6 December 2023, the removal of te reo Māori proficiency payments/allowances for public servants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, press releases or media reporting from the incoming Minister responsible for the public service in the week to 6 December 2023; true if a minister announced ending te reo Māori proficiency payments/allowances for Crown employees, false if no such announcement was made or if it concerned something materially different.

veracity.statement: In the time of my grandparents, when they were at school, they were beaten for speaking the Māori language.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori children of her grandparents' generation were physically punished at school for speaking te reo Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record of the Native Schools system, including Waitangi Tribunal Wai 11 (te reo Māori claim) findings and recorded oral testimony; true if corporal punishment of Māori pupils for speaking te reo at school in the early-to-mid twentieth century is documented, false if the record shows no such practice.

veracity.statement: Well, the petition and march for the Māori language arrived here in the year 1985.
veracity.explanation: Dates the te reo Māori petition and accompanying march to Parliament to 1985.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary and archival records of the te reo Māori petition delivered to Parliament (Ngā Tamatoa / Te Reo Māori Society) and any accompanying hīkoi; true if the petition and march reached Parliament in 1985, false if they occurred in a different year (compare also the 1985 lodging of the Wai 11 claim and the 1987 Māori Language Act).

veracity.statement: There is no research that supports that, but there is a statement that says all those things, don’t do it. They will only fall into trouble again.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no research supports military-style boot camps for young offenders and that the evidence advises against them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published evaluations of youth boot camps, including the New Zealand Military-style Activity Camp evaluations and international meta-analyses of correctional boot camps; true if the body of evaluation evidence shows no reduction in reoffending, false if credible evaluations show boot camps reduce reoffending.

veracity.statement: While I was listening to the Speech from the Throne, I didn’t hear, I didn’t see a single vision for our children and grandchildren. Not at all.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Speech from the Throne delivered on 6 December 2023 contained nothing at all directed at children and young people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Speech from the Throne of 6 December 2023; false if it contains any commitment directed at children or young people (for example education, truancy or child health measures), true only if it contains none.

focus.statement: They saw the desires of this Government, they heard the speech that came from the Governor-General from the Throne this afternoon, the desire of this Government to modify, to mess with the Treaty of Waitangi, the principles, to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora, the healthy futures of our children, the removal of section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki legislation for the family, the hapū, the iwi, the genealogy, the language of the children, of the grandchildren.
focus.explanation: Names three specific measures in the government's programme — the Treaty principles work, the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, and the removal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. This is scrutiny of named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Only one week has this Government been working on their strategy and we have seen their abusive actions to our children, our youth, the smoking, the repeal of the smoke-free legislation to pay the bills to their voters, their financial supporters also.
focus.explanation: Names a real, specific measure (the repeal of the smoke-free legislation), but the weight of the sentence is on who the other side is said to be serving rather than on what the repeal does.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They saw the desires of this Government, they heard the speech that came from the Governor-General from the Throne this afternoon, the desire of this Government to modify, to mess with the Treaty of Waitangi, the principles, to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora, the healthy futures of our children, the removal of section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki legislation for the family, the hapū, the iwi, the genealogy, the language of the children, of the grandchildren.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific statutory provision (section 7AA), a named agency (Te Aka Whai Ora) and a named constitutional workstream; someone could check each. No figures, costs or timeframes, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You should be stricken with shame, in my opinion, you who support that phenomenon, because we are regressing.
civility.explanation: Moves from the policy to the members who back it, telling them they ought to be ashamed. Short of a direct insult, but it is a moral judgement of the people opposite rather than of the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Only one week has this Government been working on their strategy and we have seen their abusive actions to our children, our youth, the smoking, the repeal of the smoke-free legislation to pay the bills to their voters, their financial supporters also.
civility.explanation: Imputes a corrupt motive — that the smoke-free repeal is being done to pay off donors and supporters — rather than arguing against the repeal on its merits.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no research that supports that, but there is a statement that says all those things, don’t do it. They will only fall into trouble again.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about a named policy: no supporting research plus evidence of failure therefore do not proceed. It leans partly on absence of evidence and cites only an unnamed 'statement', so the conclusion runs slightly ahead of what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Without doubt the Māori people will continue to protest.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Māori-led protest against the new government's programme will continue after 6 December 2023, at the gatherings she names — the Kīngitanga hui, Rātana and Waitangi.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: News and official records of Māori-led protest events between December 2023 and Waitangi Day 2024, including any Kīngitanga-called national hui, the Rātana celebrations in January 2024 and Waitangi Day 2024; true if organised Māori protest against the government's programme occurred at these occasions, false if no such protest took place.

focus.statement: As I was listening to the Speech from the Throne, I—like, honestly, I just felt it was like a grab-bag of policy gimmicks.
