specificity.explanation: Names the document, the specific paragraph, and quotes its wording — anyone could go and check it. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The best way to help vulnerable workers is to have a flexible labour market that works for all New Zealanders, where every business has the opportunity to employ more staff and have more money to pay their staff more.
specificity.explanation: A statement of direction with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure — 'flexible labour market' and 'works for all New Zealanders' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, because this Government believes that the fair pay agreement system would have made vulnerable workers worse off. This is because of disemployment effects where businesses who could not stomach the added cost to their businesses lay off workers or close up entirely or don’t offer any more jobs.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the effect of the fair pay agreement system on employment — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is he aware that 500 additional police officers over two years is not enough to even replace attrition, and is he comfortable overseeing a reduction in front-line numbers?
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment (500 additional officers over two years) and tests it against a specific measurable outcome (attrition and front-line numbers). Textbook scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Number two, police officers are actually going to be on the front line serving the communities that they work in, and, number three, you’ve got a serious Government now that actually takes public safety seriously, and the country’s going to be safer.
focus.explanation: There is a thread of policy content (front-line deployment), but the weight of the answer is party framing — "a serious Government now" contrasted implicitly with the other side, with no measure, figure or mechanism named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is a stain on our nation and a terrible indictment on the record of the previous Government.
focus.explanation: It hangs off a specific named finding, which keeps it above pure tribalism, but the sentence itself does no policy work — it converts the finding into a general verdict on the other party's record rather than a mechanism, cost or measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s because section 7AA creates a fundamental conflict between protecting the best interests of children on one hand and honouring the Treaty in the other.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — a named statutory provision and what it is said to do. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Given the ACT coalition agreement requires the Government to assess the quality of new and existing legislation and regulation, will she commit to doing a regulatory impact assessment on the impacts of removing section 7AA on Māori children?
focus.explanation: Names the coalition agreement, the specific provision being repealed and the specific accountability mechanism being asked for. Legitimate scrutiny holding the Government to a stated commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Is he aware that 500 additional police officers over two years is not enough to even replace attrition, and is he comfortable overseeing a reduction in front-line numbers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 500 additional constabulary officers over two years falls short of the number needed to replace departures over the same period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police annual reports / workforce data for constabulary attrition in 2023/24 and 2024/25: true if total constabulary departures over those two years exceed 500, false if they are 500 or fewer.

veracity.statement: The recruiting pipeline, there’s pressure on that; we’ve got the Australians here recruiting our police officers; we’ve got a lot of officers coming up to retirement age.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australian police forces were actively recruiting serving New Zealand police officers in New Zealand at the time, and that a large cohort of NZ officers was approaching retirement age.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary records of Australian state police recruitment campaigns run in New Zealand in 2023 (e.g. Queensland/Western Australia Police recruitment drives) plus NZ Police workforce age profile: true if such campaigns were operating in NZ and the age profile shows a significant near-retirement cohort, false if neither is documented.

veracity.statement: Police have made 12 arrests, issued 220 infringement notices, and suspended three licences in response to road users blocking roads and exhibiting unsafe driving behaviours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific enforcement counts arising from Operation Shadow in Hamilton and the wider Waikato: 12 arrests, 220 infringement notices, three licence suspensions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police media releases and operational reporting for Operation Shadow (Waikato, late 2023): true if the arrest, infringement and suspension counts match those stated, false if they differ materially.

veracity.statement: Given the ACT coalition agreement requires the Government to assess the quality of new and existing legislation and regulation, will she commit to doing a regulatory impact assessment on the impacts of removing section 7AA on Māori children?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National–ACT coalition agreement contains a commitment requiring the Government to assess the quality of new and existing legislation and regulation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–ACT coalition agreement (November 2023): true if it contains a commitment to assess or improve the quality of new and existing legislation and regulation, false if no such commitment appears.

veracity.statement: Section 7AA has resulted in Māori children being removed from safe, loving homes they’ve lived in for years and being placed with family they may not know, because their parents or their caregivers may happen to be the wrong ethnicity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the operation of section 7AA has caused children to be moved out of long-standing safe placements on the basis of the caregivers' ethnicity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki case records, Family Court judgments, and the findings of reviews of the section 7AA repeal (including the Waitangi Tribunal's urgent inquiry): true if documented cases show placements changed under section 7AA with caregiver ethnicity as the operative reason, false if reviews find no such documented cases.

rigor.statement: Well, they can have confidence in me and this Government because we take public safety seriously.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (the public can have confidence) rests entirely on a restatement of the speaker's own good intentions — a bare self-assertion, effectively circular, with no evidence connecting the premise to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s because section 7AA creates a fundamental conflict between protecting the best interests of children on one hand and honouring the Treaty in the other.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy asserted rather than argued: the two obligations are presented as necessarily in conflict, with nothing offered to show they cannot both be satisfied. The conclusion (unintended consequences) rests entirely on that unsupported opposition.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As Associate Professor Nicola Atwell of Otago University says, section 7AA has led to practice which is ideologically driven and neither child centred nor trauma informed.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the conclusion about how section 7AA operates in practice is carried entirely by a cited academic's characterisation, with no evidence, data or case reasoning offered alongside it.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, they can have confidence in me and this Government because we take public safety seriously.
specificity.explanation: A slogan. No figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Police have made 12 arrests, issued 220 infringement notices, and suspended three licences in response to road users blocking roads and exhibiting unsafe driving behaviours.
specificity.explanation: Three exact figures tied to a named operation and a described behaviour. Fully checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Greater accountability will include creating a truly independent monitoring and oversight agency for Oranga Tamariki and will also improve attractiveness of caregiving to give caregivers the right to make everyday decisions about a child’s life by default.
specificity.explanation: Two named mechanisms — an independent monitoring and oversight agency, and a default decision-making right for caregivers — so there is something to act on, but no timeframe, no funding and no legislative vehicle.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I recommend the member asking the question try listening carefully. She might learn something.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at a named individual rather than at her argument — the implication is that she cannot listen and needs teaching. Short of abuse, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Nothing about this change will affect the support services and programmes that Oranga Tamariki provides for Māori.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing section 7AA will leave Oranga Tamariki's support services and programmes for Māori unchanged — an outcome claim about the effect of the repeal, not a commitment to a particular action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki service and programme reporting (annual reports, iwi partnership arrangements) for the year following the repeal of section 7AA: true if no Māori-facing services, programmes or partnerships are discontinued or reduced in consequence of the repeal, false if any are.

civility.statement: I share that with you as a reminder to the House to be careful about what you talk about in public spaces, including the Koru lounge, but also just to give some evidence of the fact that it’s not just this side of the House that has no confidence in that Minister of Finance and her ability to be able to do simple sums.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named individual's competence — the Minister of Finance's ability 'to do simple sums' — repeated in the speaker's own voice rather than left in the quoted note. The target is the person, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t get the sense, despite the previous speaker’s attempt to try and make it sound like she was in touch, that the Government actually cares about New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the previous speaker personally — that she was performing being 'in touch' rather than being so. Short of a direct insult, but it questions sincerity rather than the substance of what she said.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I share that with you as a reminder to the House to be careful about what you talk about in public spaces, including the Koru lounge, but also just to give some evidence of the fact that it’s not just this side of the House that has no confidence in that Minister of Finance and her ability to be able to do simple sums.
focus.explanation: Overheard gossip about a rival's staff and internal standing. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named; the content is entirely about what the other side is 'really like'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So apparently, putting jobs on the line, pushing towards a world where more Kiwis can find themselves unemployed, equates to supporting New Zealanders with the cost of living.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measures before the House — the employment-law and Reserve Bank changes just listed — and their effect on jobs and living costs. No party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How was bashing Māori, banishing te reo Māori, encouraging social and racial division, and making moves to increase the uptake of smoking in Aotearoa New Zealand going to help New Zealanders pay for their bread and butter?
focus.explanation: Real policies sit underneath this — the smokefree repeal, te reo agency names, the te reo allowance — and questioning their relevance to cost of living is legitimate scrutiny. But the policies are named only through characterisation ('bashing Māori', 'banishing te reo'), so the weight of the sentence is framing rather than the measures themselves.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Many people have been saying outside this House—and I’m going to add my voice to it—that this Government is looking like the most backward, regressive, divisive Government that we have ever seen as a country.
focus.explanation: A global verdict on the other side with no policy, measure or outcome named. Strip out the characterisation of the government and nothing about any bill or programme remains.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The first move in the House this week is to get rid of fair pay agreements, extend 90-day trials, remove the Reserve Bank’s dual mandate to focus on keeping inflation down whilst not taking their focus off employment—and just keep in mind that Australia has just moved to put that mandate in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that the incoming government's first legislative moves in December 2023 were repealing fair pay agreements, extending 90-day trials and removing the Reserve Bank's employment mandate, and (b) that Australia has recently adopted a dual mandate for its central bank.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and the NZ legislation record for December 2023: true if the Fair Pay Agreements repeal, 90-day trial extension and Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act single-mandate amendment were among the first bills introduced/passed under urgency, false if not. For the Australian limb: the 2023 Statement on the Conduct of Monetary Policy / RBA Review outcome — true if it establishes dual price-stability and full-employment objectives for the RBA, false if the RBA retained a single inflation objective.

veracity.statement: So then the Government moves to get rid of regulatory impact statements so that New Zealanders can’t see what the impact or benefit or losses might be to them through the legislative changes?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the government has abolished regulatory impact statements. The checkable core is whether the RIS requirement was removed, as against specific bills being exempted from it when passed under urgency.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's regulatory impact analysis requirements and the Cabinet Manual/CabGuide as at December 2023, plus the RIS pages on treasury.govt.nz for the December 2023 urgency bills: false if the RIS requirement remained in force generally and only particular bills were granted exemptions, true if the requirement itself was removed or suspended.

specificity.statement: The first move in the House this week is to get rid of fair pay agreements, extend 90-day trials, remove the Reserve Bank’s dual mandate to focus on keeping inflation down whilst not taking their focus off employment—and just keep in mind that Australia has just moved to put that mandate in place.
specificity.explanation: Names three specific measures and a comparator jurisdiction's central-bank mandate. A reader could check each item against the legislative record; only the timing detail ('this week') is loose.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So apparently, putting jobs on the line, pushing towards a world where more Kiwis can find themselves unemployed, equates to supporting New Zealanders with the cost of living.
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus a leap: the government's stated position is not that unemployment supports cost of living, and no mechanism is offered linking FPA repeal, 90-day trials or a single monetary mandate to job losses. The sarcastic framing substitutes for the connecting argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I may have paid once to go to that really bad circus that one time and I won’t be going back, but I have no doubt that if the Government continues on the trajectory they are on—and they will—New Zealanders won’t just be pledging to forego tickets to the next show; they will be wanting to leave the show early and asking for a full refund.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that public support will turn against the National-led coalition during this parliamentary term, to the point that voters want it out before the term ends rather than merely declining to re-elect it.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Major published NZ political polls (1News-Verian, Newshub/Reid Research, Taxpayers' Union-Curia, Roy Morgan) across 2024-2026 and the 2026 general election result: true if the Labour/Greens/Te Pāti Māori bloc leads the National/ACT/NZ First bloc in a sustained majority of polls during the term, false if the governing bloc retains a polling lead through the term.

focus.statement: They’re feeling a little uncomfortable about their new situation, and I think that New Zealanders around the country would welcome me reminding members opposite why they lost and why they no longer control the Government benches.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's post-election discomfort and their loss of office. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — this is party framing with no policy content, which is exactly the case Focus exists to catch. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility is untouched, and there is no inference to assess, so Rigor is skipped.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What that party opposite refused to do at any juncture was reduce the income taxes that New Zealanders were paying.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy area (personal income tax settings) and a specific claimed outcome of the previous government's decisions. This is scrutiny of a named commitment, not tribalism, and scores high even though it is aimed at opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is time for responsible Government, for grown-up Government. The adults are back in charge, and New Zealanders say to the last lot: good riddance.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome appears — it is a characterisation of the two sides as adults versus the last lot, ending in a send-off. Content-free party framing, which is precisely what Focus is for; no individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have had inflation out of control for more than 2½ years, and the result for working people, for New Zealanders across the country, has been a cost of living crisis that rolled on and on and on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a duration — that inflation had been above control for more than two and a half years as at December 2023. The 'cost of living crisis' framing is rhetoric; the checkable core is the length of the above-band inflation run.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ consumers price index, annual inflation rate by quarter: true if annual CPI inflation was continuously above the Reserve Bank's 1–3% target band from at least mid-2021 through to the December 2023 quarter (i.e. more than 2½ years by the date of the statement); false if the run of above-band prints is materially shorter than 2½ years.

veracity.statement: What that party opposite refused to do at any juncture was reduce the income taxes that New Zealanders were paying.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government never once legislated a personal income tax reduction across its two terms. The dispute turns on whether any rate or threshold change counts as a reduction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand income tax legislation and Budget documents 2017–2023: true if no reduction to personal income tax rates or thresholds was enacted by the Labour-led governments over that period; false if any personal income tax rate cut or threshold adjustment was legislated (independent tax credits or transfer payments do not count as an income tax reduction).

veracity.statement: Already we have removed the bureaucratic fair pay agreement regime, which would have imposed mandatory union deals on workforces that didn’t even want a bar of it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a completed action ('already we have removed') that the Fair Pay Agreements regime was gone as at the date of the speech. The check is simply the date the repeal passed relative to 12 December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation record for the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 and its repeal bill: true if the repeal had passed all stages and taken effect on or before 12 December 2023; false if the repeal bill had only been introduced or was still before the House on that date.

veracity.statement: Because it seems disgraceful to me that we had a Government that was prepared to sign up to long-term contracts for medicines but wouldn’t put the money in the Budget to fund them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government contracted for medicines over the long term without funding those commitments in the forward Budget estimates. Turns on whether Pharmac's out-year baselines covered the contracted spend.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 appropriations and Treasury/Pharmac out-year baseline funding documents: true if Pharmac entered multi-year medicine supply contracts whose out-year costs were not provided for in forward Budget baselines; false if the forward estimates carried funding for those contracted commitments.

veracity.statement: They were prepared to keep doing what they had already done three times—move that surplus out—because fundamentally they like to spend more than they earn.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count — that the forecast return to surplus had already been deferred three times before the 2026–27 projection. Checkable directly from the sequence of Treasury forecast dates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Economic and Fiscal Updates (BEFU/HYEFU/PREFU) from 2021 to 2023: true if the forecast year of return to OBEGAL surplus was pushed to a later year on three separate occasions across those updates; false if it was deferred fewer times.

specificity.statement: So we—we—will make sure we bring Government spending under control and will prioritise the things that actually matter to working people: effective public services that are sustainable into the future and that provide good value; delivering the conditions and the infrastructure that allow private enterprise to flourish, that allow for greater innovation, that allow for greater productivity, that allow for more people to be hired.
specificity.explanation: A long list of generic virtues — sustainable, good value, flourish, innovation, productivity — with no figure, no mechanism, no named programme and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on. It is squarely about policy (high Focus) but carries almost no detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Already we have introduced 90-day trial legislation, which will mean that some people will have an employer give them a go where previously they were not prepared to.
specificity.explanation: Names an identifiable legislative measure (the 90-day trial period extension) and a stated status (introduced), so the action is checkable. Falls short of the top because the claimed effect is quantified only as 'some people' — no scale, no timeframe, no coverage figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because it seems disgraceful to me that we had a Government that was prepared to sign up to long-term contracts for medicines but wouldn’t put the money in the Budget to fund them.
civility.explanation: 'Disgraceful' is blunt, but the target is a budgeting decision, not a person — no one's character, competence or motives are attacked. Harsh criticism of a decision is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because it is a reckless Government that drives the books into ongoing deficits, and that was the intention of the members opposite.
civility.explanation: Goes past criticising the fiscal outcome to asserting that ongoing deficits were what members opposite intended. Imputing deliberate bad faith to other members is a real civility failure, though it stops short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They were prepared to keep doing what they had already done three times—move that surplus out—because fundamentally they like to spend more than they earn.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the forecast surplus would never have arrived — is carried partly by an unevidenced attribution of motive ('fundamentally they like to spend more than they earn'). That is an appeal to disposition rather than to any fiscal mechanism; the record of three deferrals is offered, but a claim about what someone likes cannot support a claim about what the books would have done.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For six years—perhaps more—rural New Zealand had been in a state of emotional decline. Many had suffered the left’s farming illiteracy.
focus.explanation: Characterises 'the left' in general terms ('farming illiteracy') over a six-year period without naming a policy, regulation, figure or outcome. Party framing carrying no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to balance places like the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee with practical people, not those that were wet behind the ears, but those who have experience on farm—vets, farmers—who understand outcome and the rigour of farming practices, not theorem.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a policy question — the composition of a named statutory body (NAWAC) and the criteria for appointing to it. No party-bashing carries the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Farmers in this building, we all collectively recognise the absolute importance of sensible, pragmatic lawmaking—something for so long we have missed out on—that achieves tenable outcomes on farm, something that the previous Government, and I have to stress this point, were so often four sheets to the wind on.
focus.explanation: Gestures at lawmaking quality but the substance of the sentence is a general characterisation of the previous Government rather than any named measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will return the live animal export trade. Trying to reconcile that is worth half a billion dollars to this country.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy reversal (the live animal export ban) and attaches a dollar figure to it, so it is checkable and actionable. Marked down only for supplying no timeframe or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to balance places like the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee with practical people, not those that were wet behind the ears, but those who have experience on farm—vets, farmers—who understand outcome and the rigour of farming practices, not theorem.
specificity.explanation: Names the body and the kind of appointee sought (vets, farmers with on-farm experience), but gives no numbers, no appointment mechanism and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Farmers in this building, we all collectively recognise the absolute importance of sensible, pragmatic lawmaking—something for so long we have missed out on—that achieves tenable outcomes on farm, something that the previous Government, and I have to stress this point, were so often four sheets to the wind on.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — 'sensible', 'pragmatic', 'tenable outcomes' — with no law, figure, mechanism or date named. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We will return the live animal export trade. Trying to reconcile that is worth half a billion dollars to this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the live animal export trade is worth half a billion dollars a year to New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI / Stats NZ export statistics on the annual value of New Zealand live animal exports by sea in the years immediately before the April 2023 ban. True if the trade was worth around NZ$500 million a year; false if materially lower (for example the roughly NZ$250–350 million a year commonly reported for 2019–2022).

veracity.statement: Farmer morale has been at an all-time low.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that farmer morale/confidence in late 2023 was at a record low, i.e. lower than at any previously measured point.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published farmer confidence series — the Federated Farmers Farm Confidence Survey and the Rabobank Rural Confidence Survey — for 2023. True if net farmer confidence reached the lowest reading in the survey's history; false if any earlier reading was lower.

rigor.statement: He had travelled ill with cancer for four hours from Kaitāia to be part of that day. He battled on with his condition; he battled on with his post-cyclone recovery, and yet he still managed the time to be there for himself, for his community. Surely there is no greater conviction, no greater belief, in rural communities.
rigor.explanation: Argument from a single anecdote plus an appeal to emotion: one man's attendance at a post-cyclone gathering is offered as establishing a general conclusion about conviction across rural communities. The inference from one case to the whole does not carry.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is my hope all parties will come in this House to know this as a truism, to know this as a fact. For to do any less is what I say to them is to have turned their back on rural New Zealand, and this is something we must absolutely not do.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: either accept the speaker's characterisation of rural New Zealand as a 'truism', or you have 'turned your back on rural New Zealand'. No middle position — disagreeing with the framing while supporting the sector — is allowed for, and nothing is offered to close the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: With that in mind, it didn’t take very long for nasty Labour to come back, did it?
focus.explanation: Characterises the opposing party as 'nasty' with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is exactly the content-free party framing Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Sorry, Ms Sepuloni, you’ve got to go back to the Labour Party caucus every single week, because I think that’s where the circus is.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal state. Strip out the jibe about the Labour caucus and no policy, measure or outcome remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bit that she forgot to say is that over six years, those poor people, the vulnerable she’s so worried about, are worse off today than they were six years ago.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of the previous government against a named outcome — the position of the poorest over its six years. Holding a government to account on a specific record is on-policy, not tribalism, even though it is framed as a rebuttal of another member.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And to anybody in this House that doesn’t understand that when rural New Zealand does well all of New Zealand does well, and when the rural economy is strong the New Zealand economy is strong, they will be on that side of the House because of all the things that Labour did to our farmers over six years.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy proposition here (the rural economy's weight in the national economy), but the sentence's weight falls on sorting the House by party and on 'all the things that Labour did', with no measure, rule or figure named.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Carmel Sepuloni was on her feet, talking—making up, actually, some text message of fake news somebody happened to send her with such intricate detail from the Koru lounge, from a drunk person.
civility.explanation: Accuses a named member of fabricating evidence to the House ('making up ... fake news'). That is an imputation of bad faith landing on the person rather than on her argument, sitting between a real civility failure and a clear personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Sorry, Ms Sepuloni, you’ve got to go back to the Labour Party caucus every single week, because I think that’s where the circus is.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at a named member — calling her caucus a circus is a sneer rather than a direct insult to her character, which is the 0.5 band.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s no wonder the then Prime Minister Chris Hipkins never came to Rotorua during the campaign. He was ashamed.
civility.explanation: Ascribes a personal motive — shame — to a named member rather than engaging any policy question. It attributes a discreditable state of mind to the person, which is a clear step past pointed criticism of a record.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The bit that she forgot to say is that over six years, those poor people, the vulnerable she’s so worried about, are worse off today than they were six years ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that low-income and vulnerable New Zealanders were materially worse off in 2023 than in 2017, i.e. across the term of the outgoing Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship and AHC 50% median measures) and household income/real wage series for the 2017/18 and 2022/23 years; true if the headline hardship and low-income measures are materially higher in 2022/23 than 2017/18, false if they are equal or lower.

veracity.statement: You know, the average kiwifruit grower gets more from their exports in international markets than kiwifruit growers anywhere else in the world and we thank them for that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand kiwifruit growers earn higher average export returns than kiwifruit growers in any other country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Zespri annual reports and FAO/industry comparative export unit-value data for kiwifruit (New Zealand vs Italy, Greece, Chile, Iran, China); true if New Zealand's average grower return per tray or per tonne exported is the highest of the producing countries, false if another country's exceeds it.

veracity.statement: In viticulture—very important—did you know, Mr Speaker, in the UK market, a very competitive wine market, New Zealand wine gets on average £1 to £2 more per bottle than anything else, which means our wine growers are not competing on price; they’re competing on quality and they are winning there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific price premium for New Zealand wine in the United Kingdom — on average £1 to £2 more per bottle than wine of any other origin.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UK off-trade retail price data by country of origin (Nielsen/WSTA figures as reported by New Zealand Winegrowers) for the year to 2023; true if the average NZ bottle price exceeds the market average by £1–£2, false if the gap is materially smaller or if another origin commands a higher average price.

veracity.statement: It took them virtually 4½ years to get anywhere near India and they’ve been there two or three times this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Labour government took roughly four and a half years from taking office before any senior ministerial engagement with India, then visited two or three times in 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT and ministerial travel records for Trade, Foreign Affairs and Prime Ministerial visits to India between October 2017 and October 2023; true if the first such visit falls around early-to-mid 2022 or later and there were two or three in 2023, false if a senior ministerial visit occurred materially earlier or the 2023 count differs.

veracity.statement: It’s no wonder the then Prime Minister Chris Hipkins never came to Rotorua during the campaign. He was ashamed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Chris Hipkins made no visit to Rotorua during the 2023 general election campaign.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Labour Party campaign itineraries and contemporaneous local media reporting (Rotorua Daily Post, NZ Herald, RNZ) for the period from the writ being issued to election day, 14 October 2023; true if no Hipkins visit to Rotorua is recorded in that window, false if any campaign appearance there is documented.

rigor.statement: And, actually, if you have a look over time, this place—they say there have been fewer members of Parliament than there have been All Blacks but if you actually look at the All Blacks, a team that all New Zealanders can be proud of, over the history of it the number of farmers that have served as our top sportspeople in itself talks to the importance of rural New Zealand to the fabric of society in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real subject, and a weak one: the number of farmers selected for a national sports team is offered as evidence of rural New Zealand's importance to the social fabric. That is a non sequitur resting on anecdote — the composition of a rugby squad carries no weight on the economic or social claim being drawn from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In viticulture—very important—did you know, Mr Speaker, in the UK market, a very competitive wine market, New Zealand wine gets on average £1 to £2 more per bottle than anything else, which means our wine growers are not competing on price; they’re competing on quality and they are winning there.
rigor.explanation: The inference from a price premium to 'competing on quality, not price' is reasonable but has a real gap: a higher shelf price is also consistent with brand positioning, varietal mix, exchange rates or distribution costs. Nothing is offered to rule those out, so the conclusion runs ahead of the single figure supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to focus on better rules, fewer rules, on the outcomes, so that our rural sector can be as strong as we need it.
specificity.explanation: Squarely about regulatory policy, but carries nothing checkable: no rule, regulation or standard is named, no count, no timeframe, no mechanism. 'Better rules, fewer rules' commits to nothing anyone could act on or measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to double that over 10 years; the building blocks will be put in place now.
specificity.explanation: A quantified target (double export value) against a stated horizon (10 years), which is checkable. It stops short of the top of the scale because no mechanism, milestone or baseline year is given, and 'building blocks ... now' is filler.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I question: did the change they voted for include more people smoking to enable the funding of tax cuts for rich New Zealanders, because that’s not what I’m hearing back.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that voters gave no mandate for repealing the smokefree measures — rests entirely on what the speaker personally hears back from people. That is an appeal to anecdote; a general election result is not evidence about any single policy either way, and no polling or other evidence is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Fair pay agreements would enable a standardised wage and a standardised set of conditions that would have meant that we did not have bus drivers leaving to become truck drivers; leaving to go to Australia—and that is what the National Government is stepping away from, and it will be their basket to carry when we see things like this occur again.
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual asserted rather than argued. Even granting that an FPA would standardise bus drivers' pay within their industry, that does not establish drivers would have stayed — the comparison driving the departures was with trucking and with Australia, both outside the agreement's scope. The conclusion outruns the mechanism offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, what I would actually like to say is it does the opposite, because if we have a standard agreement across an industry, that means in those regions that are crying out for workers that need people in there, we can have workers go from one area to another with a standard agreement on what their wages and their conditions are.
rigor.explanation: A genuine mechanism is offered — portable, industry-wide terms lower the friction of moving between employers and regions — and the conclusion about labour mobility follows from it. It is a partial rebuttal, though: it answers the mobility sense of 'flexibility' while leaving the cost objection it was raised against untouched.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The fact that we have a Māori Minister of Health who is promising to improve health outcomes for Māori while delegating responsibility for more smoking for Māori to his coalition partners is an absolute stain on the name of the new Government.
civility.explanation: Aimed at a named individual rather than the measure: it imputes bad faith to the Minister of Health personally — promising one thing while quietly handing off the opposite — and calls it a 'stain'. Short of a direct insult, but it sneers at the person's sincerity rather than contesting the smokefree repeal itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It will be a circus. There are clowns in this circus, and they are performing their roles for the greatest spectacular we will ever see in New Zealand politics.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the members of the Government rather than at anything they have done — calling ministers clowns is ridicule of the people, not criticism of a decision.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So I think it’s important to note that the first two pieces of legislation that this new Government brings to this House under urgency is targeted on jobs and employment, making sure that unemployment is removed out of the Finance Act, and also driving down workers’ wages through repealing fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the new Government's first two urgency bills were the removal of the employment objective from the Reserve Bank's mandate and the repeal of the Fair Pay Agreements Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Order Paper and Hansard record of bills taken under urgency by the incoming Government in December 2023: true if the first two bills introduced under urgency were the one removing the employment/unemployment objective from the Reserve Bank's mandate and the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill; false if other bills preceded them. Note the statute named ('Finance Act') appears to be a mis-speak — judge the claim about which two bills came first, not the statute name.

veracity.statement: It’s really interesting to note that the OECD has put out a good report available online—if anyone would like to check it out—showing that productivity actually increases under fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the OECD has published a finding that productivity rises under industry-wide bargaining of the fair pay agreement type.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD publications on collective bargaining (e.g. 'Negotiating Our Way Up', 2019): true if an OECD report finds that sector- or industry-level collective bargaining of the kind fair pay agreements establish raises productivity; false if no such OECD finding exists, or if the OECD reports no productivity effect or a negative one.

veracity.statement: Not only did the OECD agree but also so does the Treasury, who gave great advice, saying that the official advice was ignored by the Minister that Pasifika women, Māori, young people, disabled would all be adversely affected by the fact that fair pay agreements will be repealed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice on the repeal identified adverse effects on Pacific women, Māori, young and disabled workers, and that the Minister proceeded against it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement and departmental advice on the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill: true if official advice identified Pacific women, Māori, young people and disabled people as adversely affected by repeal; false if the advice named no such groups or reached the opposite conclusion.

veracity.statement: So the Public Transport Operating Model, introduced by Steven Joyce under the National Government—which was the privatisation of the public transport system—enabled a contracting race to the bottom that meant lower wages and lower working conditions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) PTOM's authorship — Steven Joyce, National Government — and (b) that it constituted privatisation of the public transport system. The second half is the contestable part: bus services were already contracted to private operators before PTOM.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative and ministerial record for the Public Transport Operating Model (Land Transport Management Amendment Act 2013 and preceding policy): true if PTOM was introduced by Steven Joyce as Minister of Transport in a National-led government and transferred public transport services to private operators; false if it was introduced by another minister or government, or if it did not shift services into private ownership or operation.

specificity.statement: So the Public Transport Operating Model, introduced by Steven Joyce under the National Government—which was the privatisation of the public transport system—enabled a contracting race to the bottom that meant lower wages and lower working conditions.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy instrument, the minister who introduced it, the government responsible and the mechanism claimed to follow from it (competitive contracting driving wages down). Someone could go and check every element of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Fair pay agreements would enable a standardised wage and a standardised set of conditions that would have meant that we did not have bus drivers leaving to become truck drivers; leaving to go to Australia—and that is what the National Government is stepping away from, and it will be their basket to carry when we see things like this occur again.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: a named instrument (fair pay agreements), a named sector, a specific workforce outcome, and what repeal is expected to do. Legitimate scrutiny of a government decision, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It will be a circus. There are clowns in this circus, and they are performing their roles for the greatest spectacular we will ever see in New Zealand politics.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. Strip out the characterisation of the other side and nothing remains — this is exactly the content-free tribalism Focus exists to catch, even though no single individual is insulted.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I look forward to being able to continue to move in a way that we see better moves for us as a country, and I want to make sure that in the upcoming weeks, months, and years, we will continue to interrogate this Government—as it struggles to find money for the tax cuts that it has promised New Zealanders, as we see that when the tobacco money runs out, as we see that there is no foreign buyers tax, and as we see that New Zealanders realise that the change that they voted for will not be delivered by this Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the promised foreign buyers tax will not materialise, and that the tax cuts will therefore lack the revenue they were costed against. The foreign buyer tax component is the checkable part.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Government tax policy announcements and legislation through to the end of 2024: false if a tax or levy on foreign buyers of residential property is enacted or announced as proceeding; true if the policy is abandoned or never legislated, leaving no foreign buyers tax in place.

civility.statement: Climate change policies in New Zealand have been driven by a tiny minority with loud voices who have no conception as to the consequences of their narrow, shallow ideas on the day-to-day functioning of the economy.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the people behind climate policy rather than the policy: they 'have no conception' and their ideas are 'narrow, shallow'. Condescension and imputed ignorance aimed at people, though no individual is named, so it sits above a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Not even Treasury or the gnomes who work in the audit department—sadly, they’re still chasing me for terrible falsehoods of the Provincial Growth Fund time—can find a sliver of evidence as to how that money has improved the capacity of families and communities to look after themselves.
civility.explanation: Mocks the officials themselves — 'the gnomes who work in the audit department' — and imputes bad faith to them ('still chasing me for terrible falsehoods'), rather than criticising the audit findings. Sneering and condescension short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We are not going to meet the 2030 dreamy, fairy-tale, aspirational figures that we’ll be freeing ourselves of fossil fuels as a source of generating energy.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand will not have removed fossil fuels from its electricity generation by 2030 (the 100% renewable electricity target). This is an outcome for the country, not merely a statement of his own government's intentions.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE Energy in New Zealand / quarterly electricity statistics for calendar year 2030: the prediction is TRUE if fossil-fuelled (coal, gas, diesel) generation still contributes a non-trivial share of electricity generation in 2030; FALSE if generation is 100% (or effectively 100%) renewable by the end of 2030.

rigor.statement: One of the great lies about climate change is that, yes, apparently, it’s a crisis. Name me one law that has changed in the last nine years expediting simplifying investors’ ability to navigate the digestive tract otherwise known as the Resource Management Act and in a timely fashion secure resource consent, find the money, deliver the project. No one in this House can.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur combined with an argument from absence of evidence: the claim that no consenting-reform law has been passed is offered as proof that calling climate change a crisis is a 'lie'. The pace of resource-consent reform has no bearing on whether the underlying problem is a crisis, and 'no one can name one' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we do not have coal and gas continuing to contribute to our power system, we’re going to have blackouts, brownouts; we’re going to have a power system that lacks security, riddled with risk; and it’ll diminish the status of our nation as a first-class, First World country.
rigor.explanation: An escalating chain of consequences — no thermal generation therefore blackouts, therefore an insecure system, therefore a diminished First World status — with nothing offered to connect any link. Slippery slope plus appeal to consequences; no supply modelling, capacity figures or evidence is supplied for the causal claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One of the great lies about climate change is that, yes, apparently, it’s a crisis. Name me one law that has changed in the last nine years expediting simplifying investors’ ability to navigate the digestive tract otherwise known as the Resource Management Act and in a timely fashion secure resource consent, find the money, deliver the project. No one in this House can.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no law enacted in the previous nine years (roughly 2014–2023) made it faster or simpler for investors to obtain resource consent under the Resource Management Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand statute book for 2014–2023: the claim is FALSE if any enacted Act created or streamlined a faster consenting pathway — check in particular the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act 2020, the Resource Management Amendment Act 2020, and the Housing Supply (Enabling Housing Supply and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021; TRUE only if no such Act exists.

veracity.statement: In those areas called the Department of Conservation (DOC) estate, where it’s stewardship land, stewardship land is not DOC land, and if there is a mineral, if there is a mining opportunity and it’s impeded by a blind frog, goodbye, Freddy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of legal status that stewardship land is not Department of Conservation land.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Conservation Act 1987 (in particular the definition of a stewardship area and s25) and DOC's own description of the public conservation land it administers: the claim is FALSE if stewardship areas are held and administered by DOC as part of the public conservation land, TRUE if they sit outside DOC's estate.

veracity.statement: I was in this House when $1.8 billion, $1.9 billion was allocated for mental health.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an appropriation of roughly $1.8–1.9 billion for mental health was made during his previous term in Parliament (2017–2020).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2019 (the 'Wellbeing Budget') documents and Vote Health appropriations: TRUE if a mental health and addiction package of approximately $1.8–1.9 billion was announced/appropriated in that term, FALSE if the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Not even Treasury or the gnomes who work in the audit department—sadly, they’re still chasing me for terrible falsehoods of the Provincial Growth Fund time—can find a sliver of evidence as to how that money has improved the capacity of families and communities to look after themselves.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neither the Treasury nor the Office of the Auditor-General has produced any evidence that the mental health funding improved outcomes for families and communities.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury and Office of the Auditor-General publications on the 2019 mental health and addiction package (including the Auditor-General's reports on mental health services and Access and Choice programme monitoring, and Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission access data cited therein): the claim is FALSE if any such report records measurable improvement — e.g. numbers of people accessing new primary mental health services — and TRUE only if these agencies report no evidence of improvement at all.

specificity.statement: We are going to extract the dividend from mother Nature’s legacy on the DOC estate in those areas previously called stewardship land.
specificity.explanation: Names a land category (stewardship land within the DOC estate) so it is not a pure slogan, but supplies no minerals, no scale, no legislative mechanism and no timeframe; 'extract the dividend from mother Nature's legacy' carries no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So if there’s ever an event that’s an indictment on the people who’ve held the health portfolio on that side of the House, it’s the $1.8 billion that got poured down the orifice of the bureaucracy, supposedly going to give you and me and our whānau better health outcomes of a mental character.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific appropriation ($1.8 billion for mental health) and a specific claimed failure of outcome, which is on-policy accountability rather than tribalism. Marked down slightly because the point is framed around 'that side of the House' and the people who held the portfolio rather than the programme's mechanism or results.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, that contribution from that member who has just resumed his seat, Shane Jones, made for incredibly painful listening, talking about the thousands of young people who have marched in our streets asking our leaders to pay more attention to addressing climate change, depicting them as a tiny minority who’ve been advocating for change, not to mention, of course, recommitting to mining on conservation land and a whole host of other policies designed to take us backwards as a nation.
civility.explanation: Pointed and dismissive of a named member's speech ("incredibly painful listening"), but the criticism lands on what he said and the policies he backed, not on his character or competence. Robust, edging toward the person without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I listened on, hoping to hear of some vision as to how they would actually deliver on this, and yet the main cornerstone of their economic policy appears to be cutting spending on things like Auckland light rail, axing Industry Transformation Plans, the Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme, the Income Insurance Scheme, and, of course, delivering tax cuts for their rich mates.
specificity.explanation: Names five specific measures being cut — Auckland light rail, Industry Transformation Plans, Lake Onslow, the Income Insurance Scheme, tax cuts. Concrete enough that someone could go and check each one. No amounts or dates, which keeps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that it will cost thousands of lives, that young people will be encouraged to take up smoking, and that it will result in $1.3 billion in terms of healthcare costs.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure ($1.3 billion in healthcare costs) and named consequences attached to an identified repeal. Checkable against the published modelling; short of the top because the lives figure is left as "thousands" and no timeframe is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All we see: sanctions, bringing back 90-day trials, repealing fair pay agreements that we know, and evidence tells us, will disproportionately benefit women, youth, Maōri, and Pacific people.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete measures (benefit sanctions, 90-day trials, fair pay agreement repeal) and identifies the specific groups affected. No figures or timeframes, and the sentence is garbled in the way live speech is, but the policy content is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I listened on, hoping to hear of some vision as to how they would actually deliver on this, and yet the main cornerstone of their economic policy appears to be cutting spending on things like Auckland light rail, axing Industry Transformation Plans, the Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme, the Income Insurance Scheme, and, of course, delivering tax cuts for their rich mates.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the incoming government's economic programme by naming the specific policies cancelled, which is legitimate scrutiny; the "rich mates" tag adds party framing on top of a real policy list.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When they talk about making lives easier, for whom, I ask? Their rich mates? The tobacco lobby? That’s who is going to benefit from the policies of this new Government, not those families that they talk about, not those families whose doors they knocked on and stories they heard.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about whose side the other party is really on — "rich mates", "the tobacco lobby" — rather than about any named measure or its effects. The gesture at tobacco is the only policy anchor; the weight is motive attribution to the opposing side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the coalition agreements say that decisions will be based on data and evidence, and yet this decision to repeal what would have been globally leading legislation—smoke-free legislation—flies in the face of data, in evidence.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the smoke-free legislation repeal) and a specific stated commitment (the coalition agreements' evidence standard), and tests one against the other. This is scrutiny of a named policy against a named promise.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Instead, just a lot of Maōri bashing—scrapping Te Aka Whai Ora, the Maōri Health Authority, just because its very point is to address health inequities; looking to scrap affirmative action to incentivise te reo in the Public Service; pushing to scrap te reo names of Public Service agencies; introducing a Treaty Principles Bill, and I want to quote on that point Dame Anne Salmond, who said it better than I can ever put it.
focus.explanation: Names four specific measures — the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, te reo incentives in the Public Service, agency naming, the Treaty Principles Bill — which is real policy content. But it is framed as "Maōri bashing" and attributes motive to the other side, which pulls weight off the measures themselves.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government that is an absolute shambles. This is a Government that will take us backwards. It’s a regressive Government, and I absolutely don’t believe that they will achieve even their own loftiest goals.
focus.explanation: A general verdict on the other side — shambolic, backwards, regressive — with no measure, figure or outcome named. Nothing here can be checked against a policy; it is characterisation of the opposing team.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Once again, we see the axing of investment in high-quality public transport networks to keep hundreds of thousands of people connected in our largest city while also reducing emissions and congestion—back on the scrap heap, but yet building another 13 new roads of national significance somehow is not wasteful spending. Somehow, that’s going to ease congestion and improve productivity. How? I don’t know.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: the alleged inconsistency between cutting transport investment as wasteful while funding 13 roads. But the conclusion rests on rhetorical incredulity — "How? I don't know" — rather than on any account of why roads would not ease congestion. Argument from the speaker's own lack of an explanation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Has it worked? No. It’s been an abject failure. Wealth doesn’t trickle down. All that happens is that the inequality gap widens, public services decline, housing is privatised, public transport is privatised, education is privatised, public transport declines, roads increase, and unemployment increases.
rigor.explanation: A long causal chain — tax cuts for high earners cause inequality, privatisation of housing, transport and education, and rising unemployment — is asserted with nothing offered to connect the links. Bare assertion shading into slippery slope; the conclusion does not follow from anything supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the coalition agreements say that decisions will be based on data and evidence, and yet this decision to repeal what would have been globally leading legislation—smoke-free legislation—flies in the face of data, in evidence.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference with a stated premise: the coalition agreements commit to evidence-based decisions, this repeal contradicts the evidence, therefore the commitment is breached. Valid in form; the gap is that the evidence itself is invoked rather than cited in this sentence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s it. That is the sum game of their ambition to clear the public housing register.
rigor.explanation: Infers the total extent of a government's housing ambition from what a single ceremonial speech happened to mention. An argument from absence of evidence — the Speech from the Throne omitting something does not establish that no policy exists.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: ACT’s proposed approach to Te Tiriti will do the opposite. I agree with Helen Clark that it would “rip us down the middle”, and with Jim Bolger that it’s a “bloody stupid” idea.
rigor.explanation: Engages a real policy but the support offered is entirely that two former Prime Ministers disapprove of it. A bare appeal to authority: nothing about the proposal's content is given as a reason for the conclusion that it would divide the country.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The last 50 years has seen a dramatic decline in taxes on the rich across advanced democracies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a historical fact about tax policy across advanced democracies over roughly 1973–2023: that taxation of high earners has fallen substantially.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD tax database top statutory marginal personal income tax rates (and top corporate rates) for member countries, ~1975 compared with ~2023; true if the cross-country average top rate has fallen substantially over the period, false if it is flat or higher.

divination.statement: We know that it will cost thousands of lives, that young people will be encouraged to take up smoking, and that it will result in $1.3 billion in terms of healthcare costs.
divination.explanation: Forecasts three consequences of the smoke-free repeal: excess deaths, increased youth smoking uptake, and $1.3 billion of additional healthcare cost. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — it forecasts outcomes in the world.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily-smoking prevalence for 15–24 year-olds in the years after the repeal takes effect, compared with the 2022/23 baseline, plus any published Ministry of Health or University of Otago costing of the repeal. True if youth smoking prevalence rises above the pre-repeal baseline and a published estimate of roughly $1.3 billion in additional healthcare cost is borne out; false if youth prevalence continues to fall and no such costing is supported.

veracity.statement: Sadly, there have been no enduring benefits for the over $200 million that has been wasted by the previous Government on this failed experiment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $200 million was spent on establishing Te Pūkenga, the merged polytechnic/ITO entity, and that it produced no lasting benefit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget appropriations, TEC and Ministry of Education reporting on Reform of Vocational Education / Te Pūkenga establishment and transition costs; true if cumulative spend attributable to the merger exceeded $200 million, false if materially below that.

veracity.statement: And we will listen to what they are saying, unlike the consultation that took place during the rogue process which established Te Pūkenga, which ignored the advice of officials, which ignored the feedback from the sector, and which ignored the concerns of communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the consultation preceding Te Pūkenga's establishment proceeded against the advice of officials and against submissions from the vocational education sector and communities.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement and departmental advice for the 2019 Reform of Vocational Education, plus the published submission analysis; true if officials' advice and the majority of sector submissions opposed the single-entity model and it proceeded regardless, false if officials recommended it and submissions supported it.

veracity.statement: I note that the Invercargill City Council’s manager of infrastructure operations has highlighted the environmental importance of this initiative, saying that there have been numerous fires in regional landfills that have been caused primarily by lithium batteries, and this recycling initiative will reduce those fires and other environmental risks.
veracity.explanation: Relays a council official's claim that multiple fires at regional landfills were caused primarily by lithium batteries. The speaker is reporting the claim rather than asserting it in her own right.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: Invercargill City Council manager of infrastructure operations
veracity.falsification_criterion: Invercargill City Council / WasteNet and Fire and Emergency NZ incident records for Southland landfill and transfer-station fires; true if multiple recorded fires are attributed primarily to lithium batteries, false if the recorded causes are otherwise or the fires are not numerous.

veracity.statement: I acknowledge the challenges that a number of our universities are working through in response to declining New Zealand domestic student numbers and international student numbers not yet being back to pre-COVID levels.
veracity.explanation: Two factual claims about the state of university enrolments at the end of 2023: that domestic student numbers were falling, and that international enrolments had not recovered to pre-COVID levels.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education Counts / Ministry of Education tertiary enrolment (EFTS) series; true if domestic university EFTS fell across 2022–2023 and 2023 international enrolments remained below the 2019 figure, false if either series had risen to or above those benchmarks.

specificity.statement: Sadly, there have been no enduring benefits for the over $200 million that has been wasted by the previous Government on this failed experiment.
specificity.explanation: Names the entity and attaches a dollar figure to it, so the spending claim is checkable; the 'no enduring benefits' half carries no measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government will stop the top-down, one-size-fits-all, Government-knows-best mantra that we have had to put up with for the past six years—and it did not work.
specificity.explanation: A string of slogans about a governing style; no policy, mechanism, figure or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will make sensible decisions about where economies of scale can be achieved, we will make sensible decisions about where shared services actually save money—not cost more—and we will ensure that maximum regional autonomy can be achieved because we know that’s where the best decisions are made.
specificity.explanation: Three repetitions of 'sensible decisions' with no named service, saving, threshold or date; nothing here could be checked against a later outcome.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government will stop the top-down, one-size-fits-all, Government-knows-best mantra that we have had to put up with for the past six years—and it did not work.
focus.explanation: Characterises the previous government's general approach over six years without naming a policy, measure or outcome; the only concrete anchor is the party-versus-party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reality is that every one of us, regardless of what we do and where we live, impacts on the environment, and therefore every single one of us has a responsibility to improve the lot of the environment.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (a shared duty to improve the environment) is drawn straight from the premise that everyone has an impact — an is/ought non sequitur, since having an effect does not by itself establish an obligation, and no bridging premise is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So, to unpack that, just for a second, we have 21 seats—21 seats—explicitly to the left of the Labour Party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 21 seats in the 54th Parliament are held by parties positioned to the left of Labour, offered as evidence for the claim that this is the most left-wing Parliament in her lifetime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the 2023 general election: seat counts for the Green Party and Te Pāti Māori (the parties conventionally placed left of Labour). True if they sum to 21; false if the total is materially different or if the parties counted are not those to Labour's left.

veracity.statement: New Zealand First said then, in 2017-2018, that the most important thing that they could do, in supporting this oil and gas ban, was give those communities an opportunity to prepare, because they knew that the writing was on the wall.
veracity.explanation: Relays what New Zealand First said in 2017-18 about why it supported the ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration — namely that it gave affected regional communities time to prepare. The speaker is reporting another party's stated rationale, not asserting it as her own.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard speeches and public statements by New Zealand First MPs during the passage of the Crown Minerals (Petroleum) Amendment Bill (2018). True if they justified their support by reference to giving Taranaki/regional communities time to transition; false if their stated rationale was materially different or if they did not support the ban.

veracity.statement: Because if we burn anywhere from one fifth to one third of what we’ve already discovered—we know because the science tells us; if the Government was interested in listening to it—we are going to burst past 1.5 degrees of warming, which is critical for retention of life as we know it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as established science that burning between one fifth and one third of already-discovered fossil fuel reserves would take warming past 1.5 degrees.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IPCC AR6 remaining carbon budget for 1.5°C compared against published estimates of the CO2 embedded in proven fossil fuel reserves. True if burning roughly 20–33% of proven reserves exhausts the 1.5°C budget; false if the fraction stated is materially off from the peer-reviewed estimate.

veracity.statement: We had the $750 million walking and cycling bridge across Auckland Harbour, which, for that amount of money, didn’t even include a bus lane.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the proposed Auckland Harbour walking and cycling crossing carried a $750 million price tag and that the design contained no bus lane.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waka Kotahi/NZTA published cost estimates and design documentation for the Northern Pathway Auckland Harbour Bridge crossing announced in 2021. True if the announced cost was approximately $750m and the design excluded a bus lane; false if the published figure differs materially or a bus lane was included.

civility.statement: Now, while this Government may be blu-tacked together by hot takes from your uncle at Christmas, you know, led not by the Three Stooges but, in fact, by the three Scrooges, who are coming for you this Christmas, trying to ram through legislation—anti the workers, anti the renters, and we’ll just wait and see when it comes to being anti the planet.
civility.explanation: Ridicules the three coalition leaders personally as 'the Three Stooges'/'the three Scrooges' — mockery of individuals rather than of a policy. Short of sustained abuse, but it lands on the people, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The last three years, we reached peak stupid when it came to infrastructure proposals.
civility.explanation: Derisive language, but aimed squarely at the previous government's infrastructure proposals rather than at any person. Harsh criticism of a record is civil under this scale; the sneering register keeps it just short of the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Projects that are under way now, like KiwiRail’s Inter-island Resilience Connection terminals in Picton and Wellington, have been managed so poorly by the sponsors in the last Government—the former Minister of Finance, Grant Robertson, the former Minister for State Owned Enterprises, Dr Duncan Webb—that this new Government is now potentially on the hook for billions of dollars to rebuild the landside and the coastal structures and to pay for these Interislander ferries.
civility.explanation: Names two individuals and charges them with poor management. That is criticism of a ministerial record rather than of character, but naming them personally edges it toward the person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, while this Government may be blu-tacked together by hot takes from your uncle at Christmas, you know, led not by the Three Stooges but, in fact, by the three Scrooges, who are coming for you this Christmas, trying to ram through legislation—anti the workers, anti the renters, and we’ll just wait and see when it comes to being anti the planet.
focus.explanation: There is a gesture at policy — legislation said to be against workers and renters — but no measure, figure or outcome is named, and the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the governing parties.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Projects that are under way now, like KiwiRail’s Inter-island Resilience Connection terminals in Picton and Wellington, have been managed so poorly by the sponsors in the last Government—the former Minister of Finance, Grant Robertson, the former Minister for State Owned Enterprises, Dr Duncan Webb—that this new Government is now potentially on the hook for billions of dollars to rebuild the landside and the coastal structures and to pay for these Interislander ferries.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project, the responsible ministers and a specific claimed consequence. This is scrutiny of a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We can have free dental care; we can have free tertiary education; we can have a guaranteed minimum-income; we can have rent controls—if we decide, as a Parliament, to move ahead with an evidence base and values of compassion, to implement policies that support both people and the planet.
