divination.statement: I just suspect that, actually, that is going to have an effect on the prices that people pay, and they will be lower than they would have otherwise been, and people can start to feel some relief from the long, hard, grinding road of inflation they’ve been subject to by the previous Government for nearly three years now where inflation has been outside the target band.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that legislating the single price-stability mandate will feed into expectations and bring price inflation down, ending the run of inflation outside the target band.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual inflation against the RBNZ 1–3% target band; true if annual CPI inflation returns to within the band within a year of this statement, false if it remains above 3% throughout that period.

specificity.statement: Kiwis have found this in their back pocket: it’s their groceries, it’s their rent, it’s their rates—it is all pervasive.
specificity.explanation: Names the categories where cost-of-living pressure is felt but supplies no figures, no period, and no measure — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to begin by reiterating how outrageous it is that the Government have pushed this law through under urgency. To refuse experts in the public the opportunity to submit is arrogant and extreme. It is reckless lawmaking.
civility.explanation: Fierce criticism of a legislative process and a decision, not of any individual. 'Arrogant and extreme' edges toward characterising the Government rather than the choice, which keeps it just below the standard, but no person is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill just fills the pockets of this Government’s rich mates.
civility.explanation: Imputes corrupt motive — legislating to enrich cronies — rather than engaging the argument. No individual is named, so it stops short of a personal insult, but attributing bad faith is a genuine civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The truth is that they have been put in these positions by wealthy donors and vested interests to look after the interests of those people, especially from the ACT Party but also from Nicola Willis, the Minister of Finance, in the National Party.
civility.explanation: A direct imputation of corruption to a named individual — that the Minister of Finance holds office to serve donors rather than the public. This lands on the person, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That’s a demonstrable lie.
civility.explanation: Accuses another member of deliberate deception rather than disputing the claim. Calling a statement a lie asserts intent, which lands on the person's honesty.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill is a solution looking for a problem. There is no economic evidence that the employment mandate has contributed to inflation over the past two years, nor that it has had any other negative economic impacts.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House, but it rests on an argument from absence of evidence: the conclusion that the bill solves nothing is carried entirely by the assertion that no contrary evidence exists, with no source or analysis offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, New Zealand’s inflation peaked at a lower level and, while CPI inflation has been slower to come down, ultimately it’s the same general shape, and that’s because the shock that affected New Zealand affected the whole world, and reserve banks around the world responded in similar ways—the constraints on people going to work, because of the COVID pandemic, did result in supply chain shortages, and there were other factors, like the invasion of Ukraine by Russia, which affected gas prices and oil prices, which flowed on to energy prices here in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: shared international shocks plus similar central-bank responses are offered as the reason for the common inflation profile, and the conclusion tracks the evidence cited. The causal step from global shock to NZ prices is asserted rather than quantified, which is the remaining gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So when you say, for example, that we’re going to reward people for being landlords—which means that they do no work and they earn a return on their asset, and they don’t pay tax on that—everyone in the country cannot get wealthy through being landlords.
rigor.explanation: A valid rebuttal of a fallacy of composition: a strategy of enrichment through landlording cannot generalise to the whole population, since not everyone can be a landlord. The inference holds; the characterisation of landlords as doing no work and paying no tax is a premise question, not a reasoning one.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This bill is a solution looking for a problem. There is no economic evidence that the employment mandate has contributed to inflation over the past two years, nor that it has had any other negative economic impacts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no economic evidence exists linking the Reserve Bank's employment mandate either to the 2021-2023 inflation episode or to any other negative economic impact.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published analysis of the dual mandate's effect on NZ inflation 2021-2023 — RBNZ Monetary Policy Statements and reviews, Treasury analysis, and peer-reviewed or IMF assessments. True if no such source identifies the maximum sustainable employment objective as a contributor to inflation or other adverse economic outcomes; false if any credible published analysis attributes such an effect to it.

veracity.statement: Unemployment is rising. Māori unemployment, as always, is rising even faster.
veracity.explanation: Two linked claims about the present direction of the labour market: that unemployment overall is rising, and that Māori unemployment is rising at a faster rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey for the quarters up to September 2023. True if the total unemployment rate rose over recent quarters AND the Māori unemployment rate rose by more percentage points over the same period; false if either the total rate was flat or falling, or Māori unemployment rose more slowly than the total.

veracity.statement: In fact, New Zealand’s inflation peaked at a lower level and, while CPI inflation has been slower to come down, ultimately it’s the same general shape, and that’s because the shock that affected New Zealand affected the whole world, and reserve banks around the world responded in similar ways—the constraints on people going to work, because of the COVID pandemic, did result in supply chain shortages, and there were other factors, like the invasion of Ukraine by Russia, which affected gas prices and oil prices, which flowed on to energy prices here in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's inflation peak was lower than that of the named comparator countries and that the disinflation has been slower, with the episode attributed to common global supply and energy shocks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peak annual CPI inflation rates from Stats NZ and the corresponding national statistics agencies (BLS, ONS, ABS, Statistics Denmark) for 2021-2023. True if New Zealand's peak annual CPI rate was below those of the United States, United Kingdom, Denmark and Australia; false if it exceeded any of them materially.

veracity.statement: Yes, I stand by my statement. The Government is going to meet its obligations and commitments that it’s made on climate change, and I also stand by the statement from the Minister of Resources as well, because he was clearly talking about the previous Government’s 100 percent renewable electricity target, which is, actually, a fairy tale and is counter-productive.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Resources' quoted remark about a 'great lie' concerned the previous Government's 100 percent renewable electricity target rather than the status of climate change as a crisis.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The full text and context of the Minister of Resources' remark quoted in the House ('One of the great lies about climate change is that, yes, apparently, it's a crisis'). True if that remark was made in reference to the previous Government's 100 percent renewable electricity target; false if it referred to the characterisation of climate change itself as a crisis.

focus.statement: This bill just fills the pockets of this Government’s rich mates.
focus.explanation: Nominally about the bill, but the content is entirely a claim about who the other side really serves; no mechanism, cost, beneficiary or provision of the bill is named to support it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The truth is that they have been put in these positions by wealthy donors and vested interests to look after the interests of those people, especially from the ACT Party but also from Nicola Willis, the Minister of Finance, in the National Party.
focus.explanation: Entirely about who the other parties really are and who funds them. No policy, measure or figure is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is he concerned about the growing contradiction, under this Government, between New Zealand’s international and climate commitments and domestic plans which undermine efforts to reduce emissions, such as reopening oil and gas drilling and cancelling the Clean Car Discount?
focus.explanation: Names two specific policy decisions and ties them to a named obligation. This is scrutiny of a government's programme against its stated commitments — squarely on the policy, not on the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The mandate should include holistic wellbeing outcomes including social, cultural, and environmental.
specificity.explanation: Offers a direction for the alternative policy but nothing checkable: no statutory wording, no measure of wellbeing, no mechanism by which the bank would weigh these outcomes. A string of broad categories.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I showed members opposite last night in the second reading on this bill, if we look at Consumers Price Index (CPI) inflation right around the globe, New Zealand tracked right along with other countries, like the United States, Denmark, the United Kingdom, and Australia.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact series (CPI) and four specific comparator countries, so the comparison could be checked, but supplies no figures, dates or magnitudes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yeah, we’re going to actually electrify New Zealand by doubling the amount of renewable electricity that’s in New Zealand so we can make the transition well and make our sectors move to clean, green energy.
specificity.explanation: Gives one quantified goal — doubling renewable electricity — but no baseline year, no target date, and no mechanism for how the doubling would be achieved.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Absolutely not. We are deeply committed to delivering on our climate goals and commitments. The way we go about doing that may be different from the previous Government, but don’t misunderstand our commitment to the targets and goals.
specificity.explanation: An assertion of commitment with nothing checkable attached: no target named, no policy identified, and the stated difference in approach is left entirely unspecified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does his Government have any targets or policies to reduce fossil fuel use across the energy and transport industry to replace the 2030 renewable electricity target, and, if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: A precise question: it names the target being replaced, its date, and the two sectors at issue, so a responsive answer would be checkable. It stops short of a figure of its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he or will he not instruct all Ministers to implement the commission’s advice in their work programmes?
focus.explanation: Names a specific body's advice and a specific mechanism (Ministers' work programmes). Squarely on the policy question, no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can he name one decision that his Government has taken to date that will materially reduce New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas emissions; if so, what is it?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny directed at a named outcome (net greenhouse gas emissions) and at government decisions, not at the other party's character. This is the opposition's job and is fully on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our Government’s committed to delivering on climate change, and our Ministers are making sure that they can do that through their respective portfolios.
specificity.explanation: A statement of commitment with no measure, figure, timeframe or named action. 'Through their respective portfolios' carries no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s our plan to actually increase and double the amount of renewable electricity.
specificity.explanation: A quantified direction ('double') attached to a named area, but no baseline, no timeframe and no mechanism, so it is only partly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That starts with our 100-day plan, which includes a number of changes to make it easier for Kiwis to be able to get ahead, make our communities safer, and deliver better health and education for our young people.
specificity.explanation: Names the 100-day plan but describes it only as 'a number of changes' followed by a string of generic goods — no policy, figure or date is supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he agree with David Seymour that ACT’s proposal to have a debate and referendum on the Treaty—“you know, the coalition Government has agreed to go halfway with that, and then re-evaluate and perhaps proceed further, and it will actually enhance the mana of the Treaty”—or does he agree with Christopher Luxon that “we will pursue a Treaty Principles Bill to select committee, and that is as far as it will go.”?
specificity.explanation: Quotes two named individuals' positions directly and names the measure (Treaty Principles Bill) and the stage at issue. Anyone could check both quotes and the contradiction alleged.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The position of the Government is that we will support the bill until select committee, through its first reading, and that’s as far the comment goes at this stage.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete, checkable position — support to first reading and select committee, no further — though it gives no reasoning or subsequent process detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that New Zealanders are struggling, which is why the Government is committed to delivering fiscally neutral tax relief next year.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy (tax relief), a constraint on it (fiscally neutral) and rough timing (next year), but no rates, thresholds, amounts or funding sources.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can she stand by that statement when Oranga Tamariki’s own public website states that section 7AA enables them to “develop strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations, including iwi authorities”?
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory provision, names the source, and quotes it verbatim. The alleged contradiction can be checked against a single identified document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: By removing section 7AA, that will not remove the ability for the 10 strategic partnerships that are currently in place and work to be made on other strategic partnerships.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure (10 existing partnerships) and a named provision, but no account of what legal basis the partnerships would rest on once the section is repealed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am proud to stand here as the Minister for Children that represents a Government that is committed to making sure that every child in New Zealand wakes up knowing today is going to be a better day.
specificity.explanation: A slogan offered where substance was called for: no policy, mechanism, figure or timeframe, and nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What’s the point of sending a bill to a select committee that the Government intends to vote down, other than to waste thousands of hours of people’s time and a lot of taxpayers’ money?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the process, but a false dilemma packaged as a loaded question: it presumes the only possible purpose is waste, excluding by construction any value in public submission or coalition process. The reasoning is about the policy, not the people, so it is scoreable here — it is just incomplete.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s a democracy. And as part of our coalition agreement with National and ACT, that is our commitment that we have made.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur plus an appeal to prior commitment: that the country is a democracy does not establish that a bill the Government will not pass should be sent to select committee, and 'we agreed to it' is a restatement of the decision rather than a reason for it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, I think it’s a bit rich for that member to talk about wasteful Government spending. He led a Government that undertook so much wasteful Government spending, it drove domestic inflation, drove interest rates up, slowed our economic growth up, and put at risk employment. So, no disrespect, not taking any lectures from that member.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the conclusion is that the questioner's point can be disregarded because of his own record, which does not bear on whether sending a doomed bill to select committee is wasteful. The causal chain from spending to inflation, rates, growth and employment is also asserted with nothing offered to connect the links.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Mr Hipkins asks what the inflation rate is in the UK, and I can inform him it is down at 4.6 percent, so he managed to do an even worse job than the UK.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur from a real figure: a cross-country inflation comparison does not establish that one individual 'did a worse job', since it holds nothing else constant — different energy exposure, monetary settings and measurement baselines all move the comparison independently of any decision the member made.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are already existing provisions within the Act that protect the rights of whānau, hapū, and iwi. I refer the member to sections 4, 5, and 13 of the Oranga Tamariki Act.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with evidence offered: the conclusion that repeal changes nothing is supported by pointing to specific surviving sections. It falls short of 1.0 because pointing to other provisions does not show they carry the same duties as the one being removed — the gap between 'other protections exist' and 'nothing is lost' is not closed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The only people implying that these partnerships will be affected are those from across the House, and I have instructed officials that they should continue working with iwi and Māori organisations where this is achieving positive outcomes for young people.
rigor.explanation: Genetic fallacy: the concern is dismissed by reference to who is raising it rather than by any reason it is unfounded. Where the objection comes from has no bearing on whether repeal affects the partnerships.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Look, I think it’s a bit rich for that member to talk about wasteful Government spending. He led a Government that undertook so much wasteful Government spending, it drove domestic inflation, drove interest rates up, slowed our economic growth up, and put at risk employment. So, no disrespect, not taking any lectures from that member.
civility.explanation: The record criticism itself is fair game, but 'it's a bit rich for that member' and 'not taking any lectures from that member' are dismissive of the person's standing to speak rather than of the argument. Short of an insult, but it has left the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because we had a finance Minister who repeatedly promised a return to surplus, and yet every time he arose to announce his next Budget, the surplus would mysteriously slip, slip, slip away.
civility.explanation: Mockery of an identifiable individual rather than of the fiscal forecasts: 'mysteriously slip, slip, slip away' imputes evasiveness to the person, and the repetition is there to ridicule. The underlying point about slipping surplus forecasts could have been made without it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is she comfortable with her legacy as Minister for Children being the person who presided over another stolen generation of indigenous children?
civility.explanation: A direct personal charge: it is framed around the Minister's legacy and casts her personally as presiding over a stolen generation, rather than putting the same objection to the policy. The severity of the imputation is aimed at the individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How can she justify this policy to whānau, hapū, and iwi Māori when she knows full well that this will lead to many more tamariki Māori being severed from whakapapa?
civility.explanation: 'She knows full well' imputes bad faith — that the Minister is knowingly pursuing a harm rather than disagreeing about its effect. The policy objection itself is legitimate; the accusation of knowing intent is what costs here.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The reports I have received confirm that inflation remains a major challenge in New Zealand, at a rate of 5.6 percent, even while inflation falls rapidly overseas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's headline inflation rate as at 12 December 2023 was 5.6 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index, annual inflation rate for the September 2023 quarter (the most recent print available on 12 December 2023); true if 5.6% ± rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Inflation in the United States fell to just 3.1 percent overnight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the US annual inflation figure released in the 24 hours before 12 December 2023 NZ time was 3.1 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: US Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI release of 12 December 2023 (November 2023 data), annual all-items rate; true if 3.1%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: However, the outgoing Government has left us with a forecast deficit this year of $11.4 billion—and that’s in the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update 2023 forecast an $11.4 billion deficit for the current (2023/24) fiscal year. The source document is named, so the claim resolves on a single published number.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury PREFU 2023, OBEGAL forecast for the year ending June 2024; true if approximately -$11.4 billion, false if materially different or if the figure quoted corresponds to a different year or measure.

veracity.statement: The only people implying that these partnerships will be affected are those from across the House, and I have instructed officials that they should continue working with iwi and Māori organisations where this is achieving positive outcomes for young people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that concern about the repeal affecting iwi partnerships came only from Opposition members — a checkable claim about who had publicly raised it by 12 December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements dated on or before 12 December 2023 by non-parliamentarians — iwi leaders, the Chief Children's Commissioner, Oranga Tamariki's partner organisations — saying that removing section 7AA would affect iwi partnerships; the claim is false if any such statement exists, true only if every such statement came from an MP.

veracity.statement: It’s my pleasure to announce to the House that as a consequence of a far-sighted politician six years ago making an investment, on behalf of the Government, in the Snowy River goldmine, the entirety of the $15 million has been paid back.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a $15 million government investment made about six years earlier in the Snowy River goldmine on the West Coast has been repaid in full.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Provincial Growth Fund / Kānoa loan records and Crown financial statements for the Snowy River goldmine investment; true if the full $15m principal is recorded as repaid by December 2023, false if any balance remains outstanding or the sum invested was not $15m.

veracity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that the National Party’s position before the election was to reverse the app tax, and it is now the position of a National-led Government that it will keep the app tax in place?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two factual premises: that National campaigned in 2023 on reversing the 'app tax' (GST on services supplied through electronic marketplaces), and that the National-led coalition Government has decided to retain it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's published 2023 tax plan / campaign statements on the app tax, and the coalition Government's post-formation announcements and legislation on GST on electronic marketplace services; true if National promised reversal and the Government subsequently retained the tax, false if either half is not borne out.

veracity.statement: The previous Government promised the scheme would be “fiscally neutral”, but, as at 30 November, $579 million has been paid out in rebates and $13.5 million has been spent on administration costs, while only $290 million has been received in charges.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific Clean Car Discount scheme figures as at 30 November 2023: $579m in rebates paid, $13.5m administration costs, $290m received in charges — against a stated prior commitment that the scheme would be fiscally neutral.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA / Ministry of Transport Clean Car Discount financial reporting to 30 November 2023; true if the rebate, administration and charge totals match within rounding, false if materially different. The 'fiscally neutral' promise checks against the scheme's original Cabinet papers and regulatory impact statement.

veracity.statement: In a 2021 report into the teaching of mathematics in New Zealand, the Royal Society found significant variation amongst schools in terms of the amount of time devoted to teaching maths, with some teachers scheduling maths for as much as seven hours a week, while others teach it for fewer than three.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 2021 Royal Society Te Apārangi report on mathematics teaching found instructional time ranging from as much as seven hours a week down to fewer than three, and recommended an hour a day of mathematics.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Society Te Apārangi 2021 report on mathematics and statistics education ('Pāngarau Mathematics and Tauanga Statistics in Aotearoa New Zealand'); true if it reports that time range and carries an hour-a-day recommendation, false if the range or the recommendation is not in the report.

veracity.statement: The 2022 national monitoring study showed that only 41.5 percent of our year 8s were at curriculum for maths after eight years of schooling.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure from the 2022 National Monitoring Study of Student Achievement: 41.5% of year 8 students at the expected curriculum level in mathematics.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2022 NMSSA mathematics and statistics report, year 8 cohort; true if the proportion at or above curriculum expectation is 41.5% within rounding, false if materially different.

specificity.statement: It’s my pleasure to announce to the House that as a consequence of a far-sighted politician six years ago making an investment, on behalf of the Government, in the Snowy River goldmine, the entirety of the $15 million has been paid back.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific investment, the amount ($15 million), the recipient and the outcome (fully repaid) — directly checkable against loan records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This means that charges will end for vehicles after 11.59 p.m. on 31 December 2023, and buyers of low-emitting vehicles will no longer be able to apply for rebates.
specificity.explanation: Exact cut-off time and date, and the precise mechanism on both sides of the scheme (charges cease, rebates close). Someone could act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The previous Government promised the scheme would be “fiscally neutral”, but, as at 30 November, $579 million has been paid out in rebates and $13.5 million has been spent on administration costs, while only $290 million has been received in charges.
specificity.explanation: Three separate dollar figures with a stated as-at date, tied to a named scheme — fully checkable against the scheme's financial reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have asked for advice on how I can organise to meet with these groups that have committed partnership agreements, and if my calendar has the space to do this, I will do so.
specificity.explanation: Names an action taken (seeking advice) and a body to meet, but supplies no date, no timeframe relative to the bill's introduction, and makes the meeting conditional on unspecified calendar availability.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In a 2021 report into the teaching of mathematics in New Zealand, the Royal Society found significant variation amongst schools in terms of the amount of time devoted to teaching maths, with some teachers scheduling maths for as much as seven hours a week, while others teach it for fewer than three.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the year, and the quantified spread of teaching hours — a reader could go to the report and check the range.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Sadly, a number of pixie-like hapū in Taranaki have sought to undermine this legitimate industry.
civility.explanation: Belittles identified groups of people as 'pixie-like' and imputes bad motive ('sought to undermine') rather than engaging their objections to seabed mining. This is mockery aimed at people, not criticism of an argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And then the grown-ups will ensure that there is security and manageable risk in our energy sector, unlike what we hear from the other side of the House. I look forward to providing that educational service to other members of Parliament.
civility.explanation: Condescension toward other members — casting his own side as 'the grown-ups' and offering opposing MPs an 'educational service' treats them as childish rather than engaging what they argued. Short of a direct insult, but sneering.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I can also be confident about delivering tax relief, because, unlike the member opposite, I actually believe New Zealanders deserve to keep more of what they earn, and they deserve a Government that won’t waste their hard-earned wages on boondoggles, like he did.
civility.explanation: Imputes to the questioner both a lack of belief that New Zealanders should keep their earnings and personal responsibility for wasting wages on 'boondoggles' — a characterisation of the person's motives and conduct rather than of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In light of her response to question No. 4, that she is proud, how can she possibly feel proud to condemn future generations of Māori tamariki to be alienated from their whakapapa, language, and culture?
civility.explanation: Goes past the policy to the Minister's character — questioning how she could 'possibly feel proud' of an outcome attributed to her personally, framing her as taking satisfaction in harming Māori children.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And then the grown-ups will ensure that there is security and manageable risk in our energy sector, unlike what we hear from the other side of the House. I look forward to providing that educational service to other members of Parliament.
focus.explanation: There is a policy thread (energy security and risk), but the weight of the passage is a contrast with 'the other side of the House' as a group; no mechanism, figure or named measure is supplied to carry the point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she say that she will deliver fiscally neutral tax relief, when she doesn’t know how much it’s going to cost?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: names the specific commitment (fiscally neutral tax relief) and presses the specific gap (unknown cost). Ordinary opposition scrutiny of a named government commitment, with no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Minister to be careful of when she sees these Māori groups, because the last Minister in her place who did that ended up voting for another political party, not Labour.
focus.explanation: No policy content at all: the subject is a former Minister's defection to another party, offered as a jibe about the opposition's internal loyalties. Names no measure, figure or outcome bearing on section 7AA or Oranga Tamariki.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How does the Minister know how frequently reading, writing, and maths is currently being taught in classrooms, given the acknowledgment, in the Ministry of Education bulletin to school principals yesterday, that many of them were already doing that and little change was needed?
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the announced policy: what evidence base exists for current teaching hours, citing the specific Ministry bulletin issued the previous day. Scrutiny of a named measure, with no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can also be confident about delivering tax relief, because, unlike the member opposite, I actually believe New Zealanders deserve to keep more of what they earn, and they deserve a Government that won’t waste their hard-earned wages on boondoggles, like he did.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: confidence about *delivering* fiscally neutral tax relief is asserted to follow from *believing* people deserve tax relief. A statement of desire supplies no support for a claim about fiscal deliverability, which was the question asked.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, the $302.5 million deficit hitting taxpayers’ pockets has contributed to thousands of subsidies to high-end vehicles costing $70,000 or more.
rigor.explanation: Reversed causation: the deficit is presented as the cause of the high-end vehicle subsidies, when on his own account in the preceding answer the rebates are what produced the deficit. The stated relationship runs the wrong way, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It depends on how someone interprets what honouring the Treaty means. And so that creates a conflict, because, when decisions are being made, the decisions may vary on the interpretation of what honouring the Treaty means.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the provision at issue, but with a gap: interpretive variation is offered as establishing a 'fundamental conflict' between the child's best interests and Treaty obligations. Variation in interpretation shows inconsistency, not that the two duties conflict — the conclusion overshoots the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In light of her response to question No. 4, that she is proud, how can she possibly feel proud to condemn future generations of Māori tamariki to be alienated from their whakapapa, language, and culture?
rigor.explanation: Complex question: the contested claim — that repealing the provision will alienate future generations of tamariki from their whakapapa — is smuggled in as a presupposition rather than argued for, so no answer is available that does not concede it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She could not provide evidence of the advice that she had received from her officials to absolutely and emphatically support her view that the Reserve Bank mandate should go back to one mandate, which is in relation to price stability.
civility.explanation: A hard criticism of the Minister's handling of the bill that stays entirely on the substance — what advice was held and whether it was produced. No imputation of bad faith, no attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On the logic of this new Government, which, again, was not evidence-based, but on their logic, inflation, therefore, should be higher in countries with a dual mandate central bank, and therefore lower in countries with a single mandate central bank.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: she reconstructs the Government's implied premise and tests it against cross-country data. The reconstruction leans toward a strawman (the case for a single mandate is usually about the speed and clarity of the response, not the level of inflation), and an uncontrolled comparison of peak rates cannot separate mandate from energy prices, fiscal stance or exchange rate. The form of the argument is sound; the step from 'no visible correlation across a handful of countries' to 'no relationship' is where it gives way.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the eurozone, which has a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, it peaked at 10.6 percent, and in Sweden, which has a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, it peaked at 12.3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two named jurisdictions, each with its mandate type and a peak inflation figure to one decimal place. Directly checkable against published statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In the eurozone, which has a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, it peaked at 10.6 percent, and in Sweden, which has a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, it peaked at 12.3 percent.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the policy question at issue — whether a central bank's mandate type is associated with inflation outcomes. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It gives me a great disheartenment to stand here in the House today to, basically, once again understand that the vision of this new Government is not to support workers, is not to support those who are employed in salary and wages—and, again, the next bill that’s coming through the House, again under urgency, with no ability to be able to scrutinise it with the public, once again shows how deaf that side of the House is to the hundreds of people who stood outside and protested, who were workers.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point inside it — a named process complaint (a second bill taken under urgency with no public scrutiny) — but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of what 'this new Government' is like and how 'deaf that side of the House' is. Policy content wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the eurozone, which has a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, it peaked at 10.6 percent, and in Sweden, which has a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, it peaked at 12.3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that euro area annual inflation peaked at 10.6 percent and Swedish inflation at 12.3 percent during the recent inflation episode.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Eurostat euro area HICP annual inflation series and Statistics Sweden's CPI series, for the 2021-23 inflation episode. True if the euro area peak annual rate is 10.6% and the Swedish peak is 12.3% (to rounding); false if either peak differs materially from the figure stated.

veracity.statement: But, you know, you look at New Zealand and Australia, we both have a central bank with dual mandates—inflation peaked at 7.2 percent and 7.8 percent for Australia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand and Australia both had dual-mandate central banks and that their annual inflation peaked at 7.2 and 7.8 percent respectively.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series and the ABS CPI annual inflation series for 2021-23. True if the New Zealand peak annual rate is 7.2% and the Australian peak is 7.8% (to rounding); false if either differs materially. Also requires that both central banks had dual (price stability plus employment) mandates at that time.

veracity.statement: We found the evidence—and The Reserve Bank is only second to the Norwegian central bank in hiking interest rates in 2021.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that among comparable central banks, only Norway's raised its policy rate earlier than the Reserve Bank of New Zealand did in 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Dates of the first post-pandemic policy-rate increases by advanced-economy/OECD central banks in 2021 (e.g. RBNZ OCR decisions, Norges Bank policy rate decisions, and those of other OECD central banks). True if only Norges Bank raised its policy rate before the RBNZ; false if any other comparable central bank raised before the RBNZ in 2021.

divination.statement: Basically, it’s going to be the working people—those who are going to be unemployed—that are going to be paying for this policy change.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the cost of returning the Reserve Bank to a single price-stability mandate will fall on workers through higher unemployment.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate in the two years following the Act's enactment, measured against the December 2023 quarter baseline. True if the unemployment rate rises materially (more than a percentage point) above that baseline over the period; false if it stays flat or falls.

civility.statement: And I suggest that the member, next time, listens more carefully to my answers.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the questioner personally rather than at her argument — a pointed suggestion that she is not paying attention. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ve asked for advice in relation to the climate report which was released yesterday, but I would say that our Government’s approach will be actually on building infrastructure rather than wasting hundreds of millions of dollars on endless reports, business cases, and actually not delivering anything, which was the past Government’s approach.
civility.explanation: Scathing about a previous Government's approach and its spending, but no individual is attacked and no bad faith is imputed to a person. Hard criticism of a record is civil under this scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, the outgoing Government had a shambolic policy in relation to police to public ratio. The coalition Government has got a very clear and concise policy.
civility.explanation: 'Shambolic' is aimed at a policy, not at any member. Blunt criticism of a policy is the expected standard here and costs nothing.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think that member is getting her numbers mixed up.
civility.explanation: Pointed and slightly personal in form, but it is a correction of a factual conflation in the question rather than an attack on the member's character or competence generally.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This will include explicit teaching, collaborative learning, activities, games, and all the other best-practice techniques teachers use to engage and develop young people’s skills.
specificity.explanation: Asked what an hour a day looks like in practice, the answer offers a list of generic pedagogical categories with no mechanism, split of time, or measurable requirement. Some direction, little checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he accept the advice from the Climate Change Commission, released yesterday, in relation to low-emissions and zero-emissions vehicles, that “Supports to address the upfront cost barrier are especially important.”, and, if so, will he implement a price incentive for zero-emissions vehicles to replace the Clean Car Discount?
specificity.explanation: Named source, dated, direct quotation of the advice, and a named policy the answer would have to address. A precise question carries as much checkable content as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our policy is to commit to an additional 500 police officers on top of the 1,800 police officers that New Zealand First delivered—New Zealand First and National, in this coalition Government, will now deliver 2,300 additional police officers.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete officer figures and the baseline they build on. Someone could check the arithmetic and the delivery against workforce records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: According to the latest benefit numbers released by the Ministry of Social Development in November, there are currently 182,340 people on jobseeker support. This is an increase of over 11,000 people this year alone. In total, there were 61,614 more people receiving the jobseeker support benefit during Labour’s time in Government.
specificity.explanation: Named source, named month, and three exact figures to the individual person. Fully checkable against the published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he agree with the comment of Christopher Luxon that the funding for additional police comes out of future operating allowances, $124 million over four years?
specificity.explanation: Names the funding mechanism, an exact dollar amount and a timeframe, all of which could be checked against fiscal documents. A precise question carries as much content as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have written to the New Zealand Transport Agency to ask them to stop work on the prior Government’s vehicle kilometres travelled reduction work programme, which was simply writing reports rather than actually delivering infrastructure. Our approach will be actually delivering infrastructure, while the last Government was all about writing reports.
focus.explanation: Names a specific work programme and a specific action taken on it, but half the answer is generalised framing about what the last Government was 'all about' rather than the policy question.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’ve asked for advice in relation to the climate report which was released yesterday, but I would say that our Government’s approach will be actually on building infrastructure rather than wasting hundreds of millions of dollars on endless reports, business cases, and actually not delivering anything, which was the past Government’s approach.
focus.explanation: Asked about specific Climate Change Commission advice, the weight of the answer is a general characterisation of the previous Government's approach rather than any named measure, cost or timeframe.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, we’re not going to continue to waste hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayers’ money to subsidise wealthy New Zealanders to be able to buy electric vehicles they can already purchase. Instead, we will invest in supercharging the electric vehicle charging network, which is a priority under this Government.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure at issue — the Clean Car Discount — with a stated reason for discontinuing it and a named alternative policy. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he accept the advice from the Climate Change Commission, released yesterday, in relation to low-emissions and zero-emissions vehicles, that “Supports to address the upfront cost barrier are especially important.”, and, if so, will he implement a price incentive for zero-emissions vehicles to replace the Clean Car Discount?
focus.explanation: Names a specific advisory report, quotes its finding, and asks about a specific policy instrument and its named replacement. Scrutiny directed entirely at the measure, not the party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, the reality is that the books were a shambles under the previous Government. So we’ve got quite a bit of work to do. The previous Government already underfunded the policy around the 1:480 numbers. So we’ve made a commitment to the 500 and we will come through with that commitment. But, believe me, we’ve got a lot of work to do to tidy up the mess that that Government made.
focus.explanation: Asked where the funding comes from, the answer names a ratio commitment and an officer number but spends most of its length on a general characterisation of the previous Government's books and 'mess'. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government is committed to supporting our front line, because it appears not only were they a soft on crime Government; they’re a soft on crime Opposition as well.
focus.explanation: The reason offered is entirely a label applied to the other party in both its past and present roles. No policy, figure or outcome is named in the clause at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is relevant today is the increase in number that that Government, when they were in charge for six years, oversaw; a massive increase in the number of people on the jobseeker benefit.
focus.explanation: Declines the comparison asked for and redirects to the other party's term, but does anchor on a named benefit and its recipient numbers rather than pure party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have written to the New Zealand Transport Agency to ask them to stop work on the prior Government’s vehicle kilometres travelled reduction work programme, which was simply writing reports rather than actually delivering infrastructure. Our approach will be actually delivering infrastructure, while the last Government was all about writing reports.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: analysis and delivery are treated as mutually exclusive, so the conclusion that the programme should stop rests on an opposition that is never established. The inference concerns a real policy, so it is assessable, and it is weak.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Yes, and I have received advice that transport is expected to achieve the first emissions budget period, 2022-2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the transport sector will come in within the pathway assumed for New Zealand's first emissions budget, covering 2022 to 2025.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Climate Change Commission final accounting for emissions budget one (2022–2025), published after the period closes; true if transport-sector emissions fall within the reduction pathway assumed for that budget, false if the sector overshoots it.

divination.statement: The tough economic conditions that our Government has inherited mean that the number of people on the jobseeker benefit is expected to keep rising until January 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that jobseeker support recipient numbers will continue to climb up to January 2025 and turn down thereafter.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development monthly jobseeker support recipient counts from December 2023 through to at least mid-2025; true if the series rises to a peak at or about January 2025 and then declines, false if it continues rising materially past January 2025 or peaks well before it.

veracity.statement: No, we’re not going to continue to waste hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayers’ money to subsidise wealthy New Zealanders to be able to buy electric vehicles they can already purchase. Instead, we will invest in supercharging the electric vehicle charging network, which is a priority under this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Clean Car Discount cost hundreds of millions of dollars and that its rebates went to wealthy buyers who could have afforded electric vehicles anyway.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / Waka Kotahi Clean Car Discount rebate expenditure figures and any published distributional analysis of rebate recipients by household income; true if total rebates paid exceeded roughly $200 million and recipients skewed materially toward higher-income households, false if the spend was substantially lower or recipients were spread evenly across income deciles.

veracity.statement: Our policy is to commit to an additional 500 police officers on top of the 1,800 police officers that New Zealand First delivered—New Zealand First and National, in this coalition Government, will now deliver 2,300 additional police officers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 1,800 additional police officers were delivered under the previous coalition arrangement involving New Zealand First, and that 500 more would take the cumulative total to 2,300.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Police sworn-officer workforce records for the 2017–2020 term against the 1,800 additional police commitment in the Labour–New Zealand First coalition agreement; true if approximately 1,800 additional sworn officers were added under that commitment, false if the number delivered was materially short of 1,800.

veracity.statement: According to the latest benefit numbers released by the Ministry of Social Development in November, there are currently 182,340 people on jobseeker support. This is an increase of over 11,000 people this year alone. In total, there were 61,614 more people receiving the jobseeker support benefit during Labour’s time in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MSD's November 2023 figures show 182,340 people on jobseeker support, an increase of over 11,000 within 2023, and a net increase of 61,614 recipients across the 2017–2023 Labour-led government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development monthly benefit fact sheets for November 2023 compared with November 2022 and with the corresponding month at the change of government in 2017; true if the November 2023 jobseeker count is 182,340, the year-on-year rise exceeds 11,000, and the increase since 2017 is 61,614; false if any of the three figures differs beyond rounding.

veracity.statement: This first piece of legislation that the Government has brought to the House has gone through under urgency, with no opportunity for submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill was passed under urgency and had no select committee stage at which the public could make submissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bill record and Hansard for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill (December 2023): true if the bill was taken under urgency and was not referred to a select committee for public submissions; false if it had a select committee stage with public submissions, or was not taken under urgency.

veracity.statement: In fact, going through the regulatory impact statement and looking at the options analysis summary, on the last page of it, shows quite clearly that the best option would be to issue a new monetary policy committee remit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Treasury's regulatory impact statement on this bill, in its options analysis summary, ranks issuing a new Monetary Policy Committee remit as the preferred option ahead of amending the Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury regulatory impact statement published for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill: true if its options analysis summary rates a new Monetary Policy Committee remit above legislative amendment; false if it rates the legislative amendment equal or higher, or expresses no preference.

specificity.statement: In fact, going through the regulatory impact statement and looking at the options analysis summary, on the last page of it, shows quite clearly that the best option would be to issue a new monetary policy committee remit.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific document, a specific section of it (the options analysis summary on the last page) and the specific option it identifies — someone could open the RIS and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is about helping all New Zealanders, particularly poor New Zealanders who inflation hits the hardest, and it’s the thief in the pocket.
specificity.explanation: A statement of intent plus a metaphor. No figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As one of their very first actions into Government, it chose to do something that was completely unnecessary and to do something that was not the best option available to it.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the evidence actually offered: the RIS is quoted as preferring the remit process, so 'not the best option available' follows. 'Completely unnecessary' overreaches slightly beyond 'the remit route existed', a small gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It tells us of this Government that not only do they want to do something that’s completely unnecessary, they do something that is harmful to workers, that is harmful to full employment in this economy, and coupled with the next piece of legislation that is coming to this House, where they intend to repeal fair pay agreements, all we can say is that this Government despises workers.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: two policy choices are offered as premises and the conclusion drawn is a motive ('despises workers'). Nothing offered connects the effect of a policy to the intent behind it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill is actually about fixing the economy, which is what we went into the election on and what people voted for the coalition Government to do.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to mandate: the electoral result is offered as the reason the bill is about fixing the economy. Winning an election shows what was voted for, not that this instrument achieves it — the conclusion does not follow from the premise given.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As one of their very first actions into Government, it chose to do something that was completely unnecessary and to do something that was not the best option available to it.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and on the departmental advice about it — named policy, named analysis, no party-character content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It tells us of this Government that not only do they want to do something that’s completely unnecessary, they do something that is harmful to workers, that is harmful to full employment in this economy, and coupled with the next piece of legislation that is coming to this House, where they intend to repeal fair pay agreements, all we can say is that this Government despises workers.
focus.explanation: Two specific measures are named (this bill and the fair pay agreements repeal), so there is real policy content, but the weight of the sentence lands on characterising the Government's attitude rather than the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What a shame it is to have a Government that like on the Treasury benches, where they will not care for low-wage workers, where they will not ensure that people have access to employment, and where they will not look after ordinary New Zealanders. It is an elitist and out-of-touch Government not guided by evidence at all.
focus.explanation: A policy debate is live, but this passage names no measure, figure or outcome — it is a characterisation of what the other side is generally like. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is what Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s time to strengthen our economy and reduce the cost of living, and it’s time to get on top of inflation.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goals — strengthen the economy, reduce the cost of living, get on top of inflation — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To allow the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to fully focus on achieving and maintaining price stability in our economy, this bill removes the maximum sustainable employment objectives.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise legislative mechanism — removal of the maximum sustainable employment objective from the Reserve Bank's mandate — and what it is meant to leave in place. Checkable against the text of the bill; missing only timing or quantified effect.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the latest forecasts, the Reserve Bank expects inflation to fall within the target range of 1 to 3 percent within the third quarter of 2024.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a numeric target range and a named quarter. Fully checkable, and an example of an opposition speaker supplying figures rather than an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our economy is driven by agriculture, but our farmers are dealing with the highest inflation in 40 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that inflation currently faced by New Zealand farmers is the highest in four decades. Two checkable components: the general CPI record claim, and whether farm input inflation specifically is at a 40-year high.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series and the Stats NZ Farm Expenses Price Index, for the quarters up to December 2023: true if the relevant annual rate is the highest recorded in any year since 1983; false if a higher rate occurred within that window (e.g. the mid-1980s or 1990).

veracity.statement: In the latest forecasts, the Reserve Bank expects inflation to fall within the target range of 1 to 3 percent within the third quarter of 2024.
veracity.explanation: A claim about the content of the Reserve Bank's most recent published projection as at December 2023 — specifically the quarter in which headline annual CPI inflation is projected to re-enter the 1–3 percent band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RBNZ November 2023 Monetary Policy Statement projection tables for annual headline CPI inflation: true if the projected annual rate first falls within 1–3 percent in the September 2024 quarter; false if the projection has it re-entering the band in a materially different quarter.

rigor.statement: Let’s put some confidence back in our primary sector, with our farmers and our growers, so we can create employment and opportunity, so we can bring down inflation, so we can provide relief for many families out there struggling, who are wondering how they’re going to pay their grocery bill, their rent, their mortgage, their petrol for the week.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain — sector confidence → employment → lower inflation → household relief — offered with nothing connecting the links. The step from creating employment to bringing inflation down is a non sequitur (more employment is, on the standard account this bill relies on, inflationary, not disinflationary), and no mechanism is supplied for any stage.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This move was strongly campaigned on during our most recent general election, and because we sit on this side of the House, one could say that the majority of those who voted agreed with the move.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity, with a non sequitur inside it: forming a government does not entail that a majority of voters endorsed any particular policy in the platform, and under MMP a governing coalition's component parties need not each have majority support for a specific measure. The conclusion about what voters agreed to does not follow from the election result.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: By returning to a single objective, the task of the monetary policy committee is clearer, it is simpler, and therefore more likely to be met.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy, with a real gap: clarity and simplicity of an objective are offered as sufficient for it being more likely achieved, but nothing is offered on whether the Bank's instruments actually become more effective. Plausible, under-supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Although I think there have been a lot of promises made—and during the course of this debate, the Minister of Finance, at one point, did say that she was going to eliminate inflation, and we might set that as a KPI for the success of this Government, since it’s been claimed in the House—the reality is, and all the experts agree, that this amendment bill will do nothing to help with the cost of living.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the conclusion that the bill will do nothing rests on an unnamed and unquantified expert consensus ('all the experts agree'), with no source, mechanism or evidence offered. The intervening remark about the Minister's claim does no work in supporting the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t buy into the rhetoric that exudes out of the Opposition members conveying that this bill will result in worse outcomes for Māori and Pasifika communities.
civility.explanation: Pointed and dismissive — 'rhetoric that exudes out of' characterises opponents' argument as mere noise rather than answering it — but it lands on the argument and on a group, not on any individual's character or competence. Robust, edging toward the person without arriving.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister and the Government chose to do it by virtue-signalling legislation that is not going to achieve a thing.
civility.explanation: 'Virtue-signalling' imputes bad faith to a named individual — that the Minister legislated for display rather than effect. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes a motive rather than engaging the choice of instrument, which the speaker had just set out and could have argued from.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By returning to a single objective, the task of the monetary policy committee is clearer, it is simpler, and therefore more likely to be met.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — what a single mandate does to the monetary policy committee's task. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In this package of repeals that we are seeing from the current Government, what we are seeing is a Government that only wants to take New Zealand backwards, a Government that has no vision, and a Government that certainly does not have a focus on jobs or wages or climate action.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent — a named package of repeals touching employment, wages and climate objectives — but the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of the government as backward-looking and visionless rather than an argument about what the repeals do.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: What we are doing here—the legislation we are passing—is not going to materially change that.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill will not materially alter the inflation path already projected — i.e. that the observed return of inflation to the 1–3 percent band will track the pre-existing forecast rather than being brought forward by the mandate change.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI outturns for 2024 compared against the RBNZ November 2023 projection: true if annual headline inflation re-enters the 1–3 percent band at or after the projected quarter (September 2024) with no material acceleration, and RBNZ commentary does not attribute a change in the path to the single-mandate amendment; false if inflation returns to band materially earlier than projected and the Bank attributes that to the mandate change.

civility.statement: What I would say in terms of the speech that we just heard from the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety is this: she should climb out of the ivory tower of right-wing economic fundamentalism, and talk to the people.
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy to the Minister herself, casting her as ideologically sealed off and out of touch with ordinary people. A clear personal characterisation rather than an attack on the argument; he had an obvious civil alternative (criticising the repeal itself), so the opportunity to score high was real.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I seriously doubt that members opposite know any of these realities, but those are the realities this bill is seeking and the parties on that side of the House should be ashamed of themselves.
civility.explanation: Moves from the bill to the members themselves, imputing that they have no experience of low-wage work and telling them to be ashamed. Aimed at people rather than the argument, and short of sustained abuse — a real Civility failure, though a mild one, and she could have made the same point about the bill's effects without it.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re two weeks out from Christmas, and what we have is a Government which is addicted to cancel culture. I thought they didn’t like cancel culture, but here they are. They’re cancelling climate action, cancelling te reo Māori, and here they are cancelling Christmas for the workers.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the Government's general disposition, roped together with unrelated policy areas (climate, te reo) and a hypocrisy jibe. There is a thread of policy content — the timing of the repeal — but the weight is party framing, not the measure before the House. No Rigor score: strip out the part about the other side and no argument remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you are stuck in one job and you want to move to another one but they’ve got completely different working conditions and pay rates, it makes it very difficult for them to move from that worksite to another. Fair pay agreements would have helped to address that.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure being repealed — how fair pay agreements would operate and what problem they address. Names the policy and the effect. He could easily have spent the same breath on the coalition's motives instead.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Somebody’s not happy on that side of the House. They like to point the finger at the workers but maybe it is one of their coalition partners—who knows?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's internal state — speculation about which coalition partner is leaking. No policy, figure or outcome is named, and nothing here bears on the bill. Exactly the tribal aside Focus exists to catch; no individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to repeal this Act so that we can leave flexibility with the employer and the employee, and give them greater control over the relationship they have.
focus.explanation: On the measure itself: what the repeal is for and what it is meant to restore to the employment relationship. No party framing at all. Vague, but vagueness is Specificity's problem, not Focus's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We will be strongly opposing this bill and this Government that appears to be anti-Māori, anti-Pasifika, anti - everything involving grassroots people, and anti-workers, and continuing to stand up and speak against this “three Scrooges” coalition.
focus.explanation: A wholesale characterisation of what the coalition is 'really like', with no policy, provision or outcome named. The 'three Scrooges' label targets the parties rather than any individual, so Civility is untroubled; the content-free party framing is what Focus measures.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: With this bill, we should have had the chance to hear from unions, from those that we saw here this morning, from workers, from employment relations, experts, and, yes, from businesses too. Denying them the right to submit on the laws of this land is a breach of fundamental democratic rights that we should uphold dearly, as we are reminded often in this country.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific, identifiable feature of how this bill is being passed — the absence of a select committee stage and public submissions — rather than the character of the parties passing it. Legitimate scrutiny of a named process.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But what it did say is that by repealing this legislation, it’s going to make working people’s lives harder.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of a leaked Government document: that official advice on the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill concluded the repeal would worsen outcomes for working people. The checkable fact is what the document says, not whether the forecast proves right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The leaked departmental advice / regulatory impact statement prepared by MBIE on the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill (December 2023). True if that document states the repeal will worsen pay or conditions for working people, and specifically for women, young, Māori and Pasifika workers; false if it contains no such assessment or reaches the opposite conclusion.

veracity.statement: In the last two coalition agreements that we’ve been part of forming, increases to the minimum wage have always been a feature that we have stuck out for.
veracity.explanation: A claim about his own party's negotiating record: that minimum wage increases were secured in both the 2017 and the 2023 coalition agreements New Zealand First was party to.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published texts of the 2017 Labour–New Zealand First coalition agreement and the 2023 National–New Zealand First coalition agreement. True if both contain a minimum wage commitment; false if either does not.

veracity.statement: My goodness, we are now meeting protests and receiving petitions at least two to three times a day.
veracity.explanation: A quantified claim about the frequency of protests and petitions directed at Parliament in the weeks following the coalition's formation — offered as a measure of public opposition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The House's record of petitions presented between the opening of the 54th Parliament (5 December 2023) and 12 December 2023, together with reported protest events at Parliament over that period. True if the combined rate is at least two per sitting day; false if it is materially below that.

rigor.statement: If you are stuck in one job and you want to move to another one but they’ve got completely different working conditions and pay rates, it makes it very difficult for them to move from that worksite to another. Fair pay agreements would have helped to address that.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference with a stated mechanism: divergent site-by-site conditions raise the cost of moving employer, and a sector-wide agreement standardises those conditions, so mobility improves. The conclusion tracks the premise. It is docked for resting on a single conversation with security guards rather than any evidence that mobility is in fact constrained this way.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Members opposite are forgetting that we represent the majority, and we also speak to our constituents.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity: the reply to a substantive objection is that her side commands the majority. Winning the election establishes authority to legislate, not that the repeal has merit, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I speak to our constituents all the time, many and most of whom are workers, and I can tell you, whether it’s hospitality workers or bus drivers, they are not looking forward to losing the relationship they have with their employer and having that taken away and put into the arms of a union.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote. A self-selected set of conversations in one electorate is offered as evidence of what workers generally want, against a question that survey or submission data could speak to. The generalisation is far wider than the sample supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason why we’re slipping so far behind Australia is because of our productivity—because we have wrapped ourselves in red tape and will not allow ourselves access to our natural resources, in many cases.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause explanation asserted rather than argued: the whole of the trans-Tasman income gap is traced to regulation and resource access, with no evidence offered and no consideration of capital intensity, scale or exchange rates. The chain from 'red tape' to the productivity gap is stated, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we are seeing in this bill today is a repeat of what we saw then.
rigor.explanation: A historical analogy asserted without the connecting work: the 1990s employment reforms and this repeal are equated, but nothing is offered about which provisions correspond or why the same consequences should follow. False analogy — the resemblance is claimed, not demonstrated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: With this bill, we should have had the chance to hear from unions, from those that we saw here this morning, from workers, from employment relations, experts, and, yes, from businesses too. Denying them the right to submit on the laws of this land is a breach of fundamental democratic rights that we should uphold dearly, as we are reminded often in this country.
