rigor.explanation: Valid inference given its premise: if no initiated agreement will have been finalised by the repeal date, there are no completed rights for transitional provisions to preserve. The gap is that it addresses only finalised agreements, not part-completed bargaining processes.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Even if you disagree with me, Minister, I’d like to understand how on earth you are justifying this and how you see the way forward in New Zealand—how you see high-wage work happening if we don’t do something differently.
civility.explanation: Exasperated in tone ("how on earth") and pressing hard on a contested repeal, but the demand is aimed at the Minister's justification for the policy, not at her as a person. Pointed rather than uncivil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s because we want a flexible labour market where employers and employees can agree to terms that suit their own unique situations. We don’t believe in having a blunt tool like a fair pay agreement, which affects all employers and employees within an occupation or an industry, which is why that goes right to the heart of why we’re repealing this Act and the bargaining process underneath it.
focus.explanation: Answers the question about already-initiated fair pay agreements by engaging the measure itself — the bargaining process being repealed and the mechanism of an occupation- or industry-wide agreement. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s because we want a flexible labour market where employers and employees can agree to terms that suit their own unique situations. We don’t believe in having a blunt tool like a fair pay agreement, which affects all employers and employees within an occupation or an industry, which is why that goes right to the heart of why we’re repealing this Act and the bargaining process underneath it.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the stated objective (agreements tailored to individual workplaces) is incompatible with an instrument that binds a whole occupation, so repeal follows. Valid given its premise, but the premise that industry-wide coverage is 'blunt' is asserted rather than supported, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have noticed throughout the discussion in the House from the Minister, she constantly uses the word “believe”—“We believe that this will be the case”, “We are doing this legislation because we believe it will be better”. Believing and having actual, grounded evidence are two different things.
rigor.explanation: A sound inference about the standard of proof: she identifies the form of the Minister's justification (stated belief), and concludes the case for the repeal is unevidenced. The distinction between assertion and evidence genuinely supports that conclusion. It falls short of 1.0 because a policy preference can legitimately rest on values rather than evidence, which she does not address.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s the position that many young people find themselves in today, where a race to the bottom in New Zealand and the kind of economic settings that we have had have meant that young people are not able to earn what their parents earned—and their parents before them—in relation to the price of other things.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single submitter's family story to the position of 'many young people', and then attributes the gap causally to 'a race to the bottom' in wage settings with nothing offered to connect the two. Appeal to anecdote plus an unsupported causal leap; house prices rising faster than wages has candidate explanations she does not rule out.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In Part 2, and I’m talking to my Amendment Paper, we see that the Ministry of Businesses, Innovation and Employment has identified the implications of the repeal of the fair pay agreement legislation on Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MBIE, as departmental adviser, has itself documented the consequences for Māori of repealing the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's Regulatory Impact Statement / departmental disclosure statement for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill (Dec 2023); true if it contains an identified analysis of impacts on Māori, false if the documents contain no such analysis.

veracity.statement: And, obviously, to be supportive to the Minister in making sure how else, for example, the Government would be consistent with Treaty of Waitangi obligations, my amendment is ensuring that we identify those who are disproportionately affected—and remember that there has been no consultation with iwi Māori, no representation groups.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no consultation with iwi Māori or Māori representative groups was undertaken before the repeal bill was brought to the House.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's Regulatory Impact Statement and departmental disclosure statement for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill, plus the House record of whether the bill went to select committee; true if the consultation section records no engagement with iwi or Māori representative bodies and no public submissions were taken, false if any such consultation is recorded.

veracity.statement: Because the Minister has presented to this committee—she has said that fair pay agreements (FPAs) were never about being fair, which is something that I disagree with.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Minister told this committee fair pay agreements were never about fairness. The claim is about what was said, not about whether it is correct.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of Brooke van Velden's contributions to the committee stage of the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill on 12 December 2023; true if she stated in substance that fair pay agreements were never about being fair, false if no such statement appears.

veracity.statement: Further, the purpose of the fair pay agreements legislation when it was enacted in 2022 was about creating an industry floor for many of these industries which are dominated by young workers who move between different employers doing very similar kinds of work.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the stated purpose of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 was to set minimum industry-wide terms, and that the covered industries she has in mind (hospitality, fast food) are dominated by young workers moving between employers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The purpose provision of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 and its explanatory note, plus Stats NZ employment-by-age data for the accommodation and food services sector; true if the Act's stated purpose is sector-wide minimum terms and the sector's workforce skews young, false if the Act's purpose is materially different or the age profile does not hold.

specificity.statement: And this amendment would provide an exemption for Māori workers who will be harmed by the repeal of the fair pay agreements.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism — a carve-out from the repeal — and the group it covers, but supplies no test for which workers qualify, which agreements would survive, or for how long. A direction with some detail, missing the how.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What those two particular repeals and replacements highlight is a returning of the onus to the worker.
specificity.explanation: She has just named the two provisions being replaced (sections 132(2) and 224(1)(a)) and, immediately after, the matters they cover — wages actually paid, hours and days, and complaints to a labour inspector. Read with that context this is a checkable claim about identified clauses and a named mechanism, though it attaches no figures or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: For the Government, whose Prime Minister has assured us that he’s got the best interests of Māori at heart, this would be one way of considering again how we could be making amendments to pull off, I guess, what has been really forced on us in a concerning urgent way.
civility.explanation: Pointed: invites the House to test the Prime Minister's stated commitment against his conduct, and calls the process forced. It edges toward the person without landing on him — no imputation of bad faith is made explicit, and the criticism stays on the Government's handling of the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But, perhaps putting myself in her shoes and appreciating the world through her ideology, I can see that she is trying to advance something which is beneficial to New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: In a contested urgency debate where an attack was readily available, she credits the Minister with good intentions and frames the disagreement as one of ideology rather than motive. Attacks no one; the reference to 'her ideology' is descriptive, not a sneer.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In my reading of the Employment Relations Act, it actually stipulates that one of the objects of the Act is to promote collective bargaining.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that promoting collective bargaining is among the stated objects of the Employment Relations Act 2000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The objects section (s3) of the Employment Relations Act 2000; true if promoting collective bargaining is listed there as an object of the Act, false if it is not.

veracity.statement: We’ve heard that there are, for example, supermarket workers, bus drivers—there’s close to 300,000 workers that will be covered by these fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fair pay agreements already initiated or under way would cover approximately 300,000 workers, including supermarket workers and bus drivers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's register of initiated fair pay agreement applications as at December 2023 and the coverage estimates published with them; true if the summed estimated coverage is near 300,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I note the regulatory impact statement for the instatement of this law—for the Fair Pay Agreements Act—actually recommended against the fair pay agreement system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the departmental regulatory impact statement prepared for the Fair Pay Agreements legislation made a recommendation against the fair pay agreement system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE Regulatory Impact Statement published with the Fair Pay Agreements Bill; true if it recommends against the fair pay agreement system, false if it recommends for it or makes no recommendation against (e.g. only notes risks or declines to assess a ministerially-directed option).

veracity.statement: Lest we forget about tobacco impact and the health and wellbeing of our people, I’m bringing us back to the kaupapa as I refer to the fact that te iwi Māori are overrepresented in the workforce that we’re talking about.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori make up a disproportionately large share of workers in the low-wage sectors covered by the fair pay agreements being repealed (cleaning, security, supermarket, bus driving, early childhood education).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census/HLFS occupational employment data by ethnicity for the sectors with initiated fair pay agreements; true if the Māori share of employment in those occupations exceeds the Māori share of the total workforce, false if it is at or below it.

specificity.statement: We’ve heard that there are, for example, supermarket workers, bus drivers—there’s close to 300,000 workers that will be covered by these fair pay agreements.
specificity.explanation: Carries a numeric coverage figure and names two of the covered sectors, so someone could go and check it; falls short of 1.0 because the figure is given as an approximation with no source or date attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As Māori, we are gravely impacted in this space, and I’d like to remind the House that we are often the buffer of all of the lowest statistics in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: Attempts to convey substance about the repeal's effect on Māori but supplies no figures, no named statistic and no mechanism — 'the buffer of all of the lowest statistics' is not something anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And so I think it’s right to have some concern, if the repeal is successful, around what actually happens to all of that data that has been collected about those workers and who holds that data.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific consequence of the measure before the House — what becomes of worker data gathered under the fair pay agreement process once the Act is repealed — rather than the opposing party's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it is not the case that these population groups would be better off under a fair pay agreement; it is also quite possible that they could be worse off, as is stated within the regulatory impact statement.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the cited source establishes only that harm is possible, which does not license the categorical conclusion that these groups would not be better off. The inference slides from 'it is possible they could be worse off' to 'it is not the case they would be better off'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My response to that is it’s not possible to have a review of a law that would be repealed, because there would be nothing to review after three years, so the whole point of that paper is null and void.
rigor.explanation: Equivocates between reviewing the Act and reviewing the impact of repealing it. The amendment sought a review of the effects of the repeal, which remains perfectly possible after the Act is gone, so the conclusion that the paper is 'null and void' does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The new system that’s available, you know, through fair pay agreements would have enabled them to all have a really good Christmas.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion with a missing causal step: no fair pay agreement had been concluded, so nothing is offered to connect the existence of the system to the immediate improvement in these workers' circumstances that the conclusion asserts.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My response to that is it’s not possible to have a review of a law that would be repealed, because there would be nothing to review after three years, so the whole point of that paper is null and void.
civility.explanation: Dismissive language, but it lands entirely on the Amendment Paper and its logic rather than on the member who lodged it; the response is on the substance of the proposal.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I know that in the advice that she received in the cover sheet of the regulatory impact statement in relation to this, it was specifically noted that Māori women, young people, Pasifika would be disproportionately impacted by this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the cover sheet of the regulatory impact statement for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill specifically identified Māori women, young people and Pasifika as groups disproportionately impacted by the repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE regulatory impact statement (and its cover sheet) for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill 2023; true if it names Māori women, young people and Pasifika as disproportionately impacted, false if it contains no such identification of those groups.

veracity.statement: Principle 9 of the Privacy Act specifies that an agency that holds personal information must not keep that information for longer than is required for the purposes for which the information may lawfully be used.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of information privacy principle 9 of the Privacy Act 2020 as it applies to retention of personal information.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of information privacy principle 9 in section 22 of the Privacy Act 2020; true if it states an agency holding personal information must not keep it longer than required for the purposes for which it may lawfully be used, false if principle 9 covers a different subject or is materially differently worded.

veracity.statement: However, I do want to stress that this bill will not make Maōri worse off, because there have not been any fair pay agreements that have been finalised.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of fact that no fair pay agreement had been finalised at the time of the repeal, despite applications having been approved.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's register of fair pay agreement applications and bargaining under the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 as at December 2023; true if no fair pay agreement had been concluded, ratified or brought into force, false if any agreement had been finalised.

veracity.statement: Because that is the reality when people are not bargaining collectively, and in many of the industries that have lodged applications for fair pay agreements, there is very little substantive collective bargaining.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that collective bargaining coverage is very low in many of the industries that had lodged fair pay agreement applications (such as cleaning, security, hospitality and bus driving).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE collective agreement coverage and union membership statistics for the sectors with lodged fair pay agreement applications; true if collective agreement coverage in most of those sectors is a small minority of the workforce, false if those sectors show substantial collective bargaining coverage.

specificity.statement: I know that in the advice that she received in the cover sheet of the regulatory impact statement in relation to this, it was specifically noted that Māori women, young people, Pasifika would be disproportionately impacted by this bill.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact document (regulatory impact statement cover sheet) and the exact groups identified, so the assertion can be located and checked; stops short of quoting figures or the wording itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Principle 9 of the Privacy Act specifies that an agency that holds personal information must not keep that information for longer than is required for the purposes for which the information may lawfully be used.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, the specific principle number, and states the operative obligation, so a listener can go and verify the legal basis for the claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So once the fair pay agreement legislation is repealed, unions will no longer have a lawful purpose for retaining this information and it will need to be deleted.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference from a stated legal premise: principle 9 limits retention to the lawful purpose, the purpose was fair pay agreement bargaining, so repeal extinguishes the purpose. The gap is that it treats bargaining as the only possible lawful purpose a union could hold member information for, which is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, I do want to stress that this bill will not make Maōri worse off, because there have not been any fair pay agreements that have been finalised.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion outruns the premise. That no agreement was finalised establishes no one has lost a wage rate already in force; it does not establish that no one is made worse off, since the objection is about forgone future gains from agreements in progress. The argument answers a narrower claim than the one raised.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, that’s a very flexible situation for the employer, but it is not flexible for the employee, particularly when times are tough in the economy and competition for jobs is intense.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises offered: where there is no collective bargaining and offers are take-it-or-leave-it, the discretion sits with one side, and loose labour market conditions weaken the other's alternatives. No fallacy; the inference is stated with the mechanism that supports it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I wanted to pick up on the flexibility arguments the Minister has presented, because to me it sounds like it’s flexibility to pay poor wages and to have a race to the bottom.
rigor.explanation: Restates the Minister's flexibility rationale in its least defensible form — flexibility to pay poor wages — and offers nothing to connect the stated position to that reading. A loaded reframing bordering on strawman; the hedge 'to me it sounds like' signals the substitution rather than justifying it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, that’s a very flexible situation for the employer, but it is not flexible for the employee, particularly when times are tough in the economy and competition for jobs is intense.
focus.explanation: Engages the bill's own stated objective — flexibility to agree employment terms — and interrogates what that flexibility means for each party. Entirely on the measure, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I wanted to pick up on the flexibility arguments the Minister has presented, because to me it sounds like it’s flexibility to pay poor wages and to have a race to the bottom.
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at the rationale advanced for the measure and at the overseas wage evidence, not at the other party's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason why this relates to Part 1 is because we are not allowing for a transition period, right? So we are not allowing for us to test the impact domestically, which means we have to then draw on overseas evidence for their sector-wide bargaining, and if we had given ourselves the chance of having at least a transition period or having a carve out for specific industries, as my amendment would have proposed, then we would have had, I guess, the ability to have evidence domestically as well.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the bill directly — the absence of a transition period, a proposed carve-out for specific industries, and the evidentiary consequence. Names his own amendment. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I think it’s important to have the voice of disabled workers raised again in this House, and it’s a pity, in my view, that they didn’t get the opportunity to submit again on this repeal bill.
focus.explanation: About the process attached to a named measure — the absence of a select committee stage on this repeal bill and who consequently could not be heard. Scrutiny of the government's handling of the bill, with no party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My concern being, of course, is that is one moving from organisations that are self-funded—through members; through associations—to one that is funded by the State.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the clause: who provides the bargaining support function and how it is funded, contrasting member-funded associations with a State-funded inspectorate. No reference to the other party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason why this relates to Part 1 is because we are not allowing for a transition period, right? So we are not allowing for us to test the impact domestically, which means we have to then draw on overseas evidence for their sector-wide bargaining, and if we had given ourselves the chance of having at least a transition period or having a carve out for specific industries, as my amendment would have proposed, then we would have had, I guess, the ability to have evidence domestically as well.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: no transition period means no domestic trial, therefore only overseas evidence is available. The chain holds, though the counterfactual step (a transition period would have produced usable domestic evidence within the timeframe) is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is by definition far more flexible than what this agreement allows for, which is a blunt tool that forces employees and employers to be part of a fair-pay agreement even if they chose not to be part of one.
rigor.explanation: The premise offered — that the status quo permits either individual or collective agreements — does support a conclusion of greater optionality. But 'by definition' substitutes for the comparison actually needed, and the characterisation of coverage as forcing participation is asserted rather than argued, so there is a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But I just wanted to once again reiterate: did she use international evidence and impact overseas of sector-wide bargaining to inform the arguments, or was it just because she campaigned on it based on vibes and without any evidence prior to coming to forming this legislation?
civility.explanation: The underlying question about the evidence base is legitimate, but the framing imputes bad faith to the Minister personally — that she legislated 'on vibes and without any evidence'. Sneering rather than a direct insult, so a genuine failure short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are a number of different submissions that were made—I mentioned earlier in the House today I think there were about 1,700 submissions made—in relation to the primary bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 1,700 written submissions were received on the original Fair Pay Agreements Bill at its select committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the Fair Pay Agreements Bill (2021-22) and the Parliament submissions record: true if the number of written submissions received is approximately 1,700 (say within a couple of hundred), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The regulatory impact statement from 2021 still well and truly applies, and within that regulatory impact statement they did not actually recommend that we had a fair pay agreements system.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions about the 2021 MBIE regulatory impact statement on Fair Pay Agreements: that Treasury's exemption means it remains the operative analysis for the repeal, and that the RIS itself did not recommend adopting an FPA system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE regulatory impact statement produced when the Fair Pay Agreements system was introduced in 2021, plus the Treasury exemption coversheet for the Repeal Bill: true if the RIS's options analysis stops short of recommending the FPA system as its preferred option, false if the RIS recommends the FPA system.

specificity.statement: I note that it wasn’t actually specific to this bill, but I do thank the member for her interest, because this is a Government that is going to have a lot of work on our hands to create a good, thriving economy for every person in New Zealand. And I can’t wait for the member to see what this Government will deliver for all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Offered as an answer to how conditions for workers will be improved, but supplies no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named policy — 'a good, thriving economy for every person' and 'what this Government will deliver' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is really important that we have a flexible labour market where we have high productivity, where we focus on the regulations and red tape that is actually stifling our economy, so that businesses have more money to pay their staff more.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods — flexibility, high productivity, less red tape — with no regulation named, no quantum, and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I refer, in my contribution, specifically to Part 1 and the part that proposes that we replace section 224(1)(a) in the Employment Relations Act 200 with “(a) an employee makes a complaint to the Labour Inspector,” and it goes on.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact provision being amended and quotes the replacement text, so the point is precisely locatable in the bill by anyone following along.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When I was at law school, I learnt that in good legislative drafting it is preferable to put a purpose clause in legislation. And the reason for that is sometimes it’s important to understand the purpose of the Parliament in creating a particular law, because, otherwise, when there’s a provision that is unclear or perhaps maybe with the passage of time, a new interpretation is possible, it helps to have a purpose.
rigor.explanation: A genuine premise-to-conclusion argument: purpose clauses are preferable because unclear provisions and later reinterpretation make Parliament's intent relevant to statutory interpretation. The reason offered does support the conclusion. Marked down slightly because the claim is introduced by personal training ('when I was at law school') rather than by the substantive reason alone — a mild appeal to authority — though the actual reason is then supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Parliamentary Counsel Office have advised that it’s not standard practice in drafting a repeal bill to include a purpose clause, because the purpose of a repeal bill is to repeal a bill.
rigor.explanation: An answer that rests mainly on an appeal to authority (PCO advice), backed by a supporting reason that is close to circular — a repeal bill needs no stated purpose because its purpose is to repeal. The appeal is to a genuinely expert body on drafting convention, so it is not a bare appeal, but the reasoning offered does not itself establish that a purpose clause would be unhelpful for later statutory interpretation, which was the point put to her.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are no fair pay agreement systems that we’ve established here based on any international system—it is very much a unique design—and so in this regard we consider that many of its features are unnecessary and negative for the employment market, especially the requirement that all employers and all employees would be drawn into a fair pay agreement if they chose not to be part of it, especially because it could be initiated by a tiny minority, 10 percent or 1,000 workers, for all.
rigor.explanation: The load-bearing inference runs from 'the design is unique / not modelled on an overseas system' to 'many of its features are unnecessary and negative' — a non sequitur bordering on an appeal to novelty, since the absence of an overseas precedent says nothing about whether a feature works. She partially rescues it by naming a concrete objection (universal coverage triggered by a minority initiation threshold), which is an actual reason, but that reason is offered as an aside rather than as what the conclusion rests on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was only during the process of the Fair Pay Agreements Act that this provision for overtime rate payments and the penalty rate payments was introduced into the law, and so, by removing this, we are going back to the status quo.
rigor.explanation: A clean valid inference: if the reference to overtime and penalty rate payments was inserted into section 132(2) by the Fair Pay Agreements Act, then deleting it restores the pre-2022 position. The conclusion follows directly from the premise, and it answers the objection actually raised rather than sidestepping it. Whether the premise is factually correct is a separate question and does not bear on the reasoning.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So the purpose that I have provided in this amendment document is to outline what I believe is the purpose of this bill, which is to ensure businesses can continue to undervalue workers, to protect New Zealand’s low-wage economy from encroachment by workers’ rights, and (c) to entrench inherent imbalance of power enjoyed by employers.
civility.explanation: A satirical mock purpose clause that imputes bad motive — that the bill exists so workers can be undervalued and employer power entrenched. No individual member is insulted and the target is the bill, so this is well short of a personal attack, but ascribing deliberate bad faith to the measure's authors falls below the civil standard of engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think in relation to some of the previous questions that we did ask, I know the Minister has responded to some of them, but I don’t really feel she’s given a true answer as to how she will address low pay for Māori.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the adequacy of the Minister's answers on a contested point, expressed with hedges ('I don't really feel') and an explicit acknowledgement that she has responded to some questions. Pointed, and it edges towards suggesting evasion, but it attacks the answer rather than the person and imputes no bad faith or incompetence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the purpose that I have provided in this amendment document is to outline what I believe is the purpose of this bill, which is to ensure businesses can continue to undervalue workers, to protect New Zealand’s low-wage economy from encroachment by workers’ rights, and (c) to entrench inherent imbalance of power enjoyed by employers.
focus.explanation: Directed at the bill actually before the committee rather than at the other party in general, and it does assert particular effects (wage levels, employer-employee power balance). But it names no mechanism, clause, figure or outcome — the content is a characterisation of motive wrapped in a drafting device, so it sits between substantive engagement and framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Unfortunately, when this was reproduced a few words were omitted, meaning that, in my view—and I’m happy to hear an alternative view from the Minister—the Employment Relations Act in fact is amended by this Part 2 of the repeal bill and, unfortunately, results in the words “including overtime payment rates, and penalty rate payments” being removed from the Employment Relations Act 2000.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact instrument (Employment Relations Act 2000), the exact part of the repeal bill, and quotes the precise words she says are deleted. Anyone can open the two texts and check it. Not a full 1.0 only because the effect is characterised in general terms ('a few words were omitted') rather than by citing the section number in this sentence.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, when this was reproduced a few words were omitted, meaning that, in my view—and I’m happy to hear an alternative view from the Minister—the Employment Relations Act in fact is amended by this Part 2 of the repeal bill and, unfortunately, results in the words “including overtime payment rates, and penalty rate payments” being removed from the Employment Relations Act 2000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the consequential amendment in Part 2 of the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill replaces section 132(2) of the Employment Relations Act 2000 with wording that drops the phrase 'including overtime payment rates, and penalty rate payments', so those words cease to appear in the ERA 2000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare section 132(2) of the Employment Relations Act 2000 as in force immediately before the repeal bill's commencement with the replacement text set out in Schedule 2, Part 1 of the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill (2023). True if the phrase 'including overtime payment rates, and penalty rate payments' appears in the former and not in the latter; false if the phrase survives in the replacement text or was never in section 132(2).

veracity.statement: The Parliamentary Counsel Office have advised that it’s not standard practice in drafting a repeal bill to include a purpose clause, because the purpose of a repeal bill is to repeal a bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about advice received and about drafting convention: that the Parliamentary Counsel Office advised that including a purpose clause is not standard practice when drafting a repeal bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary Counsel Office's published drafting guidance (PCO Drafting Manual / principles on purpose provisions) plus a survey of New Zealand repeal-only Acts of the last two decades. True if PCO guidance or that survey shows purpose clauses are not customary in repeal-only bills; false if PCO guidance recommends purpose clauses generally including for repeal bills, or if repeal-only bills commonly carry them.

veracity.statement: There are no fair pay agreement systems that we’ve established here based on any international system—it is very much a unique design—and so in this regard we consider that many of its features are unnecessary and negative for the employment market, especially the requirement that all employers and all employees would be drawn into a fair pay agreement if they chose not to be part of it, especially because it could be initiated by a tiny minority, 10 percent or 1,000 workers, for all.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual feature of the Fair Pay Agreements regime: that a fair pay agreement could be initiated by 10 percent of the covered workforce or 1,000 workers, and that once initiated it would cover all employers and employees in the sector regardless of their wish to be included.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The initiation ('representation test') and coverage provisions of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022. True if the Act permits initiation on support from 10% of covered employees or 1,000 covered employees (whichever is lower) and binds all covered employers and employees once an agreement is finalised; false if the thresholds differ materially from 10%/1,000 or if coverage is opt-in.

veracity.statement: It was only during the process of the Fair Pay Agreements Act that this provision for overtime rate payments and the penalty rate payments was introduced into the law, and so, by removing this, we are going back to the status quo.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the words in section 132(2) of the Employment Relations Act 2000 referring to overtime rate payments and penalty rate payments were inserted by the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 and did not exist in that section beforehand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The amendment schedule of the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 and the legislative history of section 132(2) of the Employment Relations Act 2000 on legislation.govt.nz. True if the phrase referring to overtime and penalty rate payments was inserted into section 132(2) by the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022; false if it appeared in section 132(2) before 2022 or was inserted by a different amending Act.

rigor.statement: Now, there are a number of people who are currently negotiating fair pay agreements, and what I would like to know from the Minister—a clear answer—is what engagement have you had with the industries and the unions that are leading the bargaining in respect of fair pay agreements, because they are directly affected by this, and by your party’s own creed, you require consultation with them.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: parties are directly affected by the repeal; the standard the Minister's own party espouses requires consulting affected parties; therefore consultation should have occurred. The consistency premise is asserted rather than quoted, but the conclusion tracks what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason why I ask this is that a lot of the families that would have benefited from fair pay agreements are families with young children and the fair pay agreements would have had an impact on child poverty reduction and would have contributed to our child poverty reduction targets.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — affected workers are disproportionately parents, so a child impact assessment was warranted — but the middle step, that fair pay agreements would in fact have moved child poverty measures, is asserted rather than evidenced, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is a really wonderful agreement and it has meant high wages in that industry and high productivity in that industry.
rigor.explanation: A causal claim drawn from a single case she was personally involved in: the dairy collective agreement is credited with both high wages and high productivity, with nothing offered to rule out the industry's own economics producing either. Argument from anecdote, and a post hoc attribution of causation to correlation.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s a significant change in our policy, and it appears to me that it’s been rushed, it’s under urgency, there’s no consultation, there’s no research done on it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three process facts about the Fair Pay Agreements repeal bill: that it is being taken under urgency, that no consultation was undertaken, and that no supporting research or analysis exists.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and the Order Paper for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill (December 2023): true if the bill was progressed under urgency without select committee referral and with no published consultation and no regulatory impact statement; false if it was referred to select committee, or if MBIE published consultation or regulatory impact analysis for it.

veracity.statement: We don’t collect the data that comes in from their individual agreements; we don’t know what’s in those individual agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no New Zealand agency collects or holds the contents of individual employment agreements, so the terms the majority of workers are on are unknown to policymakers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whether MBIE, Stats NZ or any other agency collects the contents of individual employment agreements: true if no agency holds such a dataset (MBIE's deposit requirement under the Employment Relations Act covers collective agreements only); false if a register, survey or administrative dataset of individual agreement terms exists.

focus.statement: What I see in this party is a party that says one thing and does another, and that’s utterly incoherent, it’s inconsistent, and it doesn’t come well from someone who’s now in Government.
focus.explanation: A charge of general inconsistency against the other party. There is a policy grievance behind it (the missing consultation and analysis), but this sentence itself names no measure, figure or outcome — the weight is party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason why I ask this is that a lot of the families that would have benefited from fair pay agreements are families with young children and the fair pay agreements would have had an impact on child poverty reduction and would have contributed to our child poverty reduction targets.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: which families the repeal affects and what it does to a named government target. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wanted to talk to an amendment that I’ve put on the Table which is a new clause 8, and it talks about the repeal being subject to a view undertaken in three years’ time of how terms and conditions for the workers—generally in early childhood education, bus industries, security industry, cleaning and supermarkets and hospitality have changed or have they not, also in comparison to the conditions now.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the substance of an amendment before the committee — what it would require and which workers it would cover.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I don’t want to hear from the Minister is her doctrine. I don’t want to hear her dogma.
civility.explanation: Lands on the Minister personally rather than on the repeal: it pre-emptively characterises whatever she says as doctrine and dogma, imputing that she acts from belief rather than reasoning. Short of an insult, but past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And I’d also like to know whether this legislation meets the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee guidelines, not only for its legislative quality in its wording but also the process it has gone through.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific external standard (the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee guidelines) and identifies two dimensions to test it against — drafting and process. Checkable, though it does not point to which guideline is breached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I wanted to talk to an amendment that I’ve put on the Table which is a new clause 8, and it talks about the repeal being subject to a view undertaken in three years’ time of how terms and conditions for the workers—generally in early childhood education, bus industries, security industry, cleaning and supermarkets and hospitality have changed or have they not, also in comparison to the conditions now.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the mechanism (a review of terms and conditions against current conditions), the timeframe (three years) and the six industries covered. What is missing is who would conduct the review and against what measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: These are questions based on the Regulatory Standards Bill that David Seymour had and that will no doubt be reincarnated in this Parliament.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a Regulatory Standards Bill of the kind previously promoted by David Seymour will be reintroduced during the current (54th) Parliament.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary bills register for the 54th Parliament: true if a Regulatory Standards Bill is introduced to the House before the 2026 general election; false if no such bill is introduced by then.

veracity.statement: We have also, two days after I was sworn in at Government, met with both Business New Zealand and the Council of Trade Unions, which represent the unions and businesses that represent both sides of this agreement and argument.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that she met both BusinessNZ and the NZCTU within two days of being sworn in as Minister, offered as evidence that consultation on the repeal was adequate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial diary disclosures for the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety covering late November 2023, plus BusinessNZ and NZCTU records; true if meetings with both organisations occurred within roughly two days of her swearing-in (27 November 2023), false if no such meetings are recorded or they fell well outside that window.

veracity.statement: That was done in the 2021 regulatory impact statement, but if you look at page 2 of the cover sheet to the fair pay agreements regulatory impact statement that was finalised on 28 November 2023, it does state that there was an exemption granted on the grounds that the regulatory impact statement produced when the FPA system was introduced in 2021 mostly duplicates the analysis needed to repeal the system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the cover sheet to the FPA repeal regulatory impact statement, finalised 28 November 2023, records a RIS exemption granted on the ground that the 2021 FPA RIS mostly duplicates the analysis needed for repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published MBIE/Treasury regulatory impact statement cover sheet dated 28 November 2023 for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill; true if page 2 records an exemption on duplication grounds as described, false if no exemption is recorded or it was granted on different grounds.

specificity.statement: That was done in the 2021 regulatory impact statement, but if you look at page 2 of the cover sheet to the fair pay agreements regulatory impact statement that was finalised on 28 November 2023, it does state that there was an exemption granted on the grounds that the regulatory impact statement produced when the FPA system was introduced in 2021 mostly duplicates the analysis needed to repeal the system.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, its finalisation date, the page, and the precise ground of the exemption. Anyone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question goes to: what evidence does the Minister have that small-business owners do not want to sign up to something that is better than the minimum wage and that indeed sets minimum standards across their industries?
specificity.explanation: Names what is being asked about (above-minimum pay, industry minimum standards) but carries no figures, no named evidence source and no threshold for what would count as an answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But, most importantly, we do have a clear mandate from the public, from people who voted for this Government, to repeal this law.
rigor.explanation: Offered as the closing answer to a question about whether consultation was sufficient. An election result is substituted for consultation — an appeal to popularity that does not establish the conclusion it is offered for, since a mandate to act is not the same as having consulted on how to act.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I consider that the fair pay agreements system is a blunt tool that affects all employees and all employers within scope within a particular industry, and that would negatively impact on businesses, which would negatively impact on employees, which would negatively impact, therefore, on their families.
rigor.explanation: A chain of asserted consequences — business harm, therefore employee harm, therefore family harm — with no mechanism, evidence or magnitude offered at any link. The 'therefore' does the work that argument should; the harm to children is inferred entirely from the initial characterisation as a 'blunt tool'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Absolutely nothing else has worked. We know that. We know it because they’ve experienced it.
rigor.explanation: A universal claim — that nothing other than fair pay agreements has improved security guards' wages — supported only by the personal experience of the workers cited. Appeal to anecdote, and the restatement 'we know it because they've experienced it' is circular rather than evidential. The claim is about the policy, so this is a reasoning failure rather than a Focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The worst part of it, actually—the worst part of it—is that taking something away takes us backwards, but there doesn’t seem to be any vision of how the future will be for those workers.
civility.explanation: A contested repeal he strongly opposes, so there was a real opportunity to turn on the Minister. He criticises the decision and the absence of a replacement plan and attacks nobody.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question goes to: what evidence does the Minister have that small-business owners do not want to sign up to something that is better than the minimum wage and that indeed sets minimum standards across their industries?
focus.explanation: Puts a direct question about the evidence base for the repeal, naming the specific mechanism at issue — pay above the minimum wage and industry-wide minimum standards. Scrutiny of the measure before the committee, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, we know that the research shows that if we have a good quality provision of education in those early years, that is likely to continue on and have greater outcomes when those young people move throughout the education system.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests entirely on an unnamed body of research — an appeal to authority. No study, finding or effect size is offered to connect early-years quality to later outcomes, so the inference is only as good as the uncited source.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But we don’t consider, as a Government, that we wish to have any exemptions to the repeal, because we believe that there is a better way to improve the conditions of workers, for business and employees, without having fair pay agreements, and that is through increased productivity; that is through reducing regulation.
rigor.explanation: The "because" carries no argument: productivity and deregulation are asserted as the better route to improved conditions with nothing connecting them to worker outcomes, and no reason given why that route is incompatible with granting the requested exemptions. Bare assertion in the shape of a premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When the Fair Pay Agreements Bill went through Parliament, under the previous term of Government, there was quite a substantial select committee process, and many small-business owners did make submissions against the law change.
rigor.explanation: Asked what evidence she had that small businesses did not want fair pay agreements, she pointed to submissions opposing the original bill. That is real evidence and it tracks the question, but submitters self-select, so opposition submissions do not establish what the wider population of small businesses wants — a genuine gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But a blunt tool like a fair pay agreement would have forced some businesses to close their doors, because they wouldn’t have been able to have the conditions that would have been forced on them by a third party that had no knowledge about their particular business or their particular standards within their operation.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is smuggled into the premise: describing the bargaining party as "a third party that had no knowledge" of the business assumes the very defect being argued for. Nothing is offered on what conditions would have been set, or why they would exceed what any firm could bear — question-begging rather than inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I, as a previous Minister, don’t ever recall a cover sheet providing the amount of evidence that I would need or require to make any decisions, and so I am very impressed by what this cover sheet may look like.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that this cover sheet cannot bear the evidentiary weight placed on it rests on the speaker's own recollection of other cover sheets — an appeal to personal authority and anecdote. Nothing about the actual document is examined.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, we know that the research shows that if we have a good quality provision of education in those early years, that is likely to continue on and have greater outcomes when those young people move throughout the education system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the research literature shows a causal/predictive link between high-quality early childhood education and better outcomes later in the education system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed longitudinal ECE research (e.g. NZCER's Competent Children/Competent Learners study, OECD Starting Strong reviews, Perry Preschool follow-ups); true if the weight of that literature finds sustained positive effects on later educational outcomes, false if it finds no effect or effects that wash out.

veracity.statement: When the Fair Pay Agreements Bill went through Parliament, under the previous term of Government, there was quite a substantial select committee process, and many small-business owners did make submissions against the law change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Fair Pay Agreements Bill had a substantial select committee process and that many small-business owners submitted against it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's record for the Fair Pay Agreements Bill (2021–22) on parliament.nz: the number of submissions received and the committee report's characterisation of small-business opposition; true if the committee took a large volume of submissions including many from small-business owners opposing the bill, false if submissions were few or predominantly supportive.

veracity.statement: Important to note, because between 40 and 50 percent of children living in poverty are living in working households, so it would be good to know what the cover sheet said about these particular workforces and the number of children that are living in poverty in those households.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 40–50 percent of New Zealand children living in poverty are in households where at least one adult is in paid work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics and the MSD Household Incomes Report breakdown of children in low-income households by household work status, for the most recent year available in 2023; true if the working-household share of children in poverty falls in the 40–50% band on the standard measures, false if it sits materially outside it.

focus.statement: It would leave teachers able to choose where they wish to work based on reasons like having a shared educational philosophy, wanting to work within certain demographics or in certain areas, or because they wish to upskill in certain aspects of their teaching rather than being driven by their salary packages as they are now.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — what a fair pay agreement would change about how early childhood teachers choose employers. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It would leave teachers able to choose where they wish to work based on reasons like having a shared educational philosophy, wanting to work within certain demographics or in certain areas, or because they wish to upskill in certain aspects of their teaching rather than being driven by their salary packages as they are now.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (removing salary competition between providers) and gives examples of what would replace it, but carries no figures, no coverage numbers and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But we don’t consider, as a Government, that we wish to have any exemptions to the repeal, because we believe that there is a better way to improve the conditions of workers, for business and employees, without having fair pay agreements, and that is through increased productivity; that is through reducing regulation.
specificity.explanation: "Increased productivity" and "reducing regulation" are directions, not content — no named regulation to be cut, no mechanism, no figure, no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want the Minister to respond to my question with respect to what proportion of children living in poverty are actually living in households that have bus drivers, cleaners, coach drivers, hospitality workers, security officers and guards, commercial cleaners, early childhood education workers, and supermarket workers as the household providers for those households.
specificity.explanation: A precise, answerable question: a named quantity (proportion of children in poverty) cross-tabulated against nine explicitly listed occupations. A question this exact is as checkable as an answer would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He talked about clause 5, and I really commend him for coming back to a specific part of the bill and to a clause, and I would commend any member for keeping to the bill.
civility.explanation: Genuine courtesy to an opponent, but the generalising second half ("I would commend any member for keeping to the bill") is a pointed implication that other members have not — edging toward the person without landing on anyone.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It was very difficult to listen to the contribution from the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety, because I have to say it was rather patronising.
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy to the Minister's manner, characterising her as condescending. Short of a direct insult but it is a judgement of the person rather than the argument, and no part of the contribution is engaged to support it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I, as a previous Minister, don’t ever recall a cover sheet providing the amount of evidence that I would need or require to make any decisions, and so I am very impressed by what this cover sheet may look like.
civility.explanation: "I am very impressed by what this cover sheet may look like" is sarcasm directed at the Minister's handling of the evidence base. Mockery rather than a substantive objection, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine civility failure even though no insult is made.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Therefore, I look forward to hearing from the Minister how the cover sheet—and I’ll just reiterate—covers off the impacts on child poverty for those in those workforces; how the impact on Māori, Pacific, and women is covered off in those workforces through that cover sheet; how the productivity losses because of the repeal of fair pay agreements is covered off in that particular cover sheet; and, of course, because it’s of the utmost importance to that Minister and the Government, the expenditure that has been wasted because the Government decides to no longer pursue fairness in the workplace for our workers.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the missing regulatory impact statement, the cover sheet standing in its place, and the specific impact categories it is said to cover. Scrutiny of a named document and a named repeal, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How will the Minister mitigate the disproportionate impact of stagnant lower wages for women without FPA?
focus.explanation: A direct question about the named policy and its consequences for a named group. Asks the Minister for the alternative mechanism rather than characterising her party — accountability on the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Therefore, I look forward to hearing from the Minister how the cover sheet—and I’ll just reiterate—covers off the impacts on child poverty for those in those workforces; how the impact on Māori, Pacific, and women is covered off in those workforces through that cover sheet; how the productivity losses because of the repeal of fair pay agreements is covered off in that particular cover sheet; and, of course, because it’s of the utmost importance to that Minister and the Government, the expenditure that has been wasted because the Government decides to no longer pursue fairness in the workplace for our workers.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (the cover sheet in place of the regulatory impact statement) and four distinct impact categories the Minister is asked to address, but supplies no figures, no magnitudes and no timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, the issue with reducing regulation, in so many examples in the past, is that it’s often regulations that relate to health and safety at work, that relate to conditions at work, and many of them relate to wages—such as regulations around overtime, for example, and regulations around additional pay conditions such as getting additional pay for working on weekends, or working at nights or shift allowances or meal allowances and all those sorts of things.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms — overtime rules, weekend and night rates, shift and meal allowances — which is more than a direction. But 'in so many examples in the past' cites no actual instance, and there are no figures, dates or named regulations.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Make sure, please, Minister, that when you talk about the expenditure put towards actually negotiating these fair pay agreements, you align that next to the productivity losses we can expect from those workforces because we didn’t, or they didn’t, have the courage to continue down the track of enforcing what is only right, which is fair pay agreements for these workforces.
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust. The substance — set the negotiation spend against the claimed productivity loss — is entirely about the policy, but 'didn't have the courage' imputes a character failing rather than a policy error. Edges toward the person without landing on any individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So the committee may understand why we on this side are a little bit sceptical of the claim that instead of this Act, which will be repealed by this bill, which will and has been proven to improve conditions and increase wages and get a fair standard across the board—people shake their heads, but they’re not looking at evidence; they’re only looking at their own view that they don’t want to pay higher wages.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the members opposite: not that they are mistaken, but that they are ignoring evidence because they personally do not want to pay higher wages. Ascribing a self-interested motive rather than contesting the position is a real civility failure, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem with that, of course, is that productivity is linked to wages, and there is a reason why Australia and other countries that follow what was in place in the Fair Pay Agreements Act—the Act that this bill, in Part 2, seeks to repeal—have higher productivity: the two go hand in hand.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, and a weak one: from an observed association between sector-bargaining countries and higher productivity it concludes a causal link ('the two go hand in hand'). Correlation asserted as causation, with the comparator countries selected rather than surveyed and no mechanism offered. Not fact-checked here — the premise may well be true.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s extraordinary that there are people in this House that would oppose that.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The purpose clause quoted is the Act's stated goal (improving employment terms); opposing the Act as the means of achieving it is not opposing the goal. The conclusion that opponents oppose better employment terms does not follow from their opposition to this mechanism.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Kate Sheppard fought for women’s rights and would be appalled that we are still fighting for equal rights and pay for women.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority combined with an appeal to emotion: an imagined reaction from a historical figure is offered as a reason to retain fair pay agreements. Nothing is shown about whether the Act closes the gap; the invoked authority cannot bear on the question.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Since 1991, New Zealand’s productivity has not kept up with other countries that have maintained what is in the Fair Pay Agreements Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NZ labour productivity growth since 1991 has lagged that of countries retaining sector-wide/industry bargaining of the kind the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 established.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD labour productivity (GDP per hour worked) growth series, 1991 to date, comparing New Zealand against countries with sector-wide collective bargaining (e.g. Australia, and the EU/Nordic economies with extended sectoral awards). True if NZ's cumulative productivity growth over that period is below those comparators; false if NZ matches or exceeds them.

veracity.statement: The gender pay gap for women compared to men is 8.6 percent; 8.6 percent matters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current national gender pay gap figure as 8.6 percent at the time of speaking (December 2023).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ official gender pay gap (median hourly earnings, Household Labour Force Survey / Labour Market Statistics) for the June 2023 quarter. True if the published figure is 8.6% (± rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We can be proud in New Zealand that we have reduced this gap from 16.8 percent in 1998 through concerted efforts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand gender pay gap stood at 16.8 percent in 1998, the baseline against which the reduction is claimed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ gender pay gap series (New Zealand Income Survey / Household Labour Force Survey) for 1998, and Ministry for Women published historical figures. True if the 1998 figure is 16.8% (± rounding), false if materially different.

focus.statement: Now, if the committee can remember, I said the five-year outlook: the mean hourly for cleaners was $18.60. In a sector where there is higher union membership, the mean hourly five years out is $25.30. There is actually a considerable difference which shows why having collective bargaining power is incredibly important.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: she works from the regulatory impact statement's own annex, cites union density and wage figures for named occupational groups, and ties it to a specific tabled amendment. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, if the committee can remember, I said the five-year outlook: the mean hourly for cleaners was $18.60. In a sector where there is higher union membership, the mean hourly five years out is $25.30. There is actually a considerable difference which shows why having collective bargaining power is incredibly important.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, and a weak one: she infers that collective bargaining causes the wage difference from a two-occupation comparison (cleaners at 17 percent density, drivers at 36 percent). The occupations differ in skill, licensing, hours and sector, so the comparison is confounded — a correlation-as-causation step with no control offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I come from a family of hospital cleaners, who are some of the lowest-paid workers, but, thankfully, they’ve been able to collectively bargain to be able to lift some of those wages.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the policy — collective bargaining raises low wages — but the support offered is a single family anecdote. Appeal to personal anecdote: one household's experience does not establish the general effect she is defending.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, if the committee can remember, I said the five-year outlook: the mean hourly for cleaners was $18.60. In a sector where there is higher union membership, the mean hourly five years out is $25.30. There is actually a considerable difference which shows why having collective bargaining power is incredibly important.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2021 Fair Pay Agreements regulatory impact statement records a five-year mean hourly rate of $18.60 for cleaners and laundry workers and $25.30 for automobile, bus and rail drivers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's full Regulatory Impact Statement for the Fair Pay Agreements Bill (2021), Annex Two, figures A2 and A3; true if the five-year mean hourly rates shown are $18.60 for cleaners/laundry workers and $25.30 for automobile/bus/rail drivers, false if the figures differ materially or the annex reports no such series.

veracity.statement: Back in 2021, it said that there’s going to be an estimated $150 million to $600 million per year total monetised benefits.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2021 Fair Pay Agreements regulatory impact statement estimated total monetised benefits of $150 million to $600 million per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's full Regulatory Impact Statement for the Fair Pay Agreements Bill (2021), cost-benefit section; true if the stated total monetised benefit estimate is a range of roughly $150m–$600m per annum, false if the document gives a materially different range or expresses the benefit on a different basis (e.g. one-off rather than annual).

specificity.statement: Back in 2021, it said that there’s going to be an estimated $150 million to $600 million per year total monetised benefits.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a dated document, a quantified range and a stated unit (per year, total monetised benefits). Anyone could pull the impact statement and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, the Minister did talk about productivity costs—or perhaps that was the answer that she didn’t actually provide.
civility.explanation: Pointed and barbed — it suggests the Minister dodged rather than answered — but the jab lands on the quality of the answer, not on the Minister's character, competence or motives. Robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Wage growth has not actually kept up with the small productivity gains that we have had since 1991 and since the introduction of the Employment Contracts Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that since 1991 cumulative real wage growth in New Zealand has lagged behind cumulative labour productivity growth, drawing on a FIRST Union submission.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ labour productivity index and real average hourly earnings series (or NZ Productivity Commission analysis of the wage-productivity gap) from 1991 to 2023; true if cumulative labour productivity growth exceeded cumulative real wage growth over that period, false if real wages grew at or above the rate of productivity.

veracity.statement: There was an exemption from the regulatory impact statement requirements that was provided and you can find this in the cover sheet on page 2.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a formal exemption from the regulatory impact statement requirements was granted for this bill and is recorded on page 2 of the Cabinet paper cover sheet.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet paper cover sheet for the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill (page 2) and the Treasury/MBIE regulatory impact analysis register; true if an RIS exemption is recorded for this bill, false if no exemption was granted.

veracity.statement: So while this law has been in place for about a year, many of the bargaining sides have yet to actually meet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a year after the Fair Pay Agreements Act came into force, many of the parties to initiated agreements had not yet held a bargaining meeting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's record of approved fair pay agreement bargaining initiations and their bargaining status as at December 2023; true if a substantial share of initiated bargaining sides had not yet held a first bargaining meeting, false if most had already begun meeting.

veracity.statement: That funding was $6.33 million in Budget 2021 and $9.226 million in Budget 2022, and for 23/24 the funding is approximately $16.209 million in operating expenditure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific operating-expenditure figures appropriated to MBIE and the Employment Relations Authority to establish and run the fair pay agreement system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2021 and Budget 2022 appropriations for the fair pay agreement system and the 2023/24 Estimates of Appropriations for Vote Business, Science and Innovation / Vote Labour Market; true if the operating figures match $6.33m, $9.226m and approximately $16.209m, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: One of the comments that I thought was really useful and absolutely speaks to my experience, having worked with supermarket workers, many of whom are on low wages, is that workers who are worried about money, stressed about money—often I met with workers who hadn’t had enough to eat that day—are not going to be productive workers.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy question before the House (whether wage-setting affects productivity), but the causal step is carried by an appeal to personal anecdote and to a union submission's authority rather than by any evidence connecting low pay to measured productivity.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It says because there is an existing regulatory impact statement from 2021 already providing analysis on the status quo, we would essentially be carrying out the exact same replica of analysis, so there was no need to replicate what we already had in the original regulatory impact statement.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy, but with a real gap between premise and conclusion: analysis produced in 2021 to justify introducing fair pay agreements is treated as interchangeable with analysis of repealing them, which are different counterfactuals. The conclusion is reasonable but does not fully follow from what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, on the face of it, that sounds like quite a simple question, but it is actually very complex. And that’s because the law is not actually clear who is and is not within coverage within different sectors; which types of employees can and cannot be covered.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (the requested sector-by-gender coverage statistic cannot be produced) follows from the stated premise (the statute does not define who falls within coverage), and she supplies a concrete illustration of the ambiguity. It remains an assertion about the state of the data rather than a demonstration of it, which is the only real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason for my amendment of this nature is to reflect the work that has been done but reflect as well that many of these workers who are covered by the agreements that are currently being negotiated do represent vulnerable workers.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: explains what her amendment does and who it affects. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She mentioned about a lot of the work having been undertaken by parties to the fair pay agreements already under the bargaining process, but forgot to mention that the agreements are all in their very early stages.
