veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics (enterprises and employee counts, or the RME/FTE series) for the year referenced: true if total employment divided by number of enterprises is below 4 FTE, false if 4 or above.

veracity.statement: Because in this situation, we have not even had a select committee look at this. We have not had any chance for the public to take part.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that this repeal bill was not referred to a select committee and that there was no opportunity for public submissions on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill: true if no select committee referral and no call for submissions appears in the bill's stages, false if a committee stage or submissions process is recorded.

veracity.statement: Did the Productivity Commission ask the previous Government to increase the jobseeker benefit by 66,000 over the last six years?
veracity.explanation: Embedded in the rhetorical question is the factual assertion that the number of people receiving Jobseeker Support rose by about 66,000 over the six years to the date of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets / Jobseeker Support recipient counts for the quarter ending late 2017 compared with late 2023: true if the increase is approximately 66,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: A coalition Government established the Productivity Commission 13 years ago, and it was quite effective for a season.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Productivity Commission was established roughly 13 years before January 2024, by a coalition Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Productivity Commission Act 2010 and the Commission's commencement date: true if establishment falls in 2010–2011 (i.e. about 13 years before the speech), false if materially earlier or later.

veracity.statement: We’ve got more empty houses than we’ve ever had in New Zealand, and yet we’re in the middle of a housing crisis.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current number of unoccupied dwellings in New Zealand is the highest ever recorded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ census counts of unoccupied dwellings, 2023 compared with 2018, 2013 and earlier censuses: true if the 2023 count is the highest in the series, false if any earlier census recorded more.

veracity.statement: Just going back to the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill, the infrastructure funding and financing legislation—the IFF—has been in place for some time, and yet the previous Government has done nothing with it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no use was made of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing regime between its enactment and the change of government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Levy orders and designated projects made under the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 between its commencement and November 2023: false if any levy order or funded project (e.g. a named Auckland or Tauranga scheme) was made under the Act, true if none were.

civility.statement: It’s a tragedy to lose that for something that is, in fact, as many people have said tonight, a vanity project—and it’s one based on arrogance.
civility.explanation: Moves off the merits of the replacement body and onto the motives of those advancing it — "vanity" and "arrogance" impute bad faith rather than engaging the substance. Short of a direct personal insult, but no longer civil under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So adding to the layers of irony and hypocrisy that have been present in the House tonight is the Minister in charge of this bill—who used to rail about the use of urgency, who used to tell us it was undemocratic not to give the public a say—here tonight with a silly and sad piece of legislation that he hasn’t even sought to justify.
civility.explanation: Imputes hypocrisy to the Minister personally rather than confining the attack to the bill; 'silly and sad' about the legislation would pass cleanly, but the charge of bad faith lands on the person. A real failure under the re-anchored scale, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And the fact that the ACT Party are prepared to trade that away for the vanity project that is the ministry of regulation that David Seymour has put forward is indeed very sad.
civility.explanation: 'Vanity project' attributes a self-serving motive to the named Minister rather than criticising the ministry's design or cost. Sneering at motive, which the re-anchored scale treats as a genuine failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s a real thrill to follow my fellow Otago graduate, the Hon Grant Robertson—proud Otago University Students’ Association alumni, passionate about Otago University, and I hope, with the spare time he’s got on his hands now, he spends a lot more time down there this year.
civility.explanation: A courteous frame carrying a dig at Robertson's personal circumstances — loss of office read as idleness. Pointed at the person rather than any argument, but mild and good-humoured rather than contemptuous.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I have heard many times, while I have been in this House, David Seymour rail about the use of urgency, and I do want to quote from him towards the end of 2020 when a bill was being passed in urgency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that David Seymour repeatedly criticised the use of urgency in the House, and specifically did so late in 2020 during an urgency debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of debates in the last quarter of 2020; true if Seymour is recorded speaking against the government's use of urgency in an urgency debate in that period, false if no such speech exists.

veracity.statement: This is an electorate where, in South Canterbury, 1.2 percent of the country’s population produces 7.3 percent of our food and fibre exports.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that South Canterbury holds about 1.2% of New Zealand's population while generating about 7.3% of national food and fibre export value.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for South Canterbury (Timaru/Mackenzie/Waimate districts) against national population, and MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries regional export share; true if both shares are within about a percentage point of those stated, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, it’s very simple: the schedule provides that contracts will be honoured. The identity of the counterparty will change, but what they get will be delivered as if the Productivity Commission was still the counterparty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Schedule 1 of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill preserves existing contracts in full, changing only which entity is the counterparty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Schedule 1 of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill as reported; true if it provides for contracts to transfer with obligations and entitlements unchanged, false if it permits variation or extinguishment of contractual entitlements.

focus.statement: I think members of the public would have enjoyed that opportunity to come forward to this House and put their views on the table, but they are not being given the opportunity to do that.
focus.explanation: Directed at the handling of this specific bill — the absence of a select committee stage and public submissions — rather than at the other party's character. Legitimate process scrutiny of the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To have an institution that actually supports that conversation, provides the big-picture issues, gives people an opportunity to input on that, and gives its thoughts and recommendations to the Government is a different job than a ministry of regulation.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the measure: what the body being disestablished actually does and whether the proposed replacement does the same job. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And the fact that the ACT Party are prepared to trade that away for the vanity project that is the ministry of regulation that David Seymour has put forward is indeed very sad.
focus.explanation: A real policy object is named (the ministry of regulation replacing the Commission), but the weight of the sentence is on what the ACT Party is willing to trade and the Minister's motives rather than on the mechanism or its effects.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If members opposite were so concerned about productivity, why did they spend six years strangling the most productive part of our economy?
focus.explanation: Characterises the previous government's whole record with no policy, figure or mechanism named — 'strangling' identifies no regulation and no measure. Almost entirely about the other side rather than the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s not the State that is the key to solving our productivity problems; it is people like my friend and my neighbour Miles Anderson, who many of us have spoken about tonight, the member for Waitaki, who himself took a punt on sheep scanning technology, and 4 million - odd sheep later the productivity gains in this sector speak for themselves.
focus.explanation: Engages the underlying policy question the bill turns on — whether a state body drives productivity — rather than attacking opponents, though the argument runs on a personal illustration rather than the measure's provisions.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It appears that no one’s entitled to cancel their contractual arrangements on the basis that they’ve got a new entity, even though they don’t want to contract with the ministry—whatever ministry that might be.
focus.explanation: Directed at a named provision of the bill — Schedule 1's transfer of contractual obligations — and its practical effect on counterparties. Entirely on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To have an institution that actually supports that conversation, provides the big-picture issues, gives people an opportunity to input on that, and gives its thoughts and recommendations to the Government is a different job than a ministry of regulation.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: he lists functions of the Commission (long-run analysis, public input, advice to government) and concludes a regulatory ministry is not a substitute. The functional contrast is asserted rather than demonstrated — the gap is that he does not show the ministry cannot perform those functions — but the conclusion broadly tracks what he offers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not the State that is the key to solving our productivity problems; it is people like my friend and my neighbour Miles Anderson, who many of us have spoken about tonight, the member for Waitaki, who himself took a punt on sheep scanning technology, and 4 million - odd sheep later the productivity gains in this sector speak for themselves.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: one farmer's success with scanning technology is offered as grounds for a general conclusion about the State's role in national productivity. A single case cannot support the categorical premise, and 'speak for themselves' substitutes assertion for the missing link.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is an electorate where, in South Canterbury, 1.2 percent of the country’s population produces 7.3 percent of our food and fibre exports.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures tied to a named region and a defined export category. Fully checkable against published statistics; whether the numbers are right is a separate question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It appears that no one’s entitled to cancel their contractual arrangements on the basis that they’ve got a new entity, even though they don’t want to contract with the ministry—whatever ministry that might be.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the schedule, the mechanism (obligations assumed by a new entity) and the concrete consequence (no right of cancellation). Falls short of a figure or clause-level citation, and the receiving ministry is left unnamed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, it’s very simple: the schedule provides that contracts will be honoured. The identity of the counterparty will change, but what they get will be delivered as if the Productivity Commission was still the counterparty.
specificity.explanation: States the mechanism — substitution of counterparty with performance preserved — in terms someone could check against the schedule, though no clause is cited and the question of a right to exit is not quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In turn, that will have, I guess, a kind of win-win in that we preserve all of the great works that have been done by the Productivity Commission—even though, as members have noted, they haven’t always been followed as well as they might—and yet also free up around $6 million per year of funding that can be used for better—ironically—more productive purposes.
specificity.explanation: Carries one concrete, checkable figure (about $6 million per year freed up), but the destination of that money is left as 'better, more productive purposes' with no mechanism, recipient or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In turn, that will have, I guess, a kind of win-win in that we preserve all of the great works that have been done by the Productivity Commission—even though, as members have noted, they haven’t always been followed as well as they might—and yet also free up around $6 million per year of funding that can be used for better—ironically—more productive purposes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that disestablishing the Commission frees up roughly $6 million of funding a year — a claim about the Commission's current annual budget.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Productivity Commission's annual appropriation in the Estimates/Vote papers (Vote Business, Science and Innovation) for the years immediately before disestablishment; true if annual funding is approximately $6 million, false if materially different (e.g. under $4m or over $8m).

veracity.statement: For example, the Crown Entities Act and the Ombudsman Act both have references to the Productivity Commission for the purpose of scrutiny under the Official Information Act and so on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two named Acts each contain express references to the Productivity Commission, which is why consequential amendments are needed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedules of the Crown Entities Act 2004 and the Ombudsmen Act 1975 as they stood in January 2024; true if the New Zealand Productivity Commission is named in both, false if it is absent from either.

rigor.statement: Well, that would be because the Productivity Commission is a Crown entity, and so, therefore, the employees are employees of a Crown entity.
rigor.explanation: A clean, valid inference: the Commission is a Crown entity, therefore its staff fall under the Crown Entities Act definition of 'employee', which is why the bill cross-references that Act. The conclusion follows directly from the premise with no gap or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So when we see things like the interpretation clause defining what “assets” are, it’s very important to define these terms to make sure that bills like this aren’t open to costly, lengthy judicial reviews tied up in the courts if Ministers are making decisions, or officials are interpreting the bill, in a way which isn’t in line with the interpretation.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — defined terms reduce interpretive ambiguity, therefore reduce litigation risk — and the step from premise to conclusion holds. Marked down only because the litigation-risk link is asserted rather than supported with any example of such a review.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I haven’t had the chance or the opportunity this evening to look up the Crown Entities Act 2004, but that’s an indication, to me, that we might not be talking about your bog-standard, sort of run-of-the-mill definition of “employee” that you might run into in Black’s Law Dictionary or some sort of legal dictionaries you use, but you have to actually go to the Crown Entities Act 2004 to determine what an “employee” means in this instance.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence, and by the speaker's own admission from not having checked: the mere existence of a cross-reference to another Act is taken as an indication that the defined term departs from the ordinary meaning. Statutes routinely cross-reference definitions that are entirely conventional, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I think it’s a really important point because this is an important bill and the technicalities are the meat of this, and if we get this wrong, well, we won’t be very productive and that would not be the whole point of it.
rigor.explanation: Circular reasoning: the point is said to be important because the bill is important, which restates the conclusion rather than supporting it. The only added content is a pun on 'productive'; no consequence of getting the registers clause wrong is actually identified.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I think the concept that the member is—I mean, this is the problem with going to Otago: you’ve got to really spell it out for them.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the questioner rather than at his question — the implication is that the member needs things spelled out because of where he studied. Short of a direct insult but past pointed: it mocks the member's comprehension instead of answering on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So when we see things like the interpretation clause defining what “assets” are, it’s very important to define these terms to make sure that bills like this aren’t open to costly, lengthy judicial reviews tied up in the courts if Ministers are making decisions, or officials are interpreting the bill, in a way which isn’t in line with the interpretation.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: a named clause of the bill, the specific term it defines, and the consequence of defining it. No party framing at all, in a debate stage where filler about the other side was freely available.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I say this from the perspective of small businesses—the majority of businesses in this country are small businesses—and someone who comes from a background of small business, before I became a lawyer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that small businesses form the majority of New Zealand businesses — a factual claim about the present composition of the business population, distinct from the autobiographical framing around it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Small Business Factsheet / Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics for 2023-24: true if the majority of NZ enterprises fall within the standard small-business definition (fewer than 20 employees), false if they do not.

rigor.statement: But the experience I had from that is that, effectively, good regulation, good law is the DNA of our society, so if we have good regulation and good law, that creates a good body politic, a good society, and if we don’t have it particularly effective, then it doesn’t.
rigor.explanation: An inference about regulation is offered, but it is essentially circular: 'good' regulation produces a 'good' society and bad regulation does not, with the evaluative term doing all the work. The metaphor ('the DNA of our society') supplies no connecting mechanism, so the conclusion restates the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know the need to improve productivity in this country, because, if we don’t do that, we can’t afford all the things we that we want to do, all the great public services we want, we can’t afford to pay ourselves the sort of wages that we want to pay, and we are all the worse for it.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: productivity growth is needed because real wages and public spending are ultimately funded out of output per worker. The link from productivity to affordable services and wages is standard and holds given its premises; it loses something only because the connection is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I just wanted to build on this point because you can make the argument that New Zealanders continue to get sick and therefore we should disestablish the health service because we haven’t healed everybody yet, and, actually, that argument doesn’t follow that just because Governments are too self-interested or captured by vested interests to act on recommendations isn’t a good reason to get rid of the people who thought of the recommendations.
rigor.explanation: A reductio ad absurdum aimed at the structure of the disestablishment case: if 'the problem persists' justified abolishing the body that advises on it, the same reasoning would abolish the health service. The parallel identifies a real gap — non-adoption of advice is a failure of the adopter, not of the adviser. Marked down slightly because the analogy is asserted rather than defended, and a delivery body and an advisory body are not perfectly alike.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So just the intention of this bill—how is that going to ensure these people we’re talking about, these small-business owners around the country are going to see some relief at the light at the end of the tunnel?
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at the measure before the House — the intention of the bill and its effect on a named group. No party framing or characterisation of opponents at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are others, on the opposite side of the Chamber, who are saying they’re very concerned about its loss, which I find slightly ironic.
focus.explanation: The point is about the other side's perceived inconsistency rather than about the disestablishment itself; no specific policy, figure or outcome is named. It is mild and glancing rather than sustained party-bashing, and it does attach to the Commission's loss, so not a floor score.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So just the intention of this bill—how is that going to ensure these people we’re talking about, these small-business owners around the country are going to see some relief at the light at the end of the tunnel?
specificity.explanation: Asks for 'some relief at the light at the end of the tunnel' with no figure, mechanism, threshold or timeframe that would let anyone tell whether relief had arrived. The surrounding speech supplies anecdote rather than detail. High focus, low specificity — the same statement, two different questions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I agree with that, and we’re going to be doing a lot to ensure that that is less and less the case over this term of Government.
specificity.explanation: 'Doing a lot' to make excessive regulation 'less and less the case' names no measure, no target, no mechanism and no milestone within the term. Nothing here could be checked against or acted on, and no detail is supplied nearby in the speech.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So my question to the Minister for Regulation, which he did appeal to us in the second reading debate, to come back to some of the policy decisions, which is not easy to do within Standing Orders, clause by clause here, which maybe is why he suggested it, in order to ensure that we had as little debate as possible about the substance of the bill.
civility.explanation: Imputes a bad-faith motive to the Minister — that his invitation to raise policy at the committee stage was a device to suppress substantive debate. Short of an insult, but it moves from the argument to the person's intentions, which is the 0.5 failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Then there is a question—well, it wasn’t really a question—from Joseph Mooney. It sort of started off autobiographical, then his speech sort of got into the pseudo-philosophical, and then he made the point that red tape and regulation are bad for business when it’s done badly and when it’s excessive.
civility.explanation: Mockery of another member's contribution — 'pseudo-philosophical', 'it wasn't really a question' — belittling how he spoke rather than engaging what he asked. Condescension aimed at the member, not at the substance; not a direct insult to his character, so above the personal-attack band.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the people of New Zealand issued their own opinion on economic resilience, supply chain disruptions, and all the negative effects on that, on 14 October, 2023, when they indicated to the previous Government that the way they managed the supply chain—all the red tape they imposed on the economy, or costs on employers, or raising the minimum wage without increasing productivity at all—were unacceptable to New Zealanders, who voted to remove the last Government.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity plus non sequitur: a general election result is treated as a verdict on named individual policies (red tape, employer costs, the minimum wage). Nothing is offered to show voters were rejecting those specific measures rather than anything else, and 'they voted them out' cannot establish it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, actually, the law that’s being passed tonight will self-repeal, and the reason for that is that in a years’ time, when all of the transitions and savings have been done, the business has been wound up, there is no longer a need to have this Act.
rigor.explanation: A stated premise (once the transitional and savings work is complete the Act has no remaining function) genuinely supports the conclusion (it should self-repeal). The inference holds on its own terms; no appeal or gap is being leaned on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The act of repeal has been done. The non-existence of this Act does not change the other legislation that will no longer give rise to a Productivity Commission.
rigor.explanation: Answers the revival question by distinguishing the completed act of repeal from the continuing existence of the repealing Act, and the conclusion follows directly from that distinction. No fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Crown is going to honour its commitments made through the Productivity Commission through another entity—in this case, the Treasury. From the point of view of those counterparties to contract, nothing changes.
rigor.explanation: Begs the question. Webb's premise was that some advisory contracts turn on a personal relationship of trust with the chair; the reply asserts that a Crown entity has no personal relationships and concludes nothing changes, which assumes away the disputed premise rather than answering it. Continuity of the legal obligation does not establish continuity of what the counterparty contracted for.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, the repeal Act has done its job—many Acts do do their job—but to repeal a repeal Act seems to be fundamentally an unnecessary legislative step and a little confusing.
rigor.explanation: The inference is that because the repealing Act has already had its effect, repealing it is unnecessary. There is a real gap: a spent Act can still be repealed to tidy the statute book, and nothing is offered to rule that out. Hedged ('seems'), so not a bare non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the people of New Zealand issued their own opinion on economic resilience, supply chain disruptions, and all the negative effects on that, on 14 October, 2023, when they indicated to the previous Government that the way they managed the supply chain—all the red tape they imposed on the economy, or costs on employers, or raising the minimum wage without increasing productivity at all—were unacceptable to New Zealanders, who voted to remove the last Government.
focus.explanation: Real policy content is named — supply-chain resilience, compliance costs, the minimum wage — but the weight of the passage is the previous Government's defeat at the ballot box rather than the clause before the committee. A policy point in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I mean, the repeal Act has done its job—many Acts do do their job—but to repeal a repeal Act seems to be fundamentally an unnecessary legislative step and a little confusing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill before the committee — what a self-repealing repeal Act actually does. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In answer to the member’s questions, first of all, the commission will be wound down at the end of February—interestingly, 29 February; can’t do that every year.
specificity.explanation: Answers a timing question with an exact date rather than a direction of travel. Anyone can check whether the commission ceased on 29 February 2024.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So if the Minister could clarify what the effect of a repeal of a repeal is, that would be really useful, because if a repeal of a repeal then restores what we had before, we’re going to be in all kinds of trouble on 30 June 2025.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise legal question (the effect of repealing a repealing Act) and the date on which it would bite, 30 June 2025. Checkable and actionable, though the consequence itself is left as 'all kinds of trouble'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So you might have a consultant who the chair of the commission has arranged to give advice—it’s a personal relationship of trust, it’s one that’s quite personal; might even be a solicitor-client relationship, and yet that relationship can’t be terminated because of Part 1 of Schedule 1, clause 1(2)(b).
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact provision (Part 1 of Schedule 1, clause 1(2)(b)) and a concrete class of affected contract, so the claimed effect can be read off the bill and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Second of all, the final report the member’s referred to, I’m advised, will be reported back around mid-February.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Productivity Commission's inquiry into economic resilience to supply chain disruptions will be reported back around the middle of February 2024, before the commission's wind-up.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Publication record for the Productivity Commission's 'improving economic resilience' / supply chain resilience inquiry: true if the final report was reported back or released in the first half of February 2024 (roughly 8–20 February), false if it appeared materially later, only at the 29 February wind-up, or not at all.

civility.statement: Look, just for the benefit of the children watching up and down New Zealand tonight, I think we’ve just seen that anyone can grow up to be a law professor.
civility.explanation: A sneer at Duncan Webb personally rather than at anything he argued — it addresses nothing in the questions asked and works only as mockery of his standing and competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: A law professor should know: no, it wouldn’t.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the questioner's professional competence rather than at his question. The substantive answer follows in the next sentences and needed none of this; short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m advised that the cash reserves will be adequate for its liabilities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, on official advice, that the Productivity Commission's cash reserves are sufficient to meet its liabilities on disestablishment, so that no residual liability falls on the Treasury.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Productivity Commission's final annual report / disestablishment accounts and Treasury's disclosure of transferred liabilities: true if reserves covered the commission's liabilities with no material residual liability assumed by the Treasury, false if the Treasury absorbed a shortfall.

specificity.statement: Yes, 65 percent of firearms seized by police in 2023, and 62 percent of firearms seized in 2022 had no recorded serial number.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages tied to named years and a named source of data (police seizures); directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has—in the ACT and National coalition agreement—committed to reviewing the firearms registry, starting before June 2024.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document (the ACT–National coalition agreement), the action (a review of the firearms registry) and a start-by date (June 2024). No detail on scope or who conducts it, so short of full marks.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government is committed to the smoke-free target of less than 5 percent of people smoking daily by 2025. Our plan is to repeal the 2022 smoke-free amendments that have not yet taken effect, namely reduced retailers, denicotisation, and prohibition to those born from 2009.
specificity.explanation: A numeric target with a date, plus three named measures to be repealed. Concrete enough that anyone could check what is being undone and against what benchmark.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re completely committed to targeted programmes rather than the blanket approach of the previous Government and will focus on those groups with the greatest need.
specificity.explanation: Asked for a strategy to accelerate Māori smoking cessation, the answer names no programme, no funding, no mechanism and no timeframe — 'targeted programmes' and 'greatest need' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want to call on all parents to make sure they get their kids to school this week so we can teach them the basics—an hour of maths, reading, and writing starting this year; a mobile phones ban; and an expert panel reviewing primary and intermediate school curriculum.
specificity.explanation: Three named measures with a quantum for one (an hour of maths, reading and writing) and rough timing ('starting this year'); no funding, no implementation detail and no date for the panel's report.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Yes, 65 percent of firearms seized by police in 2023, and 62 percent of firearms seized in 2022 had no recorded serial number.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 65% of firearms seized by police in calendar 2023, and 62% in 2022, had no recorded serial number.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police firearms-seizure data for calendar 2022 and 2023 on the proportion of seized firearms with no recorded serial number (as briefed to the Minister or released under OIA); true if the figures are 62% (2022) and 65% (2023) within rounding, false if materially different or if no such breakdown exists.

veracity.statement: Ninety-four percent of people who were present at or subject to a search by police in which firearms were seized last year did not possess a firearms licence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 2023, 94% of people present at or subject to police searches in which firearms were seized held no firearms licence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police data for 2023 linking firearms-seizure searches to the licence status of persons present; true if the unlicensed proportion is 94% within rounding, false if materially different or if the figure is not derivable from police records.

veracity.statement: As of mid - last year, we were down to 284,000 daily smokers from 573,000 ten years ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the number of daily smokers in New Zealand fell from 573,000 about ten years earlier to 284,000 as at mid-2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily-smoking prevalence applied to the adult population for 2022/23 and for roughly 2012/13; true if the counts are approximately 284,000 and 573,000 within rounding of the published estimates, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Given that smoking is the leading cause of premature death in Aotearoa, what is her Government’s strategy to rapidly address the inequity and accelerate smoking cessation among Māori to achieve nationwide targets?
veracity.explanation: The embedded factual premise is that smoking is the single leading cause of premature death in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Global Burden of Disease New Zealand attribution of deaths and DALYs to risk factors; true if tobacco ranks first among causes of premature or preventable death in NZ, false if another risk factor (e.g. dietary risks or high BMI) ranks above it on the standard published measure.

veracity.statement: Does she accept the Government’s modelling that suggests Māori will not reach the 5 percent national target of smoking prevalence until 2061?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Government modelling exists which projects Māori smoking prevalence reaching the 5 percent target only by 2061.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Government smokefree modelling papers current in January 2024; true if a Government projection places Māori daily smoking at 5% around 2061, false if no such modelling exists or it gives a materially different date.

veracity.statement: Is it the Minister’s position that behind this policy is the wisdom of not imposing $8.6 billion of taxation upon Māori since 2011 when it comes to cigarette smoking or having people beaten up at supermarkets on a daily basis in ram raids, all sorts of illegalities, or the black market, but by following this policy we have taken ourselves to number one in the world?
veracity.explanation: The embedded factual premise is that $8.6 billion in tobacco taxation has been imposed on Māori since 2011.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Customs/Treasury tobacco excise revenue 2011–2023 combined with New Zealand Health Survey estimates of Māori share of tobacco consumption; true if the Māori-attributable excise total is approximately $8.6 billion, false if it is materially lower or if no defensible basis for the attribution exists.

veracity.statement: In answer to supplementary questions on question No. 11, I stated that the Government’s policy was for the 500 additional police to be delivered over the course of the term, which is three years. I should have been clearer: the Government’s policy is to deliver 500 new police in the first two years of the term.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Government policy is delivery of 500 new police within the first two years of the term, not over the three-year term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–New Zealand First coalition agreement and Government policy statements on the additional-police commitment as at January 2024; true if the stated commitment is 500 additional police within two years, false if the governing documents specify the term (three years) or another period.

veracity.statement: Sadly, this has been a former Government that left us with 55 percent of our kids not going to school regularly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 55 percent of New Zealand school students were not attending school regularly at the end of the previous Government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education attendance statistics, where 'regular attendance' is attending more than 90% of half-days; true if roughly 45% attended regularly (i.e. ~55% did not) in the most recent period under the previous Government, false if the non-regular share is materially different.

veracity.statement: How can Mark Mitchell have been confused yesterday, when he said on Monday: “Realistically, 500 new staff over the next three years is what we’re aiming for.”; he said on Tuesday, “The Government’s policy is to deliver 500 additional officers over the term of this Government, which is three years.”; and claimed previously that there had been a meeting in December of the three governing parties where they agreed to change the target from two years to three years?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Mark Mitchell made the two quoted statements on the Monday and Tuesday preceding, and previously referred to a December meeting of the three governing parties agreeing to move the police target from two years to three.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and contemporaneous media transcripts for 29 and 30 January 2024; true if Mitchell used the quoted words on those days and referred to a December three-party meeting changing the target, false if the quotes are inaccurate or the December reference was not made.

rigor.statement: This suggests that criminals are using firearms that are either illegally imported, manufactured, or intentionally stripped of serial numbers, making them untraceable. The firearms registry would be unable to capture these illegally held or manufactured firearms.
rigor.explanation: The step from 'no serial number' to 'untraceable and illicitly sourced' follows reasonably. The further step to the registry being 'unable to capture' them is a partial gap: the registry's stated purpose is recording legally held firearms and their movement into illicit hands, so the absence of serials in a seized sample does not by itself establish the registry is ineffective.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The gangs and criminals are carrying and using firearms illegally, and they’re circumventing the firearms registry. Licensed firearms owners are not the problem. That’s why the Government is committed to targeting firearms illegally held by the gangs.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation from a selected sample: the statistic covers only people caught up in police firearms searches, which is by construction weighted toward the unlicensed, so it cannot support the general conclusion that licensed owners 'are not the problem' (it says nothing about diversion from licensed stock).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Cutting supply doesn’t equate to reducing demand, and the last Government’s planned approach was also going to have consequences for retailers, crime, and the growth of the black market.
rigor.explanation: Bare assertion: the claimed consequences for retailers, crime and the black market are stated, not argued for — no modelling, comparison or evidence is offered to connect the repealed measures to those outcomes, and the supply/demand premise is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is it the Minister’s position that behind this policy is the wisdom of not imposing $8.6 billion of taxation upon Māori since 2011 when it comes to cigarette smoking or having people beaten up at supermarkets on a daily basis in ram raids, all sorts of illegalities, or the black market, but by following this policy we have taken ourselves to number one in the world?
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur and conflation: tobacco excise, ram raids and the black market are chained together as though the causal link were established, and the concluding claim that 'this policy' has taken New Zealand to 'number one in the world' is attached with nothing offered to connect it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Sadly, this has been a former Government that left us with 55 percent of our kids not going to school regularly.
focus.explanation: Names a specific outcome and figure — school attendance — rather than a content-free swipe at the previous Government, so this is accountability rather than tribalism. Marked down slightly because the framing is 'a former Government' rather than a named policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can Mark Mitchell have been confused yesterday, when he said on Monday: “Realistically, 500 new staff over the next three years is what we’re aiming for.”; he said on Tuesday, “The Government’s policy is to deliver 500 additional officers over the term of this Government, which is three years.”; and claimed previously that there had been a meeting in December of the three governing parties where they agreed to change the target from two years to three years?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy commitment — 500 additional police and the delivery timeframe — using dated quotations. Holding a Minister to a specific target is scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Will the Minister bring an open mind to her review of the firearms registry, or has she an utterly predetermined approach to the usefulness of it?
civility.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of the review, but the alternative offered is an imputation about the Minister personally — that she has an 'utterly predetermined' mind — which lands on the person rather than the review's design. Pointed, and edging into imputing bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: With respect to the member’s proposals for other regulated products, are there any of those that would not increase the availability of tobacco and the profits of tobacco companies among her proposals?
civility.explanation: The question is framed to presuppose that every one of the Minister's proposals serves tobacco company profits, which imputes motive rather than testing the policy. Short of a direct insult, but not neutral scrutiny.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Electoral Act requires—as we all know—parties to submit a full record, open and in front of the public and under the law, of where they got their party funding.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that electoral law obliges parties to publicly disclose a full record of the sources of their party funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Act 1993, Part 6A (party donation and expense returns) and the Electoral Commission's published return requirements; true if parties must file a public return covering all party funding sources, false if disclosure is limited (e.g. only donations above a monetary threshold must be itemised, with smaller donations aggregated and anonymous).

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister not find it extraordinary that the Opposition that’s raising in the House today this issue nevertheless supported the very same party writing sound policy in 2018-19 which led to the biggest drop in the whole world of cigarette smoking?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2018-19 policy led to the largest fall in cigarette smoking of any country in the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WHO global report on trends in tobacco use / OECD comparative adult smoking prevalence for 2018-2020; true if New Zealand's fall in smoking prevalence over that period was the largest of any country reported, false if any other country recorded a larger fall.

veracity.statement: I think we’re incredibly proud of the lowering of smoking rates. It’s gone from 16.7 percent down to 8.6 percent and to 6.8 percent in the space of the last decade.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the smoking rate fell from 16.7% to 8.6% and then to 6.8% over the decade to the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence series, 2013/14 through 2022/23; true if the series contains readings of approximately 16.7%, 8.6% and 6.8% in that order within the decade, false if the figures or the decade-long span are materially different.

veracity.statement: Is he aware that under article 1 of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, New Zealand has an obligation to take action to prevent genocide before it occurs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Article 1 of the Genocide Convention imposes a duty on New Zealand to act to prevent genocide in advance of its commission.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of Article 1 of the 1948 Genocide Convention plus the ICJ's interpretation in Bosnia and Herzegovina v Serbia and Montenegro (2007); true if the duty to prevent is held to arise once a state learns of a serious risk of genocide, false if the obligation is held to attach only after genocide is established.

veracity.statement: The court did not make any findings that Israel has actually engaged in genocidal conduct.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ICJ order on provisional measures in South Africa v Israel, 26 January 2024; true if the order expressly declines to determine the merits and makes no finding of genocidal conduct, false if it contains such a finding.

veracity.statement: NZIER says that while a net 10 percent of firms are expecting a worsening in general economic conditions over the coming months, this is a significant decrease from a net 49 percent in the previous quarter and a net 79 percent a year ago.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZIER Quarterly Survey of Business Opinion for the December 2023 quarter; true if the net percentage expecting deterioration is about 10%, against about 49% in the September 2023 quarter and about 79% a year earlier, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: How can she say beneficiaries will be better off, when Treasury is forecasting annual wage growth to be 5.1 percent in June 2025 compared with the forecasted 2.5 percent rate of inflation in June 2025, where wage growth clearly outstrips inflation?

veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update, December 2023, forecast tables for average hourly ordinary-time earnings growth and CPI inflation in the year to June 2025; true if the figures are approximately 5.1% and 2.5% respectively, false if materially different.

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister not find it extraordinary that the Opposition that’s raising in the House today this issue nevertheless supported the very same party writing sound policy in 2018-19 which led to the biggest drop in the whole world of cigarette smoking?

specificity.statement: I think we’re incredibly proud of the lowering of smoking rates. It’s gone from 16.7 percent down to 8.6 percent and to 6.8 percent in the space of the last decade.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I think is fantastic is we have an Associate Minister with delegation for reducing smoking. She’s incredibly focused on that goal, and she’s asked her officials for a range of advice to actually lower smoking in New Zealand. That’s a good thing.

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his joint statement with the Prime Ministers of Australia and Canada in relation to Gaza made on 13 December 2023 that he supports “urgent international efforts towards a sustainable ceasefire.”, and, if so, what specific actions has his Government taken since that date to secure a sustainable ceasefire?
specificity.explanation: Names the document, the co-signatories, the exact date and quotes the commitment; a precise question is as specific as a precise answer.

specificity.statement: We have joined with many companies calling for a sustainable ceasefire and we’ll continue to do so.
specificity.explanation: Asked what specific actions had been taken, the reply names no action, no partner, no date — only that the Government has joined calls. (The 'companies' for 'countries' slip is spoken-language noise, not scored.)

specificity.statement: NZIER says that while a net 10 percent of firms are expecting a worsening in general economic conditions over the coming months, this is a significant decrease from a net 49 percent in the previous quarter and a net 79 percent a year ago.

specificity.statement: Beneficiaries will be better off under our Government because we will be dealing with the cost of living crisis. We will be growing the economy to support more job opportunities as well as improving health and education.

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister believe that the casual, lazy misuse of the word “genocide” is not only incorrect but highly offensive to those many people who, tragically, throughout history were victims of actual genocide?

civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she think snatching money away from the most vulnerable New Zealanders to pay for tax cuts is morally acceptable?

civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Beneficiaries will be better off under our Government because we will be dealing with the cost of living crisis. We will be growing the economy to support more job opportunities as well as improving health and education.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on bare assertion: no mechanism links growing the economy or improving health and education to beneficiary incomes, and the intervening premises are simply restatements of intent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can she say beneficiaries will be better off, when Treasury is forecasting annual wage growth to be 5.1 percent in June 2025 compared with the forecasted 2.5 percent rate of inflation in June 2025, where wage growth clearly outstrips inflation?
rigor.explanation: Valid inference given its premises: if wages are forecast to grow faster than prices, then indexing benefits to inflation rather than wages leaves beneficiaries relatively worse off.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Forecasts are exactly that. We’ll make decisions based on good data, and we made a commitment ahead of the election that we will index increases to benefits to inflation. That protects the real purchasing power of those on welfare.
rigor.explanation: The final inference is sound as far as it goes — CPI indexation does preserve real purchasing power — but it does not reach the contested conclusion that beneficiaries are better off, which was a comparison against wage indexation; the gap between what is shown and what is concluded is left unbridged, and 'forecasts are exactly that' dismisses the evidence without offering a reason.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That member is incorrect. What this Government is doing is providing certainty for all of those on welfare that benefit increases to inflation—which is the same way it’s been done for 31 out of the last 35 years—will protect their purchasing power, which is absolutely critical in a cost of living crisis that that member contributed to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that indexing benefit increases to inflation (CPI) is how benefits were adjusted in 31 of the last 35 years — a checkable claim about indexation policy history, given Labour moved benefits to wage indexation from April 2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD/Treasury records of the benefit indexation method used each year from 1989 to 2024; true if CPI indexation applied in 31 of the 35 years to 2024, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: There are now nearly 190,000 New Zealanders on the jobseeker benefit, meaning almost 90,000 more compared to September 2017.
veracity.explanation: Two linked factual claims: the current jobseeker support caseload (~190,000) and the size of the increase since September 2017 (~90,000).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets, Jobseeker Support recipient counts for the December 2023 quarter and the September 2017 quarter; true if the December 2023 figure is close to 190,000 and exceeds the September 2017 figure by close to 90,000, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: Young people under the age of 25 on welfare are estimated, on average, to spend 21.3 years on benefit.
veracity.explanation: A specific actuarial estimate of expected lifetime benefit duration for under-25 entrants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MSD/Treasury benefit system actuarial valuation (Taylor Fry) for the most recent year before January 2024; true if the average expected future years on benefit for clients under 25 is 21.3, false if materially different or if no such figure exists in the valuation.

veracity.statement: Why did she say in the House yesterday that her comments to media were “truthful at the time” because “Being offered something and asking for something are two separate matters.” when the document she signed on 20 December shows that she both initiated the advice and accepted the offer to provide that advice by circling an option for further advice on freezing tobacco excise tax?
veracity.explanation: The premise asserted is that a document signed by the Minister on 20 December shows her both initiating and accepting an offer of advice on freezing tobacco excise, by circling an option.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 20 December 2023 health briefing to the Associate Minister of Health as released (OIA/proactive release); true if the document bears her mark against an option requesting further advice on freezing tobacco excise, false if no such marked option appears.

veracity.statement: I haven’t yet received any of that advice, and I certainly did not specifically request a proposal on excise freeze.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts about her own dealings with officials: that no advice had yet been received, and that she made no specific request for a proposal on an excise freeze.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The released briefings and correspondence between the Associate Minister's office and Ministry of Health officials from December 2023 to January 2024; true if no request specific to an excise freeze appears and no advice had been delivered by 31 January 2024, false if a specific excise-freeze request or delivered advice is documented.

veracity.statement: Does she agree that dropping cancer screening for Māori by 10 years is an equitable approach to address the inequity that exists for Māori with cancer; if not, what is her Government proposing to address this inequity that Māori have faced for decades?
veracity.explanation: The premise is that the Government dropped a cancer screening eligibility provision that gave Māori access 10 years earlier than the general population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora bowel screening eligibility policy and the coalition Government's announcements to January 2024; true if a Māori and Pacific eligibility age set 10 years below the general age was removed or reversed, false if no such 10-year differential was in place or removed.

veracity.statement: Police arrested 15 people, of which 14 were associates or patched gang members.
veracity.explanation: A precise operational claim about arrest numbers and gang affiliation arising from the Whakatāne gang convoy response.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police media statements and operational reporting on the 2023 Whakatāne gang convoy; true if 15 arrests were made of whom 14 were patched members or associates, false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that “Mark could have expressed himself better”, and, if so, is the reason he’s struggling to express himself because a 6.5 percent cut to the police front line is unexplainable?
veracity.explanation: The embedded premise is that a 6.5 percent cut is being applied to the police front line.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 baseline savings instructions to NZ Police and the Government's stated exemptions; true if a 6.5 percent reduction was required and applied to frontline police, false if the 6.5 percent target excluded frontline staff or did not apply to Police at that rate.

civility.statement: That member is incorrect. What this Government is doing is providing certainty for all of those on welfare that benefit increases to inflation—which is the same way it’s been done for 31 out of the last 35 years—will protect their purchasing power, which is absolutely critical in a cost of living crisis that that member contributed to.

civility.statement: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that “Mark could have expressed himself better”, and, if so, is the reason he’s struggling to express himself because a 6.5 percent cut to the police front line is unexplainable?
civility.explanation: Wraps a policy point in mockery of the Minister personally — that he is 'struggling to express himself' — using the Prime Minister's criticism of him as the setup. Short of a direct insult, but it needles the person rather than the position.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are now nearly 190,000 New Zealanders on the jobseeker benefit, meaning almost 90,000 more compared to September 2017.

specificity.statement: The coalition Government believes a job is the best way out of dependence, best path to independence, and greater opportunities.

specificity.statement: I’m absolutely committed, which is the reason we do not want a broad-brush approach; we want targeted campaigns that will enable the most marginalised and most vulnerable to quit smoking.

specificity.statement: As part of the Government’s hundred-day plan, work is under way on banning gang patches and insignia in public, as well as dispersal notices and consorting prohibition notices.

rigor.statement: The fact that jobseeker benefit numbers consistently increased during prolonged periods of widespread labour shortages means the welfare system has not done enough to shift people into work.

divination.statement: Concerningly, forecasts predict that by January 2025, there will be 198,500 people on the jobseeker benefit.

focus.statement: I’m proud to be the Minister of Police in a Government that takes public safety seriously and that the public can already see is making a difference—that is, after six years of gang members operating with a sense of impunity.

veracity.statement: He beat Michael Wood, who said that Auckland light rail would be built by 2021.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Michael Wood publicly stated Auckland light rail would be built by 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard, ministerial press releases and contemporaneous media for Michael Wood's statements on Auckland light rail; true if Wood stated the line would be built/completed by 2021, false if no such statement by Wood exists and the 2021 date traces to another Labour minister (Phil Twyford's 2017 Mt Roskill pledge).

veracity.statement: Well, after $228 million of wasted money, the last Government couldn’t even deliver a single metre for their ghost train.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $228 million was spent on Auckland light rail with no metre of line constructed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Light Rail Ltd / Ministry of Transport reported programme expenditure to December 2023, and the project's construction status; true if cumulative spend was approximately $228m and no track was laid, false if the spend figure is materially different or physical construction of the line had begun.

veracity.statement: Here in Wellington, over $82 million spent on “Let’s Get Wellington Consulting”—sorry, Moving.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $82 million was spent on the Let's Get Wellington Moving programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Let's Get Wellington Moving programme expenditure reported by Waka Kotahi / Wellington City Council to end 2023; true if reported spend exceeds $82m, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: They wanted to waste $16 billion on Lake Onslow—$16 billion on Lake Onslow instead of trying to strengthen renewable energy across New Zealand and making sure we have secure energy supply.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Lake Onslow pumped-hydro scheme carried a $16 billion cost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Battery Project Lake Onslow business case cost estimate published by MBIE; true if the headline estimate is approximately $16bn, false if the published estimate is materially lower or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: We’ve put an end to this wasteful project, which could have cost taxpayers up to $29.2 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an official upper cost estimate of $29.2 billion for Auckland light rail.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland Light Rail indicative business case and Treasury/Ministry of Transport cost ranges; true if an official estimate of up to $29.2bn (whole-of-life or capital) exists, false if no published estimate reaches that figure.

veracity.statement: They wanted to slow every single State highway down to 80 kilometres per hour and they wanted every suburban street to be 30 kilometres per hour.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the previous government's speed management policy would have set 80 km/h on every state highway and 30 km/h on every suburban street.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waka Kotahi's draft Speed Management Plan and the Road to Zero speed rule; true if those documents propose 80 km/h across all state highways and 30 km/h across all suburban streets, false if the reductions applied only to identified subsets of roads.

civility.statement: He beat Michael Wood, who said that Auckland light rail would be built by 2021.
civility.explanation: Names an individual opponent and attacks his record on a delivery commitment, not his character or competence as a person.

specificity.statement: Well, after $228 million of wasted money, the last Government couldn’t even deliver a single metre for their ghost train.

specificity.statement: We’ve committed to removing the unfair Auckland regional fuel tax—legislation will be coming to the House shortly.

specificity.statement: We’ve scrapped Lake Onslow, that boondoggle of a project—$16 billion it would have cost—and we’re focusing our efforts on strengthening New Zealand’s energy security by doubling renewable energy by 2050, with a national policy statement on renewable electricity generation soon to come, and many other actions which are going to be needed to ensure that we have a strong and secure supply of energy for New Zealand.

divination.statement: The last National Government started the City Rail Link; it’s going to be completed by this National Government in this term.

divination.falsification_criterion: City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport completion and opening announcements; true if the project is declared complete (handed over or opened for passenger service) before the dissolution of the 54th Parliament, false if completion slips past that date.

rigor.statement: Their vision would have been, if they could have got away with it, to have people walking in front of our cars with a little red flag.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The last Government, they thought that co-governance was the answer to our water problems; we actually think it’s about ensuring local councils have the tools to be able to make long-term infrastructure investments and be able to have sustainable funding and financing for that investment.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy resting on a strawman: reduces the Three Waters reform to co-governance and treats council funding and financing tools as mutually exclusive with it, when the reform's stated purpose was balance-sheet separation for exactly that investment.

focus.statement: To the last Government, the word “roads” was a dirty word.

focus.statement: The last Government talked about public transport; we’re actually the Government which delivers.

veracity.statement: Yes, I am concerned, including with the fact that more than 20 beaches in Auckland in December were unswimmable because of human sewage, which reinforces that polluted rivers, lakes, and beaches are an issue to be addressed by all New Zealanders, both rural and urban.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council Safeswim monitoring records for December 2023: true if more than 20 Auckland beaches carried a no-swim or health warning attributable to human wastewater during that month; false if the count was materially lower or the contamination was not attributed to sewage.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why, then, did the Government delay freshwater improvements already in progress by pushing out the deadline for regional council plans to 2027?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the instrument (regional council plans) and the date (2027); a precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can assure the member that we will be consulting widely. We will be consulting with academics, with scientists, with iwi, and with commercial and recreational users. So we will consult widely and take a balanced approach to ensure that we come up with workable solutions.
specificity.explanation: Names the categories to be consulted but supplies no timeframe, process, or content for the changes; 'balanced approach' and 'workable solutions' are placeholders.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For instance, duties on mānuka honey production will reduce by 17.3 percent to 0; the kiwifruit growers benefit from tariff savings of $37 million on entry into force.
specificity.explanation: Named products, an exact duty rate and an exact saving; directly checkable against the tariff schedule.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, when fully implemented, the FTA is set to provide an annual boost to our GDP of up to $1.4 billion and to our exports to the EU by up to $1.8 billion each year.
specificity.explanation: Two quantified economic effects tied to a stated condition (full implementation).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have been voted into Government to get things done for this country, to get things back on track, to address the cost of living crisis, to ensure that we restore law and order, and to deliver the infrastructure that this country needs.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goals - 'back on track', 'restore law and order', 'deliver the infrastructure' - with no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named policies.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Well, when fully implemented, the FTA is set to provide an annual boost to our GDP of up to $1.4 billion and to our exports to the EU by up to $1.8 billion each year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the economic effect of the FTA once fully implemented: an annual GDP uplift of up to $1.4 billion and up to $1.8 billion more exports to the EU each year.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ and MFAT trade statistics once the FTA's tariff phase-ins are complete: true if annual New Zealand goods and services exports to the EU are up to about $1.8 billion above the pre-FTA baseline with a GDP uplift of the order claimed; false if the realised uplift is materially below that.

civility.statement: I’d like to thank the Minister for sharing his CV with us today and also reminding us who the Prime Minister currently is, because if anyone had been sitting in this House this week, they may have been under the mistaken impression that it was David Seymour.
civility.explanation: Mock thanks used to sneer at Simeon Brown for reciting his own CV, and to needle the Prime Minister as a figurehead. Short of a direct insult, but it is derision aimed at people rather than engagement with any substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How embarrassing is it for her that she has denied seeking advice on tax cuts for tobacco companies, and then today we hear different accounts from the Minister?
civility.explanation: Frames a substantive inconsistency as a personal humiliation ("how embarrassing is it for her") and implies dishonesty. The underlying point could have been made about the advice and the accounts; instead it lands on the Minister personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He either broke a promise or he is clearly not on top of the numbers in his portfolio.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on Mark Mitchell's competence and honesty — either he lied or he does not know his own portfolio's figures. The target is the man, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is disingenuous for this finance Minister, this new one, to claim that it is their work that’s doing it.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named Minister — not that the claim is wrong, but that she knows it is wrong and makes it anyway. That is the 0.5 band: short of an insult, no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: At the end of the day, as Grant Robertson said, it is his responsibility, it’s his Government, it’s his circus, and they are his clowns.
civility.explanation: Calls the Government's ministers clowns. Sustained derision of people's competence and worth, delivered as the closing line; quoting a colleague does not make it any less the speaker's own remark.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d like to thank the Minister for sharing his CV with us today and also reminding us who the Prime Minister currently is, because if anyone had been sitting in this House this week, they may have been under the mistaken impression that it was David Seymour.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's internal pecking order — who is really running the Government. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In my experience at the British Council, voluntary redundancy often results in some of the most experienced people leaving the organisation and lots and lots of money in redundancy payments. So I’m not sure that’s the answer.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named measure — MBIE's voluntary redundancy programme — and on its mechanism and cost. The reasoning is thin, but that is Rigor's deduction, not this one's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When it comes to infrastructure projects like the $1.6 billion Dunedin Hospital, the media has been asking Shane Reti about whether he is planning to fund that publicly. He will not give an assurance.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: a named project, a named cost and a specific unanswered question about how it will be funded. This is the opposition's job and carries full policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have seen political narratives this year hijacked by ACT, hijacked by the Treaty principles bill—why don’t we just call them the “Hijacked Party”, because they are 8 percent of the vote and they are hijacking 80 percent of the Government’s airtime.
focus.explanation: A measure is named in passing, but nothing is said about it. The weight of the statement is a nickname for another party and a claim about how much attention it commands — party framing rather than policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: At the end of the day, as Grant Robertson said, it is his responsibility, it’s his Government, it’s his circus, and they are his clowns.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other team's character. No policy, figure, commitment or outcome is named anywhere in it.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Matt Doocey was actually right, yesterday, when he said that voters voted for change, but they did not vote for this change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Matt Doocey said in the House the previous day that voters voted for change but not for this change. The checkable content is the attribution.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard transcript for 30 January 2024; true if Doocey made a statement to that effect in the House that day, false if no such remark appears in the record.

veracity.statement: There was no detail pre-election on how these tax cuts would be costed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no costing detail for the tax cuts was published before the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's pre-election tax and fiscal plan documents released in 2023; false if a costed funding plan for the tax package (revenue sources and totals) was published before election day, true if no such costings were released.

veracity.statement: Then we heard an announcement in recent days that inflation has dropped from 7.2 percent to 4.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific annual CPI inflation figures, a fall from 7.2 percent to a newly announced 4.7 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual inflation series; true if the release referred to (December 2023 quarter) printed 4.7% and the earlier reference point was 7.2%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: She sold it as annual reductions in back-office expenditure of 6.5 percent, and there were only going to be 24 agencies, 24 specific agencies listed on a Treasury website.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the original terms of the savings policy: 6.5 percent annual back-office reductions applying to a published list of exactly 24 agencies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 fiscal plan and the Treasury baseline-savings material; true if the announced rate was 6.5% and the published list contained 24 agencies, false if either the percentage or the agency count differs.

veracity.statement: When it comes to infrastructure projects like the $1.6 billion Dunedin Hospital, the media has been asking Shane Reti about whether he is planning to fund that publicly. He will not give an assurance.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: the Dunedin Hospital project's cost is $1.6 billion, and the Minister of Health has declined, when asked by media, to guarantee it will be publicly funded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown's published Dunedin Hospital budget figure, and Shane Reti's media statements up to 31 January 2024; false if the project's stated cost is materially different or if he gave a public-funding assurance, true if the figure matches and he declined to give one.

veracity.statement: Currently, my constituents pay about $4,500 to go up to Christchurch, plus accommodation, plus transport, to be able to access the same services that people in Christchurch get for free.
