rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Don’t raise the ire of David Seymour now that he’s in Government or he will disestablish you.
civility.explanation: Turns on the named Minister rather than the bill, imputing personal vindictiveness — abolishing a public body as retaliation for annoying him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So he’s got no care for those people whatsoever.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's character rather than on the bill's provisions — imputes total indifference to staff losing their jobs.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I was recently at the Gisborne Police Station and there was a young constable there that had been put in charge of mentoring and identifying young people in the community that may be interested in a career in Police. He has been very successful. In the latest recruit wing, I think there were four that had been recruited through that process and were proudly graduating. So I think we’re just going to have to look at many different options in terms of how we meet our target of 500 over two years.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: one constable's mentoring produced four recruits in one wing, therefore many different options should be looked at for the 500 target. The conclusion is modest, but the evidence is a single anecdote generalised to a national recruitment programme.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, I can confirm that the Minister acknowledges that an electric vehicle or plug-in hybrid, as shown here, would pay more than twice as much in road tax under his proposal on a trip from Wellington to Auckland?
rigor.explanation: The premise offered is the Minister's acknowledgement that "there are variances throughout the system". The conclusion drawn is far stronger — an acknowledgement of a specific magnitude, more than twice as much. A real gap between what was conceded and what is inferred from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s a range of variables around how much based on the fuel usage. The problem with the current system is that it charges people based on how many litres of fuel they put into their car rather than how much they use the road. We want to move to a system which charges based on how many kilometres and the weight of that vehicle, rather than what type of fuel motors that vehicle. That is the reform that we are progressing.
rigor.explanation: A coherent inference: if the charge is meant to fund road maintenance, then a base of litres consumed is a poorer proxy than distance and weight, so the proposed change follows from the stated purpose. It does not engage the magnitude point put to him, but that is a separate question from whether this argument holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No. The issue that the member continues to raise is she’s just simply looking at how much tax is paid based on the number of litres or the type of fuel used. We want to move it to being a distance and weight change, and that member’s graph that she continues to raise doesn’t take into account the full running costs of those vehicles. As everyone knows, electric vehicles are far cheaper to use and drive, as many members of this House know, but that graph that she uses misinforms the House.
rigor.explanation: A real argument about the policy, and a weak one. The key premise is carried by an appeal to common knowledge ("As everyone knows", "as many members of this House know") rather than evidence, and the conclusion does not follow: lower total running costs do not establish that a vehicle should pay more per kilometre towards road maintenance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is the Minister aware that the running charges for efficient petrol vehicles would also be lower, therefore their contribution to tax is lower than less efficient vehicles, and, therefore, what is the logical connection between cars having lower running costs and contributing less to the roads on a per-kilometre basis?
rigor.explanation: Isolates the inference under test by applying it to a parallel case: efficient petrol vehicles also have lower running costs and also pay less fuel excise, so running cost cannot be the principle that justifies charging EVs more. The counter-example does the work the conclusion needs.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I’ve appointed Professor Elizabeth Rata because she is a well-recognised and renowned educational expert. Any views that she has expressed in terms of her political views are not relevant to her appointment, which is based on her educational expertise. It would be a strange thing for the Labour Party to reveal that they actually profile people for their political views before appointing them on the basis of their expertise to get the job done and get a better curriculum for New Zealand’s kids.
rigor.explanation: Strip out the party material and an argument remains — appointed for educational expertise, so political views are not relevant — but its only support for the expertise premise is an appeal to her being "well-recognised and renowned". The closing move is a strawman: the question asked whether a particular statement was knowledge-rich, which is recast as profiling people for their political views before appointing them.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I was recently at the Gisborne Police Station and there was a young constable there that had been put in charge of mentoring and identifying young people in the community that may be interested in a career in Police. He has been very successful. In the latest recruit wing, I think there were four that had been recruited through that process and were proudly graduating. So I think we’re just going to have to look at many different options in terms of how we meet our target of 500 over two years.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the recruitment mechanism and the named 500-over-two-years target; no party content. Whether it dodged the question asked is Forthrightness's concern, not this one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes. The Government has announced that electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids will contribute towards the maintenance of our roads, as other vehicles do. The changes proposed for electric vehicles will ensure that they pay the same amount as a road-user charge as those other light vehicles which pay a road-user charge. There are variances throughout the system, and that is why the coalition agreement with ACT commits this Government to progress a fleet-wide transition to road-user charges that will result in a much fairer charging system based on how much people travel the roads and the weight of their vehicle.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure: what changes for EVs, why, and what the charging basis becomes. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I really enjoyed the co-leadership bid from the member opposite, and if she would like to table a copy of that document, I’d be very happy to have a read.
focus.explanation: A policy question about road-user charges was before him and nothing in the reply touches it. The whole content is the member's leadership ambitions.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I’ve appointed Professor Elizabeth Rata because she is a well-recognised and renowned educational expert. Any views that she has expressed in terms of her political views are not relevant to her appointment, which is based on her educational expertise. It would be a strange thing for the Labour Party to reveal that they actually profile people for their political views before appointing them on the basis of their expertise to get the job done and get a better curriculum for New Zealand’s kids.
focus.explanation: The first two-thirds genuinely engage the appointment and the basis for it; the last third pivots to what Labour would be revealing about itself. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I announced yesterday that we are looking into the credit contracts Act because our intent is to improve the regulation, which the previous Government has made an absolute hash of—hash of. What we’re intending to do is to make sure that vulnerable borrowers are still protected, but, just as importantly, making sure that credit is available to those who need it but have been excluded under the current regulations.
focus.explanation: Names the Act and identifies the substantive trade-off being addressed — protecting vulnerable borrowers against credit access for those excluded by the current rules. The swipe at the previous Government is framing around a real policy point, not a substitute for one.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the 500 new police all be constabulary or does it include authorised officers?
specificity.explanation: A precise question naming a figure and a checkable categorical distinction (constabulary vs authorised officers) — as specific as a precise answer would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes. The Government has announced that electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids will contribute towards the maintenance of our roads, as other vehicles do. The changes proposed for electric vehicles will ensure that they pay the same amount as a road-user charge as those other light vehicles which pay a road-user charge. There are variances throughout the system, and that is why the coalition agreement with ACT commits this Government to progress a fleet-wide transition to road-user charges that will result in a much fairer charging system based on how much people travel the roads and the weight of their vehicle.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (road-user charges based on distance travelled and vehicle weight) and its source (the coalition agreement with ACT), but supplies no rates, no costs and no timeframe for the fleet-wide transition.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How is it fair that the average electric vehicle or plug-in hybrid owner would pay more than double the tax of a similarly sized petrol vehicle for a return trip from Wellington to Auckland?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable comparison: a stated multiple (more than double), a matched comparator (similarly sized petrol vehicle) and a defined trip. Someone could go and calculate it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No. This Government has confirmed that the exemption, which would run out on 1 April this year—which was, actually, by the way, put in place by the last National Government to help incentivise electric vehicle uptake—will end now that 2 percent of the fleet is electric. What we’re saying is all users of our road should pay and contribute towards maintaining it.
specificity.explanation: A dated expiry (1 April), a named originating Government, and a quantified trigger condition (2 percent of the fleet). All of it checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, this Government is a coalition of three parties and the coalition agreement set out that restoring balance is exactly what the Government is committed to doing with the Aotearoa histories curriculum. The way that that will be done is set to come before Cabinet in the future, and once those policy decisions have been made, I’m sure the member will be the first to know.
specificity.explanation: Asked what "restore balance" means, the answer restates the phrase and points to an undated future Cabinet process. No content of the change, no mechanism, no timeframe beyond "in the future".
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yesterday, I announced at the Financial Services Council meeting my intention to simplify regulations, cut red tape, and reduce costs to financial institutions. There were three elements: first of all, the proposal to move from three to two regulators; secondly, to reduce from a maximum of six licences to a single licence; and thirdly, to reform the Conduct of Financial Institutions requirements to make it easier for smaller financial institutions to meet their obligations. We are committed to reducing compliance and regulation, where appropriate, and getting the economy back on track.
specificity.explanation: Three enumerated changes with concrete before-and-after figures — three regulators to two, six licences to one — and a named regime. Checkable and actionable, despite the slogan at the end.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What initiatives has he announced in respect of the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act, and how does that differ one little bit from the announcement of the last Minister on 8 August 2023?
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and pins the comparison to a dated prior announcement (8 August 2023), so the claim of no difference can be checked against the record.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: No. Unlike the previous Government, who deceived New Zealand by saying they had recruited 1,800 front-line police officers when in fact they hadn’t—it was 1,500—we will be recruiting, training, and deploying 500 sworn police officers. In relation to standards, no we will not be dropping standards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government publicly claimed 1,800 front-line police officers recruited when the actual figure was 1,500.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police constabulary workforce statistics for the increase in sworn officers over the 2017–2023 Government, set against that Government's own published statements on the number recruited. True if the stated figure was 1,800 while the delivered number was about 1,500; false if the delivered number matches the 1,800 claimed.

veracity.statement: No. This Government has confirmed that the exemption, which would run out on 1 April this year—which was, actually, by the way, put in place by the last National Government to help incentivise electric vehicle uptake—will end now that 2 percent of the fleet is electric. What we’re saying is all users of our road should pay and contribute towards maintaining it.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the light-EV road-user-charge exemption was introduced by the previous National Government to incentivise EV uptake, and that electric vehicles are now 2 percent of the fleet.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacting instrument for the light electric RUC exemption and the year and Government under which it was passed; plus Ministry of Transport / NZTA light-fleet registration statistics for early 2024 giving the electric share. True if the exemption was legislated under a National-led Government and the electric share is about 2 percent; false if either the originating Government or the share is materially different.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned about the combined disincentive effect of charging electric vehicles more tax, given the Ministry of Transport’s advice that scrapping the Clean Car Discount means transport may fail to meet its third emissions budget?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ministry of Transport advised that removing the Clean Car Discount puts the transport sector's third emissions budget at risk.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport advice to the Minister (regulatory impact statements or briefings released under the OIA) on the emissions effect of ending the Clean Car Discount. True if that advice states the third emissions budget may not be met; false if no such advice exists or it reaches the opposite conclusion.

civility.statement: No. Unlike the previous Government, who deceived New Zealand by saying they had recruited 1,800 front-line police officers when in fact they hadn’t—it was 1,500—we will be recruiting, training, and deploying 500 sworn police officers. In relation to standards, no we will not be dropping standards.
civility.explanation: "Deceived New Zealand" imputes deliberate bad faith, which costs something — but it lands on the previous Government as an institution rather than on any individual member, and it is attached to a specific numerical claim rather than to a person's character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No. The issue that the member continues to raise is she’s just simply looking at how much tax is paid based on the number of litres or the type of fuel used. We want to move it to being a distance and weight change, and that member’s graph that she continues to raise doesn’t take into account the full running costs of those vehicles. As everyone knows, electric vehicles are far cheaper to use and drive, as many members of this House know, but that graph that she uses misinforms the House.
civility.explanation: "That graph that she uses misinforms the House" moves from disputing the graph to charging the member with misleading the House — an imputation of bad faith rather than error, which is what prompted the point of order. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I really enjoyed the co-leadership bid from the member opposite, and if she would like to table a copy of that document, I’d be very happy to have a read.
civility.explanation: Mockery: the question is dismissed by inviting the member to table her leadership pitch. It is aimed at the individual rather than at anything she argued, though it stops short of attacking her character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I’ve appointed Professor Elizabeth Rata because she is a well-recognised and renowned educational expert. Any views that she has expressed in terms of her political views are not relevant to her appointment, which is based on her educational expertise. It would be a strange thing for the Labour Party to reveal that they actually profile people for their political views before appointing them on the basis of their expertise to get the job done and get a better curriculum for New Zealand’s kids.
civility.explanation: Robust, and the jab is at the Labour Party rather than at any individual. Neither the questioner nor the appointee is disparaged personally — the appointee is defended.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I announced yesterday that we are looking into the credit contracts Act because our intent is to improve the regulation, which the previous Government has made an absolute hash of—hash of. What we’re intending to do is to make sure that vulnerable borrowers are still protected, but, just as importantly, making sure that credit is available to those who need it but have been excluded under the current regulations.
civility.explanation: "An absolute hash of" is brutal about the previous Government's regulation and touches no individual. Under the re-anchored scale, hard criticism of a policy or a record sits at the top.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He’s very concerned about the quality of regulation in this country, and so concerned is he about the quality of regulation that this bill has had no submissions and no select committee hearing, it was put through under urgency, and it has no regulatory impact statement attached to it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four checkable facts about the passage of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill: no public submissions, no select committee hearing, passed under urgency, and no regulatory impact statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill (2023/24) plus the Hansard urgency motions and the Ministry for Regulation/Treasury RIS register; true if the bill was never referred to select committee, took no submissions, was accorded urgency, and has no published regulatory impact statement; false if any select committee referral, submission process or RIS exists.

veracity.statement: In their very good report in 2018, which was commissioned by the Hon Steven Joyce, a National Minister at the time, the Productivity Commission produced the Road to Net Zero report, a very substantive, long piece of work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 2018 Productivity Commission report titled 'Road to Net Zero' existed and that its inquiry was commissioned by Steven Joyce as a National Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Productivity Commission's published inquiry list and the terms of reference for its low-emissions inquiry; true if a 2018 report of that title exists and the terms of reference were issued by Steven Joyce as a Minister in the National-led government, false if the report's title or the commissioning Minister/government differs.

veracity.statement: It was referred to as the Clean Car Discount, which was implemented in the last term, and it led to a more than 1,200 percent increase in the uptake of electric vehicles.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Clean Car Discount was followed by an increase of more than 1,200 percent in electric vehicle uptake.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA motor vehicle registration statistics for battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, comparing the period before the Clean Car Discount took effect (1 July 2021) with the period after; true if any standard uptake measure rose by more than 1,200 percent, false if the largest defensible increase on registrations or fleet share is materially below that.

focus.statement: He’s very concerned about the quality of regulation in this country, and so concerned is he about the quality of regulation that this bill has had no submissions and no select committee hearing, it was put through under urgency, and it has no regulatory impact statement attached to it.
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure and specific procedural failings (submissions, select committee, urgency, regulatory impact statement) rather than attacking the other party in general; the irony framing about the sponsoring Minister is the only thing pulling it below 1.0.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think, while we can disagree, the Hon James Shaw and myself, it’s amazing how our perspectives change when we only move a few metres across the House. All of a sudden, the member is understanding the frustrations with the urgency process and the use of it which we spent a lot of time railing against only a few months ago.
focus.explanation: The weight of the remark is that the other side has changed its tune on urgency now that it is in opposition. It touches a real procedural matter but names no provision, figure or outcome of the bill before the House — it is about the other team's consistency.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So many of the contributions, especially in the committee of the whole House stage, were questions about words in the interpretation clause, which are pretty easily dealt with, and which, in fact, most of the people asking do, or ought to, know the answer to already.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to other members — that they asked questions to which they already knew the answers — and is condescending about their grasp of the interpretation clause. Short of a direct insult, but it targets the questioners rather than the questions.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think, while we can disagree, the Hon James Shaw and myself, it’s amazing how our perspectives change when we only move a few metres across the House. All of a sudden, the member is understanding the frustrations with the urgency process and the use of it which we spent a lot of time railing against only a few months ago.
civility.explanation: Imputes opportunism to a named member, but does so about his position rather than his character, and in a good-humoured register. Pointed, edging toward the person without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if you take that to its logical extreme, you would also disestablish the Treasury, and then so the bottom of The Terrace would sulk because every Government in history has continuously ignored the advice of the Treasury, and yet you don’t shut the Treasury down because you ignore its advice.
rigor.explanation: A genuine reductio ad absurdum aimed at a stated argument for the repeal (that governments ignore the commission's advice): if 'advice is ignored' justified abolition, it would justify abolishing Treasury, which nobody accepts. The inference is sound; the analogy is slightly loose in that Treasury has executive functions beyond advice, which is the only gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s very easy to make that problem go away: you set up an independent appointments panel. It’s at arm’s length from the Minister, and appointments are done on the basis of merit, the people who are appointed to the appointments panel are human resources experts and recruitment experts and not Ministers, and so on.
specificity.explanation: Proposes a named mechanism with some design detail (arm's-length panel, merit basis, HR and recruitment experts rather than Ministers), but supplies no legislative vehicle, cost or timeframe, and trails off with 'and so on'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It was referred to as the Clean Car Discount, which was implemented in the last term, and it led to a more than 1,200 percent increase in the uptake of electric vehicles.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, its implementation period and a precise numerical outcome — fully checkable, whether or not the figure survives checking.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But all I can say is the time has come for the Productivity Commission to be disestablished, and the regulations ministry will take over and do a much better job.
specificity.explanation: A conclusion with no content behind it: no measure of the commission's performance, no function the new ministry would take over, no timeframe and no test for 'a much better job'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s this coalition Government that can see, on this side of the House, saving some money to put this money into a better place.
specificity.explanation: Offers the fiscal rationale for the repeal with no amount saved, no destination for the money and no mechanism — 'some money' into 'a better place' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we know red tape is a problem, and we will be able to put this money to a better place and to a better spend.
specificity.explanation: Asserts a benefit from the repeal with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named destination for the money — "a better place and to a better spend" commits to nothing checkable, in a debate where the savings could have been quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What’s really interesting about the disestablishment of that Housing Commission, by virtue of its inconvenient advice, is that also in that final report from the Housing Commission, we had, and I quote here—or, rather, prior to quoting, just advice against the establishment of the accommodation supplement which we now see paid out to the tune of $2 billion a year.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific document, a specific policy instrument and a dollar figure — a listener could go and check the report and the appropriation. Marked down only because the year the $2 billion refers to is left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we’re going to focus on productivity, we’ve got to drive those sectors that produce, and that’s agriculture, that’s supporting our exporters, that’s supporting our businesses, and that’s supporting the places that are going to drive productivity in this country, and that is reducing red tape, reducing regulation, and reducing compliance.
specificity.explanation: A list of sectors and a list of things to reduce, with no figure, no mechanism and no timeframe — which regulations, by how much, by when, are all absent. This is the string-of-generic-virtues case.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to seriously get to work and improve the quality of regulation and reduce Government spending.
specificity.explanation: States a direction with no content attached — which regulations, improved how, spending reduced by how much or where. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The reason, though, that I think that that’s a really important issue to, kind of, call to mind as we are working through this today is that, as the Hon James Shaw highlighted in his contributions, we here are working under urgency with this legislation through a process in which there has been no public consultation nor submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that this bill is being passed under urgency without any select committee stage or public submissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill: true if the bill was progressed under urgency with no select committee referral and no call for public submissions; false if it was referred to a select committee or submissions were taken.

veracity.statement: That’s, of course, to point out, as others have, and as the Hon James Shaw has in his earlier speeches and readings on this bill, that the Productivity Commission was originally an innovation of the ACT Party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Productivity Commission was an ACT Party creation, not a National or Labour one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The origin of the New Zealand Productivity Commission: the 2008 National–ACT confidence and supply agreement and the Hansard/Cabinet record of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act 2010. True if the Commission originated as an ACT policy secured in that agreement; false if it originated with another party or outside any such agreement.

veracity.statement: What’s really interesting about the disestablishment of that Housing Commission, by virtue of its inconvenient advice, is that also in that final report from the Housing Commission, we had, and I quote here—or, rather, prior to quoting, just advice against the establishment of the accommodation supplement which we now see paid out to the tune of $2 billion a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the 1988 Housing Commission report advised against creating the accommodation supplement and that the supplement now costs about $2 billion a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Two checks: (a) the 1988 Housing Commission final report — true if it advised against establishing an accommodation supplement; (b) MSD/Treasury expenditure figures for the Accommodation Supplement in the most recent full year — true if annual spend is approximately $2 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I mean, yesterday, just for example, he said that the Productivity Commission has done some tremendous work—tremendous work—over the past decade or so and that the work will remain available as an asset or a taonga for New Zealanders, to be a guide for policy formation.
veracity.explanation: Reports what Seymour said in the House the day before, in order to charge him with inconsistency. The checkable element is whether he said it, not whether the praise was warranted.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for David Seymour's speech on this bill the preceding sitting day: true if he described the Productivity Commission's work as "tremendous" and said its work would remain available as an asset/taonga guiding policy; false if the transcript contains no such remarks or materially different ones.

focus.statement: Time and again, they have pulled out the shredder and said that they don’t like the direction that the country is headed in and decided to rip up that direction, that plan, that blueprint.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the Government's general habits rather than of the measure before the House — no policy, figure or named commitment is identified, so there is nothing here a reader could check the Government against. Some policy adjacency (it gestures at repeals) keeps it off the floor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s probably appropriate that Dr Don Brash is here to support this kaupapa, because, of course, this is yet another example of our far-right, race-baiting Government’s commitment to New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the Government's nature — "far-right", "race-baiting" — with no policy, mechanism or named commitment engaged. The bill is mentioned only as an occasion for the label. Civility is not moved: the attack lands on the Government collectively, not on an individual.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, if you’ve been reading, we’ve all heard about it: the Atlas Network, an international far-right thinktank whose extreme policy platform seeks to attack public servants, push for radical privatisation, dismantle regulation protecting workers and their environment, and champions landlords over renters.
focus.explanation: Wholly about who is alleged to be behind the other party. Nothing in it touches the Productivity Commission, the repeal, or any figure or outcome. Nothing is emitted for Rigor: strip out the material about ACT's supposed backers and no argument about the policy remains, so the guilt-by-resemblance is a focus failure, not a reasoning one.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I think it’s also really important to point out that in the respective agreements that have cobbled this Government together—the Government of the “Three Scrooges”—what we have is a commitment to data and evidence in the founding documents of this Government.
civility.explanation: The substance — that the coalition agreements commit to data and evidence — is engaged squarely, but the parenthetical epithet is mockery aimed at the three party leaders rather than at any policy. Short of a direct insult, so above the 0.5 line, but no longer clean.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There’s no doubt about that—under urgency, cancelling the Productivity Commission so that David Seymour can fund his new ministry of regulation razor gang vanity project.
civility.explanation: Imputes a personal motive — vanity — to a named member, and "razor gang" casts the ministry as an instrument of his ego rather than a policy to be argued with. Short of a direct insult to his character, but it attributes bad faith to the person rather than criticising the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we’re going to focus on productivity, we’ve got to drive those sectors that produce, and that’s agriculture, that’s supporting our exporters, that’s supporting our businesses, and that’s supporting the places that are going to drive productivity in this country, and that is reducing red tape, reducing regulation, and reducing compliance.
rigor.explanation: Circular: productivity is to be raised by backing "the places that are going to drive productivity", which restates the conclusion as its own premise. The closing jump to deregulation as the means is a non sequitur — nothing offered connects reduced compliance to output in the named sectors. Scored here rather than under Focus because it does engage the policy; it just reasons in a loop about it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If the cost being saved by ACT’s new vanity project was so easy to gain, then why can’t this new “ministry of blaming red tape” fund itself from all the cost savings they were supposedly meant to find?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if the savings are as readily available as claimed, the new body should be self-funding. The challenge is genuine, but it rests on an unstated premise that savings arrive at the same time and in the same appropriation as the set-up cost, which is not established. A reasonable point with a real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What has actually been really clear is that this Government does not care for public consultation or engagement in relation to important bills that come before the House.
focus.explanation: Directed at a real process question about this bill — the absence of a select committee stage and public submissions — rather than at the other party's character, but it is framed as a general charge about 'this Government' and names no specific provision or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government sees a better way to cut red tape and improve the productivity that this country so dearly needs.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the policy rationale for the measure before the House rather than about the opposition. It carries little detail, but Focus asks what the statement is about, not how precise it is.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Not spending more and doing less like we’ve seen over the last three years, but doing more with less, more efficiently.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the previous government's record in general. No policy, programme, figure or outcome is named, so nothing here is scrutiny of a specific commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is about David Seymour being able to control the research and narrative that comes out from his own new agency, as opposed to being able to, again, allow there to be a high-level debate, which is why this commission was set up in 2010.
civility.explanation: Imputes a self-serving motive — wanting to control research and narrative — to a named member. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes bad faith to the person rather than arguing about the agency's design.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is what is going on—an ideologically driven, one-person-knows-best solution from the Minister David Seymour.
civility.explanation: Moves from the measure to the named Minister's character — ideological, believing he alone knows best. A judgement about the person rather than about the repeal.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m quite new to the House and I learnt some good material there. “Razor gang vanity project”, “social-good vandalism”, and “overseas far-right thinktanks”. There’s some awesome material there that I can use.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mockery of a named member's speech, quoting his phrases back at him as entertainment. It targets his rhetoric rather than his character, so it stops short of a personal insult, but the register is sneering rather than civil.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: David Seymour was reported in a press conference on 5 September 2023 saying it had been “frankly hijacked” and that he wouldn’t have appointed the chair that it currently has.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Seymour, at a press conference on a named date, described the Productivity Commission as having been 'frankly hijacked' and said he would not have appointed its current chair.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous media reports or transcripts of David Seymour's press conference of 5 September 2023; true if he used the phrase 'frankly hijacked' of the Productivity Commission and said he would not have appointed the sitting chair, false if no such remarks are recorded on that occasion.

veracity.statement: It was Bill English who said it was about encouraging high-level debate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bill English described the purpose of the Productivity Commission, at its establishment, as encouraging high-level debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Bill English's recorded statements around the New Zealand Productivity Commission Bill 2010 — Hansard first/third reading speeches and ministerial press releases; true if he characterised the commission's purpose in those terms, false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: It is a bill that is the result of our coalition agreement with the ACT Party, and obviously, effectively, repeals the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act 2010.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things: that disestablishing the Productivity Commission was a commitment in the National–ACT coalition agreement, and that this bill repeals the 2010 Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the National–ACT coalition agreement (24 November 2023) and the text of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill; true if the agreement contains a commitment to disestablish the commission and the bill repeals the 2010 Act, false if either is absent.

veracity.statement: I remind the public: this Productivity Commission came up under ACT.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Productivity Commission originated as an ACT initiative.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2008 National–ACT confidence and supply agreement and the origin of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Bill 2010; true if the commission was an ACT policy commitment secured through that agreement, false if it originated elsewhere.

veracity.statement: In terms of construction costs, we are in the bottom 10 percent of the OECD—the Infrastructure Commission’s told us that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand ranks in the bottom decile of OECD countries on construction costs, and attributes that finding to the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published New Zealand Infrastructure Commission (Te Waihanga) research on international construction cost comparisons; true if it places New Zealand in roughly the worst 10 percent of OECD countries on construction costs, false if its ranking is materially different or if it makes no such comparison.

specificity.statement: David Seymour was reported in a press conference on 5 September 2023 saying it had been “frankly hijacked” and that he wouldn’t have appointed the chair that it currently has.
specificity.explanation: Names the person, the exact date, the setting and the words used — someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s an outcome that will improve people’s lives, it will improve people’s lifestyles, and it will improve people’s livelihoods.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic benefits with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or measurable outcome; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We probably needed to move to a model where the person appointed was not appointed by the Minister and we probably needed to move to a model where those reports came to Parliament and we looked at them and we had to respond to them so we all focused on the wisdom of what is the great knowledge out there in our community—the great goodwill out there in our community from people who have headed these organisations and worked for them.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete institutional mechanisms — removing ministerial appointment of the chair, and requiring reports to be tabled in and responded to by Parliament — but gives no timeframe, drafting or process for either, and trails off into generalities.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of construction costs, we are in the bottom 10 percent of the OECD—the Infrastructure Commission’s told us that.
specificity.explanation: A numeric ranking, a named comparison group and a named source, all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is it going to be able to look at the same issues? The answer is no. It’s comparing apples with pears. It’s simply not the same thing.
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference here — the preceding contrast between the commission's wellbeing and persistent-disadvantage research and a red-tape ministry's remit gives the conclusion some support — but the conclusion is delivered by answering her own rhetorical question and by analogy ('apples with pears') rather than by showing what the new ministry's terms of reference actually cover.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Lots of agencies, NGOs, and laypeople can tell us the problems. We don’t need the Productivity Commission anymore; it’s the end of a season.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: that other bodies can identify problems does not establish that the commission is redundant, since its stated function was independent research and analysis rather than problem-spotting — and he has just credited it with 'really fantastic work'. The conclusion also leans on a metaphor ('the end of a season') in place of an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s really good to have the support from the other side with regards to some of our initiatives and whakaaro, and glad that that member over there—Ryan Hamilton—is learning something.
civility.explanation: Warm about the cross-party support, but 'is learning something' is a patronising aside at a named member. Mild condescension rather than an insult, so short of the standard but well above a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In contrast to the previous speaker, Ginny Andersen, I want to focus on the importance of this bill.
civility.explanation: A pointed contrast drawn with a named member — the implication is that she was not focused on what matters — but it stops at the contrast and does not land on her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill, of course, will delay the repeal of the experience pathways to social work registration from February 2024 to February 2028.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (repeal of the experience pathway to registration) and both dates. Anyone can check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, the reality is that we have come through to 2024 and we are some 700 vacancies short and we just simply don’t have the people that we need.
specificity.explanation: Carries a checkable figure and a year, but no source and no definition of which workforce the 700 covers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s good that we’re doing more to encourage people to register and to be able to encourage that forward, but I am highly sceptical of how social investment is going to work, particularly for our social sectors, and how those communities that are the most vulnerable in New Zealand are served by social workers when a programme of 6.5 percent cuts to all social services will directly impact people like social workers in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names a percentage and a named policy direction (social investment), but does not say which agencies, which budgets, or over what period, and does not quantify the effect on social worker numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve got to do a better job of encouraging people into the sector, and part of that solution is, of course, training more into social work.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no mechanism, no target number and no timeframe: 'train more' restates the problem rather than saying how, how many, or by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This bill, of course, will delay the repeal of the experience pathways to social work registration from February 2024 to February 2028.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill before the House pushes the repeal of the experience pathway out by four years, to February 2028. Note that another speaker in the same debate describes the extension as two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill as introduced/read a second time: true if it moves the commencement of the experience-pathway repeal from February 2024 to February 2028; false if the extension is to a different date or of a different length.

veracity.statement: The Social Workers Registration Act initially brought in the rules around this, back in 2003.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the statutory registration regime for social workers dates from a 2003 Act of that name.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ statute book: true if the Social Workers Registration Act establishing the registration regime was enacted in 2003, false if the founding Act carries a different year.

veracity.statement: However, the reality is that we have come through to 2024 and we are some 700 vacancies short and we just simply don’t have the people that we need.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current national shortfall of roughly 700 social worker vacancies. The scope of the figure (whole sector, or statutory social work only) is not stated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD / Social Workers Registration Board or Oranga Tamariki workforce data for 2023–24 on unfilled social worker positions: true if the vacancy count is approximately 700, false if it is materially different (e.g. under 400 or over 1,000).

veracity.statement: So the intention of this amendment bill is to add another two years for that experience pathway, so that people who don’t have those academic qualifications but have the experience that is necessary—to ensure that we feel comfortable that they’re competent, fit, and proper—can offer these services to people in the community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the length of the extension the bill delivers is two years. This directly conflicts with Willie Jackson's February 2024 to February 2028 in the same debate, and with Lemauga Lydia Sosene's account of a proposed amendment cutting four years to two.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill as reported back and as enacted: true if the experience pathway is extended by two years (to February 2026), false if the extension is four years (to February 2028) or some other period.

veracity.statement: It’s good that we’re doing more to encourage people to register and to be able to encourage that forward, but I am highly sceptical of how social investment is going to work, particularly for our social sectors, and how those communities that are the most vulnerable in New Zealand are served by social workers when a programme of 6.5 percent cuts to all social services will directly impact people like social workers in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 6.5 percent cut applies to all social services. The 6.5 percent figure corresponds to a real savings target, so the checkable part is the word 'all' — whether the target was universal across social service agencies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget 2024 baseline savings instructions to departments: true if a 6.5 percent savings target was applied across the social service agencies as described, false if the target was a different percentage or did not apply to all social services (e.g. applied at 6.5/7.5 percent to selected departments only).

veracity.statement: The last point I wish to highlight: last night, the Minister for Social Development and Employment said in her kōrero; in her contribution—and I’m sure it’s on Hansard—that she was considering reducing the time from four years to two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Minister said in the House the previous night about shortening the proposed extension of the experience pathway. The speaker herself points to Hansard as the check.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the Minister for Social Development and Employment's speech on this bill the previous sitting evening: true if she stated she was considering reducing the extension from four years to two, false if no such statement appears or she said something materially different.

rigor.statement: I think some of the mahi that we did at ground level, particularly in the Whānau Ora space, where I would hope that this Government would continue to invest in that kaupapa, was rolled out by people who did not have the necessary academic qualifications in terms of social work. They can be some of our best people. So that is why this type of bill is really important, and that is why we as political parties—whatever our parties are—must come together to support a lot of these social workers who have great skills, who have life skills, who can change lives.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure — unqualified staff did good Whānau Ora work, therefore the pathway should be kept open — but it rests entirely on the speaker's own recollection of his organisations. Argument from anecdote, with no measure of how the unqualified cohort performs generally.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would oppose that consideration for the simple fact that many of our community members that can go through and become qualified actually are quite busy—very busy looking after their families, going through the cost of living crisis, and other duties.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure — a shorter window is harder for people carrying family and work loads, so keep four years — and the premise does bear on the conclusion. But nothing is offered on how many practitioners would actually fail to qualify inside two years, so the step from 'people are busy' to 'two years is too short' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But in some of our communities—particularly iwi, Māori, Pasifika, ethnic—there isn’t that need to become a qualified person, because you are already there.
rigor.explanation: The reason given restates the conclusion: qualification is unnecessary because the person is 'already there'. Circular — what standing in the community establishes about competence to practise is exactly what is at issue, and it is assumed rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it now that they’re actually passing Labour legislation because they’ve run out of their own bills to put?
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of the governing party and nothing about the measure remains. No policy, figure or outcome is named — it is a claim about the other side's legislative cupboard being bare.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: “Kumbaya” had broken out until Ginny Andersen got to her feet and launched an unprovoked attack on this Government when we were just trying to be the nation’s great unifiers.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. The entire content is a characterisation of an opposing member's contribution and a self-congratulatory contrast with the speaker's own side — the party-versus-policy failure Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Delaying the repeal of that experience pathway will act as a short-term mechanism to help reduce the workforce pressures in the social work sector by continuing to provide an alternative means of entering that very important profession.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what the bill does, the mechanism it uses and the problem it is aimed at. Ordinary, unremarkable, on-policy speech.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: “Kumbaya” had broken out until Ginny Andersen got to her feet and launched an unprovoked attack on this Government when we were just trying to be the nation’s great unifiers.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at a named member: 'launched an unprovoked attack' imputes bad faith, and 'we were just trying to be the nation’s great unifiers' is sneering rather than substantive. Short of a direct insult to her character, so a real failure but not contempt. Nothing is deducted here for the absence of policy content — that is Focus's job.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Delaying the repeal of that experience pathway will act as a short-term mechanism to help reduce the workforce pressures in the social work sector by continuing to provide an alternative means of entering that very important profession.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (retaining the experience pathway as an alternative entry route) and its intended effect, but carries no figure, no duration and no measure of the workforce pressure it is meant to relieve. A direction with some detail, missing the how much and the by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As the member for Northcote, Dan Bidois, has already said, the Social Workers Registration Board estimate that there are 700 unfulfilled social worker vacancies currently.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a hard figure and a stated timeframe ('currently'). Someone could go to the Board and check it. Precision is judged here regardless of whether the number turns out to be right.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this Government is committed to supporting earlier interventions, which are more effective for those most at risk.
specificity.explanation: A statement of commitment with no named programme, no funding figure, no timeframe and no definition of 'earlier interventions'. Nothing here could be checked or acted on, and the surrounding text supplies no detail for it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As the member for Northcote, Dan Bidois, has already said, the Social Workers Registration Board estimate that there are 700 unfulfilled social worker vacancies currently.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific numeric vacancy estimate and attributes it to a named body, the Social Workers Registration Board, as the current position at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board workforce reporting and public statements current as at February 2024 (SWRB annual report / workforce planning material, or the Board's submission to the Social Services and Community Committee on this bill): true if the Board estimated approximately 700 unfilled social worker vacancies, false if the Board's estimate was materially different or if no such Board estimate exists.

veracity.statement: Submitters were almost universal in their praise for this delay.
veracity.explanation: A claim about the balance of submissions received by the select committee — asserting that support for delaying the repeal was near-unanimous. Extracted because 'almost universal' is an overstatement risk that the committee record can settle.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Social Services and Community Committee's August 2023 report on the bill and the published submissions: true if the overwhelming majority of submitters supported delaying the repeal of the experience pathway, false if a substantial minority opposed the delay. The speaker's own following sentence ('There were some differing views') is part of what a checker would weigh against 'almost universal'.

rigor.statement: There were some differing views, but the National Party is satisfied that pulling in the extension from four years to two years will mean that the mandatory registration of social workers and the public safety will remain absolutely paramount.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy, and a weak one. The only support offered for the conclusion that public safety remains paramount is that the speaker's own party is satisfied it does — a bare appeal to authority. Nothing is offered to connect the specific change (four years to two) to the safety outcome, and the acknowledged 'differing views' are set aside rather than answered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So I stand here as the 30th ACT MP elected to this House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that he is the thirtieth person ever elected to Parliament as an ACT MP, counting across all MMP elections since the party's formation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Library / New Zealand Parliament records of every MP elected on the ACT list or in an ACT-held electorate from 1996 to 2023, ordered by first entry; true if Stephenson is the 30th such member, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Given that we’ve only had 10 MMP elections, being an ACT MP in one of the world’s only classical liberal parties with elected representatives is a rare and unique opportunity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand had held exactly ten general elections under MMP as at the date of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission record of general elections held under MMP; true if exactly ten general elections had been held under MMP by February 2024, false if the count differs.

veracity.statement: To the almost quarter of a million New Zealanders who voted ACT, thank you.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ACT's party vote at the 2023 general election was close to 250,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the 2023 general election, ACT New Zealand party vote total; true if the figure is within roughly 10% below 250,000, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: In the same year as I started university, Sir Roger Douglas had published Unfinished Business and then, along with the Hon Derek Quigley, founded the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Douglas published Unfinished Business and, with Derek Quigley, founded the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers, both in 1993 — the year the speaker says he began at the University of Otago.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Publication date of Roger Douglas's Unfinished Business (National Library / publisher record) and the founding date of the Association of Consumers and Taxpayers (ACT party history, Electoral Commission registration); true if both fall in 1993, false if either is a different year.

rigor.statement: It’s a great example of where the private sector is doing something no Government could or should do. No Government could manage the complexity, let alone accept the considerable cost and risks involved.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that no government could or should develop medicines — is supported only by restating it as a premise ('no Government could manage the complexity'), with no evidence, comparison or counter-example offered; and the normative 'or should' is asserted rather than argued at all. Assuming the conclusion / bare assertion. State-funded drug discovery is an obvious counter-case that is not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m committed to working with David Seymour to deliver a modern, efficient, and effective medicines access process so Kiwis can get the world’s best treatments.
specificity.explanation: Names a policy area and a colleague, but the substance is a string of generic virtues — 'modern, efficient, and effective' — with no mechanism, no funding figure, no change to Pharmac's process and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m here to play my part in how we rethink how our Government operates and delivers for Kiwis.
specificity.explanation: A statement of purpose committing to nothing: no part of government is named, no change is described, no measure or timeframe is given. 'Rethink how our Government operates' is a slogan.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I can tell you that was not my childhood—20 percent interest rates make life hard—but it was a childhood where I learnt all about work ethic and community service from the example of my parents, who did every role from school boards, to school sports, to community service groups, and beyond.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that interest rates reached 20 percent during his 1980s farming childhood in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ historical interest rate series (mortgage/farm lending rates) for New Zealand in the 1980s; true if rates reached approximately 20 percent at some point in that decade, false if the peak was materially lower.

veracity.statement: It’s hardly surprising that Invercargill was named after him and his birthplace.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the name Invercargill derives both from William Cargill and from Cargill's birthplace.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published place-name authority records (NZ Geographic Board / standard etymologies) for Invercargill; true if the name is recorded as honouring William Cargill with the prefix drawn from his birthplace, false if the prefix is instead the generic Gaelic 'inbhir' (river mouth) or Cargill's birthplace is not the source.

rigor.statement: The biggest risk to further progress is ignoring this change. If the feeling amongst farmers becomes “Why do I bother to do all this, because there is nothing I am doing that is being recognised?”, they will give up.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about environmental policy toward farming: premise that farmers are motivated by recognition, conclusion that failing to recognise progress will stall it. The causal step rests on an unevidenced assertion about farmer motivation and on his own anecdotal observation, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded — but it is a coherent argument, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, we need a regulatory framework that gives farmers the confidence to invest, but every small business in New Zealand needs that.
specificity.explanation: A policy direction with no mechanism, no named regulation, no cost and no timeframe — 'a regulatory framework that gives confidence to invest' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Contrary to expectations, statistics reveal a concerning uptick in serious workplace incidents and fatalities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official workplace-safety statistics show a rise in serious incidents and in fatalities, offered as evidence that current compliance settings are not working.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WorkSafe NZ / Stats NZ work-related fatality and serious-harm injury series for the years preceding February 2024; true if both acute work-related fatalities and serious workplace incidents show an increase over the most recent comparable periods, false if either series is flat or falling.

rigor.statement: There are also unintended winners from regulation. Big business—who can easily afford to implement complex protocols—enjoy the fact that smaller would-be competitors face barriers to open and grow.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference with a stated mechanism: compliance costs are largely fixed, so firms that can absorb them benefit from the barrier the same costs impose on smaller entrants. The conclusion follows from the premise offered; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve watched as others in health and safety compliance lobby for more rules and more complexity, with the sneaking suspicion that the increased work stream isn’t an unintended cost, but instead the whole point.
rigor.explanation: Infers intent from personal observation alone — an appeal to anecdote, plus a motive imputation that does not follow from the premise. That an industry lobbies for rules it profits from is equally consistent with sincere belief; nothing is offered to distinguish the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is imperative that we have the settings right to tackle the workplaces with appalling health and safety, and let the rest of us get on with it.
specificity.explanation: The policy prescription of the speech, and it carries no checkable content: no rule named, no threshold for which workplaces count as the bad ones, no mechanism, no figure and no timeframe. 'Have the settings right' commits to nothing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: With initiatives like partnership schools, we empower parents, students, edu-preneurs, and iwi to forge a new educational path.
specificity.explanation: Names a real, identifiable policy (partnership/charter schools), which lifts it above a slogan, but supplies no number of schools, no funding, no timeframe and no account of how the empowerment works.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As our leaders get further away from the site of production, further from how buildings are built, food is grown, fish are caught, resources harvested, and services provided, it is no wonder that we have a productivity crisis.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion (productivity crisis) is drawn from a single asserted premise (decision-makers' distance from productive work) with nothing offered to connect them — no mechanism, no evidence, no consideration of other causes. Non sequitur dressed as an explanation. Note the premise's truth is not at issue here; the gap is in the inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As with the recent examples of housing supply initiatives, tradies and property owners rightly ask: how does a Government think they can change the direction of a housing supply crisis without changing the real factors which affect our ability to provide houses and actually build more?
specificity.explanation: Squarely aimed at policy substance, but carries almost nothing checkable: 'recent examples of housing supply initiatives' names no initiative, 'the real factors' names no rule, consent process, cost or figure, and no timeframe is given. A listener could not act on it or verify it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But as the only licensed building practitioner ever elected to this House, I am here to enable my fellow tradies and everyone who thinks that New Zealand can only reach our potential if driven by our productive sectors.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about the historical composition of Parliament: that no other Licensed Building Practitioner has ever been elected as an MP. The 'ever' is the load-bearing word — a single prior LBP-holding MP falsifies it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's register of members' prior occupations cross-checked against the MBIE Licensed Building Practitioners register (the LBP scheme commenced under the Building Act 2004, with licensing from 2007). True if no MP elected since the scheme began held an LBP licence; false if any did. If no MP's LBP status can be established either way, the claim is uncheckable rather than false.

veracity.statement: The day kura hourua was stopped by the “kind” previous Government, I decided that, in whatever way I could, I would help the political party who gave—if even for a moment—that chance to Kiwi kids.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the previous (Labour-led) Government ended the kura hourua / partnership (charter) school model. The claim is about who terminated the policy, not about whether ending it was right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education Amendment Act 2018 and Ministry of Education records on the closure or conversion of partnership schools kura hourua. True if the repeal of the partnership-school provisions was enacted by the Labour-led Government that took office in 2017; false if the model was ended under a different government or was not in fact discontinued.

veracity.statement: My siblings the engineers are impacted with New Zealand’s $200 billion infrastructure deficit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's infrastructure deficit stands at $200 billion — a specific quantified claim about the present state of national infrastructure investment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published estimates of New Zealand's infrastructure deficit from Te Waihanga / the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission (or Infrastructure NZ) current as at early 2024; true if a recognised estimate of the deficit is approximately $200 billion, false if the authoritative estimates are materially different in magnitude (e.g. an order of tens of billions).

rigor.statement: We’ve already seen changes to New Zealand with this newly formed Government. The result is an unwinding and unpicking of years of progress, with real impacts. What does this mean for New Zealand? Just within my whānau, my sibling the nurse is impacted by overflowing waiting rooms in a critically underfunded healthcare system at the point of collapse.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that a Government formed roughly two months earlier has produced these impacts — does not follow from what is offered. The evidence supplied is a set of long-standing structural conditions (an infrastructure deficit the speech itself attributes to "historical under-investment", an underfunded legal system, hospital waiting rooms), and attributing them to recent changes is post hoc reasoning; no mechanism or link between the named changes and the named impacts is supplied. The anecdotal framing (impacts on individual family members) is offered in place of that link.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Participative Governments lead democratically. Having empowered and participative citizens gives the people in this Chamber access to move perspectives to help give us a wide range of options to solve New Zealand’s biggest challenges.
specificity.explanation: Advances a governance claim but supplies no mechanism, no named process for participation (citizens' assemblies, submission reform, participatory budgeting), no figures and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on — it is a general virtue statement about participation.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We ran the biggest grassroots electorate campaign in Green history and we raised $100,000, which is actually really hard when we’re all broke—probably from paying the rent in this city, as you’re all aware.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts about the speaker's own 2023 Wellington Central campaign: that it raised $100,000, and that it was the largest grassroots electorate campaign the Green Party has run. The dollar figure is the checkable half.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission candidate donations and expenses return for Tamatha Paul, Wellington Central, 2023 general election, plus Green Party campaign reporting: true if the return shows roughly $100,000 in campaign donations raised; false if the figure is materially lower. The 'biggest in Green history' comparison resolves against Green Party electorate campaign records for prior elections; treat it as unresolved if no such record is public.

veracity.statement: I’ve noticed that our new Prime Minister likes to talk about our city like it’s an ivory tower.
veracity.explanation: A factual claim about Christopher Luxon's public rhetoric — that he characterises Wellington as an insulated, elite place out of touch with the rest of the country. Asserted by the speaker in her own voice, not relayed, so the conduct on record here is her accuracy about him.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, speeches and interviews by Christopher Luxon from November 2023 to February 2024 referring to Wellington: true if he repeatedly characterised the city (or 'Wellington' as shorthand for the public service and political class) as elite, insulated or out of touch with the rest of New Zealand; false if no such characterisation appears in the record.

specificity.statement: We ran the biggest grassroots electorate campaign in Green history and we raised $100,000, which is actually really hard when we’re all broke—probably from paying the rent in this city, as you’re all aware.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named dollar figure and a named comparison class, alongside the 30,000 contacts stated immediately before. Someone could go to the donations return and check it. Not 1.0 because the 'biggest in Green history' half supplies no number to compare against.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve seen what happens when you cut wages, deny benefits, sanction people, sell State housing, strip and privatise public assets, and move people away from the land that they come from and lock them up and throw away the key.
specificity.explanation: Names seven distinct policy levers — wage restraint, benefit refusal, benefit sanctions, State house sales, asset privatisation, relocation, imprisonment — rather than gesturing at 'the system'. But no figures, no dates, no named programme and no named government, so there is a direction with real detail and no way to check or act on any single element.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The things I saw growing up there is exactly the kind of behaviour you’d come to expect when the only investment you’re getting is new liquor stores on every street corner and new pokie machines in every pub.
rigor.explanation: A real causal inference about a real policy question — that the pattern of investment a town receives shapes the social behaviour in it — reasoned from personal observation of Tokoroa. The premise-to-conclusion step is coherent and the direction is defensible, but the link between alcohol and gambling availability and the harm described is left entirely unstated and rests on anecdote rather than any evidence offered. Judged on the inference only; the 'only investment' overstatement is a Veracity matter, not deducted here.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I am very proud to be part of our new Green caucus; the biggest Green caucus ever, with such a wealth of lived experience from the Far North to the deep South.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Green Party caucus elected at the 2023 general election is the largest in the party's history, larger than any previous Green caucus.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the number of Green Party MPs returned at each general election; true if the caucus sitting after the 2023 election exceeds every previous Green caucus size, false if any earlier Parliament returned as many or more Green MPs.

veracity.statement: Secondly, the rejection by the Dunedin City Council of Aotearoa’s first community wind farm at Blueskin Bay on “visual impact” grounds.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Dunedin City Council declined the Blueskin Bay community wind farm, and that visual/landscape impact was the stated ground for the refusal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Dunedin City Council resource consent decision on the Blueskin Bay community wind farm application; true if the application was declined and the decision cites visual/landscape amenity effects among its grounds, false if it was granted, withdrawn, or declined solely on other grounds (e.g. noise, ecology, funding).

rigor.statement: The wind farm experience in Blueskin revealed two things. It showed the incredible potential to build community resilience, but it also revealed the inadequacy of the Resource Management Act, which we are going back to.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single local consent decision to a conclusion about the adequacy of an entire statute — a hasty generalisation from one anecdote.
